title: The Lankavatara Sutra
summary: On Mount Lanka the Buddha teaches the bodhisattva Mahamati that the world we see is the mind showing itself. Early Chan used it to confirm awakening.

primer.a: 一部大乘佛经。「楞伽」是一个海岛的名字，「入楞伽」就是佛来到楞伽岛说法。一般认为梵文本大约在公元四、五世纪成形，作者不详。中文有三个古译本，本站对照的古译，是唐朝实叉难陀约公元七百年译的七卷本。早期禅宗很看重这部经；传统上说，禅宗初祖菩提达摩曾把四卷本的《楞伽经》传给弟子慧可。
说法的是佛，经里称他「世尊」「如来」；他说「我」，就是指他自己。几乎所有问题都由大慧菩萨提出，佛开口多半先叫一声「大慧」，所以「你」大多是大慧。只有第一品的主角是楞伽岛的罗刹王罗婆那。散文后面常有「世尊说了偈颂」，意思是下面改用诗句，把刚才的话再说一遍。
罗婆那是印度史诗《罗摩衍那》里的十首魔王，统治楞伽岛；在史诗里他是反派，这部经却让他成了真心求法的人。楞伽岛，后人多半认为在今天斯里兰卡一带。在场听法的除了菩萨和出家人，还有夜叉、罗刹这类鬼神。佛也常常拿「外道」，也就是当时印度其他宗教和哲学派别的说法，来和自己的说法对比。

primer.q: 这部经翻来覆去讲的一件事
primer.a: 我们以为在心外的东西，这部经说其实是自己的心显现出来的。最有名的比喻是大海和波浪：心像大海，外面的境界像风，种种认识像被风吹起的波浪。人不明白这一点，就把看到的东西切成「这个」「那个」，当成真的，抓着不放，烦恼由此而来。这并不是说外面什么都没有：经里同样说，事物「不是有，也不是无」。

primer.q: 读的时候会卡住的地方
primer.a: 这部经没有一条故事线，大多是一问一答，话题跳得很快，同一个道理在好几品里重讲。常见一连串的否定，像「不是一，不是异，不是两者都是，也不是两者都不是」，意思是哪一种说法都抓不住它。比喻很多：阳焰（热天远处像水的光影）、乾闼婆城（海市蜃楼）、梦、幻术、眼病的人看到的毛团，都是「看得见，却不是真的」。第十品的梵文传抄错误多，有些偈读不通。
这些词会反复出现，先认一下。
terms: 分别
心把事物切成「这个」「那个」，起了名字，再当成真有的。这部经里它几乎都指要放下的那种心理活动，不是平常说的「区分」。
自心所现、唯心
「境界不过是自己的心所显现」。唯心就是「只是心」：看到的一切都是心的显现。
阿赖耶识（藏识）
最深的一层心，像仓库一样存着过去经验留下的种子；经里把它比作大海。
习气
过去的经验和念头在心里留下的痕迹，像衣服熏过香会留着香味，推动人以后怎样看事物。
如来藏
众生本来就有的成佛的本性。这部经说它就是被称为阿赖耶识的那个东西，又说它不同于外道所说的「自我」。
五法、三自性、八识、两种无我
佛整理出的四组名目，经里说整个大乘都在其中。五法：名、相、分别、正智、真如。三自性：凭空想出来的（遍计所执）、依条件而起的（依他起）、圆满真实的（圆成实）。八识：眼、耳、鼻、舌、身五识，加上意识、末那、阿赖耶识。两种无我：人没有常存的自我，万物也没有自体。
不生
事物从来没有真正「生出来」过。不是说什么都没有，而是说「生」只是分别出来的。
转依
心的根基彻底翻转，不再被习气推着走；经里把它当作解脱、涅槃的另一种说法。
外道
佛教以外的宗教和哲学派别，如数论、胜论、顺世论。
声闻、独觉
声闻是听佛说法而修行的弟子，独觉是自己悟道、不去教人的修行人。经里说他们只求自己解脱，还没走到菩萨和佛的地步。

primer.a: 先读第一品，它是全经唯一有故事的一品。再读短的第五品（如来是常还是无常）、第七品（化身佛）和第八品（为什么不吃肉），习惯这种问答的说法。然后读第六品，它把五法、三自性、八识讲得最集中；再读最长的第二品和第三品。第四品讲修行的阶位，第九品是咒语，第十品近九百首偈大多是重述，放到最后。每品先看「这一品在讲什么」，括号（）里的字是本站补的，不是经文。

primerEn.a: A Mahayana Buddhist sutra. Lanka is the name of an island, and the title means the Buddha's teaching coming to Lanka. The Sanskrit text is generally thought to have taken shape around the 4th or 5th century CE; its author is unknown. It was translated into Chinese three times; the classical version shown on this site is Śikṣānanda's, made around the year 700. Early Chan (Zen) valued it highly; tradition says Bodhidharma handed a copy of it to his student Huike.

The teacher is the Buddha, called "the Lord" or "the Tathagata"; when he says "I" he means himself. Almost every question comes from the bodhisattva Mahamati, and the Buddha usually begins his answer by naming him, so "you" is nearly always Mahamati. Only Chapter 1 centers on someone else: Ravana, king of the rakshasas of Lanka. A prose passage is often followed by verses that say the same thing again.

Ravana is the ten-headed demon king of Lanka in the Indian epic, the Ramayana, where he is the villain. Here he becomes a sincere seeker of the teaching. Lanka is usually identified with the area of present-day Sri Lanka. Besides bodhisattvas and monks, the audience includes yakshas and rakshasas, kinds of spirits. The Buddha often sets his teaching against the views of the tirthikas, the other religious and philosophical schools of India.

primerEn.q: The one thing the sutra keeps saying
primerEn.a: What we take to be outside the mind, the sutra says, is what one's own mind shows. Its best-known image is the ocean and its waves: the mind is the ocean, the world around us is the wind, and our perceptions are the waves the wind raises. Not seeing this, people cut what they see into "this" and "that", take it as real and cling to it, and suffering follows. This is not a claim that nothing is out there: the sutra also says things neither exist nor fail to exist.

There is no storyline after the first chapter, just question and answer, and the topics change fast; the same point comes back in several chapters. Long strings of negations are common ("not one, not different, not both, not neither"), meaning no single statement can capture the thing. The images pile up: a mirage, a gandharva city (a city seen in the clouds), a dream, a magic show, the hairs seen by someone with an eye disease. All mean "seen, but not real". The Sanskrit of Chapter 10 has many copying errors, and some verses do not parse.
These come up again and again.
terms: Conceptualizing
The mind cutting things into "this" and "that", naming them and taking them as real. In this sutra it is almost always something to let go of, not a neutral ability to tell things apart.
What one's own mind shows, mind-only
Everything we perceive is the mind's own appearing. "Mind-only" means just that: all that is seen is mind showing itself.
Storehouse consciousness
The deepest layer of mind, which holds the seeds left by past experience like a storehouse. The sutra compares it to the ocean.
Habit-energy
The traces past experiences and thoughts leave in the mind, like the scent left in cloth, shaping how we see things later.
Tathāgatagarbha
The potential for buddhahood that every being already has. The sutra says it is what is called the storehouse consciousness, and that it is not the "self" of the tirthikas.
Five dharmas, three natures, eight consciousnesses, two kinds of no-self

Four lists that the sutra says contain the whole Mahayana. Five dharmas: name, appearance, conceptualizing, right knowledge, suchness. Three natures: the imagined, the dependent, the perfected. Eight consciousnesses: the five senses, the mind consciousness, manas, and the storehouse consciousness. Two kinds of no-self: no lasting self in a person, and no self-nature in things.
Non-arising
Nothing has ever truly come into being. This does not mean nothing exists; it means that "arising" is itself a product of conceptualizing.
Turning-around of the basis
A complete reversal at the root of the mind, so that habit-energy no longer drives it. The sutra treats it as another name for liberation and nirvana.
Tirthikas
Followers of religious and philosophical schools outside Buddhism, such as Samkhya, Vaisheshika and the Lokayata.
Shravakas, pratyekabuddhas

Shravakas are disciples who practice by hearing the Buddha teach; pratyekabuddhas awaken on their own and do not teach. The sutra says both seek only their own release and fall short of bodhisattvas and buddhas.

primerEn.a: Start with Chapter 1, the only chapter with a story. Then read the short Chapters 5 (is the Tathagata permanent?), 7 (the Buddha's emanations) and 8 (why not to eat meat) to get used to the question-and-answer style. Next comes Chapter 6, the most compact account of the five dharmas, three natures and eight consciousnesses, and then the long Chapters 2 and 3. Chapter 4 is about the stages of practice, Chapter 9 is spells, and Chapter 10, nearly nine hundred verses that mostly restate earlier chapters, comes last. Read "What this chapter says" before each chapter.

compare: 前半部最难译的是一组「心」的名词。全经的核心句 svacittadṛśya，字面是「自己的心所显现、所被看见的」，实叉难陀简洁地译成「自心现」，白话说「境界不过是自己的心所显现」，英文译 what one's own mind shows，第一次出现时补一句解释。三种语言都要面对同一个难点：这句话说的是「我们以为在心外的东西，其实是心的显现」，不是「物质不存在、只有一个心存在」；中文「唯心」、英文 mind-only 都容易被读成后者。同样，ālayavijñāna 中文意译「藏识」、音译「阿赖耶」，英文用 storehouse consciousness；tathāgatagarbha 中文作「如来藏」，「藏」偏向「宝藏」，梵文 garbha 却是「胎、胎儿」，带着「孕育」的意思，所以英文保留原词、第一次出现时解释为 the Tathagata-womb。这部经最独特的一步，是把两者说成同一个东西（「如来藏名为阿赖耶识」），中英文都照原文保留「被称为」的措辞，不替它下结论。

第二个差别在 vikalpa。它是前十品出现最多的词之一，指心把东西切分成「这个、那个」并加以命名、构想。白话和古译都用「分别」，现代中文读者容易想成中性的「区分、辨别」能力；英文译作 conceptualizing，强调这些概念是心自己造出来的。与此相连的是本经对语言的态度：佛说「从成道到涅槃不说一字」，又说「依义不依文」，用「看指头的人」比喻执着文字（第六品偈颂里才明确出现「月亮」）。古译把这些译得极精炼，成了禅宗常用的话头；英文则逐字直译，读者可以看到原文本来的语气，也能看到哪些「名句」是后来才被压缩成四个字的。

《偈颂品》是全经最长的一品，近九百首偈，许多是前面各品散文的重述，也有前文没有的内容：龙树出世的预言、四个时代与诸佛出世的次序、对数论和胜论的批评。梵本这一品传抄错讹很多，有些偈颂法读不通；中文白话和实叉难陀常常顺着上下文补成一句通顺的话，英文则照梵文直译，读不通的地方直接写 meaning unclear，读者能看出哪里是原文本身就有问题。实叉难陀的本子跟梵本对得上的约三分之二，其余没有对应的古译；有几处他还把说话的人弄反了，例如开头一首把大慧的赞颂写成「尔时世尊……而说偈言」，预言一段直接写出「龙树」，梵文只说「名叫 Nāga（龙）的比丘」。

全品反复出现几个词，三种语言的意思范围不同。vikalpa 中文译「分别」，听起来像日常的「区分」，英文 discrimination 今天又容易让人想到「歧视」；梵文指的是心把一个整体切成「这个、那个」并当成实有的那种活动，所以本站英文统一用 conceptualizing（概念化），第一次出现时加了说明。svabhāva 中文是「自性」，英文用 own-nature，比 self-nature 少一点「有个自我」的联想。cittamātra「唯心」英文写 mind-only，说的是看到的一切都是 what is seen as one's own mind，不是说外面什么都没有；ālayavijñāna「阿赖耶识」英文写 storehouse consciousness，保留「仓库、储藏种子」的原意，中文音译反而看不出这层意思。
compareEn: The hardest thing to translate in the first half is a set of words for "mind." The sutra's central phrase, svacittadṛśya, literally "what is seen, or shown, of one's own mind," is rendered compactly by Śikṣānanda as 自心现 (zìxīn xiàn, "one's own mind appearing"); the plain Chinese says 境界不过是自己的心所显现 ("the realm is nothing but what one's own mind manifests"); the English says "what one's own mind shows," with an explanation on first use. All three face the same difficulty: the phrase means that what we take to be outside the mind is the mind's own appearing, not that "matter doesn't exist and only one mind does"; both the Chinese 唯心 (wéixīn, "mind-only") and the English "mind-only" are easily read the second way. Likewise ālayavijñāna is translated in Chinese as 藏识 (zàngshí, "storehouse consciousness") or transliterated as 阿赖耶 (ālàiyē), and in English as "storehouse consciousness"; tathāgatagarbha is 如来藏 (Rúlái zàng) in Chinese, where 藏 leans toward "treasury," while Sanskrit garbha means "womb, embryo" and carries the sense of gestation, so the English keeps the Sanskrit word and explains it on first use as "the Tathagata-womb." The sutra's most distinctive move is to call the two the same thing ("the tathāgatagarbha, called the storehouse consciousness"); both the Chinese and the English keep that "called" wording without drawing conclusions for the reader.

The second difference is vikalpa, one of the most frequent words in these ten chapters: the mind cutting things into "this" and "that" and naming and constructing them. The plain Chinese and the classical version both use 分别 (fēnbié), which a modern Chinese reader tends to hear as a neutral ability to "tell things apart"; the English renders it "conceptualizing," stressing that the concepts are the mind's own making. Tied to this is the sutra's attitude to language: the Buddha says he "has not uttered a single syllable" between his awakening and his nirvana, says "rely on the meaning, not on the letter," and compares clinging to words to "one who looks at the finger" (the moon appears explicitly only in a verse of Chapter 6). The classical Chinese renders these lines so tersely that they became stock phrases of Chan; the English translates them word for word, so readers can hear the original tone and see which "famous lines" were only later compressed into four characters.

The Chapter in Verse is the longest chapter of the sutra, close to nine hundred verses. Many restate the prose chapters before it, but some are found nowhere else: the prophecy of a monk named Naga, the four world ages and when buddhas appear in them, and attacks on the Samkhya and Vaisheshika schools. The Sanskrit of this chapter came down with many copying errors, and some verses simply do not parse. The plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda (the 7th-century translator) often smooth such places into a sentence that reads well from context; the English translates the Sanskrit as it stands and says “meaning unclear” where it cannot be read, so you can see where the problem lies in the original itself. Only about two-thirds of the verses have a matching line in Śikṣānanda’s version, and in a few places he changes who is speaking: the opening praise, spoken by Mahamati in the Sanskrit, becomes 尔时世尊……而说偈言 (ěrshí shìzūn … ér shuō jì yán, “then the World-Honored One spoke in verse”), and the prophecy names 龙树 (Lóngshù, “Nagarjuna”) outright, while the Sanskrit says only “a monk named Naga.”

A few words come back again and again, and their range differs across the three languages. Vikalpa is 分别 (fēnbié, “distinguishing”) in Chinese, which sounds like everyday sorting; the obvious English word, “discrimination,” now first suggests prejudice. The Sanskrit means the mind cutting one whole into “this” and “that” and taking the pieces as real; the English uses “conceptualizing” throughout and explains it on first use. Svabhāva is 自性 (zìxìng, “self-nature”) in Chinese; the English says “own-nature,” which carries less of a suggestion that there is a self inside. Cittamātra, 唯心 (wéixīn, “only mind”), becomes “mind-only”: everything we see is what is seen as one’s own mind, which is not the same as saying nothing is out there. Ālayavijñāna is “storehouse consciousness” in English, keeping the Sanskrit image of a storehouse of seeds; the Chinese transliteration 阿赖耶识 (ālàiyē shí) hides that image.

chapters.title: Opening
chapters.intro: Only the title, The Sutra of the True Dharma's Descent into Lanka, and a line of homage to the Three Jewels (the Buddha, his teaching, his community) and to all buddhas and bodhisattvas. The sutra itself begins with the next chapter.

verses.en: The Sutra of the True Dharma's Descent into Lanka

cmp.note: 梵文经名是「正法入楞伽」：「入」(avatāra)既可以理解成佛「进入」楞伽岛，也可以理解成教法在楞伽「降临、显现」。英文 Descent into Lanka 取后一层，中文「入」两层都能装下。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit title is "the True Dharma's avatāra in Lanka." Avatāra can mean the Buddha "entering" the island of Lanka or the teaching "coming down, appearing" there. The English "Descent into Lanka" leans toward the second; the Chinese 入 (rù, "enter") can hold both.

verses.en: Om! Homage to the Three Jewels! Om! Homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas!

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · Ravana's Request (Rāvaṇādhyeṣaṇā)
chapters.intro: Leaving the sea-dragon's palace, the Buddha is invited into Lanka by Ravana, king of the rakshasas, who sings to a lute. The Buddha conjures countless jeweled peaks and teaches, then everything vanishes. Wondering if it was a dream, Ravana realizes it was all his own mind. He then asks how to let go of dharma and non-dharma.

verses.en: Chapter One: Ravana's Request

This is what I heard. Once the Lord was staying in the city of Lanka, on a peak of Mount Malaya by the sea, a place adorned with flowers and jewels of every kind. With him were a great community of monks and a great host of bodhisattvas. These bodhisattvas, great beings, had gathered from many different buddha-fields, with the bodhisattva Mahamati (his name means "Great Wisdom") at their head. They played freely with countless samadhis (states of deep meditative concentration), with mastery, powers and supernatural abilities. Every buddha had laid his hand on their heads and anointed them. They were skilled at fully understanding that the world they perceive is just what their own mind shows (svacittadṛśya), the realm of their own mind appearing to itself. They knew how to guide beings by matching each one's mind, conduct, form and way of being. And they had arrived at the non-dual understanding of the five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses and the two kinds of no-self.

cmp.note: 「自心所现的境界」：这是全经的核心说法——我们看见的世界，就是自己的心显现出来的。英文第一次出现时把 svacittadṛśya 译成 what their own mind shows，并补一句解释；白话「境界不过是自己的心所显现」意思相同；实叉难陀译「境界自心现」，最简洁。
cmp.en: "The realm of what one's own mind shows": the central claim of the whole sutra, that the world we see is our own mind appearing. The English renders svacittadṛśya as "what their own mind shows" and adds an explanation on first use; the plain Chinese 境界不过是自己的心所显现 ("the realm is nothing but what one's own mind manifests") says the same; Śikṣānanda's 境界自心现 (jìngjiè zìxīn xiàn, "the realm is one's own mind appearing") is the most compact.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「五法、自性、识、无我」，没有给数目。白话补成「五法、（三）自性、（八）识、（二）无我」，实叉难陀写「五法、三性、诸识无我」。这四组是全经反复讲的纲目，英文照梵文只写名称，后文再逐一解释。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit just lists "the five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses, no-self" without numbers. The plain Chinese fills them in as five dharmas, (three) natures, (eight) consciousnesses, (two) kinds of no-self; Śikṣānanda writes 五法、三性、诸识无我 ("five dharmas, three natures, the consciousnesses, no-self"). These four lists are the framework the sutra returns to again and again; the English follows the Sanskrit and gives only the names, explaining each later.

verses.en: At that time the Lord had come up out of the palace of the naga king of the ocean after seven days there. Millions upon millions of Shakras, Brahmas and naga maidens came out to meet him. He looked at Mount Malaya in Lanka and smiled, thinking: "The tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of the past also taught, on this very peak of Mount Malaya in the city of Lanka, the Dharma that grows out of this realm: the realm of noble wisdom realized within oneself, which is not the realm of the reasoning and views of the tirthikas (outsider teachers), nor that of the shravakas (disciples) or pratyekabuddhas (solitary buddhas). Why don't I, right here, for the sake of Ravana, lord of the yakshas, bring this out and teach this Dharma too?"

cmp.note: 「自内证圣智」：每个人只能在自己内心亲身证到的圣者智慧，不是从言语或推理得来的。这是《楞伽经》的另一个关键词。英文译作 noble wisdom realized within oneself；实叉难陀译「自所得圣智证法」。
cmp.en: "Noble wisdom realized within oneself": wisdom each person can only realize inwardly, not reach through words or reasoning. Another key term of the Lankavatara. The English says "noble wisdom realized within oneself"; Śikṣānanda writes 自所得圣智证法 (zì suǒ dé shèngzhì zhèng fǎ, "the Dharma of noble wisdom one has realized oneself").

verses.en: Ravana, lord of the rakshasas, heard about this through the Tathagata's sustaining power: the Lord, it was said, had come up from the palace of the naga king of the ocean, surrounded and honored by millions of Shakras, Brahmas and naga maidens. Looking at the waves of the ocean, he had seen the minds of the beings gathered there, stirred up in the realm where the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the deepest layer of mind that stores the seeds of all experience, is an ocean and the active consciousnesses are the wind and waves. Standing right there, Ravana broke out in this cry: "Why don't I go and invite the Lord to come into Lanka? That would bring me, and gods and humans, benefit, welfare and happiness for a long time."

cmp.note: 「藏识大海」：阿赖耶识（ālayavijñāna）是最底层的心识，像大海；眼、耳等「转识」是海面上被风吹起的波浪。这是本经最有名的比喻。英文第一次出现时译成 storehouse consciousness 并解释；白话、古译都用「藏识」。梵文句子把「海」和「风」都塞进一个长复合词，英文只能拆开来说。
cmp.en: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness": the ālayavijñāna is the deepest layer of mind, like an ocean; the active consciousnesses of eye, ear and so on are the waves raised on it by the wind. This is the sutra's most famous image. The English renders it "storehouse consciousness" with an explanation on first use; the plain Chinese and the classical version both say 藏识 (zàngshí, "storehouse consciousness"). The Sanskrit packs both "ocean" and "wind" into one long compound, which English has to break apart.

cmp.note: 这里罗婆那被称作「罗刹之王」，上一段却是「夜叉之主」。梵文两种说法混用；实叉难陀统一译「夜叉王」。英文照原文各用各的。
cmp.en: Here Ravana is called "lord of the rakshasas," while the previous passage called him "lord of the yakshas." The Sanskrit uses both; Śikṣānanda makes it 夜叉王 (yèchā wáng, "yaksha king") throughout. The English keeps whichever the Sanskrit has.

verses.en: Then Ravana, lord of the rakshasas, with his retinue, climbed into the flying palace Pushpaka and went to where the Lord was. When he arrived he stepped down from the palace with his retinue and walked around the Lord three times, keeping him on his right, while musicians played drums and cymbals. He took a vina (an Indian lute) with a neck of sapphire, set with beryl and agate, and hung at its side a priceless cloth, pale yellow like the priyangu flower. Then, following the scales, modulations and notes of song (shadja, rishabha, gandhara, dhaivata, nishada, madhyama, and the kaishika mode), he played the vina gracefully and sang along in verse:
"Leader, teach here the way of the Dharma: the method of the mind's own nature, no-self, free of views and stainless, which points to the realm known only within oneself."

"Sugata (Well-Gone One), your body is gathered from pure dharmas; you show yourself in magically created forms; you delight in the Dharma of the realm known only within oneself. Sage, today is the time to go to Lanka."
"This Lanka was home to the conquerors of the past and to their sons, who take on many forms. Protector, teach the highest Dharma here; the yakshas, who take on many forms, will listen."
Then Ravana, lord of Lanka, having sung in the totaka meter, sang again in verse:
"After seven nights the Lord came up out of the ocean, the home of sea monsters, out of the palace of the ocean's king, and stood on the shore."
"As soon as the Buddha stood there, Ravana, with apsaras (celestial nymphs), with all kinds of yakshas, and with Shuka, Sarana and other wise ones,"

"traveled by supernatural power along the road to where the Leader stood. He came down from the flowery Pushpaka chariot, bowed to the Tathagata and honored him, and, sustained by the King of Conquerors, announced his name to him:"
"'I am Ravana, the ten-headed king of the rakshasas, and I have come here. Look kindly on my Lanka and on those who live in this city.'"
"'The fully awakened ones of the past, too, revealed the realm one reaches within oneself, on the jewel-studded peak in the middle of this city.'"
"'Let the Lord, too, on that same jewel-adorned peak, surrounded by the sons of the Conqueror, teach the stainless Dharma. We want to hear it today, and so do those who live in Lanka.'"
"'The Lankavatara Sutra is free from the ways of teaching in words; it is the realm reached within oneself, and the buddhas of the past praised it.'"

cmp.note: 梵文说这部经「脱离了言说之道」，强调它讲的是言语以外的亲证。实叉难陀把这半句省掉了，只留「昔佛所称赞」；他在上一首末尾倒是加了「离言自证法」，意思挪了位置。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says this sutra is "free of the way of verbal teaching," stressing that it is about realization beyond words. Śikṣānanda drops this half-line and keeps only 昔佛所称赞 ("praised by the buddhas of old"), though he adds 离言自证法 (lí yán zì zhèng fǎ, "the self-realized Dharma beyond words") at the end of the previous verse: the idea has moved.

verses.en: "'I remember the buddhas of the past, honored by the sons of the Conqueror, proclaiming this sutra. Let the Lord proclaim it too.'"
"'In time to come, the buddhas and the sons of the buddhas, those leaders, will teach this same divine way on the jewel-adorned peak, out of compassion for the yakshas.'"
"'Divine Lanka is a lovely city, adorned with many jewels, with cool, lovely terraces and canopies of jeweled nets.'"

"'Lord, there are yakshas here who are free of desire and hatred, who reflect on the realm reached within oneself, whom the buddhas of the past have already helped. They have faith in the way of the Mahayana, are settled in it, and encourage one another.'"
"'Yaksha women and yaksha sons long to understand the Mahayana. May the Lord, the Teacher, come to Mount Malaya in Lanka.'"
"'The rakshasas who live in the city, led by Kumbhakarna, devoted to the Mahayana, will hear about the realm reached within oneself.'"
"'They have done service to the buddhas before and will do so now. Out of compassion for me, come to Lanka with your sons.'"
"'Great Sage, accept my palace, the troops of apsaras, all kinds of necklaces, and the lovely Ashoka grove.'"
"'I do the bidding of the buddhas and of the sons of the Conqueror. There is nothing I would not give. Have compassion, Great Sage.'"
Hearing his words, the Lord of the three worlds said: "Lord of the yakshas, the leaders of the past, too, on this jewel mountain,
taught the Dharma realized within oneself, and you were shown compassion by them. Those to come will also teach it on this jewel-adorned mountain.
This is a dwelling place for yogis who live in the Dharma they see here and now. Lord of the yakshas, you deserve the compassion of the sugatas, and mine as well."
The Lord accepted in silence, settled in a mind at peace, and climbed into the flowery Pushpaka chariot that Ravana brought to him.
Ravana and the other fearless sons of the Conqueror went to the city with him, honored along the way by apsaras with laughter, dancing and the like.
When he reached that lovely city he was honored again: honored by Ravana and the hosts of yakshas and yaksha women, honored by yaksha sons and yaksha daughters with nets of jewels.
Ravana also placed jewel-studded necklaces on the heads of the Buddha, the Conqueror, and of the sons of the Conqueror.
Having accepted the offerings, the Lord, with the wise sons of the Conqueror, made clear the Dharma of the realm reached within oneself.

Ravana and the hosts of yakshas, having honored the best of speakers, honored Mahamati and asked him again and again: "You are the one to question all the buddhas about the realm reached within oneself.
I am a listener, and so are the yakshas and the sons of the Conqueror here. We yakshas and the wise sons of the Conqueror ask you.
Among debaters you are the great debater; among yogis you are the one who leads the practice. I ask you with devotion: fearless one, ask about this way,
which is free of the faults of the tirthikas and beyond the pratyekabuddhas and shravakas, pure through the true nature realized within, and which brings to light the stage of a buddha."
Then the Lord, right there, conjured up mountain peaks adorned with jewels, and other divine ones decorated with millions of jewels.
On each of these great mountains he showed his own form, and on each one, too, stood Ravana the yaksha.
The whole assembly could be seen on each one; all the buddha-fields were there, along with the leaders in them.
The king of the rakshasas was there, and those who live in Lanka. The Conqueror conjured up a Lanka that matched the real one, with more Ashoka groves and the beauty of their woods.

On each mountain the Protector, prompted by Mahamati, taught the yaksha the Dharma that points to the realm reached within oneself. On the mountain he taught the entire sutra of a hundred thousand lines.

cmp.note: 梵文说佛在山上讲了「十万颂」的整部经，暗示我们手上的本子只是一个缩本。实叉难陀本这段偈颂没有逐句对应，白话照梵文译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the Buddha taught the whole sutra "of a hundred thousand lines" on the mountain, implying that the text we have is a shorter version. Śikṣānanda's verses here don't line up one to one; the plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Then the Teacher and the sons of the Conqueror vanished right there, and Ravana the yaksha saw himself standing in his own house.
He thought: "What was this? Who was that? What was taught, and who heard it? What was seen, and who saw it? Where is the city? Where is the Sugata?
Where are those buddha-fields, those buddhas shining with jewels, those sugatas? Was it a dream? A magic show? What they call a city of gandharvas (a mirage city)?
Spots before failing eyes, a mirage, a dream of a barren woman giving birth, the wheel made by a whirling firebrand, smoke? What was it I saw here?
Or is this simply the true nature of things in the realm of mind, which fools do not understand, deluded by all their imaginings?

There is no seer and nothing to be seen, nothing spoken and no speaker. Apart from this, it is just conceptualizing (vikalpa) that makes the forms of Buddha and Dharma appear and stay. Those who see things the way they have seen them do not see the Leader.

cmp.note: vikalpa 是本经出现最多的词之一：心把东西切分成「这个、那个」并加以命名、构想。白话、古译都作「分别」，中文读者容易想成「区别、分辨」这种中性能力；英文 conceptualizing 强调它是心自己造出来的概念。
cmp.en: Vikalpa is one of the most frequent words in the sutra: the mind dividing things into "this" and "that," naming and constructing them. The plain Chinese and classical versions say 分别 (fēnbié, "discriminating"), which a Chinese reader may take as a neutral ability to tell things apart; the English "conceptualizing" stresses that the concepts are the mind's own making.

verses.en: When conceptualizing does not arise, one does not see a buddha. In the state where nothing arises, if one sees, that is the Buddha, the fully awakened one."

At that very moment the lord of Lanka woke up: his basis turned around, he arrived at the understanding that everything is nothing but what one's own mind shows, and he stood in a state where no conceptualizing moves. He had been moved by the roots of good he had planted before. His intelligence was trained in every treatise; he saw things as they really are and could not be led by others; he was skilled at examining with his own understanding; his vision was free of reasoning and views. He was a great yogi of the great yoga, able to take on all kinds of forms, at home in skillful means, skilled at reaching the marks of each stage, one above the other; he delighted in being free from the own-nature of mind, thinking mind (manas) and mind-consciousness (manovijñāna); his vision had cut off the three continuities; his understanding was free of all the tirthikas who teach a first cause; he had entered inwardly into the tathāgatagarbha (the Tathagata-womb, the awakened nature hidden in every being) and the stage of a buddha; his understanding was settled in the understanding of a buddha. Then he heard a voice from the sky, one known only within: "Well done, well done, lord of Lanka! Truly well done, lord of Lanka! A yogi should train just as you are training.

cmp.note: 「如来藏」：garbha 既是「胎、子宫」，也是「胎儿、种子」，意思是如来（觉悟的本性）藏在每个众生里，像胎儿在母腹中。中文「藏」偏向「宝藏、收藏」，少了「孕育」的一层；英文保留梵文原词，第一次出现时用 Tathagata-womb 解释。
cmp.en: Tathāgatagarbha: garbha means both "womb" and "embryo, seed," so the idea is that the Tathagata, the awakened nature, lies within every being like an embryo in the womb. The Chinese 藏 (zàng) leans toward "treasury, storehouse" and loses the sense of gestation; the English keeps the Sanskrit word and explains it on first use as "the Tathagata-womb."

cmp.note: 梵文是「心、意、意识」三个词。白话加了括号说明「心 = 阿赖耶识，意 = 末那识，意识 = 第六识」，这是后来唯识宗的配法，《楞伽经》本身并不总是这样一一对应。英文只照原文译出三个词。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit has three words: citta, manas, manovijñāna. The plain Chinese adds a gloss, "citta = ālaya consciousness, manas = the mental faculty, manovijñāna = the sixth consciousness," which is the later Yogācāra school's mapping; the Lankavatara itself doesn't always line them up this neatly. The English simply translates the three words.

verses.en: "The tathagatas should be seen this way, and so should all dharmas (things), just as you have seen them. Seeing them any other way is to lean on annihilation. You should examine all dharmas free of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness. Practice inwardly, without clinging to the view that there are outside objects. Do not get stuck in the views and samadhis that belong to the categories and realms the shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas attain. Do not take delight in legends and epic tales. Do not hold the view that things have an own-nature. Do not fall into the pride of royal power. Do not practice the six meditations and the like. Lord of Lanka, this is the realization of the great yogis, who crush the doctrines of others, shatter unwholesome views, are skilled at turning away from the view of a self, and skilled at the subtle turning-around of consciousness: the sons of the Conqueror who walk the Mahayana. To enter and reach the stage the Tathagata realizes within himself, you must practice yoga.

"If you do this, lord of Lanka, the path you have taken up through your skill in entering samadhi will become purer and purer. It is not the pleasant realm the shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas enter, the way it is imagined by foolish tirthika yogis: people who cling to grasping a self and to the marks of what they see; who follow elements, qualities and substances; who are attached to views conditioned by ignorance; who are thrown into confusion by emptiness and arising; who cling to conceptualizing; whose thinking has fallen into what marks and what is marked. Lord of Lanka, this realization of the Mahayana brings one to the state of taking on all kinds of forms, wakes one to the realm reached within oneself, and leads to a special kind of rebirth. Lord of Lanka, entering the yoga of the Mahayana turns back the films and sheaths and the many waves of consciousness; it does not fall back on the yoga of the tirthikas. For the yoga of the tirthikas, lord of Lanka, starts from their clinging to a self.

"Because they cling to the meaning of consciousness, own-nature and duality, the yoga of the tirthikas is not a good one. So, lord of Lanka, think well on this very meaning, as you did after seeing the Tathagata. That itself is seeing the Tathagata."

Just then Ravana thought: "I wish I could see the Lord once more: master of every yoga, who turns back the yoga of the tirthikas, who brings to light the realm reached within oneself, who is beyond magical creations and created forms. His awakened understanding is what yogis attain at the moment of realization in yoga, when they have entered the gateway of samadhi; and it is because of this attainment that the word 'yoga' is applied to yogis. I wish I could see, by that same supernatural power, that compassionate one who burns up the firewood of afflictions and conceptualizing, surrounded by the sons of the Conqueror, who enters into the minds and intentions of all beings, is everywhere and knows everything, and has turned away from the marks of doing. By seeing him I would reach what I have not yet reached, and what I have reached would grow: the practice free of conceptualizing, dwelling in the bliss of samadhi, which brings one to the stage of a tathagata."

Then the Lord, knowing that the lord of Lanka had reached acceptance that things are unborn (anutpattikadharmakṣānti), out of compassion for the Ten-Necked One, showed himself again in that same splendor, on the peak studded with many jewels and spread with jeweled nets. Daśagrīva, lord of Lanka, saw again the splendor he had seen and lived through before: on the peak, the Tathagata, the arhat, the fully awakened one, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being; and on each mountain, in front of each tathagata, each fully awakened one, he saw himself, together with Mahamati, talking about the realm the Tathagata realizes within himself, surrounded by yakshas, telling the substance of that teaching; and the buddha-fields were there too, each with its leader.

cmp.note: 「无生法忍」：kṣānti 本义是「忍耐、接受」，这里是指心能安然接受「一切法本来不生」这件事，不再抗拒。中文「忍」容易被读成「忍受」，英文 acceptance 更贴近「心里接得住」。
cmp.en: Anutpattikadharmakṣānti: kṣānti originally means "patience, acceptance," and here it means the mind can calmly accept that no thing ever truly arises, without resisting. The Chinese 忍 (rěn) is easily read as "putting up with"; the English "acceptance" is closer to the sense of the mind being able to hold it.

cmp.note: 罗婆那的别名，梵文字面是「十颈」，白话、古译都作「十首」。英文这里保留梵文名 Daśagrīva，并在前面用了 Ten-Necked One。
cmp.en: Ravana's epithet; the Sanskrit literally means "ten-necked," while the plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda say 十首 (shí shǒu, "ten-headed"). The English keeps the name Daśagrīva and uses "the Ten-Necked One" just before.

verses.en: Then the Lord looked over the assembly again, with understanding, not with his physical eyes, stretched like a lion king, and laughed a great laugh. Light streamed from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, from his sides, thighs and waist, from the shrivatsa mark on his chest, and from every pore of his body; he blazed like the fire at the end of an age, shining in a ring of light like a rainbow or the rising sun, watched from the sky by Shakra, Brahma and the guardians of the world. Seated on a peak that rivaled the summit of Mount Sumeru, he laughed a great laugh. Then the assembly of bodhisattvas, and Shakra, Brahma and the others, thought: "What is the cause, what is the reason, that the Lord, master of all dharmas, first smiles and then laughs aloud, and sends out rays of light from his body?"

Having sent out the light, he fell silent, his mind sunk in the gateway of the samadhi that is the realm of noble wisdom realized within oneself, not astonished; looking around in every direction the way a lion looks, he reflected on how Ravana's practice of yoga was going.

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, who had already been asked by Ravana, out of compassion for him, and knowing what was going on in the minds of that assembly of bodhisattvas, and looking ahead to people in the future, thought: "Beings who delight in the wording of the teachings, who cling to meaning exactly as the words sound, who cling to the yogic powers of the shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas, will be confused: 'Even the tathagatas, the lords, whose realm of consciousness has ceased, laugh out loud.'" To put an end to their wondering, he asked the Lord: "What is the cause, what is the reason for this smile?" The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati! Truly well done, Mahamati! You have looked at the nature of the world, and you have begun to ask me so that people who have fallen into wrong views may understand the mind in the three times.

"This is how wise people who know how to ask should be, for their own sake, for others, and for both. Mahamati, this Ravana, lord of Lanka, asked the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of the past two questions. Now he wants to ask me as well, to bring out the distinctions, meaning and marks of the two questions, which no shravaka, pratyekabuddha or tirthika yogi has ever tasted. This Ten-Necked One, who wants to ask, will ask the conquerors of the future too."

Knowing all this, the Lord said to the lord of Lanka: "Ask, lord of Lanka. The Tathagata has given you the opportunity. Don't hesitate, you with the swaying crown. Whatever you want to ask, I will satisfy your mind by answering that very question. With the basis of your conceptualizing turned around, skilled at overcoming what stands against each stage, examining with discerning wisdom, you will dwell in the bliss of samadhi marked by the truth realized within; embraced by the buddhas of samadhi, settled in the bliss of calm, you will go beyond the samadhis of the shravakas and pratyekabuddhas and stand on the stages called Immovable, Good Intelligence and Cloud of Dharma; skilled in the no-self of things as it really is, you will receive the consecration of the conquerors of samadhi in a palace of great jeweled lotuses.

"You will see yourself seated on matching lotuses, lotuses made by the various sustaining powers of your own body, and you will look at one another face to face. That realm is beyond thought: brought forth by a single skill in bringing forth, standing on the stage of practice. Brought forth by bringing forth that embraces skillful means, you will reach that unthinkable realm and the stage of a tathagata that changes into many forms. You will reach what shravakas, pratyekabuddhas, tirthikas, Brahma, Indra, Upendra and the rest have never seen."

Then the lord of Lanka, given leave by the Lord, rose from that jewel peak, which shone with pure light like a jeweled lotus. Surrounded by troops of apsaras, he conjured up flowers, garlands, scents, incense, ointments, parasols, banners, flags, necklaces, half-necklaces, crowns and diadems of every kind and variety, and other special ornaments never seen or heard of before; he conjured up musical instruments, drums and cymbals, finer than those of gods, nagas, yakshas, rakshasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents and humans, all the instruments there are in the whole desire realm, and the special instruments seen in other buddha-fields. He covered the Lord and the bodhisattvas with a net of jewels, raised flags of all kinds of cloth, rose seven palm trees high into the sky, rained down great clouds of offerings, made the instruments sound, then came down from the sky and sat on a second jewel peak, bright as the sun and lightning, adorned with great jeweled lotuses.

Once seated, he politely smiled first and, given leave by the Lord, asked the Lord his two questions: "I asked the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of the past, and they answered. Now I ask the Lord too. In the wording of the teaching, the buddhas and you will surely explain this. Lord, these two dharmas are spoken by created buddhas, magically formed ones; they are not spoken by the silent tathagatas. For the silent tathagatas, Lord, only bring to light the realm of the bliss of samadhi; they do not conceptualize about that realm, and they do not teach it. So may the Lord himself, master of the Dharma, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, kindly teach these two dharmas. These sons of the Conqueror and I will listen."

The Lord said: "Tell me the two dharmas, lord of Lanka." The king of the rakshasas said: "You who shine with the splendor of crown, armlets, necklaces and ornaments strung on diamond thread: dharmas themselves are to be abandoned, how much more what is not dharma. So, Lord, how are the two dharmas abandoned? What are not-dharmas, and what are dharmas? How can there be two among dharmas to be abandoned, when they have fallen into the marks of conceptualizing, have no own-nature apart from conceptualizing, are made of elements or not made of elements, have no distinct marks because the storehouse consciousness is not understood, and are like the hairnet seen by eyes with cataracts, objects of an impure and perishing knowledge? How can such things be abandoned?"

cmp.note: 「法尚应舍，何况非法」，这是《金刚经》里有名的「筏喻」。梵文的 dharma 在这里两层意思叠在一起：「教法」和「事物」。英文只能用 dharmas 原词保留歧义，中文「法」也同样两义并存。
cmp.en: "Even dharmas must be abandoned, how much more not-dharmas": the famous raft simile of the Diamond Sutra. Here dharma carries two meanings at once, "teaching" and "thing." The English keeps the ambiguity only by leaving the word "dharmas" untranslated; the Chinese 法 (fǎ) holds both meanings just as the Sanskrit does.

cmp.note: 「毛团」：患眼病的人眼前看到一团团像毛发的东西，以为是真的。本经常用它比喻根本不存在、却被看见的东西。英文译作 the hairnet seen by eyes with cataracts。
cmp.en: "The hair-tangle": someone with an eye disease sees floating hairlike shapes and takes them as real. The sutra often uses this image for things that are seen but do not exist at all. The English says "the hairnet seen by eyes with cataracts."

verses.en: The Lord said: "But surely, lord of Lanka, you have seen how pots and other things that break and perish are told apart in the realm of fools' conceptualizing. Why not take it the same way here? There is a distinction between dharma and not-dharma with respect to the conceptualizing of fools, but not in the seeing of one who has realized noble wisdom. Let us leave aside, lord of Lanka, pots and other things that have fallen into all kinds of marks, for fools but not for the noble ones. Flames of a single nature, lit from a single fire, set in a house, a mansion, a garden or a palace, are seen to differ: depending on the fuel, their light is long or short, small or great. Why not take it the same way here? There is a distinction between dharma and not-dharma. And it is not only in the fire's flame, belonging to one continuous stream, that a distinction is seen, but in its light as well.

"Even things that sprout from one seed and form one stream, lord of Lanka, differ as stalk, shoot, knot, joint, leaf, bud, flower, fruit and branch. In the same way, all dharmas that grow, outer and inner, that come out of ignorance, that belong to the heaps, elements and sense fields, that are born in the three realms, are seen to differ in pleasure, shape, ways of speaking and courses of life. The consciousnesses, though they have one mark, are seen to differ as low, high and middle when they take hold of objects, as pure and impure, as good and bad. And not only do these dharmas differ, lord of Lanka: among yogis practicing yoga on the path of yoga, differences in the marks of what each realizes within are also seen. So how could there not be a difference between dharma and not-dharma, which arise from conceptualizing? Of course there is.

"There is a distinction between dharma and not-dharma, lord of Lanka, because they are marks of conceptualizing. Which, lord of Lanka, are the dharmas here? Those imagined by the conceptualizing of tirthikas, shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and fools. Dharmas that are taught as having causes, qualities and substances behind them: these are to be abandoned. They are not to be conceptualized according to their marks. Through taking hold of the true nature of what one's own mind shows, pots and other dharmas imagined by fools do not exist; they have no body to them. For one who looks this way with insight, they are abandoned.

"Which are the not-dharmas here? Dharmas that have no self, where marks and conceptualizing do not operate, that have no cause: seeing that they do not arise, whether as real or unreal. Then dharma is abandoned. And which, again, are the dharmas without a self? The horns of a hare, a camel or a horse, the son of a barren woman, and so on. Since they have no self, they are not to be imagined in terms of marks. They are spoken of only for everyday convenience, not clung to the way pots are. Just as these are abandoned because consciousness does not grasp them, so are things that exist through conceptualizing to be abandoned. That is how both dharma and not-dharma are abandoned. You asked, lord of Lanka, how dharmas and not-dharmas are to be abandoned. That is the answer.

"You also said, lord of Lanka, 'I asked the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of the past, and they answered.' Lord of Lanka, that is just another name for conceptualizing. The past is conceptualized as 'past' in this way; so are the future and the present, by the very nature of things. The tathagatas do not conceptualize; they have gone beyond all conceptualizing and conceptual proliferation (prapañca). They are not conceptualized the way the own-nature of form is. Only for those who do not know, and for their happiness, is it explained from realization. They move in signlessness through wisdom. So the tathagatas are made of knowledge, with knowledge as their body. They do not imagine and are not imagined. Through what do they not imagine? Through the thinking mind, as self, life or person. How do they not conceptualize? Through mind-consciousness, which has objects as its cause, as in the marks, shape and look of form. So one should go beyond both conceptualizing and not conceptualizing.

cmp.note: 「戏论」：心把概念一层层铺展开来、越说越多。中文「戏论」容易被读成「开玩笑的话」；英文 conceptual proliferation 直说是「概念的繁衍」。
cmp.en: Prapañca, rendered 戏论 (xìlùn, literally "play-talk"): the mind spreading concepts out layer after layer. The Chinese is easily read as "idle joking talk"; the English "conceptual proliferation" says plainly that concepts are multiplying.

verses.en: "What is more, lord of Lanka, the activity of beings is like figures painted on a wall. The world, lord of Lanka, is motionless, without karma or action, because no dharma is real. No one here hears and nothing is heard. The world, lord of Lanka, is like a magically created image, and the tirthikas and foolish yogis do not understand this. Whoever sees it this way, lord of Lanka, sees rightly. Those who see it otherwise move in conceptualizing. Their own conceptualizing grasps things as two: like one's own reflection in a mirror, the shadow of one's body in water, the shadow of one's body in a house lit by moonlight or a lamp, or an echo. Taking hold of what their own conceptualizing has grasped, they conceptualize dharma and not-dharma. They do not move toward abandoning dharma and not-dharma; they conceptualize, they feed it, and they do not find peace.
"That peace is another name for one-pointedness of mind. This is the entry into the tathāgatagarbha, the realm of noble wisdom realized within oneself, from which the highest samadhi is born."
Here ends the first chapter, called Ravana's Request.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · Gathering All Dharmas (Sarvadharmasamuccaya)
chapters.intro: The longest chapter. Mahamati praises the Buddha and asks over a hundred questions; the Buddha answers with 108 paired statements. Then the central image: the storehouse consciousness is an ocean, the world is wind, perceptions are waves. Later topics: the three natures, two kinds of no-self, why the tathāgatagarbha is not a self, nirvana, and one vehicle versus three.

verses.en: Chapter Two, called "The Gathering of All Dharmas, in Thirty-Six Thousand"

cmp.note: 梵文品名开头有「三万六千」，没说是什么的三万六千，一般理解为「颂」或「行」。白话补了「颂」，英文只照写数字。实叉难陀本这一品叫「集一切法品」，没有数字。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit chapter title begins with "thirty-six thousand" without saying thirty-six thousand of what, usually understood as verses or lines. The plain Chinese adds 颂 (sòng, "verses"); the English keeps just the number. Śikṣānanda calls the chapter 集一切法品 ("Gathering All Dharmas") with no number.

verses.en: Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, together with bodhisattvas of great wisdom who travel through all the buddha-fields, rose from his seat by the power of the Buddha, put his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Lord, bowed, and praised the Lord in verse: "The world is free of arising and perishing, like a flower in the sky;
with wisdom you find neither being nor non-being, and you have compassion.
All dharmas are like illusions, free of mind and consciousness; with wisdom you find neither being nor non-being, and you have compassion.
The world is always like a dream, free of permanence and annihilation; with wisdom you find neither being nor non-being, and you have compassion.
How can one praise the Dharma-body, whose nature is illusion and dream? The non-arising of things that have no own-nature: that is your coming into being.
His seeing is unseen, free of senses and their objects. Sage, how can praise or blame be spoken of him?
The no-self of things and of persons, the afflictions and what is to be known, you have always purified through signlessness; you have wisdom and you have compassion.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「烦恼与所知」，白话补成「烦恼障与所知障」，这是后来唯识宗的标准说法。英文照字面译 the afflictions and what is to be known。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only "afflictions and the knowable"; the plain Chinese expands it to 烦恼障与所知障 ("the obstruction of afflictions and the obstruction of the knowable"), the standard later Yogācāra phrasing. The English translates literally: "the afflictions and what is to be known."

verses.en: You do not pass into nirvana through nirvana; nirvana abides in you. It is free of the awakened and what is to be awakened to, free of the sides of being and non-being.
Those who see the Sage like this, at peace, free of arising, become free of grasping and stainless, here and hereafter."
Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, having praised the Lord with these fitting verses, announced his name and family to the Lord:
"Lord, I am Mahamati, and I have gone the way of the Mahayana. I ask you, best of speakers, a hundred and eight questions."
Hearing his words, the Buddha, best of those who know the world, looked over the whole assembly and at the son of the Sugata and said:
"Let the sons of the Conqueror ask me, and you ask too, Mahamati. I will teach you the realm reached within oneself."
Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, given leave by the Lord, fell at the Lord's feet and questioned him:
How is reasoning purified? From what does reasoning arise? How is confusion seen? From what does confusion arise?
From what do the buddha-fields, the created forms, the marks and the tirthikas come? By what is the stage without images reached? And where do those sons of the Conqueror come from?
Where does the freed one go? Who is bound? By what is one freed? What is the realm of meditators? How do there come to be three vehicles?
What is it that is produced by conditions? What is effect and what is cause? Who talks of the two extremes, and how does it arise?
How do the formless attainments and cessation come about? How does the cessation of perception happen? How, and from what, is one freed?
By what does action arise, and the going of embodied beings? How is what is seen made clear? How does one move through the stages?
Who is it that breaks through the threefold existence? What is the place, what is the body? Where does the one who stands arise? How does one become a son of the Conqueror?
By what are the supernatural powers gained, and the masteries and samadhis? How is the mind brought into samadhi? Tell me, bull among conquerors.
How and from what is the storehouse consciousness, and mind-consciousness too? How does what is seen arise, and how does one turn away from what is seen?
How and by what are there lineages and no lineage? How is there mind-only (cittamātra)? How are the marks laid down, and how is there no-self?

cmp.note: 「唯心」：只有心。白话、古译都作「唯心」，英文 mind-only。这个词在本经里的意思是「我们以为在心外的东西，其实都是心的显现」，不是说「物质不存在、只有一个心存在」，这一点中英文都容易被误读。
cmp.en: "Mind-only": nothing but mind. The plain Chinese and the classical version both say 唯心 (wéixīn); the English says "mind-only." In this sutra it means that what we take to be outside the mind is the mind's own appearing, not that "matter doesn't exist and only one mind does"; both the Chinese and the English are easy to misread that way.

verses.en: How is it that there is no being? How is there teaching by convention? How does the view of permanence and annihilation not arise?
How is it that you and the tirthikas are not at odds in your marks? Tell me, how will there be logicians in the future?
How and by what is there emptiness? How do you mean that things break apart in an instant? How does the womb arise? How is the world without motion?
By what is the world like an illusion or a dream? How is it like a city of gandharvas? By what is it like a mirage or the moon in water? Tell me.
How and by what are the limbs of awakening? From where do the factors of awakening come? How do disturbances of the land and the view of existence come about?
How is it unborn and unceasing, like a flower in the sky? How do you understand the world? How do you speak without letters?
By what are they without conceptualizing, and how are they like the sky? How many kinds of suchness are there? How many minds, how many perfections?
By what is the order of the stages? What is the state without images? By what is no-self twofold? How is what is to be known purified?
Protector, how many kinds of knowledge are there, of moral conduct, of beings' dispositions? By whom were the mines of gold, jewels and pearls brought forth?
By what is speech born, with its variety of beings and states? How and by whom were the fields of learning and the arts made known?
How many kinds of verse are there? How are prose and poetry made? How many kinds of reasoning, and what kinds of explanation?
How do the varieties of food and drink and sexual union come about? How do there come to be kings, wheel-turning kings and regional lords?
How is a kingdom to be protected? What kinds of bodies of gods are there? By what are the earth, the stars and their groups? How are the moon and the sun?
What are the fields of learning? How many kinds of liberation and of yogis? How many kinds of disciples, and how does one become a teacher?
How many kinds of buddhas are there, and what are the birth stories like? How many kinds of Mara, and how many kinds of heretics?
How many kinds of own-nature do you teach? How many kinds of mind? How is there mere designation? Tell me, best of speakers.
By what are clouds in the sky, and wind? How do memory and clouds come about? How and by what are trees and creepers? Tell me, lord of the three worlds.
By what do horses, elephants and deer get caught by fools? By what are people (meaning unclear: uhoḍimā)? Tell me, charioteer of the mind.

cmp.note: 这个词意思不明，各家写本有异文。白话也没有硬译，英文照实标 meaning unclear。
cmp.en: The meaning of this word is unclear and manuscripts vary. The plain Chinese doesn't force a translation either; the English marks it "meaning unclear."

verses.en: By what are the six seasons grasped? How does one become an icchantika (one who has cut off the roots of good)? And how are women, men and those who are neither born? Tell me.
How does one turn back from yoga? How does yoga get going? And how are people of this kind to be set in yoga? Tell me.
What is the sign, and what the mark, of beings who come and go? How and by what is there a lord of wealth? Tell me, you who are like the sky.
How and by what is the Shakya clan? How did the Ikshvaku line come about? By what is the long-ascetic seer, and how was he made powerful?
Why are you yourself seen everywhere, in every buddha-field, with all kinds of names and forms, surrounded by the sons of the Conqueror?
Why is meat not to be eaten? How is meat forbidden? And why do those born in lineages of flesh-eaters eat meat?
By what are there buddha-fields shaped like the moon and the sun, like Mount Meru or a lotus, shaped like the shrivatsa mark or a lion? Tell me.
How are there fields upside down, head down, like Indra's net? How and by what are there fields made all of jewels? Tell me.
Shaped like a vina or a drum, like all kinds of flowers and fruit, stainless as the sun and moon: how and by what? Tell me.
By what are there transformation buddhas, by what buddhas born of ripening, and how and by what the buddhas of suchness and knowledge? Tell me.
How and by what do you not awaken in the desire realm? Tell me. Why do you awaken in the Akanishtha heaven, among those free of desire?
When the Sugata has passed into nirvana, who will uphold the teaching? How long will the Teacher last, and how long will the way last?
How many kinds of realized truth (siddhānta) do you have, and what kinds of view? How and by what are the discipline and the state of a monk? Tell me.
By what do pratyekabuddhas, sons of the Conqueror and shravakas reach the turning-around, and how the state without images? Tell me.
By what are there worldly supernatural powers, and how are there ones beyond the world? How and by what are mind and the seven stages? Tell me.
How many kinds of Sangha (community) do you have? How does a split in the Sangha come about? How and by what is the science of healing for beings? Tell me.
Why, Great Sage, do you tell the sons of the Conqueror "I am Kashyapa, Krakucchanda and Konakamuni"? Tell me.
By what is there talk of no real self? How is there talk of permanence and destruction? Why do you not teach everywhere that reality is mind-only?
By what is there a forest of men and women, a forest of myrobalan and amalaki trees? How are Mount Kailasa and the ring of iron mountains, hard as diamond?
What are the immovable mountains in between, gleaming with many jewels, crowded with seers and gandharvas? How and by what? Tell me.
Hearing this, the great hero, the Buddha, best of those who know the world, (spoke to) the mind made of the Mahayana, the heart and strength of the buddhas:
"Well done, well done, you of great wisdom, Mahamati! Listen. I will explain in order what you have asked:
arising and non-arising, nirvana, the mark of emptiness, transmigration, being without own-nature, the buddhas, the sons of the perfections,
shravakas and sons of the Conqueror, tirthikas, those who move in the formless realms, Meru, the oceans, the mountains, the continents, the fields, the earth,
the stars, the sun, the moon, tirthikas, gods and asuras, liberations, masteries and powers, strengths, meditations and samadhis,
cessations, the bases of supernatural power, the limbs of awakening and the path, the meditations and the immeasurables, the heaps, coming and going,
attainment and cessation, emerging, the teaching of mind, mind, thinking mind and consciousness, no-self, the five dharmas,
own-nature, imagining and the imagined, what is seen, how there are two views, the vehicles, dispositions and lineages, the mines of gold, jewels and pearls,
icchantikas, the great elements, bewilderment, there being one buddha, knowledge and the knowable, going and attaining, and the existence and non-existence of beings.
Tell me how and by what horses, elephants and deer are caught. How are the realized truth and the teaching joined with examples and reasons?
By what are effect and cause, the many confusions, and the way? It is mind-only; nothing seen exists; there is no order to the stages.
By what do you tell me of the hundred turnings-around to the imageless? The science of healing, the crafts, the arts and branches of learning;
how are the measures of the immovable mountains, of Meru, of the earth? Tell me how the ocean, moon and sun are measured.
How many particles are in the body of a being, low, high and middle? How many particles in each field, how many in each bow-length?
In a cubit, a bow, a krosha, a yojana and half a yojana; how many in a hare's hole, a window, a louse egg, a ram, a barley grain?
How many barley grains in a prastha, how many in half a prastha? In a drona, a khari; how many lakhs, kotis and bimbaras?
How many atoms in a mustard seed, how many mustard seeds in a rakshika? How many rakshikas make a masha, how many mashas a dharana?
How many dharanas in a karsha, how many karshas in a pala? By this the mark of a heap: how many palas would Mount Meru be? Ask me things like this, son; why do you ask otherwise?

cmp.note: 这一串重量、长度单位是佛在嘲讽：你要问就问「须弥山有几两重」这种问题吧，何必问别的？语气带反讽，白话也照字面译；英文保留问句，让读者自己读出那点讥讽。
cmp.en: This string of weights and measures is the Buddha being ironic: "If you're going to ask, ask how many palas Mount Meru weighs; why ask anything else?" The plain Chinese translates it literally; the English keeps the questions so the reader can hear the irony.

verses.en: How many atoms make the body of a pratyekabuddha, a shravaka, a buddha or a son of the Conqueror? Why don't you ask that?
How many atoms in a tongue of fire, how many atoms in the wind? How many in each sense faculty, in a pore of the skin, in the eyebrows?
By what are people lords of wealth, kings, wheel-turning kings? How are their kingdoms to be protected, and how is their liberation to come about?
How do you speak of prose and verse, of sexual union, famous in the world, the varieties of food and drink, the forests of men and women?
By what are the immovable mountains hard as diamond? Tell me how. By what are things like illusion and dream, how like a mirage?
Where do clouds come from, and from where the seasons? Why do flavors have their flavor? Why are there women, men and those who are neither?
Where are the splendors and the sons of the Conqueror? Ask me, son. How are the divine immovable mountains adorned with seers and gandharvas?
Where does the freed one go? Who is bound? By what is one freed? What is the realm of meditators? The created forms and the tirthikas?
By what is non-being, being and non-action? How does what is seen turn back? How is reasoning purified? By what does reasoning arise?
By what does action arise? Tell me how going happens. By what is perception cut off? By what is it called samadhi?
Who is it that splits apart the three worlds? What is the place, what the body? By what is there talk of no real self? How is there teaching by convention?
By what do you ask about the marks? How do you ask about no-self? Sons of the Conqueror, by what do you ask me about wombs and logicians?
By what is the view of permanence and annihilation, by what is the mind brought into samadhi? Speech, knowledge, moral conduct, lineage, sons of the Conqueror,
reasoned explanation, teacher and disciple, how beings are so various, food and drink, the sky, clouds, Maras, mere designation,
how and by what are trees and creepers? You ask me, son of the Conqueror. By what are the fields so various, and the seer of long austerities,
your clan, your teacher? By what? You ask me, son of the Conqueror. People (meaning unclear) in yoga; you do not awaken in the desire realm;
the realized truth among the Akanishtha gods: how do you ask me about reasoning? By what are worldly supernatural powers, and how is one a monk?
How do you ask me about transformation buddhas and buddhas of ripening? How are the buddhas of suchness and knowledge, and how the Sanghas?
Fields shining like vinas, drums and flowers, fields free of the world; mind and the seven stages: you ask me, son of the Conqueror. These and many other questions you ask me, son.
Each one joined with its marks, free of the faults of views: I will tell you the realized truth and the teaching. Listen to me now.
I will set out the terms; listen to me, son: a hundred and eight terms, just as the buddhas have described them."
Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "Lord, what are the hundred and eight terms?"

The Lord said: "The term 'arising' is a non-term of arising; the term 'permanent' is a non-term of permanent; 'mark', not mark; 'abiding and changing', not abiding and changing; 'momentary', not momentary; 'own-nature', not own-nature; 'emptiness', not emptiness; 'annihilation', not annihilation; 'mind', not mind; 'middle', not middle; 'eternal', not eternal; 'condition', not condition; 'cause', not cause; 'affliction', not affliction; 'craving', not craving; 'means', not means; 'skill', not skill; 'purity', not purity; 'reasoning', not reasoning; 'example', not example; 'disciple', not disciple; 'teacher', not teacher; 'lineage', not lineage; 'three vehicles', not three vehicles; 'imageless', not imageless; 'vow', not vow; 'the three circles', not the three circles; 'sign', not sign; 'the sides of being and non-being', not the sides of being and non-being; 'both', not both; 'noble wisdom realized within oneself', not noble wisdom realized within oneself; 'bliss here and now', not bliss here and now; 'field', not field; 'atom', not atom; 'water', not water; 'bow', not bow; 'element', not element; 'number and counting', not number and counting; 'supernatural power', not supernatural power; 'weariness', not weariness; 'cloud', not cloud; 'crafts, arts and learning', not crafts, arts and learning; 'wind', not wind; 'earth', not earth; 'thinkable', not thinkable; 'designation', not designation; 'own-nature', not own-nature; 'heap', not heap; 'being', not being; 'understanding', not understanding; 'nirvana', not nirvana; 'knowable', not knowable; 'tirthika', not tirthika; 'turmoil', not turmoil; 'illusion', not illusion; 'dream', not dream; 'mirage', not mirage; 'reflection', not reflection; 'wheel', not wheel; 'gandharva', not gandharva; 'god', not god; 'food and drink', not food and drink; 'sexual union', not sexual union; 'view', not view; 'perfection', not perfection; 'moral conduct', not moral conduct; 'moon, sun and stars', not moon, sun and stars; 'truth', not truth; 'fruit', not fruit; 'cessation', not cessation; 'emerging from cessation', not emerging from cessation; 'healing', not healing; 'mark', not mark; 'limb', not limb; 'arts and learning', not arts and learning; 'meditation', not meditation; 'confusion', not confusion; 'seen', not seen; 'protected', not protected; 'clan', not clan; 'seer', not seer; 'kingdom', not kingdom; 'grasping', not grasping; 'jewel', not jewel; 'prediction', not prediction; 'icchantika', not icchantika; 'woman, man and neither', not woman, man and neither; 'flavor', not flavor; 'action', not action; 'body', not body; 'reasoning', not reasoning; 'moving', not moving; 'sense faculty', not sense faculty; 'conditioned', not conditioned; 'cause and effect', not cause and effect; 'Kanishtha', not Kanishtha; 'season', not season; 'trees, shrubs, creepers and vines', not trees, shrubs, creepers and vines; 'variety', not variety; 'entering by teaching', not entering by teaching; 'discipline', not discipline; 'monk', not monk; 'sustaining power', not sustaining power; 'letter', not letter."

cmp.note: 这一百零八「句」每一对都是「某句、非某句」：每个概念说出来的同时就被否定，意思是这些都只是名言，不能执为实有。实叉难陀译成「生句非生句」，白话照这个格式。英文的第一对写得完整（The term 'arising' is a non-term of arising），之后只写 'X', not X，以免太长。
cmp.en: Each of the hundred and eight "terms" comes as a pair, "the term X, the non-term X": every concept is negated the moment it is stated, meaning these are all just words and must not be taken as real. Śikṣānanda renders it 生句非生句 ("the arising-term is a non-arising-term"), and the plain Chinese follows that pattern. The English writes out the first pair in full and then shortens the rest to "'X', not X" to keep it readable.

verses.en: These, Mahamati, are the hundred and eight terms described by the buddhas of the past."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, in how many ways do the consciousnesses arise, abide and cease?" The Lord said: "The consciousnesses arise, abide and cease in two ways, Mahamati, and reasoners don't understand this: there is cessation of the stream and cessation of the mark. The consciousnesses arise in two ways: arising of the stream and arising of the mark. They abide in two ways: abiding of the stream and abiding of the mark. Consciousness has three marks: the mark of activity, the mark of karma and the mark of birth. In brief, Mahamati, consciousness, which is described as having eight marks, is of two kinds: the consciousness that displays (khyātivijñāna) and the consciousness that conceptualizes things (vastuprativikalpavijñāna). Just as a mirror takes in forms, Mahamati, so the displaying consciousness displays. The displaying consciousness, Mahamati, and the consciousness that conceptualizes things:

cmp.note: 「现识」与「分别事识」：前者像镜子一样把一切影像显现出来（大致对应藏识），后者对这些影像起分别（大致对应其余诸识）。实叉难陀分别译作「现识」「分别事识」，英文译 the consciousness that displays、the consciousness that conceptualizes things。
cmp.en: "Displaying consciousness" and "consciousness that conceptualizes things": the first shows all images the way a mirror does (roughly the storehouse consciousness), the second conceptualizes those images (roughly the other consciousnesses). Śikṣānanda calls them 现识 (xiànshí, "manifesting consciousness") and 分别事识 (fēnbié shì shí, "consciousness that discriminates things"); the English says "the consciousness that displays" and "the consciousness that conceptualizes things."

verses.en: these two are not different in mark, and each is the cause of the other. Of these, Mahamati, the displaying consciousness is caused by the inconceivable transformation of habit-energy (vāsanā), the traces past experience leaves in the mind. And the consciousness that conceptualizes things, Mahamati, is caused by conceptualizing objects and by the habit-energy of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time.

cmp.note: 「习气」：过去的经验在心里留下的气味、印痕，像衣服熏了香，香味留在布上。中文「习气」现代多指「坏习惯」；英文 habit-energy 是本站的固定译法，第一次出现时加了解释。
cmp.en: Vāsanā, rendered 习气 (xíqì): the scent or imprint past experience leaves in the mind, like perfume lingering in cloth. In modern Chinese 习气 mostly means "bad habits"; the site's fixed English rendering is "habit-energy," explained on first use.

verses.en: The cessation of all the sense consciousnesses, Mahamati, means the cessation of the variety of habit-energy of unreal imagining in the storehouse consciousness. That, Mahamati, is the cessation of the mark. The cessation of the stream, Mahamati, is the cessation of that from which it arises. 'From which,' Mahamati, means its support and its object. Its support is the habit-energy of the coarse tendencies of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time; its object is the conceptualizings in the realm of consciousness that is what one's own mind shows. It is like this, Mahamati: a lump of clay is made of clay atoms, and it is neither different from them nor the same; so too gold and its ornaments. If the lump of clay were different from the clay atoms, Mahamati, it would not have been made from them. But it is made from those clay atoms, so it is not different. Yet if it were not different, there would be no telling the lump apart from the atoms.

In the same way, Mahamati, if the active consciousnesses were different from the mark of birth of the storehouse consciousness, they would not have the storehouse consciousness as their cause. But if they were not different, then when the active consciousnesses ceased the storehouse consciousness would also cease, and that does not happen: there is no cessation of its own mark of birth. So, Mahamati, what ceases in the consciousnesses is not their own mark of birth but the mark of karma. If its own mark of birth were to cease, the storehouse consciousness would cease. And if the storehouse consciousness ceased, this teaching would be no different from the annihilationism of the tirthikas. The tirthikas, Mahamati, teach this: when the grasping of objects stops, the stream of consciousness stops; and when the stream of consciousness stops, the stream that has run since beginningless time is cut off. And the tirthikas, Mahamati, explain the arising of the stream from a cause.

They do not explain the eye-consciousness as arising from the coming together of form and light, but from a cause. And the cause, Mahamati, is what they call primal matter, spirit, God, time or atoms.

"Again, Mahamati, the own-nature of things is of seven kinds: the own-nature of gathering, the own-nature of being, the own-nature of marks, the own-nature of the great elements, the own-nature of causes, the own-nature of conditions, and seventh, the own-nature of completion.

"Again, Mahamati, the highest truth is of seven kinds: the realm of mind, the realm of knowledge, the realm of wisdom, the realm of the two views, the realm beyond the two views, the realm of the sons of the Conqueror progressing through the stages, and the Tathagata's realm realized within himself.

"This, Mahamati, is the heart of the highest truth about the own-nature of things for the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of past, future and present. Having it, the tathagatas, with the noble eye of wisdom, set out the highest worldly and world-transcending dharmas as they fall under their particular and general marks. And they set them out so that they are not shared with the doctrines and wrong views of the tirthikas. How, Mahamati, do they come to be shared with the doctrines and wrong views of the tirthikas? Through the consciousnesses not understanding that they are views conceptualizing the realm of one's own mind. Because they have not entered into 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' Mahamati, foolish ordinary people talk about the highest truth of the own-nature of things in terms of the two views, being and non-being.

"Again, Mahamati, I will speak of turning back the suffering of the three existences that come from conceptualizing; of turning away from the conditions of ignorance, craving and karma; of seeing the illusion-like realm that is what one's own mind shows. Some ascetics or brahmins, Mahamati, hold that what did not exist comes to be; that cause and effect become manifest; that substance lasts through time; that the heaps, elements and sense fields arise and abide in conditions and, having been, pass away. These, Mahamati, end up as destroyers and annihilationists, denying continuity, action, arising and perishing, existence, nirvana, the path, karma, fruit and truth. Why? Because they have not seen this directly, and have not seen the beginning.

"It is like this, Mahamati: a pot broken into shards does not do a pot's work, and a burnt seed does not do the work of a sprout. In the same way, Mahamati, the heaps, elements and sense fields that have ceased, are ceasing and will cease are not causes, since what is seen is the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows; so there is no unbroken arising.

"If, Mahamati, consciousnesses that did not exist were to arise through the working of the three-way meeting of conditions, then turtle hair, which does not exist, would also arise, Mahamati, or oil from sand. Mahamati, their own thesis would collapse and their rules would break down, and the actions, karma and means of those who talk of being and non-being would be pointless. They too, Mahamati, have a teaching of the working of the three-way meeting of conditions; relying on the particular marks of cause and effect, staying on the level of reasoning, they will argue with reasons and scriptures that past, future and present exist or do not, driven by the faults and habit-energy of their own views. In just this way, Mahamati, foolish ordinary people bitten by wrong views, their minds warped, will call what was set out by the ignorant 'set out by the all-knowing.'

"But there are other ascetics or brahmins, Mahamati, who see that everything has no own-nature, like clouds, a whirling firebrand, a city of gandharvas; that nothing arises; that the outside world is by nature like an illusion, a mirage, the moon in water or a dream, the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows, the display of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time. They are free of conditions rooted in the conceptualizing of their own mind; free of imagined names and what they mark, of words and what words refer to; free of the grasped and the grasper in the realm of the storehouse consciousness, which appears as body, possessions and dwelling place; and they will understand the imageless realm, free of arising, abiding and perishing, which follows the arising of one's own mind. Before long, Mahamati, these bodhisattvas, great beings, will reach the sameness of samsara and nirvana.

"Through practice, Mahamati, that comes with great compassion and skill in means and needs no effort; through seeing all beings as the same as illusions and reflections; through conditions never having been set going; through freedom from inner and outer objects; through seeing nothing outside the mind; following the sustaining power of signlessness; following step by step the order of the stages and the realms of samadhi; understanding through conviction that the three realms are one's own mind, they attain the illusion-like samadhi. Entering into 'only one's own mind, without images,' they reach the abode of the perfection of wisdom, free of the working of arising, and they will attain, Mahamati, the body of a tathagata: like the samadhi called the Diamond Reflection, following the Tathagata's body, following the transformations of suchness, adorned with powers, supernatural abilities, masteries, kindness, compassion and skillful means, going into all buddha-fields and the haunts of tirthikas, free of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness, reached step by step through the turning-around. Those bodhisattvas, Mahamati, will attain the body of a tathagata.

"So then, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, who want to attain by following the Tathagata's body, should be free of conceptualizing and conceptual proliferation about the heaps, elements, sense fields, mind, causes and conditions, action, arising, abiding and perishing, and should follow mind-only.

"Seeing that the three existences are caused by the habit-energy of conceptualizing, the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, and keeping in mind the imageless, unarisen stage of a buddha, he arrives at the noble Dharma realized within, masters his own mind, arrives at effortless practice, and, like a jewel that reflects every color, with subtle created bodies that enter the minds of beings, through firmly grasping mind-only, establishes them in the sequence of the stages. So then, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should be skilled in his own realized truth."

Mahamati spoke again: "May the Lord teach me the flower of Dharma discourses about mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, the five dharmas, own-nature and marks, which the buddhas and bodhisattvas have followed; which unbinds from the realm that is what one's own mind shows; which tears open the true marks of every saying and reasoning; the heart of the words of all buddhas. For the bodhisattvas who live on Mount Malaya in the city of Lanka, please proclaim the Dharma-body that the tathagatas have sung of, the realm of the storehouse consciousness, which is like the waves of the ocean."

Then the Lord said again to the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "Mahamati, eye-consciousness arises for four reasons. Which four?
