Not understanding that what is grasped is what one's own mind shows; clinging to the habit-energy of form, the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time; the very nature of consciousness; and curiosity about the various marks of form. Through these four reasons, Mahamati, the waves of the active consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness, which is like the water of a flood.

"As with eye-consciousness, Mahamati, so in all the sense faculties, atoms and pores, arising at once or in order, as a mirror shows images of objects: just as the ocean is struck by the wind, Mahamati, so the waves on the ocean of mind, struck by the wind of objects, with unbroken marks of cause and action, never separate from one another, tightly bound by the marks of karma and birth, unable to settle the own-nature of form: in this way, Mahamati, the five groups of consciousness arise. Along with those five groups of consciousness, Mahamati, arises what is called mind-consciousness, which settles the marks that distinguish causes and objects, its body born from them as cause. And neither they nor it think, 'We here are causes of one another, arising from clinging to the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows.'

"Yet they arise together, with marks not different from one another, in distinguishing the objects of representation. And they arise in such a way that even for a yogi in meditative attainment, the subtle workings of habit-energy go unnoticed. Yogis think, 'We will stop the consciousnesses and enter attainment.' But they enter attainment with the consciousnesses not stopped: not stopped, because the seeds of habit-energy have not stopped; stopped, only in that the grasping of arising objects is lacking. So subtle, Mahamati, is the working of the storehouse consciousness that, apart from the Tathagata and bodhisattvas established on the stages, it is not easy for others, shravaka, pratyekabuddha or tirthika yogis, to understand it or make it out, even by the force of samadhi and wisdom.

"Only those who are skilled in wisdom and knowledge of the marks of the stages, who have settled the distinctions of meaning, who have stored up roots of good under countless conquerors, who are free of conceptualizing and conceptual proliferation about what one's own mind shows, and who live in forests, thickets and caves, practicing yoga at low, high or middle levels, can see the flow of what is seen from their own mind's conceptualizing and attain the consecration by conquerors in endless fields, the masteries, powers, supernatural abilities and samadhis; others cannot, Mahamati. Those led by good friends and conquerors, Mahamati, can cross the ocean of existence, of samsara: mind, thinking mind and consciousness conceptualizing the realm of the own-nature of what their own mind shows, caused by karma, craving and ignorance. For this reason, Mahamati, a yogi should undertake the practice under the guidance of good friends and conquerors."
Then the Lord spoke these verses:
"Just as the waves of the ocean, stirred by the wind as their condition, rise dancing and never cease,
so the flood of the storehouse, always stirred by the wind of objects, rolls on, dancing with its many waves of consciousness.
Like blue and red, salt, conch, milk and sugar, astringent things, fruits, flowers and the like, and the rays of the sun,
not other and not the same, so are the waves thought to be with the ocean; so too are the seven consciousnesses joined with mind.
As the ocean transforms into the variety of waves, so the storehouse in all its variety arises as what is called consciousness.

cmp.note: 这几首偈颂是全经最有名的段落：阿赖耶识像大海，七识像波浪，海与浪不一不异。中文「阿赖耶」是音译，「藏识」是意译；英文统一用 storehouse，偈颂里只写 the storehouse 以合节奏。
cmp.en: These verses are the most famous lines of the sutra: the storehouse consciousness is like the ocean, the seven consciousnesses like waves, neither one nor different. The Chinese 阿赖耶 (ālàiyē) is a transliteration and 藏识 (zàngshí) a translation; the English uses "storehouse" throughout, and in verse just "the storehouse," to keep the rhythm.

verses.en: Mind, thinking mind and consciousness are set up to explain the marks; the eight are not different in mark: there is neither marked nor mark.
Just as there is no difference between the ocean and its waves, so no transformation is found between the consciousnesses and mind.
Karma is stored up by mind, examined by thinking mind; by consciousness one knows; with the five one imagines what is seen.

cmp.note: 这里用了一个文字游戏：citta（心）和 cīyate（积集）同根。中文「心积集业」和英文 stored up by mind 都看不出这层双关。
cmp.en: A play on words: citta (mind) and cīyate (is stored up) come from the same root. Neither the Chinese 心积集业 ("mind stores up karma") nor the English "stored up by mind" can show the pun.

verses.en: 'Consciousness appears to people in kinds such as blue and red. Tell me, Mahamati, why is mind like the waves?'
'Kinds such as blue and red are not found in the waves. Mind is described as functioning only to explain the marks to fools.
It has no functioning of its own; one's own mind is free of anything grasped. When there is something grasped there is grasping, established together with the waves.
Consciousness appears to people as body, possessions and dwelling place; that is why its functioning is seen to be like the waves.'
'The ocean is clearly seen dancing as waves. Why is the functioning of the storehouse not grasped by understanding the same way?'
'Because fools lack understanding, the storehouse is compared to the ocean; its functioning is brought home by the example of the waves.'
'As the sun rises and shines alike on the low and the high, conqueror, so you, lamp of the world, should teach the truth to fools.
Having set the dharmas in place, why don't you speak the truth?' 'Even if I speak the truth, there is no truth in the mind.
Like waves on the ocean, images in a mirror, things in a dream, appearing at the same moment, so is mind in its own realm.
When the conditions of objects are incomplete, it works in sequence: by consciousness one knows, and by thinking mind one considers again.
What is seen by the five appears; in samadhi there is no sequence. As a painter, or a painter's apprentice, mixes colors for a painting, so do I teach.
The painting is not in the colors, nor in the ground, nor in the dish; to attract beings, a painting is imagined with colors. Teaching can stray, but the truth is beyond letters.
Having set the dharmas in place, I teach the truth to yogis. The truth is realized within, free of imagining and the imagined. I teach it to the sons of the Conqueror; this teaching is not for fools.
As an illusion of many kinds is seen yet does not exist, so the teaching too is given in many kinds, yet does not stray. What is a teaching for one is no teaching for another.
As a physician gives medicine to each patient, so the buddhas speak of mind-only to beings.
It is not the realm of reasoners, nor of shravakas: the realm reached within oneself, which the protectors teach.'

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva who wants to fully understand the realm of conceptualizing the grasped and the grasper as what one's own mind shows should be free of the hindrances of socializing, company, sloth and sleep. He should practice yoga, staying awake in the first, middle and last watches of the night. He should be free of the treatises and tales of wrong tirthikas and of the marks of the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles. A bodhisattva, a great being, should be thoroughly at home in the marks of conceptualizing what one's own mind shows.

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, standing firm in the arrangement of the marks of mind, consciousness and wisdom, should go further and practice the three marks of noble knowledge. And what, Mahamati, are the three higher marks of noble knowledge? The mark of imagelessness, the mark of the sustaining power of all the buddhas' own vows, and the mark of the course of noble wisdom realized within oneself. Having reached these, the yogi drops the marks of mind, wisdom and knowledge like a lame donkey, reaches the eighth stage of the sons of the Conqueror, and practices in the three marks above it.

"Here, Mahamati, the mark of imagelessness arises from familiarity with all the marks of shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas. The mark of sustaining power arises from the sustaining power of the past buddhas' own vows. The mark of the course of noble wisdom realized within oneself arises from not clinging to the marks of any dharma, from attaining a body of illusion-like samadhi, from going and moving on the course to the stage of a buddha. These, Mahamati, are the three marks of the noble ones; endowed with these three noble marks, the noble ones reach the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within. So, Mahamati, the three marks of noble knowledge should be practiced."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, again knowing what was on the minds of that assembly of bodhisattvas, sustained by the sustaining power of all the buddhas, asked the Lord about the Dharma discourse called "Examining the Matter of Noble Knowledge": "May the Lord teach me the Dharma discourse called 'Examining the Matter of Noble Knowledge,' based on the distinctions of the hundred and eight terms. Relying on it, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones teach bodhisattvas, great beings, who have fallen into particular and general marks, the distinctions in the workings of the imagined nature (parikalpitasvabhāva). Having clearly analyzed the distinctions in the workings of the imagined nature, they purify their practice of the no-self of persons and of things, become trained in the stages, go beyond the bliss of the meditations, samadhis and attainments of all shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas, and attain the body of a tathagata: the course of the Tathagata's unthinkable realm, turned away from the workings of the five dharmas and own-nature; the Tathagata, the Dharma-body, the Dharma firmly bound with wisdom and knowledge, coming forth from the illusion-like realm, reaching all buddha-fields, the Tushita heaven and the Akanishtha abode."

cmp.note: 「妄计自性」（遍计所执性）：三自性之一，指被心想象出来、以为实有的那一层。英文第一次出现时译作 the imagined nature。中文「妄计」带着「错误地计算」的贬义，梵文 parikalpita 本义只是「被构想的」，贬义来自上下文。
cmp.en: The imagined nature, one of the three natures: the layer of things that the mind imagines and takes as real. The English renders it "the imagined nature" on first use. The Chinese 妄计 (wàngjì, "falsely reckoned") carries a built-in judgment; Sanskrit parikalpita only means "constructed, imagined," and the negative sense comes from context.

verses.en: The Lord said: "Here, Mahamati, some people with tirthika and non-tirthika views cling to non-existence. Because their conceptualizing mind sees that causes are exhausted and own-nature is absent, they conceptualize that a hare has no horn: just as a hare's horn does not exist, so it is with all dharmas. Others, Mahamati, seeing differences in the shape and arrangement of elements, qualities, atoms and substances, and clinging to the idea that a hare's horn does not exist, imagine that a cow's horn does exist. These, Mahamati, have fallen into the view of the two extremes; their minds have not grasped mind-only. They feed on the conceptualizing of their own mind's realm. Mahamati, in what is only the conceptualizing of the course of body, possessions and dwelling place, one should not imagine a hare's horn, which is beyond existence and non-existence. In the same way, Mahamati, nothing at all, being beyond existence and non-existence, should be imagined.

"Those, Mahamati, who are beyond existence and non-existence and do not imagine that there is no hare's horn: they should not imagine that a hare's horn does not exist, since each depends on the other. And since, analyzing down to the atom, no real thing is found, Mahamati, one should not, apart from the realm of noble knowledge, imagine that a cow's horn exists."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "But surely, Lord, seeing the mark of conceptualizing not arising, we infer that its non-existence depends on conceptualizing not arising?" The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, its non-existence does not depend on conceptualizing not arising. Why? Because it is the cause of conceptualizing arising. Conceptualizing, Mahamati, arises based on the horn. Since conceptualizing arises based on the horn, Mahamati, and since the basis is the cause, and they are neither different nor the same, the non-existence of the hare's horn does not depend on it. If, Mahamati, conceptualizing were different from the hare's horn, it would not have the horn as its cause. And if it were not different, then, since it has that as its cause, and since analysis down to the atom finds nothing, and since it is not different from the horn, it too would not exist. Since neither of the two exists or does not exist, whose non-existence depends on what?

"So, Mahamati, since the non-existence of the hare's horn does not come about by depending on anything, one should not imagine the hare's horn as non-existent by depending on existence. Since the reasoning is unsound, Mahamati, the existence and non-existence of those who argue for existence and non-existence is not established. Others with tirthika views, Mahamati, clinging to the causes and shape of form and not skilled in making out the nature of space, see form as a boundary apart from the nature of space, and conceptualize it. But space, Mahamati, is form. Since space enters into the elements of form, Mahamati, form is space. The distinction between the two causes, form and space, Mahamati, should be understood in terms of what holds and what is held. The elements, Mahamati, as they arise, are distinct from one another in their own marks and do not rest in space; yet space is not absent from them. In the same way, Mahamati, the hare's horn exists in dependence on the cow's horn.

"Divide a cow's horn into atoms, Mahamati, and divide the atoms again, and they do not stay in the mark of being atoms. On what does its non-existence depend? And if it depends on some other thing, that thing is of the same nature."

Then the Lord said again to the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "You should be free, Mahamati, and so should other bodhisattvas, of views and conceptualizing about the horns of hares and cows, space and form. With your mind following the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows, Mahamati, you should teach the practice of what one's own mind shows in the assemblies of all the sons of the Conqueror in every field."
Then the Lord spoke these verses:
"What is seen does not exist; it is mind; mind arises as what is seen. The storehouse appears to people as body, possessions and dwelling place.
Mind, thinking mind and consciousness, own-nature, the five dharmas, and the pure twofold no-self: this is what the leaders teach.
Long and short and the like arise in relation to each other: non-existence proves existence, and existence proves non-existence.
Divide it down to the atom and one cannot conceptualize form. Mind-only is the conclusion; those with wrong views are not convinced.
It is not the realm of reasoners, nor of shravakas: the realm reached within oneself, which the protectors teach."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again about purifying the stream of what one's own mind shows: "Lord, how is the stream of what one's own mind shows purified: all at once, or step by step?" The Lord said: "The stream of what one's own mind shows is purified step by step, Mahamati, not all at once. Just as mangoes ripen one by one, Mahamati, not all at once, so the stream of what beings' own minds show is purified step by step, not all at once. Just as a potter makes pots one by one, Mahamati, not all at once, so the Tathagata purifies the stream of what beings' own minds show step by step, not all at once.

cmp.note: 「渐净非顿」：这一段和下一段先说「渐」，再说「顿」，后来中国禅宗的「顿渐之争」常引它。英文 step by step / all at once，中文「渐」「顿」，意思对得上；只是中文这两个字后来带上了宗派色彩，梵文这里只是「依次」和「同时」。
cmp.en: "Step by step, not all at once": this passage and the next first speak of the gradual and then of the sudden, and the later Chinese Chan debate over 顿 (dùn, "sudden") and 渐 (jiàn, "gradual") often cites them. The English "step by step / all at once" and the Chinese 渐 / 顿 match in meaning; but the Chinese words later took on sectarian color, while the Sanskrit here just means "in sequence" and "simultaneously."

verses.en: "Just as grasses, shrubs, herbs and trees grow up from the earth step by step, Mahamati, not all at once, so the Tathagata purifies the stream of what beings' own minds show step by step, not all at once. Just as comedy, dance, song, instrumental music, the vina and painting are mastered step by step, Mahamati, not all at once, so the Tathagata purifies the stream of what all beings' own minds show step by step, not all at once. But just as all forms appear in a mirror at once, Mahamati, without conceptualizing, so the Tathagata purifies the stream of what all beings' own minds show all at once, making it free of conceptualizing, an imageless realm.

"Just as the disks of the moon and sun light up all forms at once with their rays, Mahamati, so the Tathagata shows, all at once, the realm of the conquerors' unthinkable knowledge to beings who are free of the coarse habit-energy of what their own mind shows. Just as the storehouse consciousness makes appear at once the realm of body, dwelling place and possessions that is what one's own mind shows, Mahamati, so the outflow Buddha (niṣyandabuddha) ripens the realm of beings all at once and sets yogis to practice in the palaces of the Akanishtha heaven. Just as the Dharma-nature Buddha (dharmatābuddha) shines all at once with the rays of the outflow and transformation buddhas, Mahamati, so the mark of the Dharma of the noble course realized within shines all at once, turning people away from wrong views of being and non-being.

cmp.note: 这里出现三种佛：法性佛（dharmatābuddha，佛的本质）、等流佛（niṣyandabuddha，从法性「流出」的佛，大致相当于后来说的报身）、变化佛（nirmāṇabuddha，应化在世间的佛，大致相当于化身）。英文按字面译作 Dharma-nature Buddha、outflow Buddha、transformation Buddha，不套用后来的「三身」名目。
cmp.en: Three kinds of buddha appear here: the Dharma-nature Buddha (dharmatābuddha, the Buddha's essence), the outflow Buddha (niṣyandabuddha, the Buddha that "flows out" of the Dharma-nature, roughly what was later called the enjoyment body), and the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇabuddha, the Buddha who appears in the world, roughly the emanation body). The English translates them literally rather than borrowing the later "three bodies" labels.

verses.en: "Again, Mahamati, the Dharma-nature outflow Buddha teaches that all dharmas, which fall under particular and general marks, are bound up with the causal mark of the habit-energy of what one's own mind shows and are caused by clinging to the imagined nature; that they are not what they seem, like the many figures of people made by illusion and painting, whose variety one clings to but cannot find. Again, Mahamati, the mark of the workings of the imagined nature arises from clinging to the dependent nature (paratantrasvabhāva). Just as, relying on grass, wood, shrubs and creepers, joined with the art of illusion and a magician, the body of an illusory person appears, taking on the forms of all beings, a body that seems like a single complete being, conceptualized in all sorts of ways; yet though it appears that way, Mahamati, it is not that thing. In the same way, Mahamati, in the imagined nature resting on the dependent nature, the varied marks of the mind's many conceptualizings appear.

cmp.note: 「依他自性」（依他起性）：三自性之二，指依靠因缘而生起的那一层，是妄计赖以发生的底子。英文译 the dependent nature。这一段用幻师拿草木变出幻人来比喻：草木是「依他」，看起来像人是「妄计」。
cmp.en: The dependent nature, the second of the three natures: the layer that arises dependent on causes and conditions, the ground on which imagining happens. The English says "the dependent nature." The passage uses the image of a magician conjuring an illusory person out of grass and wood: the grass and wood are the dependent nature, the seeming person is the imagined nature.

verses.en: "Imagining from the habit-energy of clinging to the marks of things and imaginings, Mahamati, there comes to be the mark of the imagined nature. This, Mahamati, is the teaching of the outflow Buddha. The Dharma-nature Buddha, Mahamati, sets out the realm of the noble course realized within, free of the own-nature and marks of mind. The created transformation Buddha, Mahamati, sets out the practice of distinguishing the marks of giving, moral conduct, meditation, samadhi, the various kinds of wisdom and knowledge, the heaps, elements, sense fields, liberations and the workings of consciousness; and he teaches the mark of going beyond the views of the tirthikas and the formless realms. The Dharma-nature Buddha, Mahamati, has no object. He is free of objects, turned away from all marks of action, senses and means of knowledge, not the realm of fools, shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas who cling to the marks of a self. So then, Mahamati, one should practice in the special mark of the noble course realized within.
"And you should have the view that turns away from what the marks of one's own mind show.

"Again, Mahamati, the way of the shravaka vehicle has two distinct marks: the mark of the special realization of what is noble within, and the mark of clinging to the own-nature of things through conceptualizing. What, Mahamati, is the shravakas' mark of the special realization of what is noble within? Through dispassion and calming toward the truths whose realm is emptiness, no-self, suffering and impermanence, and through knowing as it really is the particular and general marks of the heaps, elements and sense fields and the mark of outer things perishing, the mind becomes concentrated. Having concentrated their own mind, Mahamati, the shravakas reach the meditations, liberations, samadhis, paths, fruits, attainments and freedom, though they are not free of habit-energy and of the inconceivable death of transformation, and they reach the happy abiding marked by the noble course realized within. This, Mahamati, is the shravakas' mark of the noble course realized within.

"Even having reached this happy abiding of the shravakas' realization of what is noble within, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not make the bliss of cessation and the bliss of attainment his own, out of regard for the work of helping beings and because of the vows he made before. This, Mahamati, is the shravakas' bliss of the mark of the noble course realized within, and a bodhisattva, a great being, should not train in that bliss. And what, Mahamati, is the shravakas' clinging to the own-nature of things through conceptualizing? Seeing the great elements, blue, yellow, hot, fluid, moving and hard, which arise without a maker and are firmly bound up with particular and general marks, reasoning, scripture and means of knowledge, they conceptualize them and cling to their own-nature. A bodhisattva, Mahamati, having understood this, should turn it back.

"Entering into the mark of the no-self of things, he should hold back the view of the mark of the no-self of persons and establish himself in the sequence of the stages. This, Mahamati, is the shravakas' mark of clinging to the own-nature of things through conceptualizing that I spoke of; it has now been answered."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "The Lord has spoken of the realm of the noble course realized within, the realm of the highest truth, as permanent and unthinkable. But surely, Lord, the tirthikas too say that their causes are permanent and unthinkable?" The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, the tirthikas' cause does not attain permanence and unthinkability. Why? The tirthikas' permanent and unthinkable, Mahamati, is not joined with the own-mark of a cause. If something permanent and unthinkable is not joined with the own-mark of a cause, Mahamati, how and by what is it shown to be permanent and unthinkable? And if the doctrine of the permanent and unthinkable, Mahamati, were joined with the own-mark of a cause, then, since its causal mark would depend on a maker, it would not be permanent and unthinkable.

"My highest-truth permanent and unthinkable, Mahamati, is joined with the cause that is the mark of the highest truth and is free of being and non-being. It has a mark because it is marked by noble realization within; it has a cause because the knowledge of the highest truth is its cause; and because, though it has a cause, it is free of being and non-being, and is of the same kind as the examples of unmade space, nirvana and cessation, it is permanent. So, Mahamati, it is not like the tirthikas' doctrine of the permanent and unthinkable. This permanence and unthinkability, Mahamati, is the suchness realized by the tathagatas' noble wisdom within. So then, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should practice to realize the permanent, unthinkable noble wisdom within.

"Again, Mahamati, the tirthikas' permanence and unthinkability rests on the reason that it differs in mark from impermanent things; it is not permanent by the power of a causal mark of its own making. If, Mahamati, the tirthikas, seeing that made things exist and then do not and are impermanent, establish the permanent and unthinkable by inference, then by that same reason, Mahamati, I too, seeing that made things exist and then do not and are impermanent, (do not) teach permanence by that reason.

"If, Mahamati, permanence and unthinkability is joined with a causal mark, then for the tirthikas, since there is neither a cause nor its own mark, Mahamati, their permanence and unthinkability is like a hare's horn, and it turns out, Mahamati, to be mere verbal conceptualizing. Why? Because a hare's horn, Mahamati, is mere verbal conceptualizing, having no causal mark of its own. My permanence and unthinkability, Mahamati, is permanent because it has the mark of noble realization within as its cause and is free of the being and non-being of made things; it is not permanent by inference from outer things existing or not, permanent or impermanent. Whoever, Mahamati, holds it permanent by inferring permanence from the non-existence of outer things does not know the own causal mark of permanence and unthinkability. They are outside the mark of the realm of noble wisdom realized within, Mahamati, and are not worth discussing with.

"Again, Mahamati, people afraid of the suffering of samsara's conceptualizing seek nirvana. Not knowing that samsara and nirvana are no different, Mahamati, they conceptualize nirvana as the absence of conceptualizing about all things and the stopping of the senses toward future objects, and not as the storehouse consciousness realized within, preceded by the turning-around, Mahamati. So, Mahamati, these deluded people talk of three vehicles, not of the imageless state that is mind-only. So, Mahamati, they do not know the realm of what one's own mind shows taught by the tathagatas of past, future and present; they cling to the realm of what the mind shows as outside. And so, Mahamati, they keep on turning on the wheel of samsara's courses.

"Again, Mahamati, the tathagatas of past, future and present say that all dharmas are unborn. Why? Because what one's own mind shows does not exist as a thing, and because they are free of arising from being or non-being, Mahamati, all things are unborn. All dharmas, Mahamati, are like the horns of a hare, horse, donkey or camel. Because they are conceptualized by the unreal imagined nature of foolish ordinary people, Mahamati, all things are unborn. The arising of the own-nature and marks of all things, Mahamati, is the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within, not the own-nature of the realm of the two kinds of conceptualizing of foolish ordinary people. The storehouse consciousness, Mahamati, whose own-nature and mark is the course of body, possessions and dwelling place, works through the marks of the grasped and the grasper; fools, their minds fallen into the two views of arising, abiding and perishing, conceptualize the arising of all things as being or non-being. Here, Mahamati, you should practice.

"Again, Mahamati, there are five lineages of realization. Which five? The lineage of realization of the shravaka vehicle, the lineage of realization of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, the lineage of realization of the Tathagata vehicle, the undetermined lineage, and fifth, no lineage. How, Mahamati, is the lineage of realization of the shravaka vehicle to be recognized? When the realization that comes from fully knowing the particular and general marks of the heaps, elements and sense fields is being taught, the hair on his body stands on end. His mind leaps toward the knowledge that is familiar with marks, but not toward familiarity with the inseparable mark of dependent arising. This, Mahamati, is the lineage of realization of the shravaka vehicle.

cmp.note: 「种性」：gotra 本义是「家族、血统」，也指「矿脉」。这里说众生按天性分成几类，像出身不同的家族。中文「种性」容易让人联想到「种姓」；英文 lineage 保留了「血统」义，但没有「矿脉」那层（含有可以开采的潜能）。
cmp.en: Gotra originally means "family, clan," and also "mine, vein of ore." Here beings are sorted into kinds by disposition, like different families. The Chinese 种性 (zhǒngxìng) can be confused with 种姓 ("caste"); the English "lineage" keeps the sense of descent but loses the "vein of ore" sense of a potential waiting to be mined.

verses.en: "Having seen the realization of the shravaka vehicle, at the fifth or sixth stage he has abandoned the afflictions that break out but not the afflictions of habit-energy; he has passed into the inconceivable death, and he roars a true lion's roar: 'Birth is ended for me, the holy life has been lived,' and so on. Having said this, through familiarity with the no-self of persons, he goes as far as thinking he has reached nirvana.

cmp.note: 这里的梵文写本有异读，白话译作「处于不可思议的死之中」，指声闻虽断了粗的生死，还有微细的「不可思议变易死」。英文照这个理解译出，但这一句原文本身不太顺。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit manuscripts vary here. The plain Chinese takes it as "abiding in the inconceivable death," meaning that although the shravaka has ended coarse birth and death, a subtle "inconceivable death of transformation" remains. The English follows that reading, but the original sentence is itself somewhat awkward.

verses.en: "Others, Mahamati, seek nirvana through awareness of a self, a being, a life, a nourisher, a soul, a person, a living being. Others again, Mahamati, seeing all dharmas as depending on a cause, think of it as the way to nirvana. Since they do not see the no-self of things, Mahamati, there is no liberation for them. This, Mahamati, is how someone of the shravaka lineage takes what is not a way out for a way out. Here, Mahamati, you should practice to turn away from wrong views.

"Now, Mahamati, one of the lineage of realization of the pratyekabuddha vehicle is someone who, when the pratyekabuddha's realization is taught, sheds tears, is thrilled, and has his hair stand on end. When the cause of not mixing with others is explained, and clinging to things, and the variety of one's own body, and the supernatural feats of dividing and the twin miracle, he is drawn in. Knowing 'he is of the lineage of realization of the pratyekabuddha vehicle,' one should speak to him in keeping with the realization of the pratyekabuddha vehicle. This, Mahamati, is the mark of one of the lineage of realization of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.

"Now, Mahamati, the lineage of realization of the Tathagata vehicle is of three kinds: the lineage of realization of dharmas as own-nature without own-nature; the lineage of realization of the noble attainment within; and the lineage of realization of the vastness of outer buddha-fields. When any one of these three is taught, Mahamati, or when the unthinkable realm of body, storehouse, possessions and dwelling place that is what one's own mind shows is taught, and he is not startled, not frightened, does not fall into terror, it should be known that he is of the lineage of realization of the Tathagata vehicle. This, Mahamati, is the mark of one of the lineage of realization of the Tathagata vehicle.

"As for one of undetermined lineage, Mahamati, when these three are taught, he should be guided toward whichever he is drawn to. This setting out of lineages, Mahamati, is for the stage of preparation; it is set out for entering the imageless stage. But a shravaka who has purified the habit-energy of his own afflictions in the storehouse within, seeing the no-self of things and reaching the happy abiding of samadhi, will attain the body of a conqueror."
Then the Lord spoke these verses:
"The fruit of stream-entry, of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship: all are confusion of mind.
I speak of three vehicles, of one vehicle and of no vehicle, for fools, for the dull-witted, and for the solitude of the noble ones.
The door to the highest truth is representation free of duality. When one stands in the imageless, how can the three vehicles be set up?
The meditations and the immeasurables, the formless attainments and samadhis, the cessation of perception: none of it exists in mind-only."

"Now, Mahamati, how is it that icchantikas do not desire liberation? Through abandoning all roots of good, and through vows made for beings since beginningless time. What is abandoning all roots of good? Rejecting the bodhisattva collection of scriptures and slandering it, saying, 'These sutras are not in keeping with the discipline and liberation': one who speaks this way has abandoned all roots of good and does not enter nirvana. The second, Mahamati, is the bodhisattva, the great being, who, because of his earlier vow and skillful means, thinks, 'I will not enter final nirvana until all beings have entered it,' and so does not enter final nirvana. This, Mahamati, is the mark of those whose nature is not to enter final nirvana, by which they reach the state of an icchantika."

cmp.note: 「一阐提」：字面是「有欲求者」，通常解释为断了善根、不能成佛的人。这一段很特别：它把「为了度众生而永不入涅槃的菩萨」也叫作一阐提，而且说断善根的一阐提靠如来加持终究还会生起善根。中文音译「一阐提」看不出字面义；英文保留原词，第一次出现时加了解释。
cmp.en: Icchantika literally means "one who desires," usually explained as someone who has cut off the roots of good and cannot become a buddha. This passage is unusual: it also calls the bodhisattva who never enters nirvana in order to save beings an icchantika, and says that the icchantika who cut off his roots of good will eventually grow them again through the Tathagata's power. The Chinese transliteration 一阐提 (yīchǎntí) hides the literal meaning; the English keeps the Sanskrit word with an explanation on first use.

verses.en: Mahamati spoke again: "Lord, which of these never enters final nirvana at all?" The Lord said: "The bodhisattva-icchantika, Mahamati, knowing that all dharmas are in final nirvana from the beginning, never enters final nirvana at all; not the icchantika who has abandoned all roots of good. For the icchantika who has abandoned all roots of good, Mahamati, through the Tathagata's sustaining power, will sometime, somewhere, raise up roots of good again. Why? Because the tathagatas, Mahamati, never abandon any being. For this reason, Mahamati, it is the bodhisattva-icchantika who does not enter final nirvana."

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should be skilled in the marks of the three natures. Here, Mahamati, the imagined nature arises from signs. How, Mahamati, does the imagined nature arise from signs? Here, Mahamati, the dependent nature appears in the form of things, signs and marks. And clinging to things, signs and marks, Mahamati, is of two kinds. The tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones set out the imagined nature as the mark of clinging to names and the mark of clinging to the things and signs that names refer to. The mark of clinging to things and signs, Mahamati, is clinging to inner and outer dharmas. Clinging to signs and marks is taking hold of the particular and general marks in those same inner and outer dharmas.

"This, Mahamati, is the twofold mark of the imagined nature. What arises from a support and an object is the dependent. And what, Mahamati, is the perfected nature (pariniṣpannasvabhāva)? It is free of conceptualizing signs, names, things and marks; it is suchness, the course of noble knowledge, the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within. This perfected nature, Mahamati, is the heart of the tathāgatagarbha."

cmp.note: 「圆成自性」（圆成实性）：三自性的第三层，去掉了妄计之后显出的真实，即真如。英文译 the perfected nature。值得注意的是这里直接说「圆成自性就是如来藏心」，把唯识的三自性和如来藏连在一起，这是《楞伽经》的特色。
cmp.en: The perfected nature, the third of the three natures: the reality that shows once the imagined is removed, that is, suchness. The English says "the perfected nature." Notably, this passage says outright that the perfected nature is "the heart of the tathāgatagarbha," joining the Yogācāra three natures to tathāgatagarbha thought, a hallmark of the Lankavatara.

verses.en: Then the Lord spoke this verse:
"Sign, name and conceptualizing are the marks of the two natures; right knowledge and suchness are the mark of the perfected."

cmp.note: 这首偈把「五法」（名、相、分别、正智、真如）和「三自性」对应起来：前三法属于妄计与依他，后两法属于圆成。白话译作「（前）两种自性」，补出了梵文省略的「前」字。
cmp.en: This verse maps the five dharmas (name, sign, conceptualizing, right knowledge, suchness) onto the three natures: the first three belong to the imagined and dependent natures, the last two to the perfected. The plain Chinese says 前两种自性 ("the first two natures"), filling in the "first" that the Sanskrit leaves implicit.

verses.en: "This, Mahamati, is the Dharma discourse called 'Examining the Marks of the Five Dharmas and the Natures,' the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within, in which you and other bodhisattvas should train.

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should be skilled in examining the marks of the two kinds of no-self. And what, Mahamati, are the marks of the two kinds of no-self? (First:) the cluster of heaps, elements and sense fields, without a self or anything belonging to a self, born of ignorance, karma and craving. Consciousness, arising from clinging to grasping form and the rest with the eye, through all the senses makes known what is conceptualized by the conceptualizing of one's own mind: the world as container, the body, and the storehouse, which are what one's own mind shows. Like a river, a seed, a lamp, the wind or a cloud, it is broken into a series of moments; restless like a monkey or a fly; impure, moving in impure realms; like fire, never satisfied; driven by the habit-energy of the realm of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time; like a water wheel or a machine's wheel, it turns on the wheel of the courses of samsara's existences, taking on all kinds of bodies and forms, like a corpse raised by magic or a mechanical puppet.
"Skill in knowing these marks, Mahamati, is called knowledge of the no-self of persons.

"And what, Mahamati, is knowledge of the no-self of things? It is understanding that the marks and own-nature of the heaps, elements and sense fields are imagined. Just as the heaps, elements and sense fields, Mahamati, have no self, being just a heap of heaps tied together by the thread of cause, karma and craving, arising through mutual conditioning without anyone moving them, so too, Mahamati, the heaps themselves have no particular or general marks; they are made to appear in many ways by the marks of unreal imagining, and are conceptualized by fools but not by the noble ones. Understanding all dharmas, Mahamati, as free of mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, the five dharmas and own-nature, a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes skilled in the no-self of things. And a bodhisattva, a great being, skilled in the no-self of things, Mahamati, soon attains the first bodhisattva stage, where he examines imagelessness.

"Through examining and understanding the marks of the stages, from Joy onward, step by step, trained in the nine stages, he attains the great Cloud of Dharma. Established there, seated in a great jeweled palace in the shape of a lotus, on a great king of lotuses adorned with many jewels and pearls, a palace brought forth by familiarity with the realm whose nature is illusion, surrounded by sons of the Conqueror like himself, he is consecrated by the hands of buddhas who come from every buddha-field, like the son of a wheel-turning king. Going beyond the stage of the sons of the Buddha, through going the course of the noble Dharma realized within, he will become a tathagata, master of the Dharma-body, because he has seen the no-self of things. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the no-self of all dharmas. Here, Mahamati, you should train, and so should other bodhisattvas, great beings."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, again said to the Lord: "May the Lord teach me the marks of superimposition and denial, so that I and other bodhisattvas, our minds free of the wrong views of superimposition and denial, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening; and having awakened, free of the views of eternalist superimposition and annihilationist denial, may not deny your guidance as Buddha."

cmp.note: 「增益」与「损减」：把本来没有的说成有（增益），把本来有的说成没有（损减）。英文 superimposition 和 denial 意思对得上，但中文这两个词更像会计用语（增加、减少），梵文 samāropa 字面是「往上放」。
cmp.en: Samāropa and apavāda: saying something exists that doesn't (superimposition), and saying something doesn't exist that does (denial). The English "superimposition" and "denial" match the sense; the Chinese 增益 / 损减 (zēngyì / sǔnjiǎn, "adding / subtracting") sound more like bookkeeping, while Sanskrit samāropa literally means "putting on top."

verses.en: Then the Lord, knowing the request of the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, spoke this verse:

"Superimposition and denial do not exist in mind-only. Those who do not understand that mind appears as body, possessions and dwelling place, those without insight, move among superimpositions and denials."

Then the Lord, to shed light on the meaning of this verse, said further: "There are four kinds of superimposing what does not exist, Mahamati. Which four? Superimposing marks that do not exist, superimposing views that do not exist, superimposing causes that do not exist, and superimposing things that do not exist. These, Mahamati, are the four kinds of superimposition.
"And what, Mahamati, is denial? When this very superimposition of wrong views is not found, and there is no examination, denial comes about. This, Mahamati, is the mark of superimposition and denial.

"Again, Mahamati, what is the mark of superimposing marks that do not exist? Clinging to particular and general marks of the heaps, elements and sense fields that do not exist: 'This is so, and not otherwise.' This, Mahamati, is the mark of superimposing marks that do not exist. This conceptualizing that superimposes marks that do not exist, Mahamati, arises from clinging to the varied habit-energy of the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time. This, Mahamati, is the mark of superimposing marks that do not exist.

"Superimposing views that do not exist, Mahamati, is superimposing on those same heaps, elements and sense fields the views of a self, a being, a life, a creature, a nourisher, a soul, a person. This, Mahamati, is called superimposing views that do not exist.

"Superimposing causes that do not exist, Mahamati, is this: the first consciousness arises without a cause; the later one, having not been, unarisen like an illusion, arises preceded by eye, form, light and attention; having arisen and existed, it perishes again. This, Mahamati, is superimposing causes that do not exist.

"Superimposing things that do not exist, Mahamati, is clinging to and superimposing space, cessation and nirvana as unmade things. But these, Mahamati, are beyond being and non-being. All dharmas, Mahamati, are like the horns of a hare, horse, donkey or camel, or the hairnet seen with cataracts, free of the sides of being and non-being. Superimposition and denial are conceptualized by fools whose minds have not grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' not by the noble ones. This, Mahamati, is the mark of superimposition and denial through conceptualizing things that do not exist. So then, Mahamati, you should be free of the views of superimposition and denial.

"Again, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, having arrived at the marks of mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, the five dharmas, the natures and the two kinds of no-self, take on many forms and guises for the good of others. Like the imagined nature resting on the dependent, like a wish-fulfilling jewel that shows every form, they go to the assemblies in every buddha-field and hear the Dharma face to face from all the tathagatas: that all dharmas are like an illusion, a dream, an appearance, a reflection, the moon in water, free of arising and perishing, of permanence and annihilation, and apart from the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles. They attain hundreds of thousands of gateways of samadhi, up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samadhis, and with these samadhis they pass from field to field.

"Devoted to honoring the buddhas, in the palaces of the gods in every place of birth they teach the Three Jewels, take on the form of a buddha, and, surrounded by hosts of shravakas and bodhisattvas, lead beings into 'nothing but what one's own mind shows' and teach that outer things do not exist, to turn them away from the sides of being and non-being."
Then the Lord spoke this verse:
"When the sons of the Conqueror see the world as mind-only, they attain a transformation body, free of action and formations, joined with the powers, supernatural abilities and masteries."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach the mark of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality and lack of own-nature in all dharmas, so that, by understanding it, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, may be free of conceptualizing existence and non-existence and quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening."

Then the Lord said to the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said: "'Emptiness, emptiness,' Mahamati: this is a term of the imagined nature. It is through clinging to the imagined nature, Mahamati, that people talk of emptiness, non-arising, non-existence, non-duality and lack of own-nature. In brief, Mahamati, emptiness is of seven kinds: emptiness of marks, emptiness of the own-nature of things, emptiness of non-activity, emptiness of activity, emptiness of all dharmas being inexpressible, the great emptiness of the highest truth, noble knowledge, and seventh, emptiness of one thing in another.

cmp.note: 「说『空、空』，这本身就是妄计自性的说法」：佛先提醒，连「空」这个词也是概念构想出来的，不能执着。中文、英文都照字面译出；这句话是本经对「空」的态度的关键。
cmp.en: "'Emptiness, emptiness': this is a term of the imagined nature." The Buddha warns first that even the word "emptiness" is a mental construction and must not be clung to. The Chinese and English both translate it literally; the line is key to the sutra's attitude toward emptiness.

verses.en: "What, Mahamati, is emptiness of marks? All things are empty of particular and general marks. Since they depend on gathering together with one another, and since when analyzed and taken apart nothing is found, Mahamati, particular and general marks do not arise. And since self, other and both do not exist, Mahamati, the mark does not hold. So it is said that all things are empty of their own marks.

"What, Mahamati, is emptiness of the own-nature of things? Since own-nature does not arise of itself, Mahamati, there is emptiness of the own-nature of things in all dharmas. So it is called emptiness of the own-nature of things.
"What, Mahamati, is emptiness of non-activity? Nirvana has never been active in the heaps. So it is called emptiness of non-activity.

"What, Mahamati, is emptiness of activity? The heaps, free of self and what belongs to a self, go on functioning through the workings of cause, reason, action and karma. So it is called emptiness of activity.

"What, Mahamati, is emptiness of all dharmas being inexpressible? Since the imagined nature cannot be expressed, all dharmas are empty in being inexpressible. So it is called emptiness of inexpressibility.

"What, Mahamati, is the great emptiness of the highest truth, noble knowledge? The realization of noble wisdom within oneself is empty of the faults and habit-energy of all views. So it is called the great emptiness of the highest truth, noble knowledge.

"What, Mahamati, is emptiness of one thing in another? Where something is not, that place is said to be empty of it. For example, Mahamati, in the mansion of Mrigara's mother there are no elephants, cows, sheep and so on; but I have said it is not empty of monks. It is said to be empty of those animals. But it is not, Mahamati, that the mansion lacks the nature of a mansion, or that the monks lack the nature of monks, or that elephants, cows, sheep and the like do not exist elsewhere. This, Mahamati, is the particular and general mark of all dharmas; they simply are not found in each other. So it is called emptiness of one thing in another. These, Mahamati, are the seven kinds of emptiness. And this emptiness of one thing in another, Mahamati, is the lowest of all; you should avoid it.

cmp.note: 梵文写本作「豺母的殿堂」(śṛgālamātṛ)，应是「鹿子母」(Mṛgāramātṛ，即毗舍佉夫人)的讹写，这是她捐给僧团的有名讲堂。白话已改正为「鹿子母（毗舍佉）」，英文也照改正后的读法译。
cmp.en: The manuscript reads "the mansion of the jackal's mother" (śṛgālamātṛ), almost certainly a corruption of Mṛgāramātṛ, "Mrigara's mother," that is, the lady Vishakha, whose famous hall was given to the Sangha. The plain Chinese corrects it to 鹿子母（毗舍佉） (Lùzǐmǔ, Vishakha), and the English follows the corrected reading.

verses.en: "They do not arise of themselves, Mahamati; yet it is not that they do not arise, except in the state of samadhi. So they are called unborn and without own-nature. With non-arising in mind, Mahamati, all things are without own-nature. And since there is no continuous stream of moments, and since things are seen to become otherwise, Mahamati, all things are without own-nature. So it is said that all things are without own-nature.

"What, Mahamati, is the mark of non-duality? Like shade and sunlight, long and short, black and white, Mahamati, things appear in pairs and do not stand separately. In the same way, Mahamati, all dharmas are non-dual, like samsara and nirvana. It is not that where nirvana is, samsara is not, Mahamati, nor that where samsara is, nirvana is not, since they do not have mutually exclusive marks. So it is said that all dharmas are non-dual, like samsara and final nirvana. So then, Mahamati, you should practice in the mark of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality and lack of own-nature."
Then the Lord spoke these verses:
"I always teach emptiness, free of permanence and annihilation. Samsara is called a dream and an illusion, yet karma does not perish.
Space, nirvana and the two cessations: fools imagine them as unmade; the noble ones see them as free of existence and non-existence."

Then the Lord said again to the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "This mark of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality and lack of own-nature, Mahamati, runs through all the sutras of all the buddhas. Whatever sutra it is, this is the meaning to be drawn out of it. A sutra, Mahamati, is a teaching suited to the dispositions of all beings, and its meaning can shift; it is not a statement that establishes the truth. Just as a mirage, Mahamati, lures deer, and they cling to it as water though there is no water in it, so the dharmas taught in all the sutras, Mahamati, are something for fools to be satisfied with in their own conceptualizing; they are not a statement establishing the truth of noble knowledge. So then, Mahamati, you should follow the meaning and not cling to the words of the teaching."

cmp.note: 「依义不依语」：后来「依义不依语、依法不依人」等「四依」常引这一类说法。这里语气很重：连一切经典都比作诱鹿的阳焰。中文、英文都照译，没有缓和。
cmp.en: "Follow the meaning, not the words": later lists such as the "four reliances" ("rely on the meaning, not the words; on the Dharma, not the person") often draw on passages like this. The tone is strong: even all the sutras are compared to the mirage that lures deer. The Chinese and English both translate it as it stands, without softening.

verses.en: Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "In the text of the sutras, Lord, you have described the tathāgatagarbha. You describe it, it is said, as luminous by nature, pure from the beginning, bearing the thirty-two marks, present inside the bodies of all beings. Like a jewel of great price wrapped in a dirty cloth, it is wrapped in the garment of the heaps, elements and sense fields, soiled with the dirt of greed, hatred, delusion and unreal imagining; and the Lord has described it as permanent, stable, auspicious and eternal. How then, Lord, is this teaching of the tathāgatagarbha not the same as the tirthikas' teaching of a self? The tirthikas too, Lord, teach a self that is permanent, a maker, without qualities, all-pervading and imperishable."

cmp.note: 大慧问的是全经最尖锐的问题：如来藏「常、恒、清凉、不变」，跟外道的「自我」（ātman）有什么不同？下一段佛的回答是：如来藏只是为了不让愚人害怕「无我」而用的方便说法，内容就是空、无相、无愿。中英文都照原文问答，没有加立场。
cmp.en: Mahamati asks the sharpest question in the sutra: if the tathāgatagarbha is "permanent, stable, auspicious, eternal," how is it different from the tirthikas' self (ātman)? The Buddha's answer in the next passage is that "tathāgatagarbha" is a skillful way of speaking, used so fools are not frightened by "no-self," and its content is emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness. The Chinese and English both give the question and answer as they stand, without taking sides.

verses.en: The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, my teaching of the tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the tirthikas' teaching of a self. Rather, Mahamati, the tathagatas give the teaching of the tathāgatagarbha for terms such as emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvana, non-arising, signlessness and wishlessness. The tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones teach the realm free of conceptualizing and images by way of the teaching of the tathāgatagarbha, so that fools may avoid the place of terror that is no-self. And here, Mahamati, the bodhisattvas, great beings, of the future and present should not cling to a self.

"Just as a potter, Mahamati, makes many kinds of pots from a single heap of clay atoms, through skill of hand, a stick, water, string and effort, so the tathagatas, Mahamati, teach that same no-self of things, turned away from all marks of conceptualizing, through many kinds of wisdom and skillful means, sometimes by the teaching of the garbha, sometimes by the teaching of no-self, with all kinds of words and phrases, like the potter. For this reason, Mahamati, the teaching of the tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the tirthikas' teaching of a self. In this way, Mahamati, the tathagatas teach by way of the tathāgatagarbha in order to draw in the tirthikas who cling to the teaching of a self, thinking: 'How can those whose minds have fallen into the view of an unreal, conceptualized self come to have minds that enter the realm of the three gates of liberation, and quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening?'

"For this purpose, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones give the teaching of the tathāgatagarbha. So it is not the same as the tirthikas' teaching of a self. So then, Mahamati, to turn away from the views of the tirthikas, you should follow the Tathagata's garbha of no-self."
Then the Lord spoke this verse:
"Person, continuity, heaps, conditions and atoms, primal matter, God, the maker: these are conceptualized by mind-only."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, looking toward people in the future, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me the realization of yoga, by which bodhisattvas, great beings, become great yogis." The Lord said: "Endowed with four dharmas, Mahamati, bodhisattvas become great yogis. Which four? Understanding what one's own mind shows; being free of the view of arising, abiding and perishing; seeing that outer things do not exist; and seeking the realization of noble wisdom within oneself. Endowed with these four dharmas, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, become great yogis.

"How, Mahamati, does a bodhisattva, a great being, become skilled in understanding what one's own mind shows? He reflects like this: 'These three realms are nothing but my own mind, without self or what belongs to self, without striving, without taking up or putting down; perfumed by clinging to the habit-energy of the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time; bound up with the names for the varied forms of the three realms; following the conceptualizing of body, possessions, dwelling place and courses of life, they are conceptualized and they appear.' In this way, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes skilled in understanding what one's own mind shows.

"And how, Mahamati, does a bodhisattva, a great being, become free of the view of arising, abiding and perishing? All things are like the coming into being of forms in an illusion or a dream; since self, other and both do not exist, they do not arise. Following 'nothing but one's own mind,' seeing that outer things do not exist, seeing that the consciousnesses do not arise and that conditions are not piled into heaps, seeing that the three realms come from conceptualizing as their condition, through not finding any inner or outer dharma, through seeing their lack of own-nature, the view of arising is turned away; following the nature of dharmas such as illusion, they attain acceptance that things are unborn. Standing on the eighth stage, through realizing the turning-around of mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, the five dharmas, the natures and the two kinds of no-self, they attain a mind-made body (manomayakāya).

Mahamati said: "Lord, why is it called a mind-made body?" The Lord said: "'Mind-made,' Mahamati, because it moves quickly and unhindered, like the mind; so it is called mind-made. Just as the mind, Mahamati, unhindered by mountains, walls, rivers, trees and the like, goes many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, recalling objects seen and experienced before, its body an unbroken stream of one's own mind, moving without hindrance; in the same way, Mahamati, together with attaining the mind-made body, through the illusion-like samadhi, adorned like a flower with the marks of the powers, masteries and supernatural abilities, born together with the family of the noble course, he moves like the mind, without hindrance, recalling the objects of his former vows, in order to ripen beings. In this way, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes free of the view of arising, abiding and perishing.

"And how, Mahamati, does a bodhisattva, a great being, become skilled in seeing that outer things do not exist? All things, Mahamati, are like a mirage, a dream, the hairnet seen with cataracts. Seeing clearly that the own-nature of all things is caused by clinging to the habit-energy of the varied ripening conceptualizing of the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, he longs for the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within. Endowed with these four dharmas, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, become great yogis. Here, Mahamati, you should practice."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me the marks of causes and conditions of all dharmas, so that, understanding them, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, free of the views and conceptualizing of being and non-being, may not imagine that all things arise step by step or all at once."

The Lord said: "The causal mark of the dependent arising of all dharmas, Mahamati, is of two kinds: outer and inner. Here is outer dependent arising, Mahamati: through conditions such as a lump of clay, a stick, a wheel, string, water and a person's effort, Mahamati, a pot comes into being. And just as a pot comes from a lump of clay, Mahamati, cloth from threads, mats from grass, a sprout from a seed, and butter from curd through churning and a person's effort, so, Mahamati, outer dependent arising should be seen as one thing following another.

"Here is inner dependent arising: dharmas such as ignorance, craving and karma, Mahamati, are given the name 'dependent arising.' The dharmas born from them, Mahamati, called the heaps, elements and sense fields, are given the name 'dependent arising.' They are not distinct, yet fools imagine them.

"Causes, Mahamati, are of six kinds: the cause that will be, the cause of connection, the cause of marks, the efficient cause, the cause that makes manifest, and sixth, Mahamati, the cause of indifference. The cause that will be, Mahamati, does the work of a cause in the arising of inner and outer dharmas. The cause of connection, Mahamati, does the work of an object in the arising of inner and outer heaps, seeds and so on. The cause of marks, Mahamati, produces what is bound up with the mark of immediately following action. The efficient cause, Mahamati, does the work of ruling and governing, like a wheel-turning king. The cause that makes manifest, Mahamati, does the work of lighting up the marks of a conceptualized thing that has arisen, as a lamp does for forms. The cause of indifference, Mahamati, at the time of stopping, breaks off the action of the stream, so that conceptualizing does not arise.

"These, Mahamati, imagined by the conceptualizing of foolish ordinary people, arise neither step by step nor all at once. Why? If they arose all at once, Mahamati, there would be no distinguishing effect from cause, since the mark of a cause would not be found. If they arose step by step, then, since what has not yet come about has no nature of its own, it would not arise step by step. Like the word 'father' before a son is born, Mahamati, connections of sequence don't hold up. Since the reasoners speak of producer and produced through the cause condition, object condition, immediately preceding condition, dominant condition and so on, Mahamati, they do not arise step by step. Because of the mark of clinging to the imagined nature, Mahamati, they do not arise all at once. Since body, possessions and dwelling place are what one's own mind shows, and outer things with particular and general marks do not exist, Mahamati, they arise neither step by step nor all at once. Only consciousness arises, because it is conceptualized by the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows.
"So then, Mahamati, you should be free of views that the marks of causes, conditions and their working arise step by step or all at once."
On this it is said:
"Nothing here arises through conditions, nor ceases. It is only the imagined conditions that arise and cease.
It is not the perishing, arising and defilement of conditions that is denied; what is denied is the conceptualizing fools make through conditions.

Since dharmas do not exist, they do not come into being among conditions; the mind, spun round by habit-energy, appears in the three existences. Nothing that was not comes to be, nor is anything stopped by conditions.
When people see the conditioned as the son of a barren woman, a flower in the sky, then grasper and grasped are seen as confusion and turn back.
There is nothing to be produced, nothing produced, and conditions too are nothing at all. Nothing exists anywhere; it is only spoken of by convention."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me the Dharma discourse called 'The Heart of the Marks of Verbal Conceptualizing,' so that, through this heart of the marks of verbal conceptualizing, clearly analyzed, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, may come to understand both words and what is expressed by words, quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and purify the understanding of words and what words express for all beings." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "There are four kinds of marks of verbal conceptualizing, Mahamati:
speech of marks, speech of dreams, speech of clinging to coarse conceptualizing, and speech of beginningless conceptualizing.

"Speech of marks, Mahamati, arises from clinging to the forms and signs one has conceptualized oneself. Speech of dreams, Mahamati, arises from recalling objects experienced before, and from the objects being absent on waking. Speech of clinging to coarse conceptualizing, Mahamati, arises from recalling what an enemy did in the past. Speech of beginningless conceptualizing, Mahamati, arises from the habit-energy of one's own seeds, the coarse tendency of clinging to conceptual proliferation from beginningless time. These, Mahamati, are the four kinds of marks of verbal conceptualizing I spoke of; that is the answer."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again about this same matter: "May the Lord teach me again the realm in which verbal conceptualizing becomes manifest. Where, from what, how and by what, Lord, do people's speech, representation and conceptualizing arise?" The Lord said: "Speech arises, Mahamati, from the coming together of head, chest, nose, throat, palate, lips, tongue and teeth." Mahamati said: "Lord, is speech different from conceptualizing, or not different?" The Lord said: "Speech, Mahamati, is neither different from conceptualizing nor not different. Why? Because verbal conceptualizing arises with that as its cause. If speech were different from conceptualizing, Mahamati, it would not have conceptualizing as its cause. And if it were not different, speech could not convey meaning; but it does. So it is neither different nor not different."

Mahamati spoke again: "Lord, is speech itself the highest truth, or is what speech expresses the highest truth?" The Lord said: "Speech is not the highest truth, Mahamati, and what speech expresses is not the highest truth either. Why? Because the highest truth is the noble bliss that speech only leads one into; the speech is not the highest truth. The highest truth, Mahamati, is reached by the course of noble wisdom realized within, not the realm of verbal conceptualizing understanding. So conceptualizing does not reveal the highest truth. Speech, Mahamati, arises and perishes, is unsteady, and arises from causes and conditions dependent on one another. Whatever arises from causes and conditions dependent on one another, Mahamati, does not reveal the highest truth. Since it has no mark of self or other, Mahamati, an outer mark does not reveal it.

"Again, Mahamati, since one follows 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' and since outer things with all their varied marks do not exist, verbal conceptualizing does not conceptualize the highest truth. So then, Mahamati, you should be free of all the varieties of verbal conceptualizing."
On this it is said:
"All things are without own-nature; speech too, though spoken, is unreal. Not seeing the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness, the fool runs about.

The own-nature of all things, and people's speech too, is imagination, and even that does not exist; nirvana is like a dream. One should examine existence and neither stay in samsara nor enter nirvana.
As a king or a rich merchant first lures his children with all sorts of clay deer and plays with them, and then gives them real deer,
so I, with varied marks of dharmas that are only reflections, tell my children of the limit of reality, which is known within oneself."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me this mark of all dharmas: free of non-existence and existence, oneness and difference, both and neither, not being and not non-being, permanence and impermanence; beyond the reach of all tirthikas, reached by the course of noble knowledge within; turned away from the imagined particular and general marks; the entry into the truth of the highest meaning; the mark of growing purer and purer through the sequence of the stages; the mark of entering the stage of a tathagata; moving through endless realms like the jewel that shows every form through former vows without effort; the mark of distinguishing the realm and course of what one's own mind shows. So that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, our views turned away from the imagined nature and from particular and general marks in matters like these, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening and fulfill all good qualities for all beings."

The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati! Truly well done, Mahamati, that you think this should be asked. You have set out on this, Mahamati, for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, good and happiness of a great multitude of gods and humans. Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "Because they do not understand 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' Mahamati, foolish ordinary people conceptualize through clinging to varied outer things and through clinging to conceptualizing caused by the habit-energy of the own-natures of non-existence and existence, oneness and difference, both, not being and not non-being, permanence and impermanence.

"Just as deer, Mahamati, imagine the water of a mirage to be water and, scorched by the summer heat, run toward it wanting to drink, not knowing that there is no water there because they do not understand the confusion of their own mind's seeing, so too, Mahamati, foolish ordinary people, their minds perfumed by the conceptualizing of many kinds of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, their minds burning with the fires of greed, hatred and delusion, longing for objects of varied forms, holding views of arising, perishing and abiding, unskilled about inner and outer being and non-being, fall into grasping oneness and difference, non-existence and existence. Just as, Mahamati, in a city of gandharvas the ignorant have the idea of a city where there is no city: the shape of a city appears through clinging to the habit-energy of the seed 'city' from beginningless time, and that city is neither a non-city nor a city.

"In the same way, Mahamati, those who cling to the habit-energy of the tirthikas' doctrines of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time cling to doctrines of oneness and difference, existence and non-existence, their minds not having grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows.' Suppose, Mahamati, a man is asleep, and in a dream he enters a country's royal city, beautiful with women and men, elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, villages, towns and markets, cows and buffalo, forests and parks, all sorts of mountains, rivers and ponds, and then he wakes up. Having woken, he remembers that country's royal city. What do you think, Mahamati: would that man be wise, recalling all the unreal variety of his dream?" Mahamati said: "No, Lord."

The Lord said: "In the same way, Mahamati, foolish ordinary people bitten by wrong views, with minds like the tirthikas', do not recognize that existence is what their own mind shows, like a dream, and they rely on views of oneness and difference, non-existence and existence. Just as fools imagine that a place a painter has made, though flat, has depths and heights, so, Mahamati, in the future there will be people fed on conceptualizing that comes from the habit-energy and intentions of tirthika views. Clinging to doctrines of oneness, difference, both and neither, ruined themselves, they will call others, who are free of the sides of being and non-being and teach non-arising, nihilists. These deny cause and effect, and with their bad views have uprooted the good causes, the bright side. They will be called people to be avoided from afar by those who seek the good. Their minds fallen into views of self, other and both, fallen into the wrong views of superimposition and denial in conceptualizing non-existence and existence, they are bound for hell.

"Just as people with cataracts, Mahamati, seeing a hairnet, say to one another, 'Look at this, look how strange this is, sirs!', yet that hairnet, never having arisen at all, is neither existent nor non-existent, since it is both seen and not seen: in the same way, Mahamati, those who cling to the intentions and conceptualizing of the tirthikas' wrong views, clinging to doctrines of the sides of being and non-being, oneness, difference, both and neither, will slander the true Dharma and ruin themselves and others. Just as fools, Mahamati, but not the wise, imagine the wheel of a whirling firebrand, which is no wheel, to be a wheel, so those whose minds have fallen into the wrong views of the tirthikas will imagine oneness, difference, both and neither in the arising of all things. Just as, Mahamati, when the sky rains, bubbles on the water look like crystal gems, and fools, clinging to the idea that they are crystal gems, run after them,

"though those water bubbles, Mahamati, are neither gems nor not gems, since they can be grasped and not grasped: in the same way, Mahamati, those perfumed by the habit-energy of the conceptualizing intentions of tirthika views will describe the arising of the non-existent through conditions and the destruction of the existent.

"Again, Mahamati, setting up the three means of knowledge and the parts of a syllogism, they will conceptualize that the thing to be realized by noble wisdom within, which is free of the two natures, exists by its own nature. But, Mahamati, for yogis whose basis of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness has turned around, who have abandoned conceptualizing the grasped and grasper of what one's own mind shows, who have reached the stage of a tathagata and the course of noble wisdom realized within, the notion of being and non-being does not arise. If, Mahamati, the grasping of being and non-being arose for yogis whose realm is such a course, that itself would be grasping a self, grasping a nourisher, a soul, a person. And whatever teaching there is, Mahamati, about the own-nature of things and their particular and general marks: that, Mahamati, is the teaching of the transformation Buddha, not the teaching of the Dharma-nature Buddha.

"A teaching, Mahamati, comes from the views that fools are inclined to; it does not bring to light the Dharma whose nature is the course of what is established, the realization of noble wisdom within, the happy abiding of samadhi. Just as, Mahamati, the reflection of a tree appears in water, and it is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, since it has the tree's shape and does not, so, Mahamati, those whose conceptualizing is perfumed by the habit-energy of tirthika views, their minds not having grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' will conceptualize oneness, difference, both, neither, non-existence and existence. Just as all the reflections of forms appear in a mirror, Mahamati, according to conditions and one's own conceptualizing, and they are neither images nor not images, since images are seen and yet are not images; and yet, Mahamati, these conceptualizings of what one's own mind shows appear to fools in the shape of images:

"in the same way, Mahamati, the reflections of one's own mind appear in the form of views of oneness, difference, both and neither. Just as an echo, Mahamati, arising from the coming together of a person, a river and wind, is heard, and it is neither existent nor non-existent, since a sound is heard and yet it is not a sound, so, Mahamati, the conceptualizings of one's own mind's habit-energy appear as views of non-existence and existence, oneness and difference, both and neither. Just as, Mahamati, on ground without grass, shrubs, creepers or trees, mirages ripple like waves when the sun strikes, and they are neither existent nor non-existent, since they lure and do not lure, so, Mahamati, the conceptualizing consciousness of fools, perfumed by the habit-energy of the coarse tendency of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, ripples like a mirage in waves of arising, abiding, perishing, oneness, difference, both, neither, non-existence and existence, even in the face of the thing realized by noble wisdom within.

"Just as a corpse raised by magic and a mechanical man, Mahamati, with no being in them, move about through the power of a spirit or a device, and fools cling to this unreal conceptualizing of their coming and going, so, Mahamati, foolish ordinary people whose minds have fallen into the wrong views of the tirthikas cling to doctrines of oneness and difference. And that is superimposing what is unreal. So then, Mahamati, you should be free of conceptualizing arising, abiding, perishing, oneness, difference, both, neither, non-existence and existence, and the realization of the thing that is noble within."
On this it is said:
"The heaps, with consciousness as the fifth, are like the reflection of a tree in water. See them as like an illusion or a dream; do not conceptualize through representation.
This threefold existence is like a hairnet, like the mistake of mirage-water, called a dream and an illusion; seeing it so, one is freed.
As a mirage ripples in summer, confusing the mind, and the deer take it for drinking water, though there is nothing real in it,
so the seed of consciousness ripples in the field of view; fools grasp it as being born, as people with cataracts grasp at spots.
In beginningless samsara, embraced by grasping things, the fool is drawn out as one wedge draws out another.
Seeing the world always like an illusion, a magic corpse, a machine, a dream, lightning or a cloud, with the three continuities cut, one is freed.
There is no representation here, as there are no mirages in the sky; knowing dharmas this way, one does not claim anything.
This representation is merely a name; it is not found as a mark. The heaps are like a hairnet, where it is conceptualized.
Mind, the hairnet, an illusion, a dream, a city of gandharvas, a firebrand, a mirage: they do not exist, yet they appear to people.
Permanent and impermanent, oneness, both and neither: fools, deluded, imagine these through their link with faults from beginningless time.
In a mirror, in water, in the eye, in vessels and in jewels, an image is seen, yet the image is not anywhere.
So mind is an appearance of things, like a mirage in the sky; it is seen in varied forms, like the son of a barren woman in a dream."

"Again, Mahamati, the tathagatas' teaching of the Dharma is free of the four alternatives: it avoids the sides of oneness, difference, both and neither, and is free of superimposition and denial of non-existence and existence. The tathagatas' teaching of the Dharma, Mahamati, starts from truth, dependent arising, cessation, the path and the working of liberation. The tathagatas' teaching of the Dharma, Mahamati, is not bound up with primal nature, God, causelessness, chance, atoms, time or own-nature.

"Again, Mahamati, to purify the two obstructions, of the afflictions and of what is to be known, they lead beings step by step, like a caravan leader, and establish them in the hundred and eight imageless terms and in the well-distinguished marks of the vehicles, stages and limbs.
