"Again, Mahamati, there are four kinds of meditation (dhyāna). Which four? Meditation practiced by fools, meditation that examines meaning, meditation whose object is suchness, and fourth, the meditation of the tathagatas. What, Mahamati, is meditation practiced by fools? It is the meditation of shravaka and pratyekabuddha yogis, starting from clinging to the no-self of persons, to the particular and general marks of things as images and skeletons, and to the marks of impermanence, suffering and impurity; seeing 'this mark is so and not otherwise,' going on from one to the next up to the cessation of perception: that is meditation practiced by fools. And what, Mahamati, is meditation that examines meaning? Having seen that the no-self of persons, particular and general marks, and the self, other and both of the outside tirthikas do not exist, one examines step by step the meaning of the marks of the stages of the no-self of things: that is meditation that examines meaning.

cmp.note: 「四种禅」：愚夫所行禅、观察义禅、攀缘真如禅、如来禅（实叉难陀译名）。后来中国禅宗推崇的「如来禅」一词就出自这里。dhyāna 中文音译为「禅」，英文译 meditation；禅宗的「禅」后来远远超出 meditation 的意思，这是中英文最大的落差之一。
cmp.en: The four kinds of dhyāna: Śikṣānanda calls them 愚夫所行禅 ("meditation practiced by fools"), 观察义禅 ("meditation examining meaning"), 攀缘真如禅 ("meditation taking suchness as object") and 如来禅 (Rúlái chán, "Tathagata meditation"). The term "Tathagata meditation," later prized by Chinese Chan, comes from here. Dhyāna is transliterated in Chinese as 禅 (chán) and translated in English as "meditation"; but Chan later came to mean far more than "meditation," one of the biggest gaps between the Chinese and the English.

verses.en: "What, Mahamati, is meditation whose object is suchness? When the conceptualizing of the imagined two kinds of no-self rests in things as they really are, and conceptualizing does not arise: this I call meditation whose object is suchness. And what, Mahamati, is the meditation of the tathagatas? Entering the form of the stage of a tathagata, dwelling happily in the three marks of noble wisdom within, and doing the unthinkable work of helping beings: this I call the meditation of the tathagatas."
On this it is said:
"Meditation that examines meaning, meditation practiced by fools, meditation whose object is suchness, and the pure meditation of the tathagatas.
Shaped like the moon and sun, like a lotus or the underworld, like sky, fire or a painting: so the yogi sees as he practices.
These varied signs lead him onto the tirthikas' path; they make him fall into the state of a shravaka, into the realm of the pratyekabuddhas.
When he shakes them all off and there is the imageless, then buddhas from every field come together, their hands shining like suns, and stroke his head, the sign that follows suchness."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, people say 'nirvana, nirvana.' Of what, Lord, is this word 'nirvana' a name?" The Lord said: "The turning-around of the habit-energy of all consciousnesses' own-nature, of the storehouse, thinking mind, mind-consciousness and the habit-energy of views, is called nirvana by all the buddhas and by me: the realm of the thing that is emptiness, the own-nature of the course of nirvana.

"Again, Mahamati, nirvana is the realm of the course of noble wisdom realized within, free of conceptualizing permanence and annihilation, being and non-being. How is it not permanent? It has abandoned conceptualizing particular and general marks; so it is not permanent. And it is not annihilation in that all noble ones of the past, future and present reach it within themselves; so it is not annihilation.

"Again, Mahamati, the great final nirvana is neither destruction nor death. If the great final nirvana were death, Mahamati, the chain of births would start again. If it were destruction, it would fall under the marks of the conditioned. For this reason, Mahamati, the great final nirvana is neither destruction nor death. Yogis reach a death that is free of passing away. Again, Mahamati, the great final nirvana is called nirvana because it is neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither one in meaning nor many in meaning.

"Again, Mahamati, the nirvana of shravakas and pratyekabuddhas comes from understanding particular and general marks and from not mixing with others. Since they see objects without distortion, conceptualizing does not arise. So they come to think of that as nirvana.

"Again, Mahamati, the mark of the two natures is of two kinds. Which two? Clinging to the own-nature of words and clinging to the own-nature of things. Clinging to the own-nature of words, Mahamati, arises from clinging to the habit-energy of verbal proliferation from beginningless time. Clinging to the own-nature of things, Mahamati, arises from not understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows.'

"Again, Mahamati, bodhisattvas sustained by two sustaining powers fall at the feet of the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones and ask them questions. By which two sustaining powers? The sustaining power of entering samadhi, and the sustaining power of consecration by hand, with the whole body and face shown. Here, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, on the first stage, sustained by the sustaining power of the buddhas, enter the bodhisattva samadhi called Light of the Mahayana. As soon as these bodhisattvas, great beings, have entered the bodhisattva samadhi Light of the Mahayana, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones who dwell in the world-systems of the ten directions show their faces and give their sustaining power, showing their whole body, face and speech.

"As with the bodhisattva Vajragarbha, the great being, Mahamati, and other bodhisattvas, great beings, endowed with such marks and qualities, so, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, on the first stage receive the sustaining power of entering samadhi.

"With roots of good gathered over a hundred thousand eons, having step by step come to know the marks of what favors and what opposes each stage, on the bodhisattva stage called Cloud of Dharma, a bodhisattva, a great being, sits in a seat in a great lotus palace, surrounded by bodhisattvas, great beings, like himself, wearing a crown adorned with every kind of jewel; then the hands of the conquerors, come from the world-systems of the ten directions, like lotuses shining with the color of orpiment, gold, champaka flowers and moonbeams, consecrate the head of that bodhisattva, the great being, seated in the lotus palace, as a sovereign wheel-turning king or Indra is consecrated, with whole body, face and hand. That bodhisattva and those bodhisattvas are said to be sustained by the sustaining power of consecration by hand.

"These, Mahamati, are the two sustaining powers of bodhisattvas, great beings, sustained by which bodhisattvas, great beings, see the faces of all the buddhas. Otherwise, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones cannot be seen.

"Again, Mahamati, whatever eloquence comes to bodhisattvas, great beings, in the form of samadhi, supernatural power and teaching, comes because they are sustained by the two sustaining powers of all the buddhas. If, Mahamati, eloquence came to bodhisattvas, great beings, without the sustaining power, it would come to foolish ordinary people too, Mahamati. Why? Because (it depends on) being sustained or not. Even grass, shrubs, trees and mountains, Mahamati, and all kinds of musical instruments, cities, mansions, houses, palaces and seats, give forth sound through the sustaining power of the Tathagata entering them. How much more, Mahamati, beings with minds: even the mute, the blind and the deaf, Mahamati, are freed from their defects. So great and special in its qualities, Mahamati, is the sustaining power of the Tathagata."

cmp.note: 「加持」：佛把自己的力量「安立、托住」在菩萨身上。中文「加持」今天多带神秘或密教色彩；英文 sustaining power 偏「撑住、护持」，比较中性。梵文本义是「站在上面、作依托」。
cmp.en: Adhiṣṭhāna, the Buddha's power "placed on" or "upholding" the bodhisattva. The Chinese 加持 (jiāchí) today often carries a mystical or tantric flavor; the English "sustaining power" leans toward "holding up, supporting" and is more neutral. The Sanskrit literally means "standing upon, a basis."

verses.en: Mahamati spoke again: "But why, Lord, do the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones give the sustaining power of consecration to bodhisattvas, great beings, when they are in samadhi and on the special stage?" The Lord said: "So that they may be free of the works of Mara and the afflictions; so that they do not fall onto the shravakas' stage of meditation; so that they may realize within the stage of a tathagata; and so that what they have realized of the Dharma may grow. For this reason, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones sustain bodhisattvas, great beings, with their sustaining powers. Without the sustaining power, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, would fall into the intentions of wrong tirthikas, shravakas and Mara and would not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. For this reason bodhisattvas, great beings, are taken in hand by the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones."
On this it is said:
"The sustaining power of the lords of men is purified by their vows: consecration, samadhi and the rest, from the first stage to the tenth."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati said to the Lord again: "When the Lord teaches dependent arising, he speaks only in terms of causes, not in terms of how his own way stands in its nature. The tirthikas too, Lord, describe arising from causes: things arise from primal matter, God, spirit, time and atoms as conditions. The Lord only describes the arising of things with another word for conditions; there is no difference in the doctrine itself. The tirthikas too, Lord, describe arising from being and non-being, and the perishing of things through conditions after they have been. And what the Lord said, 'Conditioned by ignorance are formations, and so on up to old age and death': this the Lord has described as a doctrine of no causes, not a doctrine of causes.

"'When this exists, that comes to be' holds for things that stand together at once, Lord, not for things that depend on a sequence. Indeed, Lord, the tirthikas' account is superior, not yours. Why? For the tirthikas, Lord, a cause that is not dependently arisen produces an effect. But for you, Lord, the cause depends on the effect and the effect on the cause. Causes and conditions get mixed up, and so there is an infinite regress. And when you say 'when this exists, that comes to be,' Lord, the world has no cause." The Lord said: "No, Mahamati. When I say 'when this exists, that comes to be,' my teaching does not turn into a doctrine of no cause, nor are causes and conditions mixed up, because there is no grasped and grasper, and because it is understood that everything is nothing but what one's own mind shows.

"But for those, Mahamati, who cling to grasped and grasper and do not understand 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' because of the existence and non-existence of outer objects of their own, this fault follows, Mahamati; not for me, when I speak of dependent causes."

Mahamati spoke again: "But surely, Lord, all things exist because words exist. If things did not exist, Lord, words would not arise. But they do arise. So because words exist, Lord, all things exist." The Lord said: "Words are used even for things that do not exist, Mahamati: for example, in the world words are seen for the horns of a hare, turtle hair, the son of a barren woman and so on. These, Mahamati, are neither existent nor non-existent, yet they are spoken of. So what you said, Mahamati, 'because words exist, all things exist,' that argument is refuted. And words, Mahamati, are not established in all buddha-fields. Words, Mahamati, are made.

"In some buddha-fields, Mahamati, the Dharma is taught by looking without blinking, in some by gestures, in some by raising an eyebrow, in some by movements of the eyes, in some by the face, in some by yawning, in some by clearing the throat, in some by calling the field to mind, in some by trembling. Just as, Mahamati, in the world called Unblinking and Fragrant, in the buddha-field of Samantabhadra, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, the bodhisattvas, great beings, gazing with unblinking eyes, attain acceptance that things are unborn and other special samadhis; for this very reason, Mahamati, it is not because words exist that all things exist. And this has been seen, Mahamati: in this world, special kinds of beings such as worms and flies go about their business without words."
On this it is said:
"Space, a hare's horn and the son of a barren woman do not exist, yet they are spoken of; so it is with imagining about things.
Fools imagine that things come into being from the coming together of causes and conditions. Not knowing this way, they wander in the house of the three existences."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, to what is the word 'permanent' applied?" The Lord said: "To confusion, Mahamati. For this confusion appears even to the noble ones, though not as a distortion. Just as, Mahamati, a mirage, a whirling firebrand, a hairnet, a city of gandharvas, an illusion, a dream, a reflection and a man seen with bad eyes mislead the ignorant in the world but not the wise; and yet it is not that they do not appear. That confusion, Mahamati, appears in many forms, yet that does not make confusion impermanent. Why? Because it is free of being and non-being. How, Mahamati, is confusion free of being and non-being? Because it is the varied realm of all fools; like the waves of the ocean or the water of the Ganges, which pretas see and do not see. For this reason, Mahamati, confusion is not a being.

"And since that water appears to others, it is not a non-being. So confusion, for the noble ones, is free of distortion and non-distortion. And for this reason, Mahamati, confusion is permanent: because its signs and marks do not split apart. For confusion, Mahamati, though conceptualized through all kinds of varied signs and concepts, does not come to be divided. For this reason, Mahamati, confusion is permanent.

"And how, Mahamati, does confusion become truth? For the reason, Mahamati, that in the noble ones no notion of distortion arises about this confusion, nor any notion of non-distortion. Otherwise, Mahamati, if the noble ones had any notion at all about this confusion, they would not have the notion of the thing that is noble knowledge. 'Any notion at all,' Mahamati, is the babble of fools, not the speech of the noble. And that confusion, conceptualized as distortion and non-distortion, gives rise to two lineages: the lineage of the noble ones and the lineage of foolish ordinary people. The noble lineage, Mahamati, is of three kinds: shravaka, pratyekabuddha and buddha. How, Mahamati, does confusion, conceptualized by fools, produce the lineage of the shravaka vehicle? When it is clung to through clinging to particular and general marks, Mahamati, it leads to the lineage of the shravaka vehicle.

"So, Mahamati, that confusion gives rise to the lineage of the shravaka vehicle. How, Mahamati, does that same confusion, being conceptualized, give rise to the lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle? Through clinging to the particular and general marks of that same confusion, Mahamati, together with not mixing with others, it gives rise to the lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle. And how, Mahamati, does that same confusion, conceptualized by the wise, give rise to the lineage of the buddha vehicle? Conceptualized through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows' and the non-existence of outer things, Mahamati, it gives rise to the lineage of the buddha vehicle. This, Mahamati, is lineage; this is the meaning of lineage. And confusion, conceptualized by fools as the existence of varied things, Mahamati, gives rise to the lineage of the samsara vehicle: 'it is so and not otherwise.'

"For this reason, Mahamati, fools imagine confusion as varied things. And it is neither a thing nor not a thing. That same confusion, Mahamati, when not conceptualized, through the turning-around of the noble ones' mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, coarse habit-energy, own-nature and dharmas, is called the noble ones' suchness. So it is said, Mahamati, that suchness too is free of mind. To bring out the meaning of this very term, Mahamati, I have said 'free of imaginings, apart from all imagining.'"

cmp.note: 这一段的结论很大胆：同一个「迷乱」，愚人分别它就成了轮回，圣者不分别它就叫「真如」——迷与悟不是两样东西。实叉难陀把 bhrānti 译成「迷惑」或「妄法」，英文用 confusion；白话、英文都照原文把这句话说得很直白。
cmp.en: The conclusion here is bold: the very same confusion that fools conceptualize into samsara is, when the noble ones don't conceptualize it, called suchness; delusion and awakening are not two different things. Śikṣānanda renders bhrānti as 迷惑 or 妄法 ("delusion, false dharma"); the English says "confusion." Both the plain Chinese and the English state the point as bluntly as the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Mahamati said: "Lord, does confusion exist or not?" The Lord said: "Like an illusion, Mahamati, confusion does not exist through clinging to marks. If confusion existed through clinging to marks, Mahamati, clinging to things would never be turned back. It would be like dependent arising, Mahamati, like the arising from a cause the tirthikas teach." Mahamati said: "If confusion is like an illusion, Lord, then it will be the cause of further confusion." The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, illusion is not a cause of confusion, because it does not bring the fault of coarse tendencies. Illusion, Mahamati, does not bring the fault of coarse tendencies. An illusion, Mahamati, which is not conceptualized, works through the magical knowledge of another person, not through the habit-energy of coarse tendencies of one's own conceptualizing. It does not bring faults.
"This, Mahamati, is just the delusion of mind and view of fools who cling to something or other, not of the noble ones."
On this it is said:
"The noble one does not see confusion, nor truth in the midst of it. Confusion itself would be truth, since truth is in the midst of it.
If, having shaken off all confusion, a sign arises, that itself would be his confusion, like impure cataracts."

"Again, Mahamati, it is not that illusion does not exist. All dharmas are like illusions because of seeing their likeness." Mahamati said: "Lord, are all dharmas like illusions because of the mark of clinging to varied illusions, or because of the mark of clinging to what is false? If all dharmas are like illusions because of the mark of clinging to varied illusions, then, Lord, things are not like illusions. Why? Because the varied marks of form are seen to have no cause. There is no cause at all, Lord, by which form appears in varied marks and shapes the way an illusion does. For this reason, Lord, things are not like illusions by likeness to clinging to the marks of varied illusions."

The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, it is not by likeness to clinging to the marks of varied illusions that all dharmas are like illusions. Rather, Mahamati, all dharmas are like illusions by likeness to something false and quick as lightning. Just as a flash of lightning, Mahamati, breaks off in an instant, seen and then gone, though fools see it, so, Mahamati, all things, whose marks are general marks of one's own conceptualizing, do not appear when examined, though they appear through clinging to the marks of form."
On this it is said:
"It is not that illusion does not exist; things are said to exist by likeness. They are like something false and as quick as lightning, and so they are thought of as like illusions."

Mahamati spoke again: "The Lord has said that all things are unborn and also that they are like illusions. But surely, Lord, in saying this you fall into the fault of contradicting your earlier words with your later ones, speaking of the non-arising of things as their being like illusions." The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, in speaking of the non-arising of things as their being like illusions I do not fall into the fault of contradicting earlier words with later ones. Why? Because, understanding that arising and non-arising are nothing but what one's own mind shows, and seeing that outer things, whether being or non-being, do not arise, there is no fault, Mahamati, of earlier and later words contradicting each other. Rather, Mahamati, this is said to set aside the tirthikas' arising from causes: 'all things are unborn, like illusions.' The deluded crowds of the tirthikas, Mahamati, want things to arise from being and non-being, not from the condition of clinging to the varieties of their own conceptualizing.

"But in me, Mahamati, no fear arises. For this reason, Mahamati, the word non-arising is used. And the teaching of things, Mahamati, is given to take in samsara and to hold back annihilationism, the claim that nothing exists. For my disciples, to take in the places of birth of their varied karma, samsara is taken in by taking up the word 'thing.' By pointing to the own-nature and marks of illusion as things, Mahamati, to turn foolish ordinary people away from the own-nature and marks of things, people whose minds have fallen into the marks of wrong views, who have not grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' who cling to the marks of arising through causes, conditions and action, and to hold them back, I teach that all dharmas have the own-nature and marks of illusions and dreams. These foolish ordinary people, clinging to the intentions and marks of wrong views, will mislead themselves and others about seeing all dharmas as they really stand.
"And seeing all dharmas as they really stand, Mahamati, means entering into 'nothing but what one's own mind shows.'"
On this it is said:
"In non-arising there is no cause; in being, samsara is taken in. One should see it as like an illusion and not conceptualize marks."

"Again, Mahamati, we will point out the marks of the groups of names, phrases and letters; well marked by these groups of names, phrases and letters, bodhisattvas, great beings, following meanings, phrases and letters, will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening and wake all beings in the same way. Here, Mahamati, 'group' means: the thing on which a name is based; that group is the thing. 'Group' and 'body' mean the same. This, Mahamati, is the group of names. The group of phrases, Mahamati, is the existence of a group of meanings of phrases, a settling. Ending, settling and finding mean the same. This, Mahamati, is the teaching of the group of phrases; it is an illusion. The group of letters, Mahamati, is that by which names and phrases are made manifest. Letter, sign, mark, finding and designation mean the same.

"Again, Mahamati, the group of phrases is the completion of the work of a phrase. Name, Mahamati, is the distinction in the own-nature of names and letters, from a to ha. Letters, Mahamati, are the short, long and extra-long sounds. Groups of phrases, Mahamati, are the elephants, horses, people, deer, animals, cows, buffalo, goats, sheep and so on that walk along a track, which get the name 'group of tracks.' Name and letter, Mahamati, are the four formless heaps. They are called 'name' because they are spoken of by name, and 'letter' because they are made manifest by their own mark. This, Mahamati, is the mark of names, phrases and letters, of naming and phrasing. You should become familiar with it."

cmp.note: pada 一字多义：既是「词句」，也是「足迹」。这一段就利用这个双关，说象、马、牛这些「走在路上（pada-vīthī）」的东西也叫 pada。中文「句身」只有「词句」义，英文 phrases / tracks 只能分两个词分别表达。
cmp.en: Pada means both "phrase, word" and "footstep, track." The passage plays on this, saying that elephants, horses and cattle that "walk along a track" (pada-vīthī) are also called pada. The Chinese 句身 (jù shēn, "group of phrases") has only the "phrase" sense; the English has to use two words, "phrases" and "tracks."

verses.en: On this it is said:
"In letters, in groups of phrases, and especially in names, dull-witted fools get stuck like elephants in deep mud."

"Again, Mahamati, in the future, bad reasoners with poorly trained minds, lacking understanding of reasons and causes, when asked by the wise about the way of the two extremes free of the marks of the views of oneness, difference, both and neither, will say, 'This is not a proper question, it is not well founded': for instance, whether impermanence is different from form and the rest, or not different. In the same way, nirvana from formations, mark from what is marked, quality from what has qualities, elemental from elements, seeing from what is seen, atoms from dust, the yogi from knowledge: asked about such undetermined questions in a sequence like this, they will say, 'The Lord set it aside as undetermined.' But those deluded people will not know that the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones do not answer, because of the listeners' lack of understanding, to keep beings away from a place of terror.

"And the undetermined questions, Mahamati, are not taught by the tathagatas, in order to set aside the doctrines of the tirthikas' views. For the tirthikas, Mahamati, say things like 'The soul is the body,' 'The soul is one thing and the body another,' and so on: the doctrine of the undetermined. For the tirthikas, Mahamati, who are confused about causes, there are undetermined questions, but not in my teaching. In my teaching, Mahamati, which is free of the grasped and the grasper, conceptualizing does not arise. How could there be anything to set aside for them? For those, Mahamati, who cling to the grasped and the grasper and whose minds have not grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' there is something to set aside. The tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones, Mahamati, teach the Dharma to beings by answering questions in four ways. 'To be set aside,' Mahamati, is a teaching I have given for another time, for those whose faculties are not yet ripe.
"For those whose faculties are ripe, nothing is set aside.

"Again, Mahamati, all dharmas, free of action and agent, do not arise, since there is no agent. So it is said that all dharmas are unborn. And why, Mahamati, are all things without own-nature? Because, Mahamati, when they are examined by one's own understanding, the particular and general marks are not found. So it is said that all dharmas are without own-nature. And why, Mahamati, do all dharmas neither come nor go? Because, Mahamati, the particular and general mark, when brought, is not brought, and when taken away, is not taken away. For this reason, Mahamati, all dharmas are free of coming and going. And why, Mahamati, are all dharmas unceasing? Because, since the marks of the own-nature of things do not exist, no dharmas are found. So it is said that all dharmas are unceasing.

"And why, Mahamati, are all dharmas said to be impermanent? Because the arising of marks is impermanent. So it is said that all dharmas are impermanent. And why, Mahamati, are all dharmas permanent? Because marks, arisen or unarisen, do not exist, they are permanent in their impermanence. So, Mahamati, it is said that all dharmas are permanent."
On this it is said:
"There are four kinds of answer: answering straight out, asking back, analyzing, and setting aside, to hold back the tirthikas' doctrines.
Non-arising from being and non-being is taught by the Samkhya and Vaisheshika; all the undetermined questions were brought up by them.
When things are analyzed by understanding, no own-nature is found. So they are taught as inexpressible and without own-nature."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me the distinctions in the course and marks of stream-entry for stream-enterers, so that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, skilled in the distinctions of the course and marks of stream-entry, and knowing the means and marks of once-returning, non-returning and arhatship one after another, may teach the Dharma to beings in such a way that, having purified the two marks of no-self and the two obstructions, and going beyond the marks of stage after stage, they may reach the realm of the Tathagata's unthinkable course and, like a jewel that shows every form, become a source of life for all beings, sustaining them in body and enjoyment in every realm of the Dharma."

The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "There are three distinctions, Mahamati, in the fruit of stream-entry for stream-enterers. Which three? Low, middle and excellent. The low, Mahamati, has at most seven more births. The middle, Mahamati, attains final nirvana after three or five existences. The highest, Mahamati, attains final nirvana in that very birth. For these three, Mahamati, the three fetters are weak, middling and strong. Which, Mahamati, are the three fetters? The view of a real self in the body, doubt, and clinging to moral rules and vows.

"These three fetters, Mahamati, through progressively higher stages, become for arhats the fruit of arhatship. The view of a real self in the body, Mahamati, is of two kinds: innate and imagined, like the dependent and the imagined natures. Just as, Mahamati, from reliance on the dependent nature there arises clinging to the varied imagined nature, which is neither being, nor non-being, nor both, since it has the mark of unreal imagining, yet fools conceptualize it through clinging to the marks of varied own-natures, as deer do a mirage; this, Mahamati, is the stream-enterer's imagined view of a real self in the body, built up by long clinging through ignorance. And it is abandoned by him because he no longer grasps a self of persons.

"The innate view of a real self in the body, Mahamati, is abandoned by the stream-enterer through seeing that his own body and others' are the same; because of the mark of the four heaps and form; because form arises from the elements and what is made of them; because the elements have the mark of being causes of one another; considering 'form does not truly come together,' and seeing the view of the sides of being and non-being. Since the view of a real self in the body has been abandoned, desire does not arise. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the view of a real self in the body.

"The mark of doubt, Mahamati: since he has the mark of seeing well the Dharma he has attained, and since he has already abandoned conceptualizing the two views of a real self in the body, he has no doubts about the teachings. Nor does he take any other teacher's view as pure or impure. This, Mahamati, is the mark of doubt for the stream-enterer.

"And how, Mahamati, does the stream-enterer not cling to moral rules? He does not cling because he has clearly seen the marks of suffering, birth and the sense fields. Clinging, Mahamati, is this: foolish ordinary people, longing for pleasure and enjoyment, seek birth in existence through moral rules, vows, austerities and observances. The stream-enterer does not cling like this. Instead he turns them toward going on to the special realization within. He takes up the limbs of moral conduct in the form of the mark of dharmas without conceptualizing and without outflows. This, Mahamati, is the mark of clinging to moral rules and vows for the stream-enterer. For the stream-enterer who has abandoned the three fetters, Mahamati, greed, hatred and delusion do not arise."

Mahamati said: "The Lord has taught that desire is of many kinds. Which desire is abandoned by him here?" The Lord said: "Desire for union with women, with the senses craving objects, pleasant now and the cause of suffering and birth later, with fondling, slapping, embracing, kissing, hugging, smelling and sidelong glances: in him, Mahamati, this desire does not arise. Why? Because he has gained the happy abiding of samadhi. So that is abandoned, not the desire to attain nirvana.

"And what, Mahamati, is the mark of the fruit of once-returning? Conceptualizing that shows the marks of form arises once more. Since signs, views, marked and mark no longer exist, and since he has seen well the marks of the course of meditation, he comes to this world once more and attains final nirvana to make an end of suffering. So he is called a once-returner. And how, Mahamati, is one a non-returner? Since the conceptualizing of the faults and tendencies of views, which arises as the being and non-being of the marks of form, past, future and present, does not return; and since the fetters of form are abandoned and do not return, he is called a non-returner. And one is called an arhat, Mahamati, because there is no conceptualizing of meditation, what is meditated on, samadhi, liberation, powers, supernatural abilities, afflictions and suffering."

Mahamati said: "The Lord has spoken of three kinds of arhat. To which of them, Lord, is this word 'arhat' applied? To one who has reached the path that leads only to peace, or to one confused about the roots of good practiced through the vow of awakening, or to a created transformation?" The Lord said: "To the shravaka, Mahamati, who has reached the path that leads only to peace, not to the others. The others, Mahamati, those who have practiced the bodhisattva way and the created transformations of the buddhas, because of their skillful means, roots of good and earlier vows, show themselves born in the assemblies, to adorn the assemblies of the buddhas. This, Mahamati, is a varied teaching of the shapes and courses of conceptualizing: since attaining the fruit is free of meditation, meditator and meditated, and through arriving at what one's own mind shows, the mark of attaining the fruit is taught.

"Again, Mahamati, if it occurred to the stream-enterer, 'These are the fetters, and I am not bound by them,' that would be a case of duality; he would have fallen into the view of a self and would not have abandoned the fetters.

"Again, Mahamati, to go beyond the meditations, the immeasurables and the formless realm, one must turn away from the marks of what one's own mind shows. And the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, Mahamati, as a going beyond the course of what one's own mind shows, does not fit for him, since everything is mind-only."
On this it is said:
"The meditations and the immeasurables, the formless attainments and samadhis, the cessation of perception, all of it, do not exist in mind-only.
The fruit of stream-entry, of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship: all are confusion of mind.
Meditator, meditation and the meditated, abandoning, seeing the truths: all this is just imagining. Whoever understands this is freed."

"Again, Mahamati, understanding is of two kinds: examining understanding, and understanding that sets up clinging to grasped marks of conceptualizing. Examining understanding, Mahamati, is the understanding by which the mark of the own-nature of things, when examined, is not found, being free of the four alternatives. The four alternatives, Mahamati, are what I call the fourfold set free of oneness and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence. All dharmas, Mahamati, are said to be free of these four alternatives. These four alternatives, Mahamati, should be applied in examining all dharmas. And what, Mahamati, is the understanding that sets up clinging to grasped marks of conceptualizing?

cmp.note: 「四句」：有、无、亦有亦无、非有非无（或一、异、俱、不俱）这四种可能的说法。佛说一切法都离开这四句。中文「四句」是固定术语，英文 four alternatives 只说明它是四种选项，读者要从上下文看出指的是哪四种。
cmp.en: The "four alternatives" (catuṣkoṭi): exists, does not exist, both, neither (or one, different, both, neither). The Buddha says all dharmas are free of all four. The Chinese 四句 (sì jù, "four phrases") is a fixed technical term; the English "four alternatives" only says there are four options, and the reader has to learn from context which four.

verses.en: "It is the understanding, Mahamati, by which, through clinging to grasped marks of the mind's conceptualizing, one superimposes, by superimposing what is unreal, the great elements, marked as heat, fluidity, motion and hardness, which are unreal imaginings, through clinging to thesis, reason, mark and example: that is the understanding that sets up clinging to grasped marks of conceptualizing. These, Mahamati, are the marks of the two kinds of understanding. Endowed with the marks of these two kinds of understanding, bodhisattvas, arriving at the marks of the no-self of things and persons, skilled in the stage of practice examined by imageless understanding, attain the first stage and enter a hundred samadhis. Through attaining special samadhis they see a hundred buddhas and bodhisattvas, enter a hundred eons before and after, and light up a hundred fields.

"Having lit up a hundred fields, knowing the marks and ways of each higher stage, playing in the special power of their vows, consecrated with the consecration of the Cloud of Dharma, they reach the Tathagata's stage within; their dharmas firmly bound to the ten final terms, they shine with varied rays of transformation to ripen beings, absorbed in the bliss of the course within.

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should be skilled in the great elements and what is made of them. And how, Mahamati, does a bodhisattva become skilled in the great elements and what is made of them? Here, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, trains himself in this: the truth is that in which the great elements do not come into being; and he sees that these elements, Mahamati, have not come into being. Seeing this, through understanding that a name is only conceptualizing and that everything is nothing but what one's own mind shows, and since outer things do not exist, he sees that these three realms are only a name, only the conceptualizing of what mind shows, free of the great elements and what is made of them; purified by the method of the four alternatives, free of self and what belongs to self, standing in their own mark as it really is, established in the own-mark of non-arising. And how, Mahamati, does what is made of elements come from the great elements?

"The great element that is the conceptualizing of moisture, Mahamati, produces the water element, inner and outer. The great element that is the conceptualizing of energy, Mahamati, produces the fire element, inner and outer. The great element that is the conceptualizing of movement, Mahamati, produces the wind element, inner and outer. The great element that is the conceptualizing of the division of form, Mahamati, produces the earth element, together with space, inner and outer. Through clinging to false truth, the cluster of the five heaps, the great elements and what is made of them, arises. And consciousness, Mahamati, arises in the link to another birth, caused by clinging to and longing for the realm of varied words. For the earth and the other elements and what is made of them, Mahamati, the great elements are a cause, but there is none for the great elements themselves. Why? Because, Mahamati, arising through the combination of action happens for things that have signs, marks, grasping, shape and the working of action, not for what has no sign.
"So, Mahamati, these marks of the great elements and what is made of them are conceptualized by the tirthikas, not by me.

"Again, Mahamati, we will point out the mark of the own-nature of the heaps. There are five heaps, Mahamati. Which? Form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Of these, Mahamati, four heaps are formless: feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Form, Mahamati, is made of the four great elements, and the elements differ from one another in mark. And the formless ones, Mahamati, are not countable as four, just like space. Just as space, Mahamati, is beyond the mark of number, and yet it is conceptualized, 'this is space,' so, Mahamati, the heaps, beyond the marks of number and counting, free of being and non-being, free of the four alternatives, are pointed out by fools with numbers and counting, but not by the noble ones.

"By the noble ones, Mahamati, they are made known as like varied forms and shapes made by illusion, free of being different or the same, like a man seen in a dream or reflection. Because the basis is not different, and through confusion about the course of noble knowledge, Mahamati, conceptualizing of the heaps appears. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the own-nature of the heaps. You should turn that conceptualizing back, and having turned it back, teach the Dharma of solitude. When the Dharma of solitude is taught in all the assemblies of the buddhas to hold back the views of the tirthikas, Mahamati, seeing the no-self of things is purified, and one enters the stage Gone Far. Having entered the great stage Gone Far, one becomes master of many samadhis. And through attaining a mind-made body one attains the illusion-like samadhi. Having arrived at the powers, supernatural abilities and masteries, one becomes a source of life for all beings, like the earth.
"Just as the great earth, Mahamati, is a source of life for all beings, so, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes a source of life for all beings.

"Again, Mahamati, there are four kinds of nirvana. Which four? The nirvana of the non-existence of the own-nature of things; the nirvana of the non-existence of the variety of marks; the nirvana of understanding the non-existence of own-marks; and the nirvana of cutting off the continuous stream of the particular and general marks of the heaps. These, Mahamati, are the four kinds of nirvana of the tirthikas, not of my teaching. In my teaching, Mahamati, nirvana is the turning away of the conceptualizing mind-consciousness."

Mahamati said: "But hasn't the Lord set out eight consciousnesses?" The Lord said: "I have, Mahamati." Mahamati said: "If you have, Lord, how is it that only mind-consciousness turns away, and not the seven consciousnesses?" The Lord said: "Because the seven consciousnesses arise with it as their cause and object, Mahamati. Mind-consciousness, Mahamati, arising through clinging to the distinguishing of objects, feeds the storehouse consciousness with habit-energy. The thinking mind goes along with it, clinging to grasping self and what belongs to self, in the form of thinking. With a body whose marks are not distinct, with the storehouse consciousness as cause and object, through clinging to the realm of what one's own mind shows, the cluster of mind arises, each part the cause of the others. Like waves on the ocean, Mahamati, stirred by the wind of the realm of what one's own mind shows, they rise and fall.
"So, Mahamati, when mind-consciousness turns away, the seven consciousnesses turn away."

cmp.note: 这里说「只要意识（第六识）转灭，七识就跟着转灭」，把第六识当成关键，跟后来唯识宗强调转第八识的讲法不完全一样。白话、英文都照这一段原文译。
cmp.en: Here the sutra says that "when mind-consciousness (the sixth) turns away, the seven consciousnesses turn away," making the sixth consciousness the key, which is not quite the same as the later Yogācāra emphasis on transforming the eighth. The plain Chinese and the English both follow this passage as it stands.

verses.en: On this it is said:
"I do not enter nirvana through being, action or mark; when consciousness, the cause of conceptualizing, ceases, I am in nirvana.
With that as cause and that as object, relying on the course of the thinking mind, consciousness gives the cause to mind and relies on it.
Just as when a great flood is spent no waves arise, so the variety of consciousness, once it has ceased, does not arise."

"Again, Mahamati, we will point out the marks of the ways of distinguishing the imagined nature. Having clearly penetrated these marks, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, free of conceptualizing and imagining, with understanding that sees well the noble course of one's own within and the course of the tirthikas' ways, having abandoned conceptualizing grasped and grasper, will not conceptualize the varied marks of the dependent as forms of the imagined nature. What, Mahamati, are the marks of the ways of distinguishing the imagined nature? Conceptualizing words, conceptualizing what is expressed, conceptualizing marks, conceptualizing wealth, conceptualizing own-nature, conceptualizing causes, conceptualizing views, conceptualizing reasoning, conceptualizing arising, conceptualizing non-arising, conceptualizing connection, and conceptualizing bondage and freedom. These, Mahamati, are the marks of the ways of distinguishing the imagined nature.

"What, Mahamati, is conceptualizing words? Clinging to the sweetness of varied sounds and songs. That, Mahamati, is conceptualizing words. What, Mahamati, is conceptualizing what is expressed? Conceptualizing that there is some thing to be expressed, with an own-nature, reached by the course of noble knowledge, on which words are based. What is conceptualizing marks? Clinging, through clinging to the variety of marks, to that very thing expressed, which is called a mirage: conceptualizing all things by the marks of heat, fluidity, motion and hardness. What is conceptualizing wealth? Speaking of objects of wealth: gold, silver and all kinds of jewels. What is conceptualizing own-nature? Settling the own-nature of things, 'this is so and not otherwise,' conceptualizing through the conceptualizing views of the tirthikas. What is conceptualizing causes?

"That by which, through causes and conditions, things are divided into being and non-being, through the arising of causal marks: that is conceptualizing causes. What is conceptualizing views? Clinging to the conceptualizing of the tirthikas' wrong views of non-existence and existence, oneness and difference, both and neither. What is conceptualizing reasoning? Teaching through reasoned argument about the marks of self and what belongs to self. What is conceptualizing arising? Clinging to the arising of things from being or non-being through conditions. What is conceptualizing non-arising? 'All things, never having arisen before, come to be through conditions without having been, without a body of causes.' What is conceptualizing connection? 'This is connected with that,' like gold and thread. What is conceptualizing bondage and freedom? Clinging to a cause of bondage and something bound: just as a man ties a knot in a rope with a noose and unties it.

"These, Mahamati, are the marks of the ways of distinguishing the imagined nature, to which all foolish ordinary people cling. Clinging to the dependent as being or non-being, Mahamati, they cling to the variety of the imagined nature. Just as one sees variety based on an illusion, with a mind that sees an illusion as something else, so fools conceptualize. But the illusion, Mahamati, is neither different nor not different from the variety. If it were different, the variety would not have the illusion as its cause. If it were not different, there would be no distinction between illusion and variety. But the distinction is seen. So it is neither different nor not different. For this reason, Mahamati, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should not cling to illusion as existing or not existing."
On this it is said:
"Mind is bound up with objects; knowledge works in reasoning; but in the imageless and the special, wisdom comes into play.
The imagined nature does not exist in the dependent. The imagined is grasped through confusion; the dependent is not imagined.
Just as an illusion is not real though it appears with all its parts, so the varied sign, when imagined, is not real.
The sign, made of coarse tendencies, a bond born of mind, the imagined, is conceptualized in the dependent by those who do not know.
This very thing that is imagined is the dependent; the imagined, appearing in variety, is conceptualized in the dependent.
Conventional and highest truth: a third has no cause. The imagined is called convention; when it is cut off, there is the realm of the noble ones.
Just as one thing shines in variety for yogis, yet there is no variety there, so is the mark of the imagined.
Just as those with cataracts imagine varied visions of form, and the cataract is neither form nor not form, so the unwise (imagine) the dependent.
Just as gold is pure, water free of mud, the sky clear of clouds, so the conceptualized becomes pure.
The imagined thing does not exist; the dependent does exist. Conceptualizing superimposition and denial, one is ruined.
If the imagined did not exist, then through the nature of the dependent there would be a thing without a thing, and a thing would come from no thing.
Based on the imagined, the dependent is found; from the link between sign and name the imagined is born.
The imagined is utterly unreal and does not arise from another; then the pure own-nature of the highest truth is known.
The imagined is of ten kinds and the dependent of six; suchness is to be known within oneself, so there is no distinguishing.
The five dharmas are reality, and so are the three natures. The yogi who understands this does not stray from suchness.
The sign is the dependent; the name is the imagined. The imagined sign arises from the dependent.
But examined by understanding, it is neither dependent nor imagined. The perfected is not a thing; how can it be conceptualized by understanding?
The perfected exists as a thing free of being and non-being. Being free of being and non-being, how can there be two natures?
In the imagined nature two natures are established; the imagined is seen in variety, and the pure is the realm of the noble ones.
The imagined, appearing in variety, is conceptualized by the dependent; imagined any other way, it would rest on the tirthikas' doctrine.
Imagining is called the imagined; from what is seen, the cause comes about. Free of the two conceptualizings, that itself is the perfected.

Mahamati spoke again: "May the Lord teach me the mark of the course of noble wisdom realized within, and the One Vehicle, so that, through the mark of the course of the One Vehicle within, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, skilled in the noble wisdom within and the One Vehicle, may not be led by others in the dharmas of the Buddha."

The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "With no conceptualizing based on means of knowledge or the teachings of authorities, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, alone and in seclusion, examines with his own understanding within, not led by others, free of views and conceptualizing, and strives to enter the stage of a tathagata, higher and higher. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the course of noble wisdom realized within. And what is the mark of the course of the One Vehicle? Because one realizes and understands the path of the One Vehicle, I call it the One Vehicle. What is realizing and understanding the path of the One Vehicle? When the conceptualizing of grasped and grasper rests in things as they really are and conceptualizing does not arise, the One Vehicle has been understood.

"This understanding of the One Vehicle, Mahamati, has never been reached before by other tirthikas, shravakas, pratyekabuddhas, Brahma and the rest, but only by me. For this reason, Mahamati, it is called the One Vehicle."

Mahamati said: "Why has the Lord taught three vehicles and not taught the One Vehicle?" The Lord said: "Because shravakas and pratyekabuddhas do not have the nature to enter final nirvana by themselves, Mahamati, I do not speak to them of the One Vehicle. For all shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, Mahamati, are freed through the Tathagata's teaching of discipline, solitude and yoga, not by themselves.

"Again, Mahamati, since shravakas and pratyekabuddhas have not abandoned the obstruction to what is to be known and the habit-energy of karma, there is no One Vehicle for them. Because they do not understand the no-self of things and have not reached the inconceivable death of transformation, I teach the three vehicles to the shravakas. When, Mahamati, all the habit-energy of their faults is abandoned through understanding the no-self of things, then, free of the faults of habit-energy and the intoxication of samadhi, they wake up in the realm without outflows. Then, having completed the provisions that belong to the world-transcending realm without outflows, they will attain mastery of the unthinkable Dharma-body."
On this it is said:
"The vehicle of gods, the vehicle of Brahma, and likewise that of the shravakas, the Tathagata's and the pratyekabuddhas': these vehicles I speak of.
There is no end to vehicles as long as mind goes on; but when mind has turned around, there is no vehicle and no one riding.
There is really no setting up of vehicles; I speak of different vehicles. To draw fools along, I speak of different vehicles.
So too the three liberations and the no-self of things; the knowledge of sameness and the afflictions: by liberation they are left behind.
Just as a log on the ocean is carried along by the waves, so the deluded shravaka is carried along by marks.
Bound by the afflictions of habit-energy, though free of those that break out, drunk on the intoxication of samadhi, they stay in the realm without outflows.
For him there is no final course, nor does he turn back again. Having reached a body of samadhi, he does not wake up for eons.
Just as a drunk man wakes up when the liquor wears off, so they will reach my body, which is called the dharmas of the Buddha."

cmp.note: 「醉于三昧酒」：佛把声闻停在定中比作喝醉，几劫都醒不过来，酒退了才会转向佛道。实叉难陀译作「三昧酒所醉」，中英文这个比喻都很直白。
cmp.en: "Drunk on the intoxication of samadhi": the Buddha compares shravakas resting in meditative absorption to drunks who don't wake up for eons, turning toward buddhahood only once the liquor wears off. Śikṣānanda writes 三昧酒所醉 (sānmèi jiǔ suǒ zuì, "drunk on the wine of samadhi"); the image is just as blunt in Chinese and English.

verses.en: Here ends the second chapter of the Lankavatara, called "The Gathering of All Dharmas, in Thirty-Six Thousand."

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · On Impermanence (Anityatā)
chapters.intro: Despite its title, most of this chapter is other questions: mind-made bodies, an inner reading of the five worst crimes ("killing mother and father"), the Buddha saying he never spoke a word, words versus meaning, and the finger pointing at something. He recounts debating a Lokayata brahmin, and ends by refuting eight tirthika views of impermanence.

verses.en: The third chapter, called "On Impermanence."

cmp.note: 梵文品名叫「无常品」，但这一品其实讲意生身、五无间业、佛语、「不说一字」等很多题目，几乎不谈无常。实叉难陀本把这部分并在别的品里。白话、英文都照梵文品名译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit calls this chapter "On Impermanence," yet it actually covers many topics (mind-made bodies, the five heinous deeds, the Buddha's words, "not a single syllable spoken") and hardly discusses impermanence. Śikṣānanda's version folds this material into other chapters. The plain Chinese and English both translate the Sanskrit title as it is.

verses.en: Then the Lord said again to the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "I will point out, Mahamati, the marks of the ways of distinguishing the courses of the mind-made body. Listen and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "The mind-made body, Mahamati, is of three kinds. Which three? The mind-made body of attaining the bliss of samadhi, the mind-made body of understanding the own-nature of dharmas, and the mind-made body of action, a formation born together with its kind. Yogis reach these by fully knowing the marks of the first and each higher stage. What, Mahamati, is the mind-made body of attaining the bliss of samadhi?

"On the third, fourth and fifth stages, through dwelling in the many kinds of solitude of one's own mind, the mind of blissful attainment, marked by the wave-consciousnesses arising on the ocean of mind, no longer arises; through fully knowing that the realm that is what one's own mind shows neither exists nor does not exist, it is called the mind-made body of the mind. What is the mind-made body of understanding the own-nature of dharmas? On the eighth stage, through examining and understanding that dharmas such as illusions are imageless, with the basis of mind turned around, through attaining the illusion-like samadhi and other gateways of samadhi, a body flowering with many marks, masteries and supernatural powers, as quick as thought, like an illusion, a dream or a reflection, not made of elements yet like what is made of elements, endowed with every variety of form and limb, going to the assemblies of every buddha-field: because it has arrived at the course of the own-nature of dharmas, it is called mind-made. What is the mind-made body of action, a formation born together with its kind?

"Through understanding the mark of the bliss of realizing all the Buddha's dharmas within, it is called the mind-made body of action, a formation born together with its kind. Here, Mahamati, you should practice examining and understanding the marks of the three bodies."
On this it is said:
"My vehicle, the great vehicle, is not sound, nor letters, nor truths, nor liberations, nor the imageless realm.
But the vehicle, the great vehicle, is mastery of samadhi, the varied mind-made body adorned with the flowers of mastery."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "The Lord has spoken of the five deeds with immediate retribution. Which, Lord, are the five deeds with immediate retribution by committing which a son or daughter of good family goes to the Avici hell?" The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said: "Which, Mahamati, are the five deeds with immediate retribution? Killing one's mother, father, or an arhat, splitting the Sangha, and drawing the blood of a Tathagata's body with evil intent.

"What, Mahamati, is the mother of beings? Craving, which leads to rebirth and comes with delight and passion, arises as mother. Ignorance, as father, for the arising of the village of the sense fields. Cutting off the very root of these two, mother and father, is killing mother and father. Completely uprooting the latent tendencies, which are like enemies and flare up like rat poison, is killing an arhat. What is splitting the Sangha? Completely destroying the root of the collection of heaps, whose marks are distinct from one another, is called splitting the Sangha. And completely destroying the eight groups of consciousness, Mahamati, which do not understand that the particular, the general and the outer are nothing but what one's own mind shows, through the evil conceptualizing of the three liberations without outflows: drawing the blood of the Buddha of consciousness with evil intent, one is called a doer of deeds with immediate retribution.

cmp.note: 佛把「五无间罪」全部翻成内心修行的比喻：杀母是断渴爱，杀父是断无明，杀阿罗汉是断随眠烦恼，破僧是破五蕴的聚合，出佛身血是断八识。字面上非常骇人，中英文都照字面译，让读者自己看到这个反转。
cmp.en: The Buddha turns all five "deeds with immediate retribution" into images of inner practice: killing the mother is cutting off craving, killing the father is cutting off ignorance, killing an arhat is uprooting the latent afflictions, splitting the Sangha is breaking up the heaps, and drawing the Buddha's blood is destroying the eight consciousnesses. Literally it is shocking; the Chinese and English both keep the literal wording so the reader sees the reversal.

verses.en: "These, Mahamati, are the five inner deeds with immediate retribution, committing which a son or daughter of good family becomes a doer of deeds with immediate retribution and one who has realized the Dharma.

"Again, Mahamati, I will point out to you the outer deeds with immediate retribution, so that, once they are pointed out, you and other bodhisattvas will not be confused in the future. Which are they? The deeds with immediate retribution described in the texts of the teaching, committing which one does not realize any of the three liberations, except through realization sustained by a created form. For a shravaka sustained by a created form, Mahamati, is sustained by the power of a bodhisattva or a Tathagata. For anyone else who has committed a deed with immediate retribution and is tormented by remorse, to turn away his view of remorse, so that one who has laid down his burden may be free of the view of remorse, and thinking, 'he will be encouraged again,' I show realization sustained by a created form.

"There is no realization at all, Mahamati, for one who has committed a deed with immediate retribution, except that, through understanding that everything is nothing but the cultivation of what one's own mind shows, and seeing that he is free of conceptualizing body, possessions, dwelling place and courses, and free of grasping self and what belongs to self, at some time, somewhere, meeting a good friend, in the link to another birth, he is freed from the faults of his own conceptualizing."
On this it is said:
"Craving is called the mother, and ignorance the father; consciousness, from being aware of objects, is taught as the Buddha.
The arhats are the latent tendencies, the Sangha is the cluster of the five heaps; by cutting off what is without gap, the deed is 'immediate.'"

Mahamati spoke again: "May the Lord teach me about the buddhas, the lords: how, Lord, is the buddhahood of the buddhas?" The Lord said: "Through understanding the no-self of things and of persons, Mahamati, through fully understanding the two obstructions, through reaching the two kinds of death and abandoning the two kinds of affliction, Mahamati, there is the buddhahood of the buddhas, the lords. By reaching these same dharmas, Mahamati, there is the awakening of shravakas and pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, Mahamati, I teach the One Vehicle."
On this it is said:
"The two kinds of no-self, the afflictions and the two obstructions; through reaching the death of inconceivable transformation, one is a Tathagata."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "With what in mind did the Lord say, in the midst of the assembly, 'I am all the buddhas of the past, and the variety of births in the birth stories; at that time, on that occasion, I was King Mandhatar, the elephant, the parrot, Indra, Vyasa, Sunetra,' and so on, teaching hundreds of thousands of birth stories?" The Lord said: "With four kinds of sameness in mind, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones speak in the midst of the assembly, saying, 'At that time, on that occasion, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni and Kashyapa.' Which four kinds of sameness? Sameness of letters, sameness of speech, sameness of Dharma and sameness of body.

"With these four kinds of sameness in mind, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones speak in the midst of the assembly. What, Mahamati, is sameness of letters? The letters by which my name is 'Buddha' are the very letters for those buddhas, the lords; those letters, Mahamati, are no different, being letters by nature. This, Mahamati, is sameness of letters. What, Mahamati, is the sameness of speech of the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones? For me there arises speech with the sixty-four qualities of the sound of Brahma's voice; and for those tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones too, Mahamati, there arises in just the same way speech with the sixty-four qualities of the sound of Brahma's voice, no less, no more, no different, with the nature of the kalavinka bird's sweet, Brahma-like voice. What is sameness of body?

"I and those tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones are the same, no different, in the Dharma-body and in the body of form with its marks and minor signs, except as needed for those to be trained. The tathagatas show varied forms according to the different courses of beings here and there. And what, Mahamati, is sameness of Dharma? They and I have attained the thirty-seven dharmas on the side of awakening. With these four kinds of sameness in mind, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones speak in the midst of the assembly."
On this it is said:
"'I am Kashyapa, Krakucchanda and Konakamuni': I say this to the sons of the Conqueror, rising up in sameness."

Mahamati spoke again: "The Lord has said: 'From the night the Tathagata awoke to the night he will enter final nirvana, in between, the Tathagata has not uttered a single syllable and will not utter one; not speaking is the Buddha's speaking.' With what in mind did the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one say, 'Not speaking is the Buddha's speaking'?" The Lord said: "I said this, Mahamati, with two dharmas in mind. Which two? With the true nature realized within in mind, and with the ancient, abiding true nature in mind. With these two dharmas in mind, Mahamati, I said this. What is the connection with the true nature realized within oneself? What those tathagatas attained, I too have attained, no less, no more: the realm of the course within, free of verbal conceptualizing, free of the two courses of letters.

cmp.note: 「从成道之夜到涅槃之夜，不说一字」：这是本经最常被禅宗引用的句子之一，实叉难陀译「我于某夜成最正觉，乃至某夜入般涅槃，于其中间不说一字」。英文 not a single syllable 对应 akṣara（字母、音节），中文「一字」对应得也很准。
cmp.en: "From the night of his awakening to the night of his final nirvana, he has not uttered a single syllable": one of the sutra's lines most quoted in Chan. Śikṣānanda writes 于其中间不说一字 ("in between, not a single word was spoken"). The English "syllable" matches akṣara (letter, syllable), and the Chinese 一字 (yī zì, "one character") matches it closely too.

verses.en: "And what is the ancient, abiding true nature? It is ancient, Mahamati, like the true nature; like veins of gold, silver and pearl, Mahamati, the realm of Dharma abides: whether tathagatas arise or do not arise, the true nature of these dharmas stands, the abiding of dharmas, the fixed order of dharmas. Like an ancient city's road, Mahamati. Suppose, Mahamati, a man wandering in a forest were to see an ancient city with an unbroken road leading in. He would enter that city, and having entered it and settled there, he would enjoy the pleasures of city life. What do you think, Mahamati: did that man make the road by which he entered the city and (enjoyed) its variety?" Mahamati said: "No, Lord."

The Lord said: "In the same way, Mahamati, what I and those tathagatas have attained is this: the true nature simply stands, the abiding of dharmas, the fixed order of dharmas, suchness, reality, truth. For this reason, Mahamati, I said: 'From the night the Tathagata awoke to the night he will enter final nirvana, in between, the Tathagata has not uttered a single syllable and will not utter one.'"
On this it is said:
"Between the night of my attainment and the night of my final nirvana, I have revealed nothing at all.
I said this with the abiding true nature realized within in mind; between those buddhas and me there is no difference at all."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me the mark of non-existence and existence in all dharmas, so that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, free of non-existence and existence, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said: "This world, Mahamati, relies on two things: it relies on existence and it relies on non-existence. It has fallen into views driven by desire for being and non-being, and takes what is no way out for a way out. How, Mahamati, does the world rely on existence?

"It says the world arises from causes and conditions that exist, not from ones that do not exist; what arises exists as it arises, not as non-existent. Saying this, Mahamati, one holds that things, causes and conditions exist and that the world has a cause. And how, Mahamati, does one rely on non-existence? Having accepted greed, hatred and delusion, one then conceptualizes greed, hatred and delusion as being and non-being. Mahamati, there is one who does not accept the existence of things, since they are free of the marks of things; and one who does not accept the greed, hatred and delusion of buddhas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, since they are free of the marks of things, (and says) they do not exist. Which of these, Mahamati, is the destroyer?" Mahamati said: "The one, Lord, who, having accepted greed, hatred and delusion, does not accept them again."

The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati! Truly well done, Mahamati, that you have spoken this way. Not only is he a destroyer because of the being and non-being of greed, hatred and delusion, Mahamati; he is also a destroyer of buddhas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why? Because the afflictions are not found inside or outside. Greed, hatred and delusion, Mahamati, are not found inside or outside, since they have no body. And because he does not accept the non-existence of greed, hatred and delusion, Mahamati, he becomes a destroyer of buddhas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas. Those buddhas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are free by nature, since there is no one to be bound and no cause of bondage. Where there is someone to be bound, Mahamati, there is bondage and a cause of bondage. Saying such things too, Mahamati, one is a destroyer. This, Mahamati, is the mark of non-existence and existence.

"And with this in mind, Mahamati, I said: 'Better a view of a person as big as Mount Sumeru than the view of emptiness of one who is proud about non-existence and existence.' For one proud about non-existence and existence, Mahamati, is a destroyer. His mind fallen into the view of particular and general marks, not acknowledging that everything is nothing but what one's own mind shows, and because he does not acknowledge it, seeing outer things as impermanent, he conceptualizes, apart from the letters of imagining, that the heaps, elements and sense fields, broken into a series of moments, cease by the stopping of their continuous stream; and so again he is a destroyer."

cmp.note: 「宁取人见如须弥山，不起空见怀增上慢」：这是佛教里有名的警句，意思是执着「有我」虽错，却比自以为懂了「空」而落入虚无要好。实叉难陀译「宁起我见如须弥山，不起空见怀增上慢」。中英文都把这层轻重保留了下来。
cmp.en: "Better a view of a person as big as Mount Sumeru than the view of emptiness of one who is proud": a famous Buddhist warning, meaning that clinging to a self is wrong, but still better than thinking one has understood emptiness and falling into nihilism. Śikṣānanda writes 宁起我见如须弥山，不起空见怀增上慢 ("rather raise a self-view as big as Sumeru than hold the emptiness-view with conceit"). Both the Chinese and English keep this weighing.

verses.en: On this it is said:
"'It is' and 'it is not' are both extremes, as far as the mind's realm reaches. When the realm has ceased, the mind truly ceases.
Since nothing is grasped in objects, there is cessation, yet not non-existence. The thing that is suchness exists, as the realm of the noble ones.
Those for whom what was not comes to be, or what was perishes, who hold being and non-being through conditions, do not stand in my teaching.
Not by tirthikas, nor by buddhas, nor by me, nor by anyone, is existence established through conditions; how then could there be non-existence?
Who has established existence through conditions, so that there is non-existence of it? Through the wrong view of the doctrine of arising, 'is not' and 'is' are conceptualized.
For one for whom nothing arises and nothing ceases, there is no 'is' and 'is not'; he sees the world as empty."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Sugata teach me, may the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, best of speakers, teach me the mark of the way of the realized truth, so that, having clearly penetrated it, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, arriving at the mark of the way of the realized truth, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening and not be led by any reasoners or tirthikas." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "The mark of the way of the realized truth, Mahamati, is of two kinds for all shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas: the way of the realized truth (siddhāntanaya) and the way of teaching in words (deśanānaya). The way of the realized truth, Mahamati, is the special mark of realization within, free of verbal conceptualizing and letters, leading to the course of the realm without outflows, the own-mark of the course and stage reached within, free of all reasoners, tirthikas and Maras. Having struck down those tirthikas and Maras, the course within shines forth. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the way of the realized truth. What is the way of teaching? It is the varied teaching of the ninefold scripture, free of the sides of different and not different, being and non-being, starting from the method of skillful means, a way of bringing beings to see. Whatever someone is inclined to, that should be taught to him. This, Mahamati, is the mark of the way of teaching.

cmp.note: 「宗通」与「说通」（实叉难陀译）：前者是自己亲证、离开文字的真理，后者是因人施教、用种种言教说法。后来禅宗「宗门」「教门」之分常引这一对。英文译 the way of the realized truth / the way of teaching in words，把字面意思说开；中文两个「通」字简洁，但不加解释很难懂。
cmp.en: Siddhāntanaya and deśanānaya, rendered by Śikṣānanda as 宗通 (zōngtōng) and 说通 (shuōtōng): the first is truth realized oneself, beyond letters; the second is teaching suited to each listener in many kinds of words. The later Chan distinction between the "school of the essence" and the "school of the teachings" often cites this pair. The English spells out the literal meaning, "the way of the realized truth / the way of teaching in words"; the two Chinese terms are compact but hard to understand without explanation.

verses.en: "Here, Mahamati, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should practice."
On this it is said:
"The realized truth and the way, and the teaching within: those who see these, knowing the distinction, do not fall under the sway of reasoning.
Things do not truly exist as fools conceptualize them. Why don't the reasoners want liberation through non-existence?
Looking at the conditioned as bound up with arising and perishing, they feed the two views and, through distortion, do not see.
Only one thing is true: nirvana, free of thinking. One should see the world as conceptualized, like the trunk of a plantain or an illusion.
Greed does not exist, nor hatred, nor delusion, nor a person. The heaps arise from craving; they exist like a dream."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Sugata teach me, the mark of unreal imagining (abhūtaparikalpa). How, what, by what and of what, Lord, does unreal imagining arise? People speak of 'unreal imagining, unreal imagining,' Lord. Of what dharma, Lord, is 'unreal imagining' a name? Or conceptualizing what does one have unreal imagining?" The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati! Truly well done, Mahamati, that you think this should be asked. You have set out on this, Mahamati, for the good of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, good and happiness of a great multitude of gods and humans.

"Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "Conceptualizing arises, Mahamati, from clinging to the unreal imagining of the many kinds and varieties of objects. For people who cling to grasped and grasper, Mahamati, whose minds have not grasped 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' who have fallen to the sides of the views of being and non-being, Mahamati, and who are fed by the habit-energy of the conceptualizing of the tirthikas' views, from clinging to perceiving varied outer objects, the cluster of mind and mental factors called conceptualizing arises, through clinging to self and what belongs to self."

Mahamati said: "If then, Lord, people's conceptualizing arises from clinging to the unreal imagining of the many kinds and varieties of objects; if, for those fallen to the sides of the views of being and non-being, fed by the conceptualizing of the tirthikas' views of grasped and grasper, the cluster of mind and mental factors called conceptualizing arises from clinging to perceiving varied outer objects, from not understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' and from clinging to varied things that exist and do not exist; then, Lord, just as the mark of varied outer objects, which has fallen to the sides of being and non-being, is free of being and non-being and turned away from the marks of views, so too, Lord, the highest truth is turned away from the marks of means of knowledge, senses, parts of a syllogism, examples and reasons.

"How then, Lord, does varied conceptualizing arise in one case, conceptualizing the clinging to varied unreal objects, but not arise in the other, conceptualizing the clinging to the mark of the highest truth? Surely, Lord, saying that it arises in one case and not in the other, you fall into a doctrine of uneven causes. And in speaking of the arising of the views of unreal conceptualizing that cling to the sides of being and non-being, conceptualizing it as a single form completed from the varied limbs of an illusory person, and with conceptualizing (accounting for) the being and non-being of varied marks, and the turning away of conceptualizing, you fall into the views of the Lokayata materialists." The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, conceptualizing neither arises nor turns away. Why?

"Because conceptualizing about being and non-being does not arise, because outer things that are seen do not exist, and through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' Mahamati, conceptualizing neither arises nor turns away. But for fools, Mahamati, because they imagine the conceptualizing of the variety of their own mind, I say that conceptualizing, preceded by the arising of action, arises from clinging to the marks of varied things. How else, Mahamati, could foolish ordinary people, through understanding that their own conceptualizing is mind-only, with their views of self and what belongs to self turned away, with the faults of effect, cause and condition turned away, with the basis of mind turned around through understanding their own mind-only, trained in all the stages, attain the Tathagata's realm of the course within and the turning away of conceptualizing views about the five dharmas, the natures and things?

"For this reason, Mahamati, I say: conceptualizing arises from clinging to the variety of unreal objects, and one is freed through fully knowing, as they really are, the objects that are the variety of one's own conceptualizing."
On this it is said:
"Those for whom the world arises from causes and conditions, caught up in the four alternatives, do not know my way.
The world is not born from non-being, nor from being, nor anywhere from both being and non-being, through conditions and causes, as fools conceptualize.
When one sees the world as neither being nor non-being nor both, then the mind turns away and reaches no-self.
All things are unborn, since they come from conditions; all conditions are effects, and existence is not born from an effect.
An effect is not born from an effect; that would mean the effect is two. And since it cannot be two, no thing is found coming from an effect.
