When one sees the conditioned as free of object and objectifying, it is settled: mind-only. Mind-only is what I teach.
'Only' means own-nature standing free of things through conditions; the end of things, the highest Brahman: this 'only' is what I teach.
The self is true as a designation; as a substance it does not exist. So too the heap-ness of the heaps is by designation, not as substance.
Sameness is of four kinds: of marks, of what is born from causes, and of no-self; the fourth belongs to yogis in yoga.
The turning away of all views, free of imagined and imagining, not finding, and non-birth: this is mind-only, I teach.
Not being, nor non-being, free of being and non-being, suchness free of mind: this is mind-only, I teach.
Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvana, the realm of Dharma, the varied mind-made body: this is mind-only, I teach.
Bound by the habit-energy of conceptualizing, varied, born of mind, it appears to people as outside: what is worldly is mind-only.
What is seen does not exist outside; mind is seen in its variety: body, possessions and dwelling place. Mind-only is what I teach.

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "The Lord has said that a bodhisattva, a great being, and others should not take the meaning to be just as the words sound. How, Lord, does a bodhisattva, a great being, avoid grasping the meaning just as the words sound? What are the words, and what is the meaning?" The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "What, Mahamati, are the words? Conceptualizing joined with speech and letters, the talk between people that comes out through teeth, jaw, palate, tongue and lips, caused by the habit-energy of conceptualizing: that is called words. And what, Mahamati, is the meaning?

"When a bodhisattva, a great being, alone and in seclusion, with the wisdom that comes from hearing, reflecting and cultivating, by his own understanding, on the path that leads to the city of nirvana, preceded by the turning-around of the basis of habit-energy, examines the course of the marks of the special meaning in each stage and place of the realm of the course within, he becomes skilled in meaning.

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, skilled in words and meaning sees that words are neither different nor not different from meaning, and meaning from words. If meaning were different from words, Mahamati, it could not be made manifest by words. But meaning is entered through words, as wealth is seen by a lamp. Just as, Mahamati, a man might take a lamp and look at his wealth, 'this is my wealth, of this kind, in this place,' so too, Mahamati, by the lamp of words, of verbal conceptualizing, bodhisattvas, great beings, free of verbal conceptualizing, enter the noble course within.

"Again, Mahamati, regarding 'unceasing,' 'unborn,' 'in nirvana by nature,' the three vehicles and the One Vehicle, the five minds, own-natures and the like: one who clings to the meaning just as the words sound falls, through clinging, into the views of superimposition and denial. Conceptualizing what stands one way as standing another, like conceptualizing the sight of the variety of an illusion. Just as, Mahamati, the variety of an illusion is to be seen one way and is imagined another way by fools, but not by the noble ones."
On this it is said:
"Conceptualizing according to the words, they superimpose on the true nature, and through that superimposition they fall into the house of hell.
The self is not found with the heaps, nor are the heaps in the self. They are not as they are conceptualized, nor are they non-existent.
If the existence of all things were as fools conceptualize it, if they were as they are seen, everyone would see reality.
If all dharmas did not exist, there would be no defilement and no purity. They are not as they are seen, nor are they non-existent."

"Again, Mahamati, I will point out to you the marks of knowledge (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna), so that, having clearly penetrated them, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, arriving at the marks of knowledge and consciousness, will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Knowledge, Mahamati, is of three kinds: worldly, world-transcending, and most world-transcending. Consciousness arises and perishes; knowledge neither arises nor perishes. Again, Mahamati, consciousness falls into sign and no sign and is caused by the varied marks of non-existence and existence; knowledge has the mark of going beyond sign and no sign. Again, Mahamati, consciousness has the mark of accumulating; knowledge has the mark of diminishing. And knowledge is of three kinds: the one that settles particular and general marks, the one that settles arising and passing away, and the one that settles non-arising and non-ceasing.

cmp.note: 「智」与「识」：两个字同根（jñā，知），vi- 是「分开」，所以 vijñāna 是「分别着知」，jñāna 是「直接的知」。中文「智」「识」看不出同根；英文 knowledge / consciousness 也看不出。这一段的整个对比都建立在这个字形上。
cmp.en: Jñāna (knowledge) and vijñāna (consciousness) share the root jñā, "to know"; the prefix vi- means "apart," so vijñāna is "knowing by dividing" and jñāna "direct knowing." The Chinese 智 (zhì) and 识 (shí) don't show the shared root, and neither do the English "knowledge" and "consciousness." The whole contrast in this passage rests on the form of the words.

verses.en: "Worldly knowledge belongs to all the tirthikas and foolish ordinary people who cling to the sides of being and non-being. World-transcending knowledge belongs to all the shravakas and pratyekabuddhas whose minds cling to falling into particular and general marks. The most world-transcending knowledge belongs to buddhas and bodhisattvas; through examining imageless dharmas and seeing non-ceasing and non-arising, free of the sides of being and non-being, it arises from realizing no-self at the stage of a tathagata.

"Again, Mahamati, knowledge has the mark of no attachment, and consciousness has the mark of attachment to the variety of objects. Again, Mahamati, consciousness has the mark of being joined with the arising and ending of the three attachments; knowledge has the mark of the own-nature of no attachment. Again, Mahamati, knowledge has the mark of not attaining; it is the realm of the course of noble wisdom within, since it neither enters nor leaves, like the moon in water.
On this it is said:
"Karma is stored up by mind and arranged by knowledge; by wisdom one reaches the imageless and its power.
Mind is bound up with objects; knowledge works in reasoning; but in the imageless and the special, wisdom comes into play.
Free of mind, thinking mind, consciousness, perception and conceptualizing, it is shravakas who reach the nature of conceptualizing, not the sons of the Conqueror.
In the peaceful, special acceptance, the pure knowledge of the Tathagata is born for the special meaning, free of active workings.
Wisdom for me is of three kinds, by which the noble ones are empowered: by which marks are imagined, and by which things are chosen.
Wisdom free of the two vehicles, free of non-existence, works for shravakas through clinging to existence; wisdom through entering mind-only is held to be the Tathagata's."

"Again, Mahamati, the tirthikas who teach transformation hold nine kinds of views of transformation: transformation of shape, transformation of marks, transformation of causes, transformation of reasoning, transformation of views, transformation of arising, transformation of things, transformation as manifestation through conditions, and transformation as manifestation through action. These, Mahamati, are the nine views of transformation, on the basis of which all the tirthikas teach transformation as arising from the sides of being and non-being.

"Transformation of shape, Mahamati, comes from seeing a shape become otherwise, like seeing gold change into all kinds of ornaments. Just as, Mahamati, gold transformed into bracelets, armlets, swastikas and so on is seen transformed into varied shapes, yet the gold itself does not transform, so, Mahamati, the transformation of all things is conceptualized by some tirthikas, and by others as coming from a cause. They are neither so nor otherwise, as far as imagining goes. All the distinctions of transformation should be seen this way, like curd from milk, liquor and the ripening of fruit.

"Just as, Mahamati, the tirthikas conceptualize transformation in each of curd, milk, liquor, fruit and so on, a transformation of conceptualizing, and yet nothing here transforms, since outer things, being or non-being, that are what one's own mind shows, do not exist; so, Mahamati, should the arising of foolish ordinary people's cultivation of their own mind's conceptualizing be seen. Here, Mahamati, no dharma arises or turns back, like seeing forms arising in an illusion or a dream. Just as, Mahamati, arising and ending are perceived in a dream, like the birth and death of a barren woman's son."
On this it is said:
"Transformation, time and shape in elements, things and senses, and taking up the intermediate existence: those who imagine these are not wise.
The conquerors do not imagine the world as dependently arisen; rather, the world itself is conditions, like a city of gandharvas."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, to untie the knots of meaning in all dharmas, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, teach me the marks of attachment and non-attachment in all dharmas, so that, having clearly penetrated them, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, skilled in the means regarding all attachments and non-attachments, may not fall into the attachment of clinging to meaning just as the words sound; so that, through skill in the attachment and non-attachment of all dharmas, having struck down conceptualizing about speech and letters, moving with understanding through the assemblies of all buddha-fields, sealed well with the seal of the powers, masteries, supernatural abilities and dharanis, with varied rays of transformation, in the ten final terms,

cmp.note: saṃdhi 一词多义：「结、连接、缠缚」，也有「密意、隐含的意思」。这一段主要取「缠结」义，用蚕作茧比喻众生被自己的分别缠住。实叉难陀译「相续」或「缠缚」，白话随文译。英文这里统一译 attachment，在偈颂里用 knots / net 补出「结」的形象。
cmp.en: Saṃdhi has many meanings: "knot, joining, binding," and also "hidden intention." Here the main sense is "entanglement": beings are wrapped up in their own conceptualizing like silkworms in a cocoon. Śikṣānanda renders it 相续 ("continuity") or 缠缚 ("binding"), and the plain Chinese varies with context. The English uses "attachment" throughout this passage, bringing out the "knot" image with "knots" and "net" in the verses.

verses.en: "with understanding firmly bound, like the effortless moon, sun, jewel and great elements in their course and conduct, with views turned away from the marks of their own conceptualizing on all the stages, seeing all dharmas as dreams, illusions and the like, entering the basis of the stage of a buddha, drawing in the whole realm of beings by teaching the Dharma as each deserves, they may establish them in what is free of the sides of being and non-being of all dharmas, which are like dreams and illusions, free of conceptualizing perishing and arising, relying on the meaning being otherwise than the words." The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati. Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "Countless, Mahamati, are the attachments in all dharmas: attachment through clinging to meaning just as the words sound; attachment through clinging to marks; attachment through clinging to conditions; attachment through clinging to being and non-being; attachment through clinging to conceptualizing arising and non-arising; attachment through conceptualizing and clinging to ceasing and non-ceasing; attachment through conceptualizing and clinging to vehicle and no vehicle; attachment through conceptualizing and clinging to the conditioned and unconditioned; attachment through conceptualizing and clinging to the own-marks of stages and no stages; attachment through conceptualizing one's own conceptualized realization; attachment through conceptualizing that relies on the tirthikas' sides of being and non-being; attachment through conceptualizing the realization of three vehicles and one vehicle.

"These and others, Mahamati, are the attachments of foolish ordinary people's own conceptualizing. Attached to these, foolish ordinary people keep conceptualizing and, like silkworms, wrap themselves and others in the thread of attachment to their own conceptualizing views, delighting in that thread, clinging to the marks of attachment to being and non-being. But here, Mahamati, there is no attachment and no mark of attachment, since all dharmas are seen as solitary. Since conceptualizing does not arise, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, lives seeing all dharmas as solitary.

"Again, Mahamati, through understanding the mark that outer being and non-being are what one's own mind shows, following imageless mind-only, and seeing all things, being and non-being, as free of the attachment of conceptualizing, there is neither attachment nor the mark of non-attachment in any dharma. Here, Mahamati, no one is bound and no one is freed; only through understanding fallen into falsehood are bondage and liberation known. Why? Because in all dharmas no attachment to being or non-being is found.

"Again, Mahamati, there are three attachments of foolish ordinary people: greed, hatred and delusion. And craving, which leads to rebirth and comes with delight and passion, attached to which the attachments of the courses of rebirth are born. Here beings are attached to the five courses of rebirth; when the attachment is cut, Mahamati, neither attachment nor the mark of non-attachment is known. Again, Mahamati, attachment comes from clinging to the working of conditions through the three-way meeting. Through the unbroken arising of the consciousnesses, from clinging, there is attachment to existence. When the conditions of the three-way meeting are turned away and the consciousnesses see the three liberations, no attachments arise."
On this it is said:
"Unreal imagining is called the mark of attachment; through knowing it as it really is, the net of attachments clears.
Grasping at things, knowledge and words, fools without insight into attachment are bound by their own conceptualizing, like silkworms."

Mahamati spoke again: "The Lord has said: 'Whatever things are conceptualized by whatever conceptualizing, that is not their own-nature; it is only imagined.' If, Lord, it is only imagined and not a settling of the mark of the own-nature of things, then surely, Lord, in saying this you fall into denying defilement and purification, since all dharmas would be made of the imagined nature." The Lord said: "It is as you say, Mahamati. The own-nature of things is not as foolish ordinary people conceptualize it. That, Mahamati, is only imagined, not a settling of the mark of the own-nature of things. But as the own-nature of things, Mahamati, is settled by the noble ones, through noble knowledge, noble vision and the noble eye of wisdom, so is the own-nature of things."

Mahamati said: "If, Lord, the own-nature of things is as it is settled by the noble ones through noble knowledge, noble vision and the noble eye of wisdom, not by the divine or the physical eye, and not as foolish ordinary people conceptualize it, how, Lord, will the conceptualizing of foolish ordinary people be turned away, since they do not understand the thing that is noble? And, Lord, they are neither distorted nor undistorted. Why? Because they do not understand the own-nature of the noble thing, and see the working of the marks of being and non-being. And even for the noble ones, Lord, the thing is not as it is conceptualized, since its own mark is not within the reach of objects. For them too, Lord, the mark of the own-nature of things appears as just the imagined nature, because one speaks of cause and no cause.

"Because, having fallen into the view of the own-mark of things, it becomes the realm of others and not as it is for them. So, Lord, there follows an infinite regress, since the mark of the own-nature of things is not understood. And, Lord, the mark of the own-nature of things is not caused by the imagined nature. How then, being conceptualized by imagining, will it not be as it is imagined? The mark of conceptualizing is one thing, Lord, and the mark of own-nature is another. The marks of conceptualizing and of own-nature have dissimilar causes. When foolish ordinary people imagine them in terms of each other, they will not be so. But this is said in order to turn beings away from conceptualizing: 'As they are conceptualized, so they do not exist.'

"Why, Lord, having held beings back from the view of non-existence and existence, do you then throw them back into a view of non-existence through clinging to the own-nature of a thing, through clinging to the realm of noble knowledge; and why do you do away with the teaching of the solitary Dharma by teaching a thing whose own-nature is noble knowledge?" The Lord said: "I do not do away with the teaching of the solitary Dharma, Mahamati, nor do I throw people into a view of existence by pointing out the own-nature of the noble thing. Rather, Mahamati, to keep beings away from a place of terror, for those who have clung since beginningless time to the marks of the own-nature of things, I teach the solitary Dharma by way of the view that clings to the mark of the own-nature of the thing that is noble knowledge. I do not teach the own-nature of things, Mahamati. Rather, Mahamati, they will come to live in the solitary Dharma, attained by themselves as it really is.

"Seeing confusion as signless, entering 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' their views turned away from the being and non-being of outer things that are seen, they will live in the solitary Dharma, reached as it really is through the three liberations. With signless views of confusion, sealed well with the seal of what really is, reached through the three liberations, they will live in direct experience of the own-nature of things, with understanding realized within, free of views of non-existence and existence as things.

"Again, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not make the thesis that all dharmas are unborn. Why? Because a thesis has the nature of all own-natures, and has the mark of arising from its causes. A bodhisattva, a great being, Mahamati, who states the thesis that all dharmas are unborn and argues it, defeats his own thesis. The thesis 'all dharmas are unborn' is defeated, because the thesis itself arises in dependence on that. And if that thesis too is unborn, being inside all dharmas, since the thesis has the mark of non-arising, then the argument 'all dharmas are unborn' collapses. Through the parts of the thesis and its reasons, the thesis is unborn from being and non-being. For that thesis, Mahamati, is inside all things, since being and non-being have the mark of non-arising.

"If, Mahamati, they make the thesis 'all things are unborn' with that unborn thesis, even so the thesis is defeated. Since the thesis has the mark of being unborn from being and non-being, no thesis should be made. Their thesis, Mahamati, has the mark of the own-nature of being unborn. So, Mahamati, no thesis should be made by you. Since the parts are spoiled by many faults, and since the parts are made from mutually dissimilar causes, no thesis should be made: that is, that all dharmas are unborn. In the same way, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not make the thesis that all dharmas are empty and without own-nature. Rather, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should teach that all things are like illusions and dreams, since they have the mark of being seen and not seen.

"And because all dharmas confuse view and understanding, things should be taught as like illusions and dreams, except where it is to keep fools away from a place of terror. For foolish ordinary people, Mahamati, fallen into views of non-existence and existence, may be terrified. And when terrified, Mahamati, they move far away from the Mahayana."
On this it is said:
"Not own-nature, nor representation, nor thing, nor storehouse: these are conceptualized by fools, bad reasoners who are like corpses.
'All dharmas are unborn,' to win over all the tirthikas; for no things joined with conditions have ever been born for anyone.
'All dharmas are unborn': one should not conceptualize this with wisdom. Since it has a cause and is established by that, their understanding collapses.
Just as people with cataracts wrongly grasp a hairnet, so fools wrongly conceptualize this conceptualizing of things.
The three existences are mere designation; there is no own-nature of things. The reasoners will imagine designations as real things.
Sign, thing, representation, and that trembling of the thinking mind: going beyond these, my sons move free of conceptualizing.
Like grasping water where there is no water, a mirage in the sky: so what is seen differs for fools and for the noble ones.
The vision of the noble ones is pure, born of the three liberations, free of arising and perishing, moving in the imageless.
For yogis, the imageless is not in the non-being of things. Through the sameness of being and non-being the fruit of the noble ones is born. How does the non-being of things make sameness, how?
When the mind does not know the moving outer and inner, then it brings about the ending, the mind that sees sameness."

Mahamati spoke again: "The Lord has said: 'When knowledge does not find an object to grasp, then mere representation is established. Since there is nothing grasped by representation, the grasper too is not grasped. Since nothing is grasped, the knowledge called conceptualizing does not arise.' Now, Lord, does knowledge not find (its object) because it does not understand the variety of particular and general marks of things, which are not different? Or does it not find it because the own-nature of things, the variety of particular and general marks, overwhelms it? Or does knowledge not find what is to be known because it is screened off by walls, mats, ramparts, enclosures, earth, water, wind or fire, or because it is too far or too near? Or does knowledge not find the object to be known because the senses are those of a child, a blind man or an old man? If, Lord, knowledge does not find it because it does not understand the variety of particular and general marks, which are not different, then, Lord, it should not be called knowledge.

"It is ignorance, Lord, when one does not find an object that exists. And if knowledge does not find it because the own-nature of things, the variety of particular and general marks, overwhelms it, then it is ignorance, Lord, not knowledge. Knowledge arises, Lord, when there is something to be known, not from its absence. And it is because it is joined with what is to be known that it is called knowledge. And if it does not find it because it is screened off by walls, mats, ramparts, enclosures, earth, water, wind or fire, or too far or too near, or knowledge does not find it because of defective senses, as with a child, an old man or a blind man; if it does not find it in this way, Lord, that is not knowledge. It is just ignorance, because of a defect of understanding about an object that exists."

The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, that is not ignorance in this way. That is knowledge, Mahamati, not ignorance. And I did not say, with that in mind, 'When knowledge does not find an object to grasp, then mere representation is established.' Rather, through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' since outer things, being or non-being, do not exist, knowledge too does not find an object. Since it does not find it, knowledge and the knowable do not arise. Following the three liberations, knowledge too is not found. But the reasoners, whose minds have been perfumed since beginningless time by the conceptual proliferation of being and non-being, do not understand it this way. Not understanding, they make outer substances, shapes and marks into being and non-being, and will point to the non-arising of conceptualizing as mind-only. Clinging to grasping the marks of self and what belongs to self, not understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' they conceptualize knowledge and the knowable.
"And through conceptualizing knowledge and the knowable, since examining outer being and non-being finds nothing, they fall back on the view of annihilation."
On this it is said:
"If knowledge does not see an object that exists, that is ignorance, not knowledge: this is the way of the reasoners.
If knowledge does not see because the marks are not different, or because of a screen, distance or nearness, that is called false knowledge.
If knowledge does not arise because one is a child, old or blind, while the knowable exists, that is called false knowledge."

"Again, Mahamati, foolish ordinary people, conceptualizing for themselves the coarse tendencies of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, dancing as in a play, unskilled in teaching the way of their own realized truth, clinging to the marks of outer things that are what their own mind shows, cling to the texts of teachings given as skillful means and do not understand the way of their own realized truth, made pure by the method of the four alternatives." Mahamati said: "It is as you say, Lord. May the Lord teach me the mark of the ways of teaching and realized truth, so that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, skilled in the ways of teaching and realized truth, may not be deceived in the future by bad reasoners, tirthikas, and followers of the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "The way of the Dharma of the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones of past, future and present, Mahamati, is of two kinds: the way of teaching and the way of the established, realized truth. The way of the texts of teaching, Mahamati, is the varied teaching of the sutras that gather the provisions. They teach beings according to their minds and inclinations. And what, Mahamati, is the way of the realized truth? That by which yogis turn away from conceptualizing what their own mind shows: not falling to the sides of oneness, difference, both and neither; beyond mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness; the realm of the noble course within oneself; turned away from the marks of reasons, reasoning and views; never tasted by bad reasoners, tirthikas, and followers of the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles, who have fallen into the two extremes of non-existence and existence: that I call the realized truth.
"This, Mahamati, is the mark of the ways of realized truth and teaching, in which you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should practice."
On this it is said:
"My way is twofold: realized truth and teaching. I give the teaching to fools and the realized truth to yogis."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "The Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, said once, at one time, that a Lokayata (materialist) with clever, varied spells and eloquence should not be served, honored or attended, since one who serves him gathers worldly gain and not Dharma. Why, Lord, did you say this about the Lokayata with clever, varied spells and eloquence, that one who serves him gathers worldly gain and not Dharma?" The Lord said: "The Lokayata with clever, varied spells and eloquence, Mahamati, confuses fools with varied reasons, words and letters that are not reasonable and not tied to meaning. He teaches just any old babble of fools.

"For this reason, Mahamati, he is called the Lokayata with clever, varied spells and eloquence. He draws in fools with the polish of varied letters, but does not enter the way of truth. Not understanding any dharma himself, he confuses fools with views fallen into the two extremes and ruins himself. Since he is not freed from attachment to the courses of rebirth, since he does not understand 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' and since he clings to the own-nature of outer things, his conceptualizing does not turn away. For this reason, Mahamati, the Lokayata with clever, varied spells and eloquence, not freed at all from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief and despair, confuses fools with varied words and letters, reasons, examples and conclusions.

"Even Indra, Mahamati, whose understanding was trained in many treatises and who wrote his own treatise on grammar, was defeated. A disciple of the Lokayata, taking on the form of a naga, made a wager in Indra's hall in heaven: 'Either your thousand-spoked chariot is broken, or each of my naga hoods is cut off.' And by fair debate the Lokayata's disciple in naga form defeated Indra, lord of the gods, broke his thousand-spoked chariot, and came back to this world. So it is, Mahamati, with the Lokayata, bound up with varied reasons and examples: even animals who learn it confuse the worlds of gods and asuras with varied words and letters, and make them cling to the view of gain and loss; how much more humans. For this reason, Mahamati, the Lokayata is to be avoided, since he carries the causes of suffering and birth; he should not be served, honored or attended.

"For the Lokayatas, Mahamati, teach, with varied words and letters, only what is perceived as the realm of body and understanding. The Lokayata, Mahamati, is a hundred thousand (lines). But in the later world, in the last five hundred years, it will be broken up, because it was made from bad reasoning, reasons and views. It will be broken up because no disciples take it up. In this way, Mahamati, the broken-up Lokayata, bound up with varied reasons, is taught by tirthikas who cling to their own causes, not as their own way. And no tirthika, Mahamati, has a way of his own treatise; they teach only the Lokayata in many forms, through hundreds of thousands of doors of causes. They do not know their own way, and in their delusion do not know that this is Lokayata."

cmp.note: 「顺世论」：古印度的唯物论派，只承认感官所见的世界。佛在这里把它扩大成一个总称：凡是执着外境、凭推理论证有无的学说，都是「顺世」。实叉难陀译「卢迦耶陀」（音译）。英文第一次加注 materialist，后文保留 Lokayata。
cmp.en: Lokāyata, the materialist school of ancient India, which accepted only the world the senses perceive. Here the Buddha broadens it into a catch-all: any doctrine that clings to outer objects and argues about being and non-being by reasoning is "Lokayata." Śikṣānanda transliterates it 卢迦耶陀 (Lújiāyētuó). The English glosses it "materialist" on first use and keeps "Lokayata" afterward.

verses.en: Mahamati said: "If, Lord, all the tirthikas teach only the Lokayata, with varied words and letters, examples and conclusions, and not their own way, clinging to their own causes, then does the Lord too teach only the Lokayata to the gods, asuras and humans who come from many lands and gather here, with varied words and letters, and not his own view, since it is contained within the teaching of all the tirthikas' views?" The Lord said: "I do not teach the Lokayata, Mahamati, nor coming and going. Rather, Mahamati, I teach neither coming nor going. 'Coming,' Mahamati, is the heap of arising that arises from the coming together of a collection. 'Going,' Mahamati, is destruction. 'Neither coming nor going' is a name for non-arising. I do not teach, Mahamati, what is contained in the conceptualizing of the tirthikas. Why?

"Because outer things do not exist, there is no clinging; standing in 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' conceptualizing that works in two ways does not arise. Since there is no realm of signs, through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows does not arise. Through entering the three liberations of signlessness, emptiness and wishlessness, one in whom conceptualizing does not arise is called freed.

"I remember, Mahamati, I was staying in a certain place on earth. Then a Lokayata brahmin came to where I was. Having come, without even asking leave, he said to me: 'Everything, Gautama, is made.' I said to him, Mahamati: 'If everything is made, brahmin, that is the first Lokayata.' 'Everything, Gautama, is unmade.' 'If everything is unmade, brahmin, that is the second Lokayata.' So too 'Everything is impermanent, everything is permanent, everything is born, everything is unborn': 'This, brahmin, is the sixth Lokayata.' Again, Mahamati, the Lokayata brahmin said to me: 'Everything, Gautama, is one; everything is different; everything is both; everything is neither; everything depends on causes, since we see things arise from varied causes.' 'This too, brahmin, is the eleventh Lokayata.'

"'Again, Gautama: everything is undetermined, everything is determined; there is a self, there is no self; this world exists, this world does not exist; the other world exists, the other world does not exist; the other world both does and does not exist; there is liberation, there is no liberation; everything is momentary, everything is not momentary; space, cessation not by analysis, and nirvana, Gautama, are made, are unmade; there is an intermediate existence, there is no intermediate existence.' To him, Mahamati, I said: 'If so, brahmin, this too is just Lokayata, not mine. This Lokayata is yours, brahmin. I, brahmin, describe the three existences as caused by the coarse tendencies of the habit-energy of conceptualizing and conceptual proliferation from beginningless time. Conceptualizing arises, brahmin, from not understanding "nothing but what one's own mind shows," not from perceiving outer things.

"'It is not with me as with the tirthikas, for whom (cognition arises from) the contact of the three, self, sense and object. I, brahmin, am neither a teacher of causes nor of no causes; rather, I designate conceptualizing itself as grasped and grasper, and teach dependent arising. People like you and others do not understand this, because your continuity has fallen into grasping a self.' Of nirvana, space and cessation, Mahamati, not even the reality is found in counting; how much less their being made.

"Again, Mahamati, the Lokayata brahmin said: 'Are these three existences, Gautama, caused by ignorance, craving and karma, or are they without cause?' 'Both of these, brahmin, are Lokayata.' 'All things, Gautama, fall under particular and general marks.' 'This too, brahmin, is just Lokayata. As long as there is the trembling of the thinking mind, brahmin, the conceptualizing that clings to outer objects, so long there is Lokayata.'

"Again, Mahamati, the Lokayata brahmin said to me: 'Is there anything, Gautama, that is not Lokayata? Gautama, it is mine that all the tirthikas teach as established, with varied words and letters, reasons, examples and conclusions.' 'There is, brahmin, what is not yours, and yet it is not unestablished and not untaught, not without varied words and letters, and not without meaning.' 'What is that non-Lokayata that is not established and yet is taught?' 'There is, brahmin, a non-Lokayata where the understanding of all the tirthikas and of you does not reach, since you cling to the conceptualizing and conceptual proliferation of what is unreal because of outer things: the non-arising of conceptualizing. Through understanding that being and non-being are nothing but what one's own mind shows, conceptualizing does not arise. Since outer objects are not grasped, conceptualizing rests in its own place and is seen.

"'This is the non-Lokayata, mine and not yours. "Rests in its own place" means it does not arise. The non-arising of conceptualizing about non-arising is what it is called. This, brahmin, is what is not Lokayata. In brief, brahmin, wherever there is the coming, going, passing away and rebirth of consciousness; seeking, clinging and attachment; seeing, view, position and adherence; clinging to varied marks; the coming together of beings; and clinging to craving and causes: that, brahmin, is your Lokayata, not mine.' This, Mahamati, is how the Lokayata brahmin who came to me questioned me. And answered by me in this way, he went off in silence.

"Then a naga king of the dark fortnight, coming in the form of a brahmin, said to me: 'Then, Gautama, the other world does not exist at all.' 'Then, young man, where have you come from?' 'I have come here, Gautama, from the White Island.' 'That, brahmin, is the other world.' Then the young man, at a loss for words, defeated, vanished without asking me anything more, thinking about how to make a statement of his own position: 'The son of the Shakyas is outside my way, a poor fellow, a teacher of the cause that is the mark of non-arising; through understanding the marks of what is seen by one's own conceptualizing, he describes the non-arising of conceptualizing.' And now, Mahamati, you ask me why one who serves the Lokayata with clever, varied spells and eloquence gathers worldly gain and not Dharma." Mahamati said: "What is the meaning, Lord, of the terms 'Dharma' and 'gain'?" The Lord said: "Well done, well done, Mahamati!

cmp.note: 这一句写本文字混乱，「释迦之子在我的道理之外，可怜的家伙……」应是龙王化身的婆罗门心里的话，但句读和归属都有疑问。英文按这个理解译出，读者应知道这里原文本身不清楚。
cmp.en: The manuscript text here is muddled. "The son of the Shakyas is outside my way, a poor fellow..." seems to be the thought of the naga king disguised as a brahmin, but both the punctuation and who is speaking are uncertain. The English follows this reading; readers should know the original itself is unclear here.

verses.en: "You have begun to inquire into the two terms looking toward the people of the future. Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "What, Mahamati, is gain (āmiṣa)? Gain is what is touched, drawn in, rubbed, adhered to, tasted; clinging to outer objects; entering the two extremes. Through wrong views, the heaps appear again, and there arise birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief and despair, beginning with craving that leads to rebirth. This is called gain by me and by the other buddhas, the lords. This, Mahamati, is gathering gain and not Dharma, which one gets by serving the Lokayata: the Lokayata.

cmp.note: āmiṣa 本义是「肉、诱饵」，引申为「世俗的好处、财利」，与「法」相对。中文「财」「食」只取引申义，英文 gain 也是；「诱饵」那层被吃掉的味道，中英文都没保留下来。
cmp.en: Āmiṣa originally means "flesh, bait," and by extension "worldly gain," set against Dharma. The Chinese 财 (cái, "wealth") or 食 (shí, "food") and the English "gain" all take only the extended sense; the flavor of "bait" that gets swallowed survives in neither.

verses.en: "And what, Mahamati, is gathering Dharma? Through understanding one's own mind and the two kinds of no-self of things, seeing the marks of the no-self of things and persons, conceptualizing does not arise; through fully knowing the higher stages, mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness turn away; the course of consecration by the knowledge of all buddhas; taking up the terms without sustaining power; effortless mastery of all dharmas: this is called Dharma, since one does not fall into the two extremes of all views, conceptual proliferation, conceptualizing and things. For the doctrine of the tirthikas, Mahamati, mostly makes fools, not the wise, fall into the two extremes: annihilation and permanence. Taking up a doctrine of no cause, the view of permanence arises; from the destruction of causes and the absence of a cause, the view of annihilation arises. But I say it is Dharma from seeing arising, abiding and perishing. This, Mahamati, is the settling of Dharma and gain, in which you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should train."
On this it is said:
"One should tame beings with the means of gathering them, bring them under control with moral conduct, destroy views with wisdom, and help them grow with the liberations.
All this that the tirthikas falsely teach is Lokayata; through the view that cause and effect exist, there is no realized truth of their own.
I alone teach my disciples a realized truth of my own, free of cause and effect, free of the Lokayata.
It is mind-only; nothing seen exists; mind is seen as two, as grasped and grasper, free of permanence and annihilation.
As long as mind arises, so long there is Lokayata. Where conceptualizing does not arise, the world sees its own mind.
'Coming' is the effect coming about; 'going' is seeing the effect. Through fully knowing coming and going, conceptualizing does not arise.
Permanent and impermanent, made and unmade, this world and the other: all these and the like are the way of the Lokayata.

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, people say 'nirvana, nirvana.' Of what is this word 'nirvana' a name, as all the tirthikas conceptualize it?" The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you how the tirthikas conceptualize nirvana, and that nirvana is not as they conceptualize it." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "Some tirthikas, Mahamati, (say that) through the cessation of the heaps, elements and sense fields, through dispassion toward objects, and through not seeing the nature of things, the cluster of mind and mental factors does not arise.

"They describe it as the non-arising of conceptualizing, through not recalling past, future and present objects, as when the grasping stops, like a lamp, a seed or a fire. So they take that to be nirvana. But, Mahamati, one does not reach nirvana through a view of destruction.

"Others describe liberation as going to another place, like the wind, when conceptualizing objects stops. Other tirthikas describe liberation as the destruction of the seeing of knower and known. Others imagine liberation as the non-arising of conceptualizing through seeing permanent and impermanent. Others, unskilled in 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' describe the conceptualizing of varied signs as what brings suffering and birth; afraid of signs, through seeing signs, they think of nirvana as a sign of longing for happiness. Others, through understanding the particular and general marks of all inner and outer dharmas, imagine nirvana as the non-destruction and existence of past, future and present things.

"Others imagine nirvana as the non-destruction of self, being, life, nourisher, soul, person and all dharmas. Other tirthikas, Mahamati, of poorly trained understanding, imagine nirvana through seeing the difference between primal nature and spirit, and the transformation of the qualities as the maker. Others, through the exhaustion of merit and demerit. Others, through the exhaustion of afflictions by knowledge. Others imagine nirvana through seeing God as the independent maker of the world. Others, (saying) the world comes about through mutual arising, not from a cause; but that itself is clinging to a cause, and in their delusion they do not understand it; not understanding it, they imagine nirvana. Other tirthikas, Mahamati, imagine nirvana as reaching the path of truth. Others think of nirvana through seeing quality and the qualified as bound together, as one, different, both or neither.

"Others conceptualize nirvana by seeing the own-nature of things as arising from own-nature, like the colors of a peacock, the variety of jewels in a mine, the sharpness of a thorn. Others, Mahamati, through understanding the twenty-five principles; others imagine nirvana as the king's taking up the teaching of the six qualities of policy. Others, seeing time as the maker, (say) the world's arising depends on time, and imagine nirvana as understanding that. Others again, Mahamati, imagine nirvana through existence, others through non-existence, others through fully knowing existence and non-existence, others through seeing no difference between existence and nirvana.

"Others again, Mahamati, roaring the lion's roar of the all-knowing, describe it this way: through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows'; through not clinging to the existence and non-existence of outer things; free of the four alternatives; seeing things standing as they really are; not falling into the two extremes of conceptualizing what one's own mind shows; not finding grasped and grasper; seeing that no means of knowledge grasps or arises; since (grasping) bewilders reality, reality is not grasped; setting that aside, realizing the noble Dharma within oneself; understanding the two kinds of no-self; turning away the two kinds of affliction; purifying the two obstructions; through the higher and higher stages, the stage of a tathagata, the illusion-like and every samadhi, and the turning away of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness: they imagine nirvana. And other (notions) made up by reasoners and wrong tirthikas, unreasonable, rejected by the wise: all these, Mahamati, imagine nirvana with a continuity fallen into the two extremes.

cmp.note: 这一段很特别：在一长串外道的涅槃说之后，佛把几乎就是本经自己的观点（自心所现、离四句、转依、二无我）也列成「有人这样构想涅槃」。白话、英文都照原文列出，读者可以看出：连正确的说法，一旦被当作「构想」来执着，也同样不是涅槃。
cmp.en: This passage is unusual: after a long list of tirthika ideas of nirvana, the Buddha lists what is almost the sutra's own view (what one's own mind shows, freedom from the four alternatives, the turning-around, the two kinds of no-self) as yet another way "some imagine nirvana." The plain Chinese and English list it as it stands, so readers can see that even a correct account, once clung to as a concept, is not nirvana either.

verses.en: "With conceptualizings like these, Mahamati, all the tirthikas imagine nirvana. But here nothing arises or turns back. The nirvana of each tirthika, Mahamati, examined by the understanding of his own treatise, falls apart. It does not stand as they conceptualize it. Because of the thinking mind's trembling coming and going, no one has nirvana. Training here, Mahamati, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should turn away all the tirthikas' views of nirvana."
On this it is said:
"The tirthikas conceptualize views of nirvana each in their own way; it is only their imagining, and there is no means of liberation.
Free of bound and bonds, and without means, the tirthikas conceptualize liberation, yet there is no liberation.
The way of the tirthikas is seen split into many divisions; so there is no liberation for them. Why do the deluded conceptualize?
All the tirthikas are deluded by the badness of cause and effect; so there is no liberation for those who teach the sides of being and non-being.

Fools delight in chatter and conceptual proliferation and do not set their minds wide on reality. Chatter is the womb of the suffering of the three realms; reality is the cause of the destruction of suffering.
Just as a form is seen in a mirror and yet does not exist, so in the mirror of habit-energy fools see mind as two.
From not fully knowing what mind shows, conceptualizing is born as two; from fully knowing what mind shows, conceptualizing does not arise.
Mind itself is varied, free of marked and mark; it has the form of what is seen, but nothing seen exists, as fools conceptualize.
The three existences are only conceptualizing; outer objects do not exist. Conceptualizing is seen in variety, yet fools do not understand.
In sutra after sutra conceptualizing is spoken of, under other names for perception; apart from naming, what is named is not perceived."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord: "May the Lord, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, teach me the buddhahood of his own awakening, so that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, skilled in the Tathagata's own (nature), may awaken ourselves and others." The Lord said: "Then ask, Mahamati, yourself. As you see fit, so I will answer." Mahamati said: "Lord, is the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, made or unmade, effect or cause, marked or mark, naming or named, understanding or what is understood? With words and terms like these, is the Lord different or not different?"

The Lord said: "No, Mahamati, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, with words and terms like these, is neither unmade nor made, neither effect nor cause. Why? Because faults follow on both sides. If the Tathagata were made, Mahamati, he would be impermanent. Being impermanent, everything made would be the Tathagata. That is not acceptable to me or to the other tathagatas. If he were unmade, since he would have no self, the provisions gathered would be pointless; he would be like a hare's horn, like the son of a barren woman, being unmade. And what, Mahamati, is neither effect nor cause is neither being nor non-being. And what is neither being nor non-being is outside the four alternatives. The four alternatives, Mahamati, are worldly convention. What is outside the four alternatives becomes mere words, like the son of a barren woman.

"For the son of a barren woman, Mahamati, is mere words and does not fall within the four alternatives. Not falling within them, it is not a measure for the wise. In this way the wise should understand all the terms for the Tathagata. And when I said that all dharmas are without self, Mahamati, the meaning of that too should be understood. No-self, Mahamati, is the absence of a self-nature. All dharmas exist with their own self, not with another's, like a cow and a horse. Just as, Mahamati, a cow's being is not of the nature of a horse, nor a horse's being of the nature of a cow, and it is not that they are neither existent nor non-existent, nor that they do not exist by their own marks, but they do exist by their own marks; so, Mahamati, all dharmas do not fail to exist by their own marks. They do exist. And by that, foolish ordinary people understand the meaning of no-self through conceptualizing, not without conceptualizing. In this way emptiness, non-arising and lack of own-nature in all dharmas should be understood.

"In the same way the Tathagata is neither different nor not different from the heaps. If he were not different from the heaps, he would be impermanent, since the heaps are made. If he were different, then, since there are two, he would be otherwise, like a cow's horns.

"Here, from seeing likeness, all things are not different; from seeing short and long, they are different. The right horn of a cow, Mahamati, is different from the left, and the left from the right. So with short and long in relation to each other, and so with the variety of colors. And so it is different, not in relation to each other. And the Tathagata is not different from the heaps, elements and sense fields. In the same way the Tathagata is neither different nor not different from liberation. The Tathagata himself is taught by the word 'liberation.' If the Tathagata were different from liberation, he would be joined with the mark of form; joined with the mark of form, he would be impermanent. If he were not different, there would be no distinction in the mark of attainment for yogis. But yogis have seen the distinction, Mahamati. So he is neither different nor not different. In the same way knowledge is neither different nor not different from what is known.

"For what, Mahamati, is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither effect nor cause, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither understanding nor understood, neither marked nor mark, neither the heaps nor other than the heaps, neither named nor naming, not bound up with oneness, difference, both or neither: that is turned away from all means of knowledge. What is turned away from all means of knowledge becomes mere words. What is mere words is unborn. What is unborn is unceasing. What is unceasing is like space. And space, Mahamati, is neither effect nor cause. What is neither effect nor cause has no object. What has no object is beyond all conceptual proliferation. What is beyond all conceptual proliferation is the Tathagata. This, Mahamati, is perfect, full awakening. This is the buddhahood of the buddhas, turned away from all means of knowledge and senses."
On this it is said:
"Free of means of knowledge and senses, neither effect nor cause, free of understanding and understood, free of marked and mark,
the fully awakened one, dependent on the heaps, has never been seen by anyone anywhere. How can one who has never been seen by anyone anywhere be understood?
Not made, not unmade, not effect, not cause, not the heaps, not other than the heaps, nor anything else through mixing.
What is not seen as the thing it is imagined to be is not to be taken as simply non-existent: it is the true nature of dharmas.
Non-existence presupposes existence, and existence presupposes non-existence. So one should not take it as non-existent, nor imagine it as existent.
Confused about self and no-self, clinging to mere sound, sunk in the two extremes, they are lost and they ruin fools.
When they see my way free of all faults, then they see rightly and do not slander the Leaders."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Sugata teach me: in the texts of the teaching the Lord has spoken of the unceasing and the unborn. And you have said that 'unceasing and unborn' is a name for the Tathagata. Is this unceasing and unborn, Lord, a non-existence, or is it another word for the Tathagata? The Lord says that all dharmas are taught by the Lord as unceasing and unborn, since the sides of being and non-being are not seen. If all dharmas are unborn, Lord, then no dharma can be grasped, since all dharmas are unborn. And if this is another word for some dharma, please tell me, Lord." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you."

"Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "The Tathagata, Mahamati, is not a non-existence, nor is the unceasing and unborn a grasping of all dharmas. It does not depend on conditions, nor do I speak of the unborn without meaning. Rather, Mahamati, this is a name for the Tathagata, whose Dharma-body is mind-made, the realm not reached by any tirthika, shravaka or pratyekabuddha, nor by bodhisattvas established in the seventh stage. That unborn is the Tathagata. This, Mahamati, is a synonym. Just as, Mahamati, Indra, Shakra and Purandara; hand, hasta and pani; body, deha and sharira; earth, bhumi and vasundhara; sky, akasha and gagana: for each of these things there are many words, synonyms, that are conceptualized.

"And it is not that, because of the many names, many things are conceptualized; nor that there is no own-nature. In the same way, Mahamati, I too, in this Saha world, come within hearing of fools under three hundred thousand countless names. They call me by these, without knowing that these are names and synonyms for the Tathagata. Some, Mahamati, know me as Tathagata; some as Self-Born; some know me as Leader, Guide, Director, Buddha, Seer, Bull, Brahma, Vishnu, Ishvara, Pradhana, Kapila, End of Beings, Arishtanemi, Soma, the Sun, Rama, Vyasa, Shuka, Indra, Bali and Varuna.

cmp.note: 佛说人们用三十万个名字称呼他，其中包括毗湿奴、自在天、迦毗罗、罗摩、毗耶娑这些印度教的神与圣者。白话、英文都照译；这一段在宗教比较上很重要，但我们不加评论。实叉难陀本也有这串名字。
cmp.en: The Buddha says people call him by three hundred thousand names, including Hindu gods and sages such as Vishnu, Ishvara, Kapila, Rama and Vyasa. The plain Chinese and English both translate it as it stands; the passage matters for comparative religion, but we add no comment. Śikṣānanda's version also has this list.

verses.en: "Others know me as the unceasing and unborn, emptiness, suchness, truth, reality, the limit of reality, the realm of Dharma, nirvana, the permanent, sameness, non-duality, the unceasing, the signless, the condition, the teaching of the Buddha's causes, liberation, the truths of the path, the all-knowing, the Conqueror, the mind-made. With these and others, Mahamati, a full three hundred thousand countless names, no fewer and no more, here and in other worlds, people know me, like the moon in water, neither entering nor leaving. But fools do not understand, because their continuity has fallen into the two extremes. And yet they honor me, respect me, esteem me and make offerings to me; unskilled in the meanings and explanations of words, they take the names as not different, and, clinging to the words and texts of the teaching, they do not know their own way.

"They will imagine the unceasing and unborn to be non-existence, and will not believe it is another word, another name, for the Tathagata, like Indra, Shakra and Purandara; nor will they believe in the texts that establish their own way, since they follow the texts of all dharmas whose meaning is just as the words sound. And those deluded people, Mahamati, will say: 'The meaning is just as the words sound; the meaning is not different from the words.' Why? 'Since meaning has no body, meaning is not something other than the words; the words themselves are the meaning,' they say, with untrained understanding, not fully knowing the nature of words. They will not know, Mahamati, that words arise and perish, while meaning neither arises nor perishes. Words, Mahamati, fall into letters; meaning does not fall into letters. Since it is free of being and non-being, it is unborn and has no body. And the tathagatas, Mahamati, do not teach a Dharma that falls into letters, since letters are not found as being or non-being.

"Unless, Mahamati, one's mind has fallen into letters: whoever teaches a Dharma that falls into letters is babbling, since the Dharma is beyond letters. For this reason, Mahamati, it is said in the texts of the teaching by me and other buddhas and bodhisattvas that the tathagatas do not utter or answer with a single syllable. Why? Because dharmas are beyond letters. Yet they do not utter what is not joined with meaning. They do utter, by taking up conceptualizing. Without taking it up, Mahamati, the teaching of all dharmas would vanish. And if the teaching vanished, there would be no buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, shravakas and bodhisattvas. And without them, what would be taught to whom? For this reason, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not cling to the words of the texts of the teaching. The texts of the teaching, Mahamati, can stray.

"Because it follows the dispositions of beings, the teaching of the Dharma is given by me and other tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones to beings of various inclinations, to turn away mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness; it is not given as an establishing of the realization of noble wisdom within oneself, which comes from understanding that all dharmas are imageless and nothing but what one's own mind shows, through turning away twofold conceptualizing. A bodhisattva, a great being, Mahamati, should rely on the meaning, not on the letter. A son or daughter of good family who follows the letter, Mahamati, ruins himself and does not lead others to understand. With a continuity fallen into wrong views, he leads his own side astray, along with wrong tirthikas who are unskilled in the own-marks of all dharmas and stages and do not know words and their explanations.

cmp.note: 「依义不依文」：这正是后来「四依」中的一条。中文「文」、英文 letter 都对应 vyañjana（字、音节、外在的标记）。
cmp.en: "Rely on the meaning, not on the letter": exactly one of the later "four reliances." The Chinese 文 (wén) and the English "letter" both render vyañjana (syllable, letter, outward mark).

verses.en: "But those skilled in the own-marks of all dharmas and stages, at home in words, synonyms and explanations, skilled in the meaning and reasoning of things, delight themselves with the bliss of the truly signless and establish others rightly in the Mahayana. And when the Mahayana is rightly taken up, Mahamati, buddhas, shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas are taken up. When buddhas, bodhisattvas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are taken up, all beings are taken up. When all beings are taken up, the true Dharma is taken up. When the true Dharma is taken up, Mahamati, the lineage of the Buddha is not cut off. Since the lineage of the Buddha is not cut off, the attainments of special births are known.

"So, in these attainments of special births, bodhisattvas, great beings, taking up birth, to establish beings in the Mahayana, taking on varied forms and guises with the ten masteries, following the marks and courses of the particular tendencies of beings, teach the Dharma for the sake of suchness.

"Suchness here is being not otherwise: reality. The mark of neither coming nor going, the calming of all conceptual proliferation, is called reality. So, Mahamati, a son or daughter of good family should not be skilled at clinging to meaning as the words sound, since reality is beyond letters. One should not be one who looks at the finger. Just as, Mahamati, someone might point something out to someone with a finger, and that person would stick to looking at the tip of the finger; in the same way, Mahamati, like children, the crowds of foolish ordinary people, clinging to the fingertip of words as they sound, will die without leaving behind the fingertip-meaning of words as they sound and coming to the highest meaning. Just as, Mahamati, food is to be eaten by children only when it has been prepared,

cmp.note: 「看指头的人」：这就是后来中国人熟悉的「以指指月」比喻的出处之一。这里梵文只说「指头指着某样东西」，没有提月亮；实叉难陀译「如为愚夫以指指物，愚夫观指不得实义」。中文读者常记成「指月」，那是后来的说法。
cmp.en: "One who looks at the finger": one of the sources of the image Chinese readers know as 以指指月 (yǐ zhǐ zhǐ yuè, "pointing at the moon with a finger"). The Sanskrit here only says "a finger pointing at something," with no moon; Śikṣānanda writes 如为愚夫以指指物 ("as when one points at a thing for a fool with a finger"). The "moon" in the familiar Chinese version is a later addition.

verses.en: "and if someone were to eat it unprepared, he would be thought mad, not understanding the step-by-step preparation of food; in the same way, Mahamati, non-arising and non-ceasing are not fine without preparation. There must be preparation here, and not like grasping the fingertip as the meaning. For this reason, Mahamati, one should devote oneself to the meaning. Meaning, Mahamati, is solitary, the cause of nirvana. Words are bound up with conceptualizing and carry one along in samsara. And meaning, Mahamati, is gained from those who have learned much. Having learned much, Mahamati, means skill in meaning, not skill in words. Skill in meaning is a view not mixed up with any tirthika doctrine, so that one does not fall oneself or make others fall. When it is like this, Mahamati, in meaning, there is great learning.
"So those who desire meaning should serve such people. Those of the opposite kind, who cling to meaning as the words sound, should be avoided by one who seeks reality."

Again Mahamati, sustained by the Buddha's sustaining power, spoke thus: "The Lord's view of the unceasing and unborn is not special in any way. Why? The causes of all the tirthikas, Lord, are also unborn and unceasing. For you too, Lord, space, cessation not by analysis and the realm of nirvana are unceasing and unborn. The tirthikas too, Lord, describe the arising of the world as caused by causes and conditions. The Lord too describes the arising of the world from the conditions of ignorance, craving, karma and conceptualizing, making a distinction only in giving another name to that same cause: 'conditions.' So too outer things from outer conditions. They and you (speak of conditions) for the arising of things. So, Lord, this doctrine is no different from the tirthikas' doctrine. Atoms, primal matter, Ishvara, Prajapati and the rest, together with the nine substances, are unceasing and unborn.

"For you too, Lord, all things are unborn and unceasing, since they are not found as being or non-being. And since the elements are indestructible, their own mark neither arises nor ceases. Whatever course it goes to, an element does not give up the nature of an element. This change of conceptualizing the elements, Lord, is conceptualized by all the tirthikas and by you. For this reason this doctrine is not special. Or else the difference should be stated here by which the Tathagata's doctrine is distinguished and not all the tirthikas' doctrine. If, Lord, your own doctrine is not distinguished, then the tirthikas too would turn out to be buddhas, since they have the cause of the unceasing and unborn. And the Lord has said that it is impossible, that there is no occasion, for many tathagatas to arise in one world-system. Yet many tathagatas would follow, if your own doctrine is not distinguished from taking up effects that exist and do not exist."

The Lord said: "My unceasing and unborn, Mahamati, is not like the tirthikas' doctrine of non-arising and non-ceasing, nor like the doctrine of arising and impermanence. Why? For the tirthikas, Mahamati, the own-nature of things exists, reaching the mark of being unborn and unchanging. Mine does not fall into the sides of being and non-being like that. Mine, Mahamati, is free of the sides of being and non-being, without arising and perishing, neither being nor non-being; it is not non-being, like seeing the varied forms of an illusion. How is it not being? Because the marks of the own-nature of form are not grasped, since it is seen and not seen, grasped and not grasped. For this reason all things are neither being nor non-being. But through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' since conceptualizing does not arise, the world is at rest and without action. Fools imagine it as acting, but not the noble ones. This, Mahamati, is a confusion of conceptualizing unreal objects, like a city of gandharvas or an illusory person.

"Just as, Mahamati, someone of childish kind, in a city of gandharvas, might imagine a varied caravan of illusory people and beings going in or coming out: 'these went in, those came out'; yet no one there went in or came out, and it is just a state of confused conceptualizing: in the same way, Mahamati, this confusion of arising and non-arising belongs to fools. Here nothing is conditioned or unconditioned, as with the arising of an illusory person. And the illusory person neither arises nor ceases, since being and non-being do nothing. In the same way all dharmas are free of perishing and arising. But fools, with perception fallen into falsehood, imagine arising and ceasing; not the noble ones. 'False' here, Mahamati, means: not as the own-nature of things is imagined, nor otherwise. If it were imagined otherwise, there would just be clinging to the own-nature of all things.

"There would be no seeing of solitude, and from not seeing solitude there would be no turning away of conceptualizing. For this reason, Mahamati, seeing the signless is better, not seeing signs. Signs are worse, since they are the cause of birth. 'Signless,' Mahamati, is the non-arising of conceptualizing; I call the unborn nirvana. Nirvana, Mahamati, is seeing the place of things as they really are, preceded by the turning-around of the cluster of conceptualizing mind and mental factors. I call nirvana the realization of the Tathagata's noble wisdom within."
On this it is said:
"To turn away arising, establishing non-arising, I teach a doctrine of no cause, and fools do not understand it.
All this is unborn, yet things are not non-existent; things called a city of gandharvas, a dream, an illusion, exist without cause.
How are they unborn by nature and empty? Tell me. Freed from combination, a thing is not grasped by understanding. So I call it empty, unborn, without own-nature.
Combination, and each one too, does not exist since what is seen does not exist; not through the dissolving of the tirthikas' views does combination not exist.
Dream, hairnet, illusion, gandharva city, mirage are seen without cause; so is the variety of the world.

Restraining with the doctrine of no cause, one should establish non-arising. When non-arising is established, my guidance does not perish. When the doctrine of no cause is taught, fear is born in the tirthikas.

How, by what, from where, where would a causeless coming-into-being be? When they see the conditioned as neither without cause nor from causes, then the view that teaches perishing and arising turns away.
Is non-arising non-existence, or looking toward conditions? Or is it a name for a thing, or meaningless? Tell me.
Non-arising is not non-existence, nor looking toward conditions, nor a name for a thing, nor a meaningless name.
What is beyond the reach of shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas, and of those on the seventh stage: that is the mark of non-arising.
Turning away causes and conditions, stopping the cause, establishing mind-only: this I call non-arising.
The causeless working of things, free of imagined and imagining, freed from the sides of being and non-being: this I call non-arising.
Mind freed from what is seen, free of the two natures, the turning-around of the basis: this I call non-arising.
Not outer things, not their absence, nor grasping by the mind; dream, hairnet, illusion, gandharva city, mirage; the abandoning of all views: that is the mark of non-arising.
So one should understand all the terms, empty, without own-nature and the rest: never empty with emptiness, but with the emptiness of non-arising.
The cluster of conditions arises and turns back; apart from the cluster, nothing is born, nothing ceases.
No thing exists anywhere that is other, apart from the cluster, as the tirthikas conceptualize it, as one or as separate.
A thing that is not is not born, nor anywhere what is or both is and is not; only this cluster arises and turns back.
This is only convention, a chain of mutual dependence; there is no other meaning apart from the chain of conditions.
Since there is nothing to be born, non-arising, free of the tirthikas' faults: I teach that it is only a chain, and fools do not understand.
Whoever holds that some thing to be born exists anywhere apart from the chain should be known as a teacher of no cause, a destroyer of the chain.
If someone holds that any thing exists anywhere apart from the chain, then the chain would be like a lamp that reveals kinds of substances.
Without own-nature, unborn, like the sky by nature, are the dharmas the unwise imagine as separate from the chain.
Another and another non-arising: the true nature of the noble ones' attainment. For one for whom the non-arising of birth is so, there may be acceptance of non-arising.
When one sees this whole world as only a chain, as nothing but a chain, then the mind becomes settled.
Ignorance, craving, karma and the like are the inner chain; space, clay, pot, wheel and so on, seed, element and the like, the outer.
For whom a thing is born from another, through conditions, anywhere, (for him) it is not only a chain; such people do not stand in reasoning or scripture.
If there is no thing to be born, from what condition would understanding come about, and whose? These produce one another; that is why they are called conditions.
Hot, fluid, moving and hard: these dharmas are conceptualized by fools. This is a cluster; there is no dharma; so there is lack of own-nature.
Just as physicians vary the treatment according to the patient, yet there is no difference in the treatise, the difference coming from the difference in the illness,
so I, knowing the streams of beings, spoiled by the faults of afflictions, and the strength of their faculties, teach the way to living beings.
My teaching does not divide because of differences in afflictions and faculties. There is only one vehicle: the eightfold path, which is peace.

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, all the tirthikas conceptualize 'impermanence, impermanence.' And in all your texts of the teaching you teach: 'Alas, formations are impermanent, subject to arising and passing away.' Is this true or false, Lord? How many kinds of impermanence are there, Lord?" The Lord said: "All the tirthikas, Mahamati, imagine impermanence in eight ways, but I do not. Which eight? Some, Mahamati, say: impermanence is the ceasing of a beginning. A beginning, Mahamati, is arising; non-arising is impermanence. Others describe impermanence as the ceasing of shape. Others say form itself is impermanent. Others say impermanence is the change of form into something else.

"(Others say:) through unbroken continuity, all dharmas break apart and divide by their own nature, like milk changing into curd, unseen and gone; it is at work in all things, and there is no permanence. Others imagine impermanence as a thing. Others imagine impermanence as being and non-being. Others imagine impermanence as the non-arising of all dharmas, since impermanence is included within them. Here, Mahamati, impermanence as being and non-being means: the destruction of the own-marks of elements and what is made of them is not found, and the own-nature of the elements does not arise. Impermanence as non-arising means: permanent and impermanent, being and non-being do not arise; no dharma is seen; examining down to the atom, nothing is seen. This is a name for non-arising, not for arising. This, Mahamati, is the mark of impermanence as non-arising; not understanding it, all the tirthikas fall into the doctrine of impermanence as arising.

"Again, Mahamati, for one for whom impermanence is a thing, impermanence is permanent only by his own mind's conceptualizing; impermanence is not a thing. Why? Because impermanence itself would not be destroyed. Here, Mahamati, the non-existence of all things would be the effect of impermanence. And without impermanence, the non-existence of all things is not found, as with a stick, a stone or a hammer, breaker and broken. They are seen as not different from each other. So impermanence is the cause and the non-existence of all things the effect. And there is no difference between effect and cause, 'this is impermanence, this is the effect.' Since effect and cause are not different, all things are permanent, since impermanence is the cause of no thing. For the non-existence of all things, Mahamati, has no cause. And foolish ordinary people do not understand this. And a cause does not produce an unlike effect.

"If it did, then the impermanence of all things would be an unlike effect, and there would be no distinguishing effect from cause. But for them a distinction between effect and cause is seen. Or if impermanence were a thing, it would fall into the mark of being a cause of action, or it would be complete in all things as a single thing. And since it falls into the mark of being a cause of action, impermanence itself would be permanent, and all things, which are impermanent and so on, would be permanent, simply permanent.

"And if impermanence is within all things, it would fall into the three times. Then past form would have perished together with it. The future too is not born. Since form is not born, it has the same mark as present form too. And form is a particular arrangement of the elements. The nature of the elements and what is made of them is not destroyed, since it is free of different and not different. Since, for all the tirthikas, all the elements are indestructible, the whole three existences are elements and what is made of them, in which arising, abiding and change are designated. What else, free of elements and what is made of them, is impermanent, whose impermanence the tirthikas imagine? And the elements neither arise nor turn back, because of clinging to the marks of own-nature.

"Here, impermanence as the ceasing of a beginning: elements do not begin other elements again; because of their mutually distinct own-marks, no distinction is begun. Because they are not distinct, because they do not begin again, because of the twofold connection, people think of impermanence as not beginning.

"Impermanence as the ceasing of shape: the elements and what is made of them are not destroyed until dissolution. Dissolution, Mahamati, is examining down to the atom; the destruction of elements and what is made of them is seeing the shape become otherwise, not finding long and short. It is not in the atoms and elements; from the destruction of the elements, seeing the ceasing of shape, they fall into the doctrine of the Samkhya.

"Impermanence of shape: for one for whom form itself is impermanent, the impermanence is of shape, not of the elements. If the elements were impermanent, there would be no worldly convention. Without worldly convention, one would fall into the view of the Lokayata, since all things would be mere words. But not from seeing the arising of own-marks.

"Impermanence as change: seeing form become otherwise, not the elements, like seeing a change in the shape of gold ornaments. The gold is not destroyed as a thing; rather, the shape of the ornament is destroyed.

"And there are others, fallen into change: in these and other ways the tirthikas conceptualize the view of impermanence. The elements, though burned by fire, are not burned, because of their own marks. If they each lost their own marks, the existence of the great elements and what is made of them would be cut off.

"For me, Mahamati, things are neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because I do not accept outer things; because I teach that the three existences are mind-only; because I do not teach varied marks; the particular arrangement of the great elements neither arises nor turns back. It is not because of elements and what is made of them that conceptualizing arises in two ways, the marks of grasped and grasper. Through fully knowing the two ways conceptualizing arises, through getting rid of views of outer being and non-being, through understanding one's own mind-only, conceptualizing arises through the shaping of conceptualizing, not for one who does not shape it. Through getting rid of the being and non-being of the mind's conceptualizing, there is neither permanence nor impermanence for any dharmas, worldly, world-transcending or most world-transcending. Not understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' with a continuity fallen into the two extremes through wrong views, not understanding their own conceptualizing, all the tirthikas, storytellers who have never established anything, imagine impermanence.

"And the mark of all dharmas, Mahamati, worldly, world-transcending and most world-transcending, for all the tirthikas, is threefold, coming out of verbal conceptualizing. And foolish ordinary people do not understand it."
On this it is said:
"The ceasing of a beginning, the becoming-otherwise of shape, the thing, impermanence, form: these the deluded tirthikas imagine.
There is no destruction of things; the elements stand in their own nature. Sunk in many views, the tirthikas imagine permanence.
For no tirthika is there destruction or coming into being. The elements are permanent in their own nature; whose impermanence do they imagine?
All this is mind-only; mind arises as two, as grasped and grasper; there is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
Up to the realm of Brahma and the rest, I say it is mind-only. Apart from mind-only, Brahma and the rest are not found."
Here ends the third chapter, On Impermanence, in the Lankavatara, a Mahayana sutra.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · Direct Realization (Abhisamaya)
