chapters.intro: Mahamati asks how practitioners enter the attainment of cessation, where thought stops entirely. From the sixth stage on, the Buddha says, they can; the eighth stage is nirvana for shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, but buddhas hold bodhisattvas back from resting in that bliss so they go on toward buddhahood. The closing verses say the stages have no real order.

verses.en: The fourth chapter, called "Direct Realization."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me skill in the marks of the sequence and connection of cessation for all bodhisattvas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, so that, through skill in the marks of sequence and connection, I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, may not be bewildered at the gateway of the bliss of the attainment of cessation, and may not fall into the confusion of shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "From the sixth stage on, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, and all shravakas and pratyekabuddhas enter cessation. On the seventh stage, moment of mind by moment of mind, bodhisattvas, great beings, enter it by setting aside the marks of the own-nature of all things, but shravakas and pratyekabuddhas do not. For the attainment of cessation of shravakas and pratyekabuddhas is contrived and has fallen into the marks of grasped and grasper. So they do not enter it on the seventh stage moment of mind by moment of mind, lest they reach the mark of no distinction among all dharmas. And there is the absence of varied marks. Because they do not understand the marks of the own-nature of good and bad, there is an attainment of all dharmas. So on the seventh stage they do not have the skill in attainment, moment of mind by moment of mind, by which they might enter it.

"On the eighth stage, Mahamati, for bodhisattvas, great beings, and for shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, the conceptualizing and perception of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness turn away. On the first to sixth stages one sees the three realms as only mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness, free of self and what belongs to self, arising from one's own mind's conceptualizing, not fallen into the variety of marks of outer things, but only one's own mind. Fools, transforming their own knowledge in two ways, as grasped and grasper, do not understand, perfumed by the habit-energy of the conceptual proliferation and conceptualizing of coarse tendencies from beginningless time.

"On the eighth stage, Mahamati, there is nirvana for shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas. But bodhisattvas are held back from that bliss of samadhi by the buddhas of samadhi, so that they do not enter final nirvana, since the stage of a tathagata is not yet complete. If they were not held back, all their work would come to a stop, and the family line of the tathagatas would be cut off. And those buddhas, the lords, teach the unthinkable greatness of a buddha. So they do not enter final nirvana. But shravakas and pratyekabuddhas are carried away by the bliss of samadhi, and so they think of that as final nirvana.

"On the seven stages, Mahamati, I make distinctions among the dharmas on the side of awakening: skill in familiarity with the marks of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness; with self and what belongs to self, grasped and grasper, the arising and ending of the no-self of things and persons, and particular and general marks; skill in settling the four analytical knowledges; the stages, tasting the bliss of mastery, and entering the sequence of stages. (I do this) so that bodhisattvas, great beings, not understanding particular and general marks and unskilled in the sequence and connection of the stages, may not fall onto the path of the tirthikas' wrong views; for this reason the order of the stages is set up. But here, Mahamati, nothing arises or turns back, except that this is nothing but what one's own mind shows: the sequence and connection of the stages and the varied practices of the three realms. And fools do not understand. Because fools do not understand, the teaching of the sequence and connection of the stages and the varied practices of the three realms are set up, and the abode of the Buddha's dharmas.

"Again, Mahamati, on the eighth bodhisattva stage, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, drunk on the intoxicating bliss of the attainment of cessation, unskilled in 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' fallen into the obstruction of particular and general marks, habit-energy, and the views that grasp the no-self of persons and things, take conceptualizing to be nirvana, not the solitary Dharma. But bodhisattvas, Mahamati, seeing the gateway to the bliss of the samadhi of cessation, filled with compassion and with their former vows, knowing the distinctions of the courses of the final terms, do not enter final nirvana. And yet they are in nirvana, since conceptualizing does not arise in them. Their conceptualizing of grasped and grasper has turned away. Through understanding 'nothing but what one's own mind shows,' conceptualizing about all dharmas does not arise. (Fools) conceptualize, clinging to the marks of the own-nature of mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness and outer things.
"So again the cause of the Buddha's dharmas does not arise (that way); it arises preceded by knowledge, through reaching the Tathagata's own stage within, like the man in a dream crossing a flood.

"Just as, Mahamati, someone asleep, in a dream, with great effort and urgency, tries to carry himself across a great flood, and wakes up before he has crossed; and having woken, he examines it: 'Was this true or false?' And he sees it like this: 'It was neither true nor false; rather, the habit-energy of conceptualizing what has been seen, heard, thought, known and experienced, varied forms and shapes fallen into conceptualizing from beginningless time, free of conceptualizing views of non-existence and existence, experienced by mind-consciousness, are seen in a dream.' In the same way, Mahamati, bodhisattvas, great beings, on the eighth bodhisattva stage, seeing that conceptualizing does not arise, having moved through the first to the seventh stages, through the realization of all dharmas, through the sameness of dharmas such as illusion, seeing that the eagerness for all dharmas and the conceptualizing of grasped and grasper have stopped, and seeing the spread of the conceptualizing of mind and mental factors, apply themselves to the Buddha's dharmas.

cmp.note: 「梦中渡河」：在梦里拼命渡过大河，还没渡到就醒了，醒来才知道没有河也没有渡。这个比喻说明八地菩萨看清分别不生，却并不因此入灭，而是继续修佛法。白话、英文都照原文译，比喻本身没有歧义。
cmp.en: "Crossing a flood in a dream": in a dream one struggles to cross a great river, wakes before reaching the other side, and only then knows there was neither river nor crossing. The image explains how bodhisattvas on the eighth stage see that conceptualizing doesn't arise, yet don't pass into cessation and keep practicing the Buddha's dharmas. The plain Chinese and English both translate it as it stands; the image itself is unambiguous.

verses.en: "This effort to reach what has not been reached, Mahamati, is the nirvana of bodhisattvas, not destruction; and through getting rid of the conceptualizing and perception of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness, acceptance that things are unborn is attained. And here, Mahamati, in the highest truth, there is neither sequence nor connection of sequence, since what is taught is the solitary Dharma, free of images and conceptualizing."
On this it is said:
"The abodes in mind-only, in the imageless, and the stage of a buddha: this the buddhas have spoken, speak and will speak.
The seven stages are mind; the eighth here is imageless. The two stages are the abode here; the remaining stage is my own.
Realized within and pure, this stage is my own: the highest place of Maheshvara, the Akanishtha, shines.
Just as rays stream out from a fire, varied, delightful and gentle, they create the three existences.
Having created the three existences, some now, some created before, there I teach the vehicles: this stage is my own.
The tenth would be the first, and the first would be the eighth; the ninth would be the seventh, and the seventh the eighth.

cmp.note: 「十地即初地，初地即八地……」：佛在这里故意把诸地的次序打乱，说明在无影像的境界里根本没有次第可言（下一首最后一句：「无影像中，哪有次第？」）。白话、英文都照数字直译，不去「理顺」它。
cmp.en: "The tenth would be the first, the first the eighth...": the Buddha deliberately scrambles the order of the stages to show that in the imageless there is no sequence at all (the next verse ends: "in the imageless, how can there be an order?"). The plain Chinese and English both translate the numbers literally without trying to "straighten them out."

verses.en: The second would be the third, the fourth the fifth, and the third the sixth. In the imageless, how can there be an order?"
Here ends the fourth chapter, Direct Realization, in the Lankavatara.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · Is the Tathagata Permanent or Impermanent? (Tathāgatanityānityatva)
chapters.intro: Mahamati asks whether the Tathagata is permanent or impermanent. Neither, the Buddha says: calling him permanent makes him like the tirthikas' creator-cause, calling him impermanent makes him a made thing like a pot or cloth. Only the knowledge he realized can be called permanent. Both views come from conceptualizing.

verses.en: The fifth chapter, called "Is the Tathagata Permanent or Impermanent?"

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "Lord, is the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, permanent or impermanent?" The Lord said: "The Tathagata, Mahamati, is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because faults follow on both sides. Either way, Mahamati, faults would follow. If he were permanent, he would turn into a creating cause. For the causes of all the tirthikas, Mahamati, are permanent and unmade. So the Tathagata is not permanent, (in the sense of) the permanence of the unmade. If he were impermanent, he would turn into something made. Since there would be no heaps, marked or mark, the destruction of the heaps would be annihilation. But the Tathagata is not annihilated. For everything made, Mahamati, is impermanent: pots, cloth, grass, wood, bricks and so on. If everything became impermanent, the provisions of the knowledge of the all-knowing would be pointless, being made.
"For everything made would be the Tathagata, since there would be no special cause. For this reason, Mahamati, the Tathagata is neither permanent nor impermanent.

"Again, Mahamati, the Tathagata is not permanent. Why? Because then the provisions would be as pointless as space. Just as, Mahamati, space is neither permanent nor impermanent, setting aside permanent and impermanent, it cannot be spoken of in terms of the faults of oneness, difference, both, neither, permanence and impermanence.

"Again, Mahamati, he would be like the horn of a hare, horse, donkey, camel, frog, snake, fly or fish, being permanent through non-arising. So, since he would turn into the permanence of non-arising, the Tathagata is not permanent.

"Again, Mahamati, there is a sense in which the Tathagata is permanent. Why? The Tathagata is permanent because the knowledge reached in realization is permanent. The knowledge reached in realization, Mahamati, of the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones, is permanent. Whether tathagatas arise or do not arise, this true nature simply stands, the fixed order of dharmas, the abiding of dharmas, in the realizations of all shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas. But the abiding of dharmas is not in the sky. And foolish ordinary people do not understand. The knowledge reached by the tathagatas, Mahamati, comes from wisdom and knowledge. The tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones, Mahamati, do not come from mind, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, the heaps, elements, sense fields, ignorance and habit-energy. For the whole three existences, Mahamati, come from unreal conceptualizing; and the tathagatas do not come from unreal conceptualizing.

"Where there is duality, Mahamati, there is permanence and impermanence, not where there is non-duality. For duality, Mahamati, is solitary, since all dharmas have the mark of non-duality and non-arising. For this reason, Mahamati, the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones are neither permanent nor impermanent. As long as verbal conceptualizing arises, Mahamati, the fault of permanence and impermanence follows. Through the ending of conceptualizing understanding, Mahamati, fools' grasping of permanence and impermanence is held back, but not through the ending of the understanding that sees solitude."
On this it is said:
"Those who always see the buddhas as free of permanence and impermanence, yet brought forth by permanence and impermanence, do not fall under the sway of views.
With permanence and impermanence, the gathering (of merit) would be pointless; through the lack of conceptualizing understanding, permanence and impermanence are held back.
As long as a thesis is made, everything is mixed up. Seeing nothing but one's own mind, one would not start a dispute."
Here ends the fifth chapter, Is the Tathagata Permanent or Impermanent?, in the Lankavatara.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · On Momentariness (Kṣaṇika)
chapters.intro: First the tathāgatagarbha, also called the storehouse consciousness: an ocean carrying the waves of seven consciousnesses. Then how the five dharmas, three natures, eight consciousnesses and two kinds of no-self fit together, why "buddhas like Ganges sands" is only a figure, and three levels of the six perfections. The title comes from the end: not everything perishes in an instant.

verses.en: The sixth chapter, called "On Momentariness."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Sugata teach me, the arising and ending of the heaps, elements and sense fields. If there is no real self, whose arising or ending is it? Fools, relying on arising and ending, not understanding the ending of suffering, do not know nirvana." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "The tathāgatagarbha, Mahamati, is the cause of good and bad; it makes all births and courses of life; like an actor, it moves through the narrow paths of the courses of rebirth, free of self and what belongs to self. Because it is not understood, the working of the three-way meeting of conditions arises. And the tirthikas, clinging to their causes, do not understand. Perfumed by the habit-energy of the coarse tendencies of many kinds of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, it is given the name storehouse consciousness; together with the seven consciousnesses born on the ground of the habit-energy of ignorance, like the waves of the great ocean, it goes on always, its body unbroken, free of the fault of impermanence, turned away from the doctrine of a self, utterly pure by nature.

cmp.note: 「如来藏名为阿赖耶识」：这一品把如来藏和藏识直接等同起来——同一个东西，清净面叫如来藏，被习气熏染时叫藏识。这是《楞伽经》最独特、后世争论最多的说法之一。中英文都照原文保留「被称为」(saṃśabdita) 这层措辞。
cmp.en: "The tathāgatagarbha, called the storehouse consciousness": this chapter directly identifies the tathāgatagarbha with the storehouse consciousness, one thing, called tathāgatagarbha in its pure aspect and storehouse consciousness when perfumed by habit-energy. This is one of the Lankavatara's most distinctive and most debated claims. The Chinese and English both keep the wording "given the name / called" (saṃśabdita).

verses.en: "The other consciousnesses, thinking mind, mind-consciousness and the rest, which arise and pass away, are momentary. All seven depend on the coming together of particular shapes and forms produced by unreal imagining as cause; they cling to names and signs; they do not understand the marks of form that are what their own mind shows; they do not feel pleasure and pain; they are not causes of liberation; they produce and are produced by the passions that break out from names and signs, with those as cause and object. When those that have been taken up, called the senses, are exhausted and cease, and others do not immediately arise, then for yogis who do not feel the pleasure and pain of their own mind's conceptualizing, who have entered the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, skilled in the four meditations, the truths and the liberations, there arises the thought of liberation, because (the consciousnesses) do not arise.

"But as long as the storehouse consciousness, called by the name tathāgatagarbha, has not turned around, the seven active consciousnesses do not cease. Why? Because the consciousnesses arise with that as cause and object; and because it is not the realm of any shravaka, pratyekabuddha or tirthika yogi. Through understanding their own no-self of persons, through taking up particular and general marks, the tathāgatagarbha goes on in the heaps, elements and sense fields. Through seeing the five dharmas, the natures and the no-self of things, it turns back, through the turning-around in the sequence and connection of the stages. It cannot be examined by the paths and views of the tirthikas. Then, established on the bodhisattva stage called Immovable, one attains the paths of the ten gateways of the bliss of samadhi.

"Upheld by the buddhas of samadhi, looking to the unthinkable Buddha-dharmas and his own vows, held back from the limit of reality that is the bliss of samadhi, through paths of yoga reached by the noble course within, not shared with any shravaka, pratyekabuddha or tirthika, he attains the path of the ten noble lineages, and a body made of knowledge and mind, free of the shaping of samadhi. So then, Mahamati, the tathāgatagarbha called the storehouse consciousness should be purified by bodhisattvas, great beings, who seek what is special.

"If, Mahamati, the tathāgatagarbha called the storehouse consciousness were not here, then, Mahamati, without the tathāgatagarbha called the storehouse consciousness, there would be neither arising nor ending. But there is arising and ending, Mahamati, for fools and noble ones. And yogis, who have not laid down the burden and are hard to penetrate, dwell in the happy abiding, here and now, of the noble course within. This realm of the tathāgatagarbha and storehouse consciousness, Mahamati, though pure by nature, appears to all shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas, with their speculative views, as if impure, because it is soiled by adventitious afflictions; but not to the tathagatas. For the tathagatas, Mahamati, it is a realm directly seen, like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand.

"This, Mahamati, is what I taught in the text of the teaching about Queen Shrimala, and, sustaining other bodhisattvas of subtle, sharp and pure understanding: the tathāgatagarbha called the storehouse consciousness, together with the seven consciousnesses, to show the no-self of things to shravakas who cling to arising. Sustaining Queen Shrimala, I taught the realm of the Tathagata, not the realm of the reasoning of shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and other tirthikas. Rather, Mahamati, the tathāgatagarbha, the realm of the storehouse consciousness, is the realm of the Tathagata only, and of bodhisattvas, great beings, like you, whose minds and understanding are subtle and sharp in making distinctions, who rely on meaning; not of all other tirthikas, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas who cling to the texts of the teaching as the words sound.

cmp.note: 「胜鬘夫人」：指《胜鬘经》，那部经以王后胜鬘为说法者，专讲如来藏。这里《楞伽经》自己引用它，说明两经的思想关系。英文 Queen Shrimala 第一次出现，没有另加说明经名，读者可从上下文看出。
cmp.en: "Queen Shrimala": a reference to the Shrimala Sutra, in which Queen Shrimala is the speaker and the subject is the tathāgatagarbha. Here the Lankavatara cites it itself, showing the connection between the two sutras. The English "Queen Shrimala" appears here for the first time without naming the sutra separately; readers can tell from context.

verses.en: "So then, Mahamati, you and other bodhisattvas, great beings, should practice fully knowing this tathāgatagarbha and storehouse consciousness, which is the realm of all the tathagatas. You should not be satisfied with merely hearing about it."
On this it is said:
"The garbha of the tathagatas, joined with the seven consciousnesses, arises from grasping at duality and turns back through full knowledge.
Mind, cultivated by thought since beginningless time, is seen like a reflection. For one who sees as it really is, there is the form of an object but no object.
As a fool looks at the fingertip and not at the moon, so one attached to letters does not know my reality.

cmp.note: 这首偈里梵文明确出现了「月亮」(niśākara，字面「造夜者」)：愚人只看指尖，不看月亮。前面第三品那段只说「以指指物」，这里才是「指月」比喻的直接出处。
cmp.en: In this verse the Sanskrit explicitly has "the moon" (niśākara, literally "night-maker"): the fool looks at the fingertip and not the moon. The earlier passage in Chapter 3 only spoke of "pointing at a thing"; this verse is the direct source of the "finger pointing at the moon" image.

verses.en: Mind dances like an actor; the thinking mind is like a jester; consciousness, with the five, imagines what is seen as on a stage."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, asked the Lord again: "May the Lord teach me, may the Sugata teach me, the marks of the distinctions and courses of the five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses and the two kinds of no-self, so that through them I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, may understand these dharmas in the sequence and connection of all the stages, so that through these dharmas there may be entry into all the Buddha's dharmas, and through entering all the Buddha's dharmas, entry even into the Tathagata's own stage within." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "I will teach you, Mahamati, the marks of the distinctions and courses of the five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses and the two kinds of no-self: name, sign, conceptualizing, right knowledge and suchness. Entry into the Tathagata's noble course within, free of views of permanence, annihilation, being and non-being, the happy abiding of attainment and of bliss here and now, comes face to face for yogis in yoga. Here, Mahamati, through not understanding the five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses, the two kinds of no-self, and the being and non-being of outer things that are what one's own mind shows, conceptualizing arises for fools, but not for the noble ones."

Mahamati said: "How, Lord, does conceptualizing arise for fools and not for the noble ones?" The Lord said: "Through clinging to names, perceptions and conventions, Mahamati, fools follow the mind. Following it, through the practice of various marks, their minds fallen into views of self and what belongs to self, they cling to a wealth of colors. Clinging, covered by ignorance, they become attached. Attached, they shape karma born of greed, hatred and delusion. Having shaped it again and again, their minds wrapped in their own conceptualizing like silkworms, fallen into the ocean and wilderness of the courses of rebirth, like a water wheel, they cannot get beyond it. And in their delusion they do not know that all dharmas are free of imagined self and what belongs to self, like illusions, mirages and the moon in water by nature; that they come from unreal conceptualizing, are free of marked and mark, turned away from perishing, arising, abiding and going; that they come from the conceptualizing of what one's own mind shows, and not from Ishvara, time, atoms or primal matter.
"Carried along by names and signs, Mahamati, fools follow signs.

"Here, Mahamati, the sign is what comes into appearance for eye-consciousness and is called form. In the same way, for ear, nose, tongue, body and mind consciousness, what is called sound, smell, taste, touch and dharmas: this I call the sign. Conceptualizing, Mahamati, is that by which one utters a name. It reveals the sign: 'This is so and not otherwise.' What is called elephant, horse, chariot, foot soldier, woman, man and so on: that is conceptualizing at work. Right knowledge, Mahamati, is that through which name and sign are not found. Since they are adventitious to each other, consciousness does not arise; since it does not fall into annihilation or permanence, or onto the stages of any tirthika, shravaka or pratyekabuddha, it is called right knowledge. Again, Mahamati, through right knowledge a bodhisattva, a great being, does not make a name into a thing, nor make a sign into a non-thing.

"Free of the wrong views of the two extremes of superimposition and denial, it is the non-arising of consciousness regarding name, sign and object. This I call suchness. And established in suchness, Mahamati, a bodhisattva, a great being, having attained the imageless realm, attains the bodhisattva stage called Joy.

"Having attained the bodhisattva stage called Joy, he turns away from all the bad courses of the tirthikas and arrives at the course of world-transcending dharmas. Through familiarity with marks, understanding the course of all dharmas beginning with illusion, the mark of the course of the noble Dharma within oneself, his curiosity about reasoning and views turned away, step by step up to the stage called Cloud of Dharma. After the Cloud of Dharma, he attains the stage of a tathagata, flowering with samadhi, powers, masteries and supernatural abilities. Having attained it, he shines with varied rays of transformation to ripen beings, like the moon in water. With dharmas firmly bound to the eight terms, he teaches the Dharma to beings according to their various inclinations, with a body free of mind and representation. This, Mahamati, is what bodhisattvas, great beings, attain by entering suchness."

Mahamati spoke again: "Lord, are the three natures contained in the five dharmas, or are they established by their own marks?" The Lord said: "Right here, Mahamati, the three natures are contained, and the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of no-self. Here, name and sign should be known as the imagined nature. And the conceptualizing that arises based on them, Mahamati, called mind and mental factors, rising at the same time, like the sun with its rays, with varied marks and nature, holding up the conceptualizing: that nature, Mahamati, is called the dependent. Right knowledge and suchness, Mahamati, since they are indestructible, should be known as the perfected nature.

"Again, Mahamati, clinging to what one's own mind shows, conceptualizing divides eightfold. Since the sign is imagined with unreal marks, and through the calming of the two graspings, of self and what belongs to self, the two kinds of no-self are born. In these five dharmas, Mahamati, all the Buddha's dharmas are contained, and the sequence and connection of the divisions of the stages of shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, and the tathagatas' entry into noble wisdom within.

"Again, Mahamati, the five dharmas: sign, name, conceptualizing, suchness and right knowledge. Here, Mahamati, the sign is what is seen with the marks of shape, form, particular appearance, form and the like: that is the sign. The making of a perception such as 'pot' about that sign, 'this is so and not otherwise': that is name. That by which one utters the name, revealing the sign, or (calling it) of the same nature: that, Mahamati, called mind and mental factors, is conceptualizing. The utter not-finding of name and sign, through the dissolving of understanding, since these dharmas are not experienced by each other and not imagined: that is suchness. Reality, the real, certainty, the end, nature, own-nature, not finding: that is the mark of suchness.

"Having followed it, I and the other tathagatas have taught it as it is, made it known, opened it up and made it plain. Following which, through right understanding, conceptualizing does not arise, without annihilation or permanence; in keeping with noble wisdom within oneself, with the mark of not being reached by the tirthikas, the other side, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas: that is right knowledge. And these, Mahamati, are the five dharmas. In these are contained the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of no-self, and all the Buddha's dharmas. Here, Mahamati, you should become skilled by your own mind, and lead others to do so too. You should not be led by others."
On this it is said:
"The five dharmas and own-nature, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of no-self: these take in the whole of the Mahayana.
Name, sign and imagining are the marks of the two natures; right knowledge and suchness are the mark of the perfected."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "The Lord has said in the texts of the teaching that the tathagatas of the past, future and present are as many as the sands of the Ganges. Should this be taken in the meaning just as the words sound, Lord, or is there some other, special meaning? Please tell me, Lord." The Lord said: "It should not be taken as the words sound, Mahamati. The number of buddhas of the three times is not measured by the sands of the Ganges. Why? Because what goes beyond the world's excellence, Mahamati, makes the example no example, since it is both like and unlike. And the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones, Mahamati, do not set out an example that is like and unlike and goes beyond the world's excellence.

"This, Mahamati, is just a comparison set out by me and by those tathagatas: that the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones are as many as the sands of the Ganges. It is to shake up foolish ordinary people who cling to permanence and impermanence, who hold the wrong views of the tirthikas' intentions, who follow the wheel of samsara and existence, (thinking:) 'How might they, shaken up, seeking something special, begin to strive for the special, out of the narrow wheel of the courses of existence?' To show that buddhahood is easy to reach, so that they will set to work with energy, thinking 'the arising of tathagatas is not like the udumbara flower.' In the texts of the teaching, though, looking to the people to be trained, I have taught that tathagatas appear as rarely as the udumbara flower. Yet no one has ever seen an udumbara flower, Mahamati, nor will anyone. But tathagatas, Mahamati, have been seen in the world and are seen now.

cmp.note: 「优昙钵花」：传说三千年一开、象征佛出世难遇的花。这里佛自己说：「从来没有人见过优昙花，以后也不会有，可是如来却有人见过、现在也看得见」，等于承认这是因人施设的比喻。中英文都照译。
cmp.en: The udumbara flower, said to bloom once in three thousand years, a symbol of how rarely a buddha appears. Here the Buddha himself says "no one has ever seen an udumbara flower, nor will anyone; but tathagatas have been seen and are seen now," in effect admitting it is a figure of speech suited to the listener. The Chinese and English both translate it as it stands.

verses.en: "It is not with reference to the statement establishing my own way that tathagatas are said to appear as rarely as the udumbara flower. When the statement establishing my own way is being taught, Mahamati, examples that go beyond the world's excellence are made fitting, since it is hard to believe, and it would be unbelievable to foolish ordinary people. In the realm of noble wisdom within oneself, examples do not work at all. And the tathagatas are reality. So examples are not set out for them.

"Rather, Mahamati, this is just a comparison: the tathagatas are like the sands of the Ganges, the same and not uneven, because they do not imagine or conceptualize. Just as, Mahamati, the sands of the Ganges, stirred up by fish, turtles, porpoises, crocodiles, buffalo, lions, elephants and the like, do not imagine or conceptualize, 'We are stirred up' or 'We are not,' but are free of conceptualizing, clear and free of dirt; in the same way, Mahamati, the sands of the powers, supernatural abilities and masteries in the great river Ganges of the noble wisdom within of the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones, though stirred up by all the tirthikas and the fools, fish and opponents, do not imagine or conceptualize. Because of the tathagatas' former vows, and to fulfill all the attainments of bliss for beings, they do not imagine or conceptualize. So the tathagatas are like the sands of the Ganges, without distinction, since they are free of favor and aversion.

"Just as, Mahamati, the sand of the Ganges, having the mark and nature of earth, is earth, and even burned in the fire at the end of an eon does not give up the nature of earth; and the earth, Mahamati, is not burned, since it is bound up with the element of fire; only foolish ordinary people, with a continuity fallen into falsehood, imagine it burning, but it is not burned, since it is the cause of that fire; in the same way, Mahamati, the Dharma-body of the tathagatas is like the sands of the Ganges, indestructible. Just as, Mahamati, the sands of the river Ganges are countless, so, Mahamati, the light of the tathagatas' rays is countless; to ripen and urge on beings, the tathagatas spread it out over all the assemblies of the buddhas.

"Just as, Mahamati, the sands of the river Ganges do not take on another nature than sand, sand staying just as sand; so, Mahamati, for the tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones there is neither arising nor ending in samsara, since the cause of the arising of existence has been cut off. Just as, Mahamati, from the sands of the river Ganges, taking some away makes no difference that is noticed, nor does adding some; in the same way, Mahamati, the knowledge of the tathagatas neither decreases nor increases through ripening beings, since the Dharma has no body. For what has a body, Mahamati, there is destruction, not for what has no body. And the Dharma has no body.

"Just as, Mahamati, the sands of the river Ganges, pressed by those who want ghee or oil, have no ghee or oil, so, Mahamati, the tathagatas, pressed by the sufferings of beings, do not give up the bliss of their vow as masters of the realm of Dharma, Mahamati, since they are filled with great compassion, until all beings have been brought to nirvana by the tathagatas. Just as, Mahamati, the sands of the river Ganges flow along with the current, not where there is no water, so, Mahamati, the tathagatas' teaching of all the Buddha's dharmas flows along with the current of nirvana. That is why the tathagatas are said to be like the sands of the Ganges. The meaning of 'going' does not apply to the tathagatas, Mahamati. The meaning of 'going,' Mahamati, is destruction. And the first beginning of samsara, Mahamati, is not known. Since it is not known, how could I speak of it in terms of going?
"The meaning of 'going,' Mahamati, is annihilation. And foolish ordinary people do not understand this."

Mahamati said: "If, Lord, the first beginning of beings wandering in samsara is not known, how then is the liberation of living beings known?" The Lord said: "The turning away of the cause, the habit-energy of conceptualizing the coarse tendencies of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, Mahamati; the turning-around of the basis of conceptualizing through fully knowing that outer objects are what one's own mind shows, Mahamati: that is liberation, not destruction. So, Mahamati, talk of the endless does not do anything. 'Endless limit,' Mahamati, is just another word for conceptualizing. Here there is no other being apart from conceptualizing, whether examined by understanding inwardly or outwardly. For all dharmas, Mahamati, are free of knowledge and the knowable. Only through not fully knowing one's own mind's conceptualizing does conceptualizing arise; through understanding it, it turns back."
On this it is said:
"Those who see the Leaders as like the sands of the Ganges, whose course ends in no destruction, see the tathagatas.
Just as the sands of the Ganges are free of all faults, flowing with the current, and permanent, so is the buddhahood of the Buddha."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "May the Lord teach, may the Sugata, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, teach me the momentary breaking of all dharmas and their mark of division. How, Lord, are all dharmas momentary?" The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "'All dharmas, all dharmas,' Mahamati, means good and bad, conditioned and unconditioned, worldly and world-transcending, blameworthy and blameless, with outflows and without outflows, taken up and not taken up.

"In brief, Mahamati, the five heaps of grasping, caused by the habit-energy of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness, are imagined as good and bad by foolish ordinary people fed by the habit-energy of mind, thinking mind and mind-consciousness. The attainments of the bliss of samadhi, Mahamati, as the happy abiding here and now, are called good and without outflows for the noble ones. Good and bad, Mahamati, are the eight consciousnesses. Which eight? The tathāgatagarbha called the storehouse consciousness, the thinking mind, mind-consciousness, and the five groups of consciousness described by the tirthikas. Here, Mahamati, the five groups of consciousness together with mind-consciousness arise divided by a succession of good and bad moments, their bodies undivided by the binding of a continuous stream. Having arisen, they perish. Not understanding what one's own mind shows, when one ceases, immediately another consciousness arises.

"Mind-consciousness, which grasps particular shapes and forms, arises joined with the five groups of consciousness, not lasting for a moment of time. This I call momentary. The storehouse consciousness, Mahamati, called the tathāgatagarbha, together with the thinking mind, is momentary through the habit-energy of the active consciousnesses, and not momentary through the habit-energy without outflows. And foolish ordinary people, clinging to the doctrine of momentariness, do not understand this momentariness and non-momentariness of all dharmas. Not understanding it, with a view of annihilation they will destroy even the unconditioned dharmas. The five groups of consciousness, Mahamati, do not transmigrate; they do not experience pleasure and pain; they are not causes of nirvana. But the tathāgatagarbha, Mahamati, together with the cause of experiencing pleasure and pain, arises and turns back, numbed by the four kinds of habit-energy.

cmp.note: 这里说藏识（如来藏）「就有漏习气而言是刹那的，就无漏习气而言不是刹那的」——同一个东西既刹那又不刹那。实叉难陀也照此译出。这是对当时说一切法刹那生灭的部派的回应。
cmp.en: Here the storehouse consciousness (the tathāgatagarbha) is said to be "momentary through the habit-energy of the active consciousnesses, and not momentary through the habit-energy without outflows": one and the same thing is both momentary and not. Śikṣānanda renders it the same way. It is a response to the schools of the time that held all dharmas to arise and perish in a moment.

verses.en: "And fools, their minds perfumed by the conceptualizing of the view of momentariness, do not understand.

"Again, Mahamati, gold, diamond and the relics of the Conqueror, which keep their weight and last for an eon, are special attainments that do not break. If, Mahamati, the attainment of realization were momentary, the noble ones would be not noble. But the noble ones are not not noble. Gold and diamond, Mahamati, keep the same weight; even lasting an eon, when weighed they neither lose nor gain. How then do fools, unskilled in teaching with hidden intention, conceptualize all inner and outer dharmas as momentary?"

Mahamati spoke again: "The Lord has said that buddhahood is reached by fulfilling the six perfections. Which are these six perfections? And how are they fulfilled?" The Lord said: "There are three distinctions in the perfections, Mahamati. Which three? Worldly, world-transcending and most world-transcending. Here, Mahamati, the worldly perfections: clinging to grasping self and what belongs to self, grasping the two extremes, for the sake of varied births in existence, longing for objects such as form, (people) fulfill the perfection of giving. In the same way, Mahamati, fools fulfill the perfections of moral conduct, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom. And they bring forth supernatural powers, to become Brahma. With the world-transcending perfections, shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, their minds fallen into grasping nirvana, apply themselves to giving and the rest, just as fools do, longing for nirvana as their own happiness.

"The most world-transcending perfections, Mahamati: through grasping that what one's own mind shows is only conceptualizing, through understanding the duality of one's own mind, since conceptualizing does not arise, since there is no taking up and grasping, and since one does not cling to the marks of form of one's own mind, the perfection of giving is born, for the good and happiness of all beings, in bodhisattvas, great beings, yogis of the highest yoga. That they practice the non-arising of conceptualizing toward that very object: that is moral conduct, and that is its perfection. Bearing the non-arising of that same conceptualizing, through fully knowing grasped and grasper: that is the perfection of patience. The energy by which one strives in the first and last parts of the night, through seeing what accords with yoga, through the turning away of conceptualizing: that is the perfection of energy. Not falling into grasping the nirvana of the tirthikas through the ending of conceptualizing: that is the perfection of meditation.

"The perfection of wisdom is this: when, since one's own mind's conceptualizing does not exist, examining with understanding, one does not fall into the two extremes, through the destruction of former karma preceded by the turning-around of the basis, and one applies oneself to attaining the noble course within: that is the perfection of wisdom. These, Mahamati, are the perfections. This is the meaning of perfection. On this it is said:
"Fools imagine the conditioned as empty, impermanent and momentary; with the examples of a river, a lamp and a seed, the meaning of momentary is conceptualized.
Without activity, momentary, solitary, free of ending, and the non-arising of dharmas: this I teach as the meaning of momentary.
I do not teach fools that things break immediately after arising; through the unbroken (succession) of things, conceptualizing trembles in its course.
Ignorance is their cause, which sets minds going. In between, what state is it in, until form is born?
Destroyed immediately, another mind arises. Form does not last in time; on what will it depend to arise?
Since the mind that arises from whatever has a false cause, it is not established; how can its momentary breaking be settled?
The attainment of yogis, gold, the relics of the conquerors, and the palaces of the Abhasvara gods are unbreakable by any worldly cause.
The abidings, the attained dharmas, the buddhas' wealth of knowledge, being a monk, reaching the truth: seen like this, how are they momentary?
Forms such as a gandharva city and illusions: are they not momentary? Unreal and real, some real ones come to hand."

cmp.note: 最后半句写本可能有讹误，字面「有些真实的到了手上」，意思不太通。英文照字面译，读者应知此处原文不明。
cmp.en: The last half-line may be corrupt in the manuscripts; literally "some real ones have come to hand," which doesn't make clear sense. The English translates it literally; readers should know the original is unclear here.

verses.en: Here ends the sixth chapter, On Momentariness, in the Lankavatara.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · On Transformation (Nairmāṇika)
chapters.intro: Mahamati asks: the Buddha predicts arhats will become buddhas and says he never spoke a word, yet he was slandered and once came home with an empty bowl. How is he faultless? The predictions, the Buddha says, encourage people toward the Mahayana, and much is done by emanated buddhas; the real Buddha is neither in them nor apart from them.

verses.en: The seventh chapter, called "On Transformation."

Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, said to the Lord again: "The Lord has predicted that arhats will reach unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and that beings whose nature is not to enter final nirvana will reach tathagatahood. And between the night the Tathagata awoke to unsurpassed, perfect awakening and the night he entered final nirvana, the Lord has not uttered or spoken a single syllable. The tathagatas are always in samadhi; they do not reason or reflect; and they conjure up transformations and do the work of a tathagata through them. Why then is the mark of the consciousnesses being divided into a succession of moments taught? And Vajrapani always, constantly, follows close behind. And the first beginning is not known, yet the ending (nirvana) is made known. And there are Maras, the works of Mara, and the remnants of karma.

"As with the young woman Chincha, the wandering nun Sundari, the washed bowl and so on, Lord, obstacles of karma are seen. How then, Lord, has the knowledge of all aspects been reached with faults not abandoned?" The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied. The Lord said to him: "(The prediction to arhats was made) with the realm of nirvana without remainder in mind, to encourage those who have practiced the bodhisattva way. For there are, Mahamati, those who practice the bodhisattva way, here and in other buddha-fields, who long for the nirvana of the shravaka vehicle. To turn them away from their liking for the shravaka vehicle and to encourage them toward the course of the Mahayana, the transformation bodies predict (awakening) to transformation shravakas, not the Dharma-nature buddhas.

cmp.note: 旃遮摩那祇、孙陀利：两则佛传故事，都是外道雇女子诬陷佛陀（一个假装怀孕，一个被杀后诬为佛弟子所害）；「洗钵」指佛曾乞食空钵而回。大慧引这些来问：佛既已断尽过失，为什么还会遭受这些「业报」？中英文都只照写人名，没有展开故事。
cmp.en: Chincha and Sundari: two episodes in the Buddha's life in which rival teachers used women to slander him (one faked pregnancy; the other was murdered and her death blamed on the Buddha's monks); "the washed bowl" refers to the Buddha returning from an alms round with an empty bowl. Mahamati cites these to ask why, if the Buddha has ended all faults, he still met with such "karmic results." The Chinese and English both just give the names without retelling the stories.

verses.en: "With this in mind, Mahamati, the prediction to shravakas was taught. For there is no difference, Mahamati, between shravakas and pratyekabuddhas (and buddhas) in abandoning the obstruction of the afflictions, since liberation has a single taste. But here the obstruction to what is to be known is not abandoned. The obstruction to what is to be known, Mahamati, is purified through the special seeing of the no-self of things. The obstruction of the afflictions is abandoned, preceded by practice of seeing the no-self of persons, through the ending of mind-consciousness. Freedom from the obstruction of dharmas is purified through the ending of the habit-energy of the storehouse consciousness. With the ancient abiding of the Dharma in mind, and since there is nothing new or final, the Tathagata teaches the Dharma with the very letters (taught) before, without reasoning or reflecting. Since he acts with full awareness and his mindfulness is never lost, he does not reason or reflect; since he has abandoned the four grounds of habit-energy, is free of the two kinds of death, and has abandoned the two obstructions, of the afflictions and of what is to be known.

"The seven, Mahamati, thinking mind, mind-consciousness, eye-consciousness and the rest, are momentary, since habit-energy is their cause; they lack the side of the good and without outflows; they do not transmigrate. But the tathāgatagarbha, Mahamati, transmigrates, the cause of nirvana, pleasure and pain. And foolish ordinary people, their minds thrown into confusion by emptiness, do not understand. Vajrapani follows at the side of the created transformation tathagatas, Mahamati, not of the original tathagatas, arhats and fully awakened ones. For the original Tathagata, Mahamati, is turned away from all the means of knowledge and senses of all fools, shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and tirthikas. Those who dwell in the bliss here and now reach him through the acceptance of the knowledge of the Dharma of realization. So Vajrapani does not follow them. For all the transformation buddhas are not born of karma. The Tathagata is not in them, nor is the Tathagata apart from them.

"Like a potter working with his materials, (the transformation buddha) does the work of beings, and teaches what is endowed with marks, but not the statement establishing his own way, the realm of the noble course within. Again, Mahamati, from the cessation of the six groups of consciousness, foolish ordinary people fall back on the view of annihilation, and through not understanding the storehouse, they come to views of permanence. The first beginning of one's own mind's conceptualizing, Mahamati, is not known. Liberation is known through the turning away of one's own mind's conceptualizing. Through abandoning the four kinds of habit-energy, all faults are abandoned."
On this it is said:
"Three vehicles and no vehicle: for the buddhas there is no (final) nirvana. All are predicted to buddhahood, and they are taught as free of faults.
The knowledge that ends in realization, the course without remainder, and encouragement for the faint-hearted: this was taught with that in mind.
The knowledge brought forth by the buddhas, the path taught by them: by that alone they go, and by no other; so there is no (final) nirvana for them.
The habit-energy of existence, desire, form and views is fourfold; born of mind-consciousness, they stay in the storehouse and the thinking mind.
With mind-consciousness, the eye and the rest, there is annihilation because of impermanence; and permanence through the beginningless, nirvana, for those with views."
Here ends the seventh chapter, On Transformation, in the Lankavatara Sutra.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · On Not Eating Meat (Māṃsabhakṣaṇa)
chapters.intro: Mahamati asks about the faults of eating meat. The Buddha gives many reasons: every being was once your relative; meat frightens animals and brings scorn on the teaching; killing happens because people buy meat. He never allowed disciples meat, he says; earlier rules allowing meat not killed for them were only steps, and here it is banned outright.

verses.en: The eighth chapter, called "On Eating Meat."

cmp.note: 梵文品名只是「食肉品」，没有「断」字；白话据实叉难陀的品名「断食肉品」加了「讲为什么不该吃肉」。英文照梵文译 On Eating Meat，目录里的章名则用 On Not Eating Meat，取这一品的结论。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit chapter title is just "On Eating Meat," without "not"; the plain Chinese follows Śikṣānanda's title 断食肉品 ("Giving Up Meat") and adds "why one should not eat meat." The English translates the Sanskrit line as "On Eating Meat," while the table-of-contents title uses "On Not Eating Meat," taking the chapter's conclusion.

verses.en: Then the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, having questioned the Lord in verse, made a further request: "May the Lord, the Tathagata, arhat, fully awakened one, teach me the merits and faults of eating meat, so that I and other bodhisattvas, great beings, in the present and future, may teach the Dharma to beings perfumed by the habit-energy of past lives as flesh-eating animals, greedy for meat, to help them give up their craving for flavor; so that those meat-eating beings, giving up their craving for flavor and longing for the food of the flavor of Dharma, loving all beings as an only child, may gain great kindness toward one another; and having gained it, trained on all the bodhisattva stages, may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening; or, resting on the stages of shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, may move on to the unsurpassed stage of a tathagata.

"Lord, even other tirthikas whose teachings are badly taught, who cling to Lokayata views and teach being and non-being, annihilation and permanence, forbid eating meat and do not eat it themselves; how much more should the fully awakened one, whose single flavor is compassion, the protector of the world, (forbid it). Yet in your teaching people eat meat themselves, and eating it is not forbidden. So may the Lord, who has compassion for the whole world, who sees all beings alike as an only child, the greatly compassionate one, out of compassion teach me the merits and faults of eating meat, so that I and other bodhisattvas may teach the Dharma to beings as it truly is." The Lord said: "Then listen, Mahamati, and keep it well in mind. I will tell you." "Yes, Lord," the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being, replied.

The Lord said to him: "For countless reasons, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. I will give only the main points. Here, Mahamati, among living beings wandering through samsara on this long road, there is hardly a single being who has not been your mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, or some other relative or kin. That relative, having changed bodies in another birth, has come to be among the wombs of wild animals, livestock and birds. How could a bodhisattva, a great being, who wants the Buddha's Dharma and wants to regard all beings as himself, eat meat that comes from all creatures and living things?

"Even rakshasas, Mahamati, hearing this excellent nature of the tathagatas' Dharma, give up their rakshasa nature, become compassionate, and turn away from eating meat; how much more people who love the Dharma. So, Mahamati, since in birth after birth all beings are to be thought of as relatives and kin, and to cultivate the thought of all beings as an only child, all meat is not to be eaten. Meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. And because of adulteration, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva of good conduct. For the meat of dogs, donkeys, camels, horses, oxen, humans and so on, Mahamati, is not eaten by people; and yet, Mahamati, butchers in the back streets sell it for money as if it were edible. For that reason too, Mahamati, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva.

"And because it comes from semen and blood, Mahamati, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva who wants purity. And because it frightens beings, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva yogi who wants kindness. Just as, Mahamati, dogs, seeing from far off meat-eating people such as Dombas, Chandalas and fishermen, bark in fear, and some are frightened half to death, thinking 'they will kill us too'; in the same way, Mahamati, other small creatures living in the air, on land and in water, seeing meat-eaters from far off and catching their smell with their keen noses, run away fast, as people do from a rakshasa, and some fear for their lives. So, Mahamati, because it frightens beings, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva yogi who dwells in great kindness; it is the food of ignoble people and smells bad.

"And because it brings disrepute and is avoided by noble people, Mahamati, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva. Noble people, Mahamati, eat the food of seers, not meat and blood. For that reason too meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva.

"And to protect the minds of many people, if one wishes to keep the teaching from being slandered, Mahamati, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. For there are people in the world, Mahamati, who slander the teaching: 'What kind of ascetics are these, and where is their brahminhood? They have abandoned the food of the seers of old and, like flesh-eating beasts, eat meat and fill their bellies, terrifying the small creatures living in the air, on land and in water, wandering all over this world frightening everything. Their asceticism is ruined, their brahminhood destroyed; they have neither Dharma nor discipline.' With minds hostile in many ways, they slander the teaching itself. So, to protect the minds of many people, if one wishes to keep the teaching from being slandered, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion.

"And because it shares the repulsive stench of a corpse, Mahamati, meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva. When the flesh of a dead human being is burned, Mahamati, and the flesh of other creatures, there is no difference in the smell. Both kinds of flesh smell equally bad when burned. For that reason too, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva yogi who wants purity.

"For those who live in cemeteries, Mahamati, and in remote dwellings in forests and wilds haunted by spirits, for yogis and practitioners of yoga who dwell in kindness, for holders of spells who want to master their spells, (meat) obstructs mastering spells and liberation; and sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahayana see that it obstructs the accomplishment of all yoga. So, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva who wants the good of himself and others. And because it produces a taste for flavor in the consciousness whose object is form, all meat is not to be eaten by a compassionate bodhisattva who regards all beings as himself. And because even the gods avoid such a person, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion.

"And because his mouth smells terrible even in this life, Mahamati, all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion. He sleeps badly and wakes badly. They have evil dreams that make the hair stand on end. When he lives alone in an empty house or in seclusion, spirits steal his vitality. He is startled, sometimes terrified, and falls into fear for no reason. He does not know moderation in food, and what he eats, drinks and chews does not digest properly or nourish him. His belly fills with worms and is a source of leprosy; he has many illnesses; and he does not gain the perception of food as repulsive.

"When I teach that food should be taken as if it were the flesh of one's own son, or as medicine, Mahamati, how could I allow my disciples meat and blood as food, which is eaten by ignoble people, avoided by noble ones, brings many faults, lacks all merits, is not the food of seers, and is not proper?

cmp.note: 「如食子肉」：佛教常用的比喻，说出家人吃东西要像一对夫妇在荒野中不得已吃自己孩子的肉那样，没有贪着，只为活命。白话直译，英文也照字面，不加淡化。
cmp.en: "As if it were the flesh of one's own son": a common Buddhist image saying that a renunciant should eat the way a couple stranded in the wilderness might, out of sheer necessity, eat their own child's flesh: without relish, only to survive. The plain Chinese translates it literally, and so does the English, without softening it.

verses.en: "What I have allowed, Mahamati, is the food eaten by all noble people, avoided by the ignoble, bringing many merits, free of many faults, the food of all the seers of old: food made from rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, beans, lentils and so on, with ghee, oil, honey, molasses, raw sugar, sugar lumps, candy and the like; this I consider proper. But in the future, Mahamati, some deluded people, who argue all sorts of theories about the discipline, perfumed or not by the habits of flesh-eating families, set on craving flavor, will not like this fine food.

"But I say it (is fitting) for those, Mahamati, who have done service under the conquerors of the past, who have planted roots of good, who have faith and do not conceptualize, many in number, sons and daughters of good family of the Shakya clan, not attached to body, life or possessions, not greedy for flavor, not covetous, compassionate, wanting to regard all beings as themselves, looking on all beings with love as an only child: the bodhisattvas, great beings.

"Once long ago, Mahamati, in the past, there was a king named Simha Saudasa. Indulging excessively in eating meat, utterly set on the craving for flavor, he even ate human flesh. Because of this he was abandoned by friends, ministers, relatives and kin, let alone the people of the city and the countryside. Losing his kingdom and lands, he met with great disaster because of meat.

"And even Indra, Mahamati, who had become lord of the gods, because of the faulty habit-energy of eating meat in a former birth, took the form of a hawk and chased Vishvakarman, who had taken the form of a dove; and (the king) put himself on the scales. Because of this, King Shibi, who had compassion for innocent beings, was made to suffer greatly. So, Mahamati, even for Shakra, who had become king of the gods, what was practiced over many births brought harm to himself and others; how much more to others.

cmp.note: 尸毗王割肉喂鹰的本生故事：帝释化鹰、毗首羯磨化鸽，试验尸毗王，王割下自己的肉放上秤去换鸽子的命。梵文这一句省略了「尸毗王」这个主语，句子不太通顺，白话用括号补了出来，英文也加括号补出 the king。
cmp.en: The birth story of King Shibi, who cut off his own flesh to feed a hawk: Indra became a hawk and Vishvakarman a dove to test King Shibi, who put his own flesh on the scales to ransom the dove's life. The Sanskrit sentence leaves out "King Shibi" as subject and reads awkwardly; the plain Chinese supplies it in parentheses, and the English adds "(the king)."

verses.en: "And other kings, Mahamati, carried off by their horses and wandering in the forest, mated with a lioness out of fear for their lives and fathered children. Through descent from that union with a lion, princes such as Kalmashapada, because of the faulty habit-energy of eating meat in former births, even after becoming rulers of men, became meat-eaters. And in this very life, Mahamati, even in a village of seven huts, through great greed for meat and excessive indulgence, people become terrible eaters of human flesh, dakas and dakinis. And in the round of births, Mahamati, through the same attachment to the flavor of meat, they fall into the wombs of great meat-eaters such as lions, tigers, leopards, wolves, hyenas, cats, jackals and owls, and into the still more terrible wombs of rakshasas and the like, which eat even more flesh. Fallen there, they reach a human womb again only with difficulty, let alone nirvana.

"These and other faults of eating meat, Mahamati, arise in those who indulge in it; and in the opposite case there are many more merits. But foolish ordinary people, Mahamati, do not understand these and other merits and faults. Seeing merits and faults like these, Mahamati, I say that all meat is not to be eaten by a bodhisattva whose nature is compassion.

"If no one ate meat in any way at all, Mahamati, no one would kill for it. For innocent creatures, Mahamati, are mostly killed for money, and seldom for any other reason. It is terrible, Mahamati: those who indulge excessively in the craving for flavor eat even human flesh; how much more the flesh of other animals, birds and creatures. Mostly, Mahamati, it is deluded people tormented by craving for the flavor of meat who have set out nets and traps of every kind, so that bird-catchers, butchers, fishermen and the like slaughter innocent creatures that move in the air, on land and in water, in many ways, for money. Their minds have grown hard and harsh, Mahamati; like rakshasas, they have lost all pity; killing and eating creatures while knowing them to be living beings, they never feel any pity.

"And there is no meat, Mahamati, that is proper because it was not done by oneself, not ordered, and not intended, on which basis I might allow it to shravakas. But in the future, Mahamati, there will be deluded people who go forth in my own teaching, claim to be sons of the Shakya, carry the banner of the ochre robe, their minds damaged by wrong thinking, arguing all sorts of theories about the discipline, holding the view of a real self in the body, set on craving flavor, who will compose various specious reasons for eating meat. They will think they can falsely accuse me. Making up an occasion for this or that, they will say: 'On this occasion this happened; the Lord allowed eating meat as proper.' And it is said among the fine foods, and the Tathagata himself, they say, ate it.

cmp.note: 「不是自己杀、不是叫人杀、不是专为自己杀」：这就是早期戒律里允许比丘吃的「三净肉」的三个条件。《楞伽经》在这里明确否定了这条开许。白话、英文都照梵文直译，不替任何一方辩护。
cmp.en: "Not done by oneself, not ordered, not intended": these are the three conditions of the "threefold pure meat" that the early monastic code allowed monks to eat. Here the Lankavatara explicitly rejects that allowance. The plain Chinese and English both translate the Sanskrit directly, without arguing for either side.

verses.en: "But nowhere in any sutra, Mahamati, have I allowed it to be eaten, or taught it as proper among the fine foods.

"If, Mahamati, I had wished to allow it, or if it were proper for my shravakas to eat it, I would not forbid all meat-eating for yogis and practitioners of yoga who dwell in kindness, for cemetery-dwellers, and for sons and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahayana, to cultivate the thought of all beings as an only child; but I have forbidden it. Here, Mahamati, for sons and daughters of good family who love the Dharma, who have set out in any vehicle, cemetery-dwellers, those who dwell in kindness, forest-dwellers, yogis and practitioners of yoga, for the accomplishment of all yoga, to cultivate the thought of all beings as an only child, all meat is forbidden.

"In various texts of the teaching, I set out the rules of training in order, as one places the steps of a ladder: binding it with the three conditions, I did not forbid what was not done on their account. Then I forbade even the ten kinds of meat, including those that died naturally. But here in this sutra, all of it, entirely, in every way, without exception, is forbidden. For, Mahamati, I have not allowed meat-eating to anyone, I do not allow it, and I will not allow it. I say, Mahamati, that eating meat is not proper for those who have gone forth. And as for those, Mahamati, who will think they can falsely accuse me, saying 'the Tathagata too ate it,' that will bring long harm and misfortune to those deluded people, covered by the obstruction of the faults of their own karma.

cmp.note: 「像安排梯子的阶梯」：这一段承认戒律是逐步制定的（先有三净肉的开许，后来连十种肉也禁），而到这部经才全面禁止。这是对「为什么早期戒律允许吃肉」的一种解释。白话、英文都照原文译出。
cmp.en: "As one places the steps of a ladder": this passage concedes that the rules were laid down step by step (first the allowance of threefold pure meat, later a ban on ten kinds of meat), and only in this sutra is meat banned entirely. It is one explanation of why the early monastic code allowed meat. The plain Chinese and English both translate it as it stands.

verses.en: "For noble shravakas, Mahamati, do not eat the food of ordinary people, let alone meat and blood, which are improper. My shravakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, Mahamati, live on the food of Dharma, not on the food of flesh; how much more the tathagatas. For the tathagatas, Mahamati, are Dharma-bodies, living on the food of Dharma, not flesh-bodies, not living on any food of flesh. They have vomited up the habit-energy of craving and seeking for the requisites of all existence; they are free of the habit-energy of all afflictions and faults; their minds and wisdom are well freed; they know all and see all; they see all beings alike as an only child; they are greatly compassionate. Since I think of all beings as my only child, Mahamati, how could I allow my shravakas to eat the flesh of my own son, let alone eat it myself? That I allowed it to shravakas or ate it myself, Mahamati: there is no possibility of that."

cmp.note: 这里 āmiṣa 用的是本义「肉」，与 dharma 对举：「以法为食，不以肉为食」。前面第三品同一个词译成 gain（世俗利养），这里译 flesh。中文「法食 / 肉食」对得很整齐，英文 the food of Dharma / the food of flesh 也保留了这个对比。
cmp.en: Here āmiṣa is used in its root sense, "flesh," set against Dharma: "living on the food of Dharma, not on the food of flesh." In Chapter 3 the same word was rendered "gain" (worldly profit); here it is "flesh." The Chinese 法食 / 肉食 ("Dharma-food / flesh-food") pair neatly, and the English "the food of Dharma / the food of flesh" keeps the contrast.

verses.en: On this it is said:
"Liquor, meat and onions should not be eaten, great sage: so say the bodhisattvas, great beings, and the bulls among conquerors.
Favored by the ignoble, foul-smelling, bringing disrepute, the food of flesh-eaters: tell us, great sage, that meat is not to be eaten.
The faults there are in eating it, and the merits in not eating it: Mahamati, understand the faults there are in eating meat.
Because they were kin, because of adulteration, because it comes from semen and blood, because it frightens creatures, the yogi should avoid meat.
Meats and onions, liquors of all kinds, leeks and garlic too: the yogi should always avoid them.
He should avoid rubbing on oil, not sleep on beds pierced with spikes, (nor) in the holes and hollows of creatures, a place of great fear.
From food comes arrogance; from arrogance, imagining; from imagining, passion is born. So for that reason too one should not eat it.
From imagining, passion is born; through passion the mind is deluded; the deluded one gets entangled, is born, and is not freed.
For gain a creature is killed; for meat, money is paid. Both of these are evil deeds, and both are cooked in Raurava and the other hells.
The fool who goes against the Sage's word and eats meat, ordained in the Shakya's teaching, does so to ruin both worlds.
Those evildoers go to the most terrible hell; meat-eaters are cooked in the fierce Raurava and the rest.
Meat that is pure in three ways, not intended, not asked for, not prompted, does not exist. So one should not eat meat.
The yogi should not eat meat; it is condemned by me and by the buddhas. Beings eat one another, born in families of flesh-eaters.
He is born foul-smelling, despised, and mad, in families of Chandalas, Pukkasas and Dombas, again and again.
From the womb of a dakini he is born into a meat-eating family; that lowest of men is born in the womb of a rakshasi or a cat.
In the Hastikakshya, the Mahamegha, the Nirvana and the Angulimalika sutras, and in the Lankavatara Sutra, I have forbidden meat.

cmp.note: 这首偈列出几部「禁肉」的大乘经：《象腋经》《大云经》《涅槃经》《央掘魔罗经》，以及《楞伽经》本身。经中引用自己的名字，一般认为说明这一品是后来增补的。英文照写经名，不作评论。
cmp.en: This verse lists several Mahayana sutras that forbid meat: the Hastikakshya, the Mahamegha, the Nirvana and the Angulimalika sutras, plus the Lankavatara itself. A sutra citing itself by name is generally taken as a sign that this chapter was added later. The English gives the titles without comment.

verses.en: Condemned by buddhas, bodhisattvas and shravakas: if one eats it shamelessly, one is always born mad.
By avoiding meat and the like, one is born among brahmins or in a family of yogis, wise and wealthy.
Because of what is seen, heard or suspected, one should avoid all meat. Reasoners, born in families of flesh-eaters, do not understand.
Just as passion is an obstacle to liberation, so meat, liquor and the like are obstacles.
In time to come, meat-eaters speaking out of delusion will say: 'Meat is proper and blameless, praised by the Buddha.'
Taking food as medicine, again like the flesh of one's son, in moderation and as repulsive, the yogi should go for alms.
For those who dwell in kindness it is always condemned by me in every way; (eating it) one would be born together with lions, tigers, wolves and the like.
So one should not eat meat, which frightens people; since it goes against the Dharma of liberation, (not eating it) is the banner of the noble ones."
Here ends the eighth chapter, On Eating Meat, from the Lankavatara, the heart of the words of all the buddhas.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Dharanis (Dhāraṇī)
chapters.intro: The Buddha gives Mahamati several spells (dharanis), which he says all buddhas past, present and future teach, to protect those who preach this sutra. No spirit can harm someone who keeps and recites them; recited 108 times over someone possessed, they drive the demon off. The spells are given in their original sounds, untranslated.

verses.en: The ninth chapter, called "Dharanis."

cmp.note: 「陀罗尼」：持诵的咒语，字面是「能持」。这一品的咒语全是音节，没有可译的意思；中英文都只音写，不翻译。实叉难陀本也有这一品。
cmp.en: Dhāraṇī, a spell for recitation, literally "that which holds." The spells in this chapter are pure syllables with no translatable meaning; the Chinese and English both only transliterate them. Śikṣānanda's version also has this chapter.

verses.en: Then the Lord addressed the bodhisattva Mahamati, the great being: "Take up, Mahamati, the mantra syllables in the Lankavatara that the buddhas, the lords, of the past, future and present have spoken, speak and will speak. I too will speak them now, to protect the preachers of the Dharma. They are: tutte tutte, vutte vutte, patte patte, katte katte, amale amale, vimale vimale, nime nime, hime hime, vame vame, kale kale, kale kale, atte matte, vatte tutte, jnette sputte, katte katte, latte patte, dime dime, cale cale, pace pace, bandhe bandhe, ance mance, dutare dutare, patare patare, akke akke, sarkke sarkke, cakre cakre, dime dime, hime hime, tu tu tu tu (four times), du du du du (four times), ru ru ru ru (four times), phu phu phu phu (four times), svaha!" (These syllables are recited for their sound and are not translated.)

"These, Mahamati, are the mantra syllables in the Lankavatara, a Mahayana sutra. Whatever son or daughter of good family, Mahamati, takes up, holds, recites and masters these mantra syllables, no one will find an opening to harm them: no god or goddess, naga or nagini, yaksha or yakshini, asura or asuri, garuda or garudi, kinnara or kinnari, mahoraga or mahoragi, gandharva or gandharvi, bhuta or bhuti, kumbhanda or kumbhandi, pishaca or pishaci, ostaraka or ostaraki, apasmara or apasmari, rakshasa or rakshasi, daka or dakini, ojohara or ojohari, katapūtana or katapūtani, no non-human male or female: none of them will find an opening.

"If someone is possessed by an evil spirit, (that spirit,) when the mantra is recited over him a hundred and eight times, will go off weeping and wailing, who knows which way." (The Sanskrit of this sentence is garbled; meaning partly unclear.)

"Again, Mahamati, I will speak more mantra syllables. They are: padme padmadeve, hine hini hine, cu cule culu cule, phale phula phule, yule ghule yula yule, ghule ghula ghule, pale pala pale, munce munce munce, chinde bhinde bhanje marde pramarde dinakare svaha!" (Recited for their sound; not translated.)

"Whatever son or daughter of good family, Mahamati, takes up, holds, recites and masters these mantra syllables, no one will find an opening to harm them: no god or goddess, naga or nagini, yaksha or yakshini, asura or asuri, garuda or garudi, kinnara or kinnari, mahoraga or mahoragi, gandharva or gandharvi, bhuta or bhuti, kumbhanda or kumbhandi, pishaca or pishaci, ostaraka or ostaraki, apasmara or apasmari, rakshasa or rakshasi, daka or dakini, ojohara or ojohari, katapūtana or katapūtani, human male or female: none of them will find an opening. Whoever recites these mantra syllables will have recited the Lankavatara Sutra."
These mantra syllables were spoken by the Lord to ward off rakshasas.
Here ends the ninth chapter, called Dharanis, in the Lankavatara.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Verses (Sagāthaka)
chapters.intro: Nearly nine hundred verses, most restating in verse what the prose chapters taught. Some material is new: a prophecy that after the Buddha's death a monk named Naga will arise in the south, the four world ages and when buddhas appear, attacks on Indian schools such as Samkhya and Vaisheshika, and rules for monks' robes and food.

verses.en: The Chapter in Verse (Sagāthaka).

cmp.note: sagāthaka 字面就是「带偈颂的（一品）」，梵本只给了这个标题。实叉难陀把它定名为「偈颂品第十」，白话也照这个意思加了括注说明全品都是偈颂。
cmp.en: Sagāthaka literally means “(the chapter) with verses”; the Sanskrit gives only this bare title. Śikṣānanda names it 偈颂品第十 (jìsòng pǐn dì shí, “Chapter Ten, Verses”), and the plain Chinese adds a note that the whole chapter is in verse.

verses.en: Then Mahamati, the bodhisattva and great being, said this to the Blessed One:

cmp.note: 梵本说这些偈是大慧菩萨对世尊说的；实叉难陀的译本却写成「尔时世尊……而说偈言」，变成世尊重宣经义。白话和英文都照梵本，说话的人是大慧。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit it is Mahamati who speaks these verses to the Blessed One. Śikṣānanda’s version instead has 尔时世尊……而说偈言 (ěrshí shìzūn … ér shuō jì yán, “then the World-Honored One … spoke in verse”), making the Buddha the speaker. Both the plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit: the speaker is Mahamati.

verses.en: The world is free of arising and perishing, like a sky-flower (the spots a person with an eye disease sees floating in the air). Through your wisdom and compassion, you see that it can be found neither as existing nor as not existing.
The world is always like a dream, beyond both permanence and annihilation. Through your wisdom and compassion, you see that it can be found neither as existing nor as not existing.
All phenomena are like a magic show, beyond mind and consciousness. Through your wisdom and compassion, you see that they can be found neither as existing nor as not existing.
You always know that neither phenomena nor persons have a self, and you know the two obstructions: the afflictions and the knowable. You are pure, free of signs, through your wisdom and compassion.

cmp.note: 梵文只写 kleśa-jñeya「烦恼与所知」两个词，没有「障」字。白话按佛教惯例补成「烦恼障和所知障」，英文也补了 obstructions，这是读者需要知道的增补。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit just says kleśa-jñeya, “afflictions and the knowable,” with no word for “obstruction.” The plain Chinese follows Buddhist convention and fills in 烦恼障和所知障 (fánnǎo zhàng hé suǒzhī zhàng, “the obstruction of afflictions and the obstruction of the knowable”); the English adds “obstructions” too.

verses.en: You do not pass into nirvana, you do not stay in nirvana, and nirvana does not stay in you. It is beyond the knower and the known, beyond the two sides of existence and non-existence.
Those who see the sage (muni, a name for the Buddha) this way, as peaceful and free of arising, stop grasping and remain unstained, in this life and the next.
In summer a mirage shimmers and fools the mind; deer take it for water, but there is nothing really there.

In the same way, this thing whose seed is consciousness shimmers in the field of what is seen. Fools take it as something being born, just as people with an eye disease grab at the dark spots in their sight.
The meditator, the meditation, the object of meditation, letting go, seeing the truth: all of this is only imagining. Whoever understands this is set free.
These phenomena have no solid core; they arise from conceiving. And the very conceiving by which one thinks of them as “empty” is itself empty.

cmp.w: sāpyatra manyanā śūnyā yayā śūnyeti manyate
cmp.note: 梵本说的是：连「把它们想成空」的那个念头也是空的。实叉难陀译成「以分别即空，所分别非有」，变成「分别是空，所以被分别的东西不存在」，重点从「空见也要放下」移到了对象不存在。白话和英文都照梵本。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that even the thought by which one thinks “they are empty” is itself empty. Śikṣānanda has 以分别即空，所分别非有 (yǐ fēnbié jí kōng, suǒ fēnbié fēi yǒu, “since conceptualizing is empty, what is conceptualized does not exist”), shifting the point from “let go of the idea of emptiness too” to “the object does not exist.” The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The aggregates (skandhas, the five heaps that make up a person), with consciousness as the fifth, are like the reflection of a tree in water. What is seen is like a magic show or a dream; one should not conceptualize it by way of representation.
