Whoever sees the world as a magic show, a corpse made to walk by a spell, a mechanical puppet, a dream, lightning, or a cloud, and sees it cut off from its threefold continuity, is set free.
Through improper conceptualizing, consciousness starts running. It is eightfold or ninefold, many-colored, like waves on the great ocean.

cmp.note: 梵文是「八重、九重」，只是说识有八种或九种样子，没说是哪几种。实叉难陀写成「八九识」，读起来像在讲第八识、第九识这种具体名目。白话照梵文字面。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “eightfold, ninefold,” meaning consciousness takes eight or nine forms, without naming them. Śikṣānanda writes 八九识 (bā jiǔ shí, “eight or nine consciousnesses”), which reads like a reference to specific numbered consciousnesses. The plain Chinese stays literal.

verses.en: Constantly fed by habit-energy (vāsanā, the leftover traces of past actions), with intellect as its root and a firm base, the mind wanders among its objects, the way iron is drawn to a magnet.

It rests in all beings; it is the ground of the spiritual lineage, beyond reasoning. Freed from activity and beyond knowledge and the known, it turns back. (What “it” refers to is unclear in the Sanskrit.)
You will see the samādhi (deep meditative absorption) that is like illusion, which reaches beyond the ten stages, and you will see the king of mind, free of perception and consciousness.
When the mind has turned around, it then abides permanently, in a palace like a lotus, which arises from the realm of illusion.
Settled there, having reached the state where action takes no effort, one does what beings need, like a jewel that shows every color.
There is nothing conditioned or unconditioned apart from conceptualizing. Fools, confused, grasp at them, like a barren woman holding a son in a dream.
The person, the aggregates, the stream of continuity, the conditions and the elements should be known as without own-nature and unarisen; they are emptiness, beyond existence and non-existence.
My teaching is a skillful means; I do not teach any real mark. Fools grasp both the mark and the thing marked as truly existing.

I know everything, yet I am not an “all-knower”; I am in the midst of everything, yet there is no “everything.” Fools conceptualize, and say the world is awakened (meaning unclear); but I neither awaken to anything nor awaken anyone.

cmp.note: 梵文用了一个文字游戏：vettā「知者」带宾语 sarvasya「对一切」，跟复合词 sarva-vettā「一切知者」（一种头衔）对照。白话译成「知道一切，又不是知一切者」，英文用引号标出那个头衔，都尽量保住这个对照；实叉难陀压成「一切知非知」，对照就看不出来了。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit plays on words: vettā, “knower,” with the object sarvasya, “of everything,” set against the compound sarva-vettā, “all-knower,” a title. The plain Chinese and the English (with the title in quotation marks) keep the contrast; Śikṣānanda compresses it to 一切知非知 (yīqiè zhī fēi zhī, “knowing all is not knowing”), where the contrast is lost.

verses.en: This is just a designation, a mere name; as a mark it cannot be found. The aggregates that fools conceptualize there look like the tangle of hairs seen by someone with an eye disease.

Nothing comes into being that did not exist before, and nothing perishes through conditions. When one sees the conditioned as a barren woman’s son or a sky-flower, then, seeing grasper and grasped as confusion, one turns away from them.

I do not enter nirvana as an existing thing, through activity, or through a mark. I am at peace because consciousness, the cause of conceptualizing, has stopped. (An extra line follows: “where the mark that fools conceptualize does not perish.”)
When a great flood has drained away, no waves can rise; in the same way, once the variety of consciousness has stopped, it no longer runs on.
These things are empty, without own-nature, like illusions, never born. They cannot be found as existing or as not existing; they are like a dream.
I teach a single own-nature, free of reasoning and representation: the divine realm of the noble ones, free of the other two own-natures.

cmp.note: 「离开两种自性」指三自性里的遍计所执性和依他起性，剩下的「一种自性」就是圆成实性。梵文没点名，白话加了「另外」两字提示，英文也写 the other two；实叉难陀译成「自性无有二」，读起来像「自性不二」，意思偏了。
cmp.en: “Free of the two own-natures” refers to two of the three natures, the imagined and the dependent; the “single own-nature” left is the perfected. The Sanskrit names none of them; the plain Chinese adds 另外 (lìngwài, “other”) as a hint, and the English says “the other two.” Śikṣānanda’s 自性无有二 (zìxìng wú yǒu èr, “own-nature has no two”) reads like “own-nature is non-dual,” which shifts the meaning.

verses.en: A drunk person sees all sorts of firefly-like sparks that are not really there; they are seen because the body’s elements are thrown out of balance. The world is like that by nature.
An illusion can shine out on grass, sticks and potsherds, and yet that illusion does not really exist. Phenomena are like that by nature.
There is no grasper and nothing grasped, no one bound and no bond. It is like an illusion, a mirage, what we call a dream, like the spots seen by a diseased eye.
When someone seeking the truth sees without conceptualizing and without stain, then, having entered yoga, he will see me; there is no doubt.
There is no representation here at all, just as there are mirages in the sky. Knowing phenomena this way, one asserts nothing.
Phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, do not arise from conditions. It is because the mind is confused in the three realms that it appears in so many forms.

A dream and the world have the same nature, for in a dream too all kinds of forms are seen: enjoyment and touch just the same, even the world’s teacher passing out of the body, and actions. (The second half is hard to construe.)

cmp.note: 后半句梵文语法松散，大意是梦里也能看到种种享用、触觉、身死、世间导师和种种作为。实叉难陀却译成「若能如是见，身为世所尊」，变成「能这样看的人，会成为世间所尊敬的人」，和梵文差得很远。白话和英文都照梵文。
cmp.en: The second half of the Sanskrit is loosely built; roughly, in a dream too one sees enjoyment, touch, death, the world’s teacher, and actions. Śikṣānanda instead has 若能如是见，身为世所尊 (ruò néng rúshì jiàn, shēn wéi shì suǒ zūn, “whoever sees this way becomes honored by the world”), which is far from the Sanskrit. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The mind is the womb of the three realms; it is the confused mind that is seen, here and in the next world. Knowing that this is how the world goes, one should not imagine the world, since these things do not exist.
Fools, through delusion, see arising and passing away. One who has wisdom sees neither arising nor passing away.
In the divine Akanishtha heaven (the highest heaven of the form realm), free of every evil, they stay always in yoga, without conceptualizing, free of mind and mental factors.
Having gained the powers, the higher knowledges and the masteries, and having reached the goal of that samādhi, the fully awakened ones awaken there; it is an emanation that awakens here.
Countless millions of emanations go out from the buddhas. Everywhere, fools hear the Dharma from them, as though hearing an echo (the last word is uncertain in the Sanskrit).
It is free of beginning, middle and end, free of existence and non-existence; all-pervading, unmoving, pure; without variety itself, yet the source of all variety.
Covered over by the lineage of representation, it lies hidden in all embodied beings. Illusion exists because of confusion; illusion is not the cause of confusion.

Whatever exists at all exists through the mind’s delusion. Bound to the two own-natures and produced by the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) are the world, which is representation-only, the flood of views, and phenomena and persons.

cmp.note: vijñapti-mātra 是「唯识」的「唯」与「表/了别」，英文用固定译名 representation-only。白话写「只是了别」，意思对但不像术语；实叉难陀译成「惟有假施设」，把它说成「只是假名安立」，和 prajñapti（施设）混在一起了。
cmp.en: Vijñapti-mātra is the technical term behind 唯识 (wéishí, “consciousness-only”); the English uses the fixed rendering “representation-only.” The plain Chinese 只是了别 (zhǐshì liǎobié, “merely cognizing”) is right in sense but does not read as a term. Śikṣānanda has 惟有假施设 (wéi yǒu jiǎ shīshè, “only provisional designation”), which blurs it with prajñapti, “designation.”

verses.en: Having examined the world like this, once one has turned around at the base, one becomes my son, who keeps the perfected Dharma turning.
Heat, wetness, motion and hardness: fools conceptualize these phenomena. It is a superimposition of what is unreal; there is neither a thing marked nor a mark.

cmp.note: 热、湿、动、坚就是火、水、风、地四大的特性。梵文只列性质，没提「四大」；英文和白话都照字面，读者要知道这其实是在说四大元素。
cmp.en: Heat, wetness, motion and hardness are the defining qualities of the four great elements: fire, water, wind and earth. The Sanskrit lists only the qualities and never says “elements”; both the plain Chinese and the English stay literal, but the reader should know the four elements are meant.

verses.en: This body’s shape and its senses, made of eight substances (the four elements plus color, smell, taste and touch): fools, confused, imagine it as form, caught in the cage of samsara.
Fools imagine that things arise when causes and conditions come together. Not knowing this principle, they wander in the house of the three realms of existence.

All things are without own-nature, and so is people’s speech; and what is produced by imagining does not exist. Existence is like a dream. One should examine it this way; then one neither wanders in samsara nor enters nirvana. (The verse is metrically broken and partly unclear.)
The varied mind, called “the seed” (bīja), appears as the mind’s own field. When it appears, fools, attached to the two kinds of imagining, imagine that something arises.
Ignorance, craving and karma, the mind and its mental factors: from these it runs on, and so it is held to be dependent (the dependent nature). (The words “na mārakam” are corrupt; meaning unclear.)

cmp.note: 这两个字在梵本里讲不通，大概是抄错了。白话把运转的主语补成「世间」，实叉难陀则写「诸心依彼生」，主语是心。英文照实标出「意思不明」，没有硬补。
cmp.en: These words make no sense in the Sanskrit and are probably a copying error. The plain Chinese supplies 世间 (shìjiān, “the world”) as the subject that runs on, while Śikṣānanda has 诸心依彼生 (zhū xīn yī bǐ shēng, “minds arise depending on these”), making mind the subject. The English marks the spot as unclear rather than filling it in.

verses.en: And the “thing” they imagine is the mind’s confusion about its own field. In imagining it is never actually established; it is conceptualized through false confusion.
For embodied beings, the mind runs on tied to conditions. A mind set free of conditions I do not see; this is what I say.
Set free of conditions and without any mark of its own, when it no longer stays in the body, it is therefore outside my range.
It is like a king or a rich merchant who coaxes his sons with all kinds of toy deer, plays with them at home, and (later takes them) to the forest to meet real deer;
In the same way, I use the varied marks of phenomena as images, and tell my sons about the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi, the very edge of what is real), which each must come to know within himself.
Just as the ocean’s waves, raised by the wind, keep running on and dancing, never broken off,
so the flood of the storehouse consciousness, always stirred by the wind of sense-objects, keeps running on and dancing with its varied wave-consciousnesses.
The mind of embodied beings bends toward things in terms of grasped and grasper. What is seen has no such mark as fools conceptualize in it.

The storehouse consciousness is supreme, and representation is, again, the store. Because grasped and grasper have fallen away, I teach suchness (tathatā, things just as they are). (The first line is hard to construe.)
In the aggregates there is no self, no living being, no person. Consciousness arises, and consciousness ceases.
In a painting, hills and hollows are seen, yet they are not there. In the same way, the “thingness” of things is seen, yet it is not there.
Like a gandharva city (a phantom city seen in clouds or haze) or a mirage, what is seen always appears like this; but to wisdom it is not there.

It is free of the means of knowing and the senses; it is neither effect nor cause; it is beyond knower and known, beyond the thing marked and the mark. (The first word could also mean “produced by” rather than “free of”; the reading is uncertain.)
The fully awakened one, spoken of in dependence on the aggregates, has never been seen by anyone, anywhere. If no one anywhere has seen him, how could he be made out?
With conditions, reasons and examples, with a thesis and its ground, with the dream, the gandharva city, the fire-wheel (a torch whirled in a circle), the mirage, the moon and the sun,

cmp.note: pratijñā（宗）、hetu（因）、dṛṣṭānta（喻）是印度逻辑立论的三个环节。白话译成「主张」「理由」「譬喻」，英文用 thesis、reason、example，都是白话说法；实叉难陀用的是因明术语「因缘及譬喻，以此而立宗」，读者能看出这是在讲辩论格式。
cmp.en: Pratijñā (thesis), hetu (reason) and dṛṣṭānta (example) are the three steps of an argument in Indian logic. The plain Chinese uses everyday words, 主张 (zhǔzhāng, “claim”), 理由 (lǐyóu, “reason”) and 譬喻 (pìyù, “example”), and the English does the same. Śikṣānanda keeps the technical logic terms, 以此而立宗 (yǐ cǐ ér lì zōng, “with these one establishes the thesis”), so his reader sees it is about the format of debate.

verses.en: and with examples like the firebrand and the rest, I teach about non-arising. The imagined world is empty; it is what we call a dream, a confusion, an illusion. (The Sanskrit here is corrupt.)

cmp.note: 这行梵文抄坏了：adṛśyaṃ kulādi 讲不通，而且字面是「我宣说生」，跟上下文不合。实叉难陀读作「火焰毛等喻，以此显无生」，可见原本应是 alāta（火把）一类譬喻、内容是「无生」。白话和英文都按这个读法修正，英文加注说明原文有讹。
cmp.en: This line is corrupt: adṛśyaṃ kulādi makes no sense, and the words literally say “I teach arising,” which contradicts the context. Śikṣānanda reads 火焰毛等喻，以此显无生 (huǒyàn máo děng yù, yǐ cǐ xiǎn wúshēng, “with examples like flame and hair I show non-arising”), which suggests the original had something like alāta, “firebrand,” and “non-arising.” The plain Chinese and the English follow that reading, and the English flags the corruption.

verses.en: Relying on nothing in the three worlds, neither inside nor outside, and seeing existence as unarisen, one gains the acceptance of non-arising (anutpattikakṣānti, the calm acceptance that nothing is ever really born).
Then come the illusion-like samādhi and the mind-made body, the higher knowledges, the masteries, the powers, and the mind’s endless variety.
Things are unarisen, empty and without own-nature. What arises about them is confusion, and it is that confusion which ceases through conditions. (The construction is ambiguous.)
The mind appears to the mind, and outside it appears as things with form. What is seen is nothing other than this, not the way fools conceptualize it.
Well-trained practitioners, by way of designation, call up the chain of bones, the image of the Buddha, and the breaking down of the elements: the varied world.
Body, dwelling place and enjoyments are the three representations of the grasped. Manas (the thinking mind), the grasping representation and conceptualizing are the three on the grasper’s side.
As long as conceptualizing and the conceptualized stay within the range of words, reasoners will not see reality, because their reasoning confuses them.
When yogis see with wisdom that things have no own-nature, then the yogi rests, settled in the signless.
Ignorant people take a rooster smeared with soot for some other bird, though it is the same bird. Fools who do not understand treat the three vehicles the same way.

cmp.note: 梵文的关键是 sa evāyam「其实还是那一只」：涂了黑墨的公鸡被当成别的鸟，其实没变；三乘也是同一乘被看成三个。白话只说「当真」，没把「还是同一只」译出来；实叉难陀直接点明「实无有三乘」。英文照梵文补了「同一只鸟」。
cmp.en: The key Sanskrit phrase is sa evāyam, “it is the very same one”: a rooster blackened with soot is mistaken for another bird but has not changed; likewise the three vehicles are one vehicle seen as three. The plain Chinese only says 当真 (dàngzhēn, “taken as real”) and leaves out “the same one,” while Śikṣānanda states it outright: 实无有三乘 (shí wú yǒu sānshèng, “in truth there are no three vehicles”). The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Here there are really no disciples (śrāvakas) and no followers of the solitary buddhas’ vehicle. The forms of disciple and of the Victor (jina, a name for a buddha) that are seen are emanations displayed by bodhisattvas who are compassion itself.
The three realms of existence are representation-only, imagined through the two own-natures. When one turns around, there is suchness, free of the coming and going of phenomena and persons.
The sun, the moon, a lamp’s flame, the elements and jewels all work without conceptualizing. The buddhahood of a buddha is like that.
Just as people with an eye disease wrongly take a tangle of hairs to be real, fools wrongly conceptualize things in this same way.
Free of staying, perishing and arising, beyond permanent and impermanent, the things called defiled or purified are all like that tangle of hairs.
It is like someone who sees the whole world as golden: there is no gold there at all, yet the ground looks golden. (The first word is corrupt; meaning unclear.)

cmp.note: puttalika 字面像是「小人偶」，放在这里讲不通，多半是抄错。实叉难陀写「如着陀都药」，即吃了曼陀罗类的药（dhattūra），看什么都是金色。白话按这个意思补了「因药物」，英文不硬补，只标「意思不明」。
cmp.en: Puttalika looks like “little doll,” which makes no sense here and is probably a copying error. Śikṣānanda writes 如着陀都药 (rú zhuó tuódū yào, “as one who has taken the datura drug”), dhattūra, which makes everything look golden. The plain Chinese adds 因药物 (yīn yàowù, “because of a drug”) on that basis; the English does not fill it in and just marks the word as unclear.

verses.en: In the same way, fools, tainted by beginningless mind and mental factors, grasp as real things that arise from illusion and mirage.
One seed and no seed, the ocean as one and the single seed, and also all seeds together: see that this is the varied mind. (The meaning of this verse is unclear.)

When the one seed is pure and has turned around, it is seedless; it is even, because it is free of conceptualizing. From an overflow (of habit-energy) comes the tangle of births; it carries the varied seeds, and so it is called “all seeds.”
Here nothing arises through conditions and nothing ceases. What arise and cease are only the imagined conditions themselves.
The three realms of existence are mere designation (prajñapti, a name put on things); there is no real thing by own-nature. Reasoners will imagine the designation as a real thing.
Inquiring into the own-nature of things does not stop confusion. Seeing that the own-nature of things never arises: that is how one is set free.

cmp.note: 梵文是「（探求事物自性）并不能遮止迷乱」，白话和英文都照此译。实叉难陀写成「迷惑不待遣」，意思是「迷惑不必去遣除」，口气相反：一个说这条路行不通，一个说根本用不着去除。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that inquiring into the own-nature of things “does not stop confusion,” and the plain Chinese and the English follow that. Śikṣānanda writes 迷惑不待遣 (míhuò bù dài qiǎn, “confusion need not be dispelled”), which has the opposite tone: one says this method fails, the other says there is nothing to remove.

verses.en: Things are not called illusions because they resemble non-existence, nor is existence claimed for them. They are false and quick, like lightning; that is why they are said to be like illusions.
Nothing is about to be born and nothing has been born, and no conditions at all are found anywhere; it is only in conventional speech that such things are said.
Arising, perishing and defilement are not held back by conditions; what is held back by conditions is what fools conceptualize. (The sense is unclear.)
There is no own-nature, no representation, no real thing, and no store. These are all conceptualized by fools, bad reasoners who are under the sway (of conceptualizing).
When the Victor’s sons see the world as mind-only, they gain a body like nirvana, free of activity and formations, endowed with the powers, the higher knowledges and the masteries.
When the mind runs on, showing every kind of form, there is here neither mind nor forms; there is only the beginningless confused mind.
Then the yogi sees with wisdom that the world has no appearance. Going beyond signs, the representation of real things, and the stirring of manas, my sons walk free of conceptualizing.
A gandharva city, an illusion, a tangle of hairs, a mirage: unreal, they appear as real. So it is with how people imagine things.
All things are unarisen; only confusion is seen. Fools, attached to the two kinds of imagining, imagine that the confusion itself has arisen.
The mind that is a link in rebirth, varied and born of habit-energy, runs on as a flood of waves. When that is cut off, it no longer runs.
If a picture of varied objects appears in the mind, why does it not appear in the same way in empty space or on a wall? (The point of the argument is not clear.)

cmp.note: 梵文把虚空和墙并列：心里能现出图画，为什么虚空和墙上不能同样现出？白话照这个读法加「如果」。实叉难陀则把墙当成比喻：「心缘诸境起，如画依于壁」，心依境起就像画要画在墙上，虚空里画不出画。两种读法论证方向不同。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit pairs space and the wall: if a picture can appear in the mind, why not in space and on a wall in the same way? The plain Chinese reads it like that, adding 如果 (rúguǒ, “if”). Śikṣānanda makes the wall a simile instead: 心缘诸境起，如画依于壁 (xīn yuán zhū jìng qǐ, rú huà yī yú bì, “mind arises depending on objects, as a painting depends on a wall”), and a painting cannot be made on empty space. The two readings argue in different directions.

verses.en: If the mind only runs by taking some sign as its support, then the mind is produced by conditions, and “mind-only” does not hold.
It is mind that grasps mind; nothing has a cause outside it. The true nature of mind is pure; in the sky there is no habit-energy.
It is by clinging to one’s own mind that the mind runs on. Outside there is nothing that is seen; that is why it is mind-only.
Mind (citta) is the storehouse consciousness. Manas is what has thinking as its nature. That by which it grasps objects is called consciousness (vijñāna).

cmp.note: 这里给三个词下定义：citta 是藏识，manas 以思量为本质，vijñāna 是了别境界的识。中文传统对应「心、意、识」，白话照用；英文 mind、consciousness 在日常英语里常混用，所以保留梵文原词并把 manas 直接留作术语。
cmp.en: This verse defines three words: citta is the storehouse consciousness, manas is whatever has thinking as its nature, and vijñāna is the consciousness that grasps objects. Chinese tradition maps them neatly to 心、意、识 (xīn, yì, shí, “mind, intention, consciousness”), and the plain Chinese keeps that. In everyday English “mind” and “consciousness” blur together, so the English keeps the Sanskrit words in parentheses and leaves manas untranslated.

verses.en: Mind is always morally neutral (neither wholesome nor unwholesome). Manas moves on both sides. The consciousness at work in the present is both wholesome and unwholesome.
The gate to the highest truth is free of the two kinds of representation. Where it stands without any appearance, how could three vehicles be set up?
Mind-only, freedom from appearance, the abodes, and the buddha-stage: this is what the buddhas have taught, teach, and lead others to teach.

cmp.note: 梵文是「已说、正说、并使（别人）说」，第三个动词是使役式，不是将来式。白话译成「过去说过、现在正说、将来也会说」，套用了三世诸佛的常见说法；英文照梵文译成 lead others to teach。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “have taught, teach, and cause (others) to teach”; the third verb is causative, not future. The plain Chinese has 过去说过、现在正在说、将来也会说 (guòqù shuō guò, xiànzài zhèngzài shuō, jiānglái yě huì shuō, “said in the past, saying now, will say in future”), borrowing the familiar “buddhas of the three times” formula. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The first seven stages are mind; the eighth is free of appearance; two stages are the abode; the rest is the stage that is my own.
The stage that is pure and known only within oneself is the stage that is my own. It is the highest place of Maheshvara (the Great Lord), shining in Akanishtha.
Just as rays stream out from a fire, many-colored, lovely and gentle, and give form to the three realms of existence,
having formed the three realms, some now and some long before, they teach the vehicles there. This is the stage that is my own.

There is no set time for realization, nor is it a matter of passing through the stages (bhūmi, the levels of the bodhisattva path) or moving from one buddha-field to another. Going beyond mind-only, the fruit rests in what has no appearance.
Nonexistence and existence are seen, and all kinds of variety. Fools are turned upside down by their grasping; the variety itself is the inversion.

If knowledge is free of conceptualizing (vikalpa, the mind’s habit of carving things up into concepts), it makes no sense to say a real thing exists. Since the mind is not forms, that knowledge is free of conceptualizing.
The senses are called illusion; their objects are like dreams. The doer, the deed, and the doing do not exist in any way at all.

The meditations (dhyāna), the immeasurables (boundless kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity), the formless concentrations, and the complete cessation of perception: none of these exist in mind-only.
The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship: these are all confusions of the mind.
Fools imagine conditioned things as empty, impermanent, and momentary. With examples like a river or a lamp flame, they conceptualize the meaning of “momentary.”
But “momentary” means without activity, set apart, free of doing. The non-arising of things is what I mean by “momentary.”

cmp.note: kṣaṇika 平常就是「刹那生灭」。这里佛故意改了它的意思：真正的「刹那」不是一闪一闪地生灭，而是根本不生。白话照这个意思译；英文 momentary 保留原词，再用引号标出这是被重新定义的词。
cmp.en: Kṣaṇika normally means “arising and perishing in an instant.” Here the Buddha deliberately redefines it: true momentariness is not flickering birth and death but no arising at all. The plain Chinese follows that; the English keeps “momentary” and puts it in quotation marks to show it is being redefined.

verses.en: The non-arising of what is and what is not was taught by the Sankhya and Vaisheshika schools; it was they who brought up all the undetermined questions (avyākṛta, questions the Buddha set aside unanswered).

There are four ways of answering: a direct, one-sided answer; answering with a counter-question; answering by drawing distinctions; and setting the question aside. These hold back the doctrines of tirthikas (tīrthikas).

Everything exists conventionally; in the ultimate sense nothing exists. That things are without own-nature is seen even in the ultimate sense. Apprehending something where there is no own-nature: that is why it is called conventional.

cmp.note: upalabdhi 是「认得、抓得到」，意思是：在没有自性的地方却认得出东西来，这就叫世俗。白话译成「不可得、无自性」，正好把 upalabdhi 的意思说反了。实叉难陀的古译只有前四句，没有这一句。
cmp.en: Upalabdhi means “apprehending, getting hold of”: apprehending something where there is no own-nature is what makes it conventional. The plain Chinese renders it 不可得 (bù kě dé, “cannot be grasped”), which reverses the sense. Śikṣānanda’s classical version has only four lines and leaves this one out.

verses.en: If a thing that is caused by words had an own-nature, then a thing born of words could not be said not to exist.

cmp.note: 梵文这一颂是反驳的口气：「如果由言说而来的东西有自性，那就不能说它不存在。」实叉难陀的古译却写成正面的定义：「在无自性中，因言说而有物生起，叫做俗谛」，意思接近前一颂的最后一句。白话和英文都跟梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit argues by reductio: “if a thing that comes from words had own-nature, it could not be called nonexistent.” Śikṣānanda’s classical version instead gives a positive definition, 于无自性中，因诸言说故，而有物起者，是名为俗谛 (“where there is no own-nature, things arise because of words; this is conventional truth”), closer to the last line of the previous verse. The plain Chinese and the English both follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Words have no real thing behind them, so they do not exist even conventionally. And because the inversion would then be a real thing, there is no apprehension (meaning unclear).

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「因为颠倒是实物」，没有否定词。白话译成「既然颠倒不是实物」，多加了一个「不」。这半句本来就难懂，英文照字面译，并注明意思不清楚。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit literally says “because the inversion is a real thing,” with no negative. The plain Chinese renders 既然颠倒不是实物 (jìrán diāndǎo bú shì shíwù, “since the inversion is not a real thing”), adding a “not.” The half-line is obscure anyway; the English stays literal and flags it as unclear.

verses.en: If inversion really existed, then the lack of own-nature would not exist. Because inversion would be treated as a real thing, whatever is apprehended would have to be without own-nature, and that does not exist in any way at all.
This variety that is seen is the mind, perfumed by its coarse faults (dauṣṭhulya, the heavy residue of past error). Grasping appearances of form as if they were outside is the mind’s confusion.
Through conceptualizing and non-conceptualizing, conceptualizing is abandoned. Through conceptualizing and non-conceptualizing, the truth of emptiness is seen.

cmp.note: vikalpena avikalpena 可以读成「用分别和无分别」，也可以读成「以无分别对待分别」。白话取前者。实叉难陀分开说：「分别是可断，无分别能见」，把两句的功能分给两个词。英文照字面并列。
cmp.en: Vikalpena avikalpena can be read “by conceptualizing and non-conceptualizing” or “by non-conceptualizing toward conceptualizing.” The plain Chinese takes the first. Śikṣānanda splits the roles: 分别是可断，无分别能见 (“conceptualizing can be cut off; non-conceptualizing can see”). The English keeps the literal pairing.

verses.en: Like an illusory elephant painted in many colors, or leaves made to look like gold, so what is seen appears to people when their mind is perfumed by ignorance.
The noble one does not see delusion, nor any truth inside it. If truth were inside delusion, delusion itself would be truth.
If, after shaking off all delusion, some sign (nimitta, a mark or image the mind fixes on) still arises, that very sign is his delusion, like an eye disease not yet cured.
Just as someone with an eye disease mistakenly grasps at a tangle of hairs, so fools’ grasping at objects goes on.
Whoever sees the three realms of existence as like a tangle of hairs, like water in a mirage, like a dream or an illusion, is set free.
Conceptualizing, what is conceptualized, and the working of conceptualizing; the binding, what is bound, and the one bound: these six are the causes of liberation.

cmp.note: 梵文后半是「束缚、所缚、被缚者」。实叉难陀译成「转所转转因」，像是他依据的本子这里是和「转」有关的词，而不是「缚」。白话和英文跟梵文。
cmp.en: The second half of the Sanskrit lists “binding, what is bound, the one bound.” Śikṣānanda has 转所转转因 (zhuǎn suǒ zhuǎn zhuǎn yīn, “turning, what is turned, the cause of turning”), suggesting his manuscript had a word for “turning” rather than “binding.” The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: There are no stages, no truths, no buddha-fields, and no transformation bodies. Buddhas, solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddha), and disciples (śrāvaka) are all imagined too.

The person, the mental continuum, the aggregates (skandha, the five heaps that make up a person), conditions, and atoms, as well as primal matter, the Lord God, and a creator: all are conceptualized within mind-only.
Mind is everything; it is present everywhere and in every body. The unwise grasp it as varied, but mind-only has no marks.
There is no self in the aggregates, and the aggregates are not in a self. They are not the way they are conceptualized, yet it is not that they do not exist.
If all things existed the way fools conceptualize them, if they were just as they are seen, then everyone would be seeing the truth.
If no things existed at all, there would be neither defilement nor purity. They are not the way they are seen, yet it is not that they do not exist.

Delusion, signs, and conceptualizing are the mark of the dependent (paratantra, what arises from conditions). The name placed on that sign is the mark of the imagined (parikalpita, what conceptualizing projects).

When name, sign, and conceptualizing no longer arise for him, and conditions are known as mere convention with no real thing behind them, that is the mark of the perfected (pariniṣpanna, things as they truly are).

The buddhas of the reward body (vaipākika, the body that ripens from merit), the Victors (jina, a name for a buddha) of the transformation body, beings, bodhisattvas, and buddha-fields in every direction,
the Victors that flow out of the Dharma and the Victors of the transformation body: all of them come forth from Amitabha’s Land of Bliss (Sukhavati).

cmp.note: amitābha 是「无量光」。白话译成「无量光佛」，照字面；实叉难陀用的是「无量寿」，那是同一尊佛的另一个名字 amitāyus。英文直接用名字 Amitabha。
cmp.en: Amitābha means “boundless light.” The plain Chinese 无量光佛 (wúliàng guāng fó, “Buddha of Boundless Light”) is literal; Śikṣānanda uses 无量寿 (wúliàng shòu, “boundless life”), the other name of the same buddha, Amitāyus. The English simply uses the name Amitabha.

verses.en: What the transformation buddhas have taught, and what the buddhas born of ripening have taught, the way of the extensive sutras (vaipulya): understand its hidden intent.
What the Victor’s children have spoken and what the guides speak is spoken by the transformation buddhas, not by the Victors of the reward body.
These things are unborn, yet it is not that they do not exist. They are like a city of gandharvas (a mirage city in the sky), a dream, an illusion, a magical creation.
It is mind that sets things going, and mind that is set free. Mind is what is born, nothing else, and mind is what ceases.
People’s minds appear as objects; mind shows itself as something imagined. There are no objects: this is mind-only. Whoever is free of conceptualizing is set free.
The coarse residue of conceptual proliferation (prapañca, the mind spinning out ideas) piled up since beginningless time has cultivated conceptualizing, and from it false appearances arise.

Within consciousness, where objects appear, there is a knowledge whose field is suchness (tathatā, things just as they are). Once turned around at the base, it has no appearances; it lies in the field of the noble ones.
Meditation that examines meanings; meditation as fools practice it; meditation that takes suchness as its object; and the pure meditation of the Tathagatas.
In terms of the imagined own-nature, all things are unborn. Leaning on the dependent, people’s conceptualizing wanders in confusion.
When the dependent is cut loose from conceptualizing, it is pure. Turned around at the base, it is suchness, a dwelling free of imagining.

Do not conceptualize conceptualizing; conceptualizing does not truly exist. For one who conceptualizes delusion there is in fact no grasped and no grasper. Seeing objects as outside is imagining: that is the imagined own-nature.
The imagining with which people imagine has an own-nature that arises from conditions. Seeing outer objects is false; there are no objects, only mind.
For those who look closely with sound reasoning, grasping and the grasped come to an end. Outer objects do not exist the way fools conceptualize them.

The mind, stirred up by habit-energies (vāsanā, the traces past experience leaves in the mind), goes on appearing as objects. When the two kinds of imagining cease, there is knowledge whose field is suchness.
It arises without appearances, inconceivable, the field of the noble ones. Name, sign, and conceptualizing are the mark of the two natures; right knowledge and suchness are the mark of the perfected.

From the union of mother and father, joined with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) and manas (the thinking mind), it grows along with the semen, like a mouse in a jar of ghee.

cmp.note: 梵文的比喻是「酥油瓶里的老鼠」，在瓶里泡着、越长越大。白话照字面。实叉难陀写成「如苏在于瓶」，只剩酥油在瓶里，老鼠不见了。英文照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit image is “a mouse in a jar of ghee,” soaking there and growing. The plain Chinese is literal. Śikṣānanda writes 如苏在于瓶 (rú sū zài yú píng, “like ghee in a jar”): only the ghee is left, the mouse is gone. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Passing through the soft lump, the firm mass, the swelling, and the blister, impure and shaped by karma, it is driven by the wind of karma and the great elements and comes forth like a ripened fruit.
Five, five, and five (meaning unclear: perhaps the groups of five that make up the body), and nine openings like wounds; covered with nails, teeth, and hair, it is born, quivering.
As soon as it is born it is like a worm in excrement, or like a person just woken from sleep. Its eyes flicker toward forms, and it grows through imagining.
Through the meeting of palate and lips, sounds are pinned down by conceptualizing. So human speech starts up, and people conceptualize the way a parrot talks.
The doctrines of tirthikas are fixed; the Great Vehicle (Mahayana) is not fixed. It works according to the dispositions of beings, and wrong views find no footing in it.
(Mahamati asks:) This vehicle, known only by inner realization, is beyond the reach of logicians. Tell me: after the Protector has gone, in later times, who will uphold it?
(The Buddha answers:) After the Sugata (the Well-Gone, a name for the Buddha) has passed into nirvana, time will go by. Mahamati, understand this: there will be one who upholds the guiding teaching.

In Vedali, in the southern region, there will be a monk, glorious and of great fame, called Naga (traditionally identified as Nagarjuna). He will tear apart the positions of existence and nonexistence.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「名叫 nāga（龙）的」，没有说全名。白话照字面译成名字叫「龙」；实叉难陀直接写「龙树」，把传统的认定写进了经文。英文写 Naga，括号说明传统认为是龙树。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit only says “called Nāga” (“serpent, dragon”), not a full name. The plain Chinese stays literal with 龙 (lóng, “dragon”); Śikṣānanda writes 龙树 (Lóngshù, Nagarjuna) outright, putting the traditional identification into the text. The English says Naga and notes the tradition in parentheses.

verses.en: He will make my vehicle known in the world, the unsurpassed Great Vehicle; reaching the stage of Joy (the first bodhisattva stage), he will go to the Land of Bliss.
When things are examined with understanding, no own-nature can be pinned down. That is why they are taught as inexpressible and without own-nature.

For a thing produced by conditions, neither “it is not” nor “it is” holds. Those who imagine a thing within conditions as existing or not existing hold, I think, the views of tirthikas and have strayed far from the teaching.
The names of all things have been practiced over hundreds of lifetimes, and are still being practiced, as people conceptualize for one another.
If nothing were named, the whole world would fall into confusion. So names are made, to clear confusion away.
Fools conceptualize things with three kinds of conceptualizing: delusion, conceptualizing through names, and conceptualizing produced by conditions.
Things that by nature neither cease nor arise, that are like the sky, and that have no own-nature: these have the mark of the imagined.
And there are things that arise like a reflection, an image, an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a whirling firebrand, a gandharva city, or an echo.

cmp.note: 梵文这一颂只列出比喻，没有说它们属于哪一种自性。按上下文是讲依他起；实叉难陀直接补了一句「是则依他起」。白话用括号补「还有一类」，英文也只照梵文列出。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit verse only lists the similes and does not say which nature they belong to. From context it is the dependent nature, and Śikṣānanda adds 是则依他起 (shì zé yītāqǐ, “this is the dependent”). The plain Chinese bridges with “there is another kind”; the English likewise just lists them.

verses.en: Non-duality, suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, the true nature of things, and non-conceptualizing: these, I teach, have the mark of the perfected.
The field of words and mind is false; what is true is discerned by wisdom (meaning unclear). The mind falls into the two extremes, so wisdom is not imagining.
Existence and nonexistence are the two extremes, as far as the mind’s field reaches. When that field is shaken off, the mind truly ceases.
With no grasping of objects and with cessation, nothing is there; yet the state of suchness exists, as the field of the noble ones (meaning uncertain).
Things do not appear to fools the way they appear to the wise. To the wise they appear like this: all things are without marks.
As fools take a fake necklace for gold, something that is not gold but looks like gold, so do poor logicians take things.
Those who hold that a thing arises after not being, perishes after being, and by conditions both is and is not, do not stand in my teaching.
Since there is no beginning and no end, things stand in the mark of what is real. The world is “like cause and maker” (meaning unclear), and logicians do not understand.

cmp.note: kāraṇa-kara-vat 字面是「像因和作者那样」，读不通，可能原文有讹。白话和实叉难陀都译成「世间没有造作」，等于把它读成否定。英文照字面并注明意思不清楚。
cmp.en: Kāraṇa-kara-vat literally reads “like cause and maker,” which makes little sense and may be corrupt. The plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda both read it as a negation, 世间皆无作 (shìjiān jiē wú zuò, “the world has no making”). The English stays literal and flags it as unclear.

verses.en: The past thing exists, the future thing exists, the present thing exists; therefore things are unborn.
Those who imagine change, time, shape, the elements, existence, the senses, and a taking-up in the intermediate state between lives are not wise.
The Victors do not describe the world as dependently arisen; rather, this world is nothing but conditions, like a city of gandharvas.

cmp.note: 梵文说诸佛「不说世间是缘起的」，而是说世间只是缘、像海市蜃楼。实叉难陀的古译完全不同：「诸缘和合故，说有法；离和合则不生不灭」，像是另一个版本。白话和英文跟梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the buddhas “do not describe the world as dependently arisen,” but as mere conditions, like a mirage city. Śikṣānanda’s version is quite different: 诸缘和合故，是故说有法；若离于和合，不生亦不灭 (“because conditions combine, things are said to exist; apart from combination, nothing arises or ceases”), apparently from another recension. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: This is only a convention about things; on that basis we say “this” and “that.” Apart from convention, it is neither born nor does it cease.
In a mirror, in water, in an eye, in vessels and in jewels, an image is seen, yet the image is not anywhere at all.
In the same way the mind appears as things, like a mirage in the sky. It is seen in many forms, like a barren woman’s own son seen in a dream.
My vehicle, the Great Vehicle, is not sound, not letters, not the truths, not the liberations, and not the field without appearances.
Rather, the Great Vehicle is mastery over concentrations (samādhi), and a body made of mind, many-formed, adorned with the flowers of the masteries.
Within conditions, a thing is not established either as one or as separate. Arising is called just a coming together, and ceasing is just a falling apart.

cmp.note: samāsa 有两个意思：「聚合」和「简略」。白话取「聚合」，说生就是诸缘聚在一起；实叉难陀取「简略」，译成「略说以为生，广说则为灭」。英文跟白话，取「聚合」。
cmp.en: Samāsa has two meanings: “coming together” and “in brief.” The plain Chinese takes the first, arising as conditions gathering; Śikṣānanda takes the second, 略说以为生，广说则为灭 (“said briefly it is arising, said at length it is ceasing”). The English follows the plain Chinese.

verses.en: Emptiness of the unborn is one kind; emptiness in what has been born is another. Emptiness of the unborn is the higher; emptiness of the born perishes.
Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvana, the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the many-formed mind-made body: I have taught these as different names for the same thing.
Those who imagine they become pure through the sutras, the monastic code, and the Abhidharma, going by the words and not the meaning, are not relying on selflessness.
Existence has never been established through conditions, not by tirthikas, not by buddhas, not by me, not by anyone. So how could there be nonexistence?
Who has ever established through conditions an existence that could then turn into nonexistence? It is the wrong view that things arise that makes people conceptualize “is not” and “is.”
For one who sees the world as quiet and set apart, nothing arises and nothing ceases; he does not fall into “is” or “is not.”
Something called a hare’s horn is seen: people’s conceptualizing is what exists. Those who imagine are deluded, like deer chasing a mirage.
Conceptualizing keeps running because of clinging to conceptualizing. Conceptualizing without a cause would not even make sense as conceptualizing.
Grasping at water where there is no water, like a mirage in the sky: objects are seen by fools, but the noble ones see nothing set apart in them (meaning uncertain).
The seeing of the noble ones is pure. It comes from the three gates of liberation (emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness), is free of arising and breaking apart, and moves in what has no appearance.
Depth, vastness, and breadth, knowledge, buddha-fields, and powers: these I teach to the Victor’s children (bodhisattvas). To the disciples I teach impermanence.

cmp.note: 梵文说：对声闻弟子，我讲的是无常。实叉难陀写成「非为诸声闻」，只说这些不是讲给声闻听的，把「无常」略掉了，下一颂才讲。白话和英文跟梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that to the disciples the Buddha teaches impermanence. Śikṣānanda has 非为诸声闻 (fēi wèi zhū shēngwén, “not for the disciples”), dropping “impermanence,” which only comes up in the next verse. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: That the three realms are impermanent and empty, with no self and nothing belonging to a self: these general marks I teach to the disciples.
No attachment to any thing, solitude, living alone: this fruit, beyond reasoning, I teach to the Victor’s children who are solitary buddhas.
Embodied beings take outer things as having an own-nature that is imagined, and the dependent too. Not seeing their own confusion, the mind starts running from there.
The tenth stage would be the first, and the first would be the eighth; the ninth would be the seventh, and the seventh would be the eighth.
The second would be the third, the fourth would be the fifth, and the third would be the sixth. Where there are no appearances, how could there be any order of steps?
For yogis, the absence of appearances is not the nonexistence of things. Through the sameness of existence and nonexistence, the fruit of the noble ones is born.

How can the nonexistence of things bring about sameness? How indeed? When the mind no longer takes outer and inner as things in motion, then it brings things to an end, by seeing the mind as sameness.
In samsara without beginning, the mind is wrapped up in grasping at things. As one peg is used to knock out another, fools are coaxed and turned back.
Having that as its cause and that as its support, and resting on the movement of manas, it provides the cause for the mind, and consciousness rests on it (what “that” refers to is unclear).

Supernormal powers (abhijñā) are gained in four ways: from the ripening of karma, from empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna, a buddha’s sustaining power), from being born into a certain class of beings, and in dreams.
Those gained in a dream, those gained by the Buddha’s grace, and those that come with one’s class of being, destiny, and lineage: these are born from the ripening of consciousness.

cmp.note: 梵文最后说：这些都是「识的果报所生」。实叉难陀却写「皆非报得通」，说它们都不是果报得来的神通，意思正好相反，可能他依据的本子不同。白话和英文跟梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit ends by saying these powers are all “born from the ripening of consciousness.” Śikṣānanda writes 皆非报得通 (jiē fēi bào dé tōng, “none are powers gained by ripening”), the exact opposite, perhaps from a different manuscript. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The mind, steeped in habit-energies, goes on appearing as things. As long as fools do not understand, one should teach them in terms of arising.
As long as speech conceptualizes a thing as having marks, the mind keeps perceiving it that way, not seeing its own confusion.
(Mahamati asks:) Why is arising spoken of? Why is the seen not spoken of? What is seen is in fact unseeable: so to whom, what, and from where could anything be spoken?
(The Buddha answers:) The mind is clear by its own-nature; manas is what muddies it. And manas, together with the consciousnesses, keeps casting habit-energy into it.
The storehouse consciousness leaves the body; manas seeks its next destiny. Consciousness appears as objects, sees the delusion, and is drawn in.
What is seen is my own mind; outer objects do not exist. Contemplate delusion this way, and keep suchness in mind.
The field of meditators, karma, and the greatness of the buddhas: these three are inconceivable. The field of consciousness is inconceivable too.
The future, the past, nirvana, the person, and speech: these I teach in conventional terms. The ultimate is beyond letters.

Followers of the schools and the tirthikas (tīrthikas) both lean on one-sided views. Confused about mind-only (cittamātra, the teaching that all we experience is mind), they imagine things as existing outside.

cmp.note: naikāyika 指各部派的追随者，也就是声闻部派的人。白话译「部派的人」照字面；实叉难陀译成「二乘」，把范围扩大到声闻和独觉。英文 followers of the schools 照梵文。
cmp.en: Naikāyika means adherents of the (early Buddhist) schools. The plain Chinese 部派的人 (bùpài de rén, “people of the schools”) is literal; Śikṣānanda renders it 二乘 (èrchéng, “the two vehicles”), widening it to disciples and solitary buddhas. The English “followers of the schools” follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Solitary-buddha awakening, buddhahood, arhatship, seeing the Buddha: whoever attains these in a dream has a hidden seed (bīja) of awakening.

cmp.note: 梵文说梦中成就这些的人「有隐藏的菩提种子」。实叉难陀译成「种子坚成就，梦佛灌其顶」，多出了佛在梦中为他灌顶的情节，梵文里没有。白话和英文都照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says that whoever attains these in a dream has a “hidden seed” of awakening. Śikṣānanda writes 种子坚成就，梦佛灌其顶 (zhǒngzǐ jiān chéngjiù, mèng fó guàn qí dǐng, “the seed is firmly ripened; in a dream the Buddha anoints his head”), adding an anointing scene that is not in the Sanskrit. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: (Mahamati asks:) If the mind is like an illusion and utterly at peace, why do you teach the two sides, existence and non-existence? Tell me: where, to whom, how, why, and for what purpose? (The opening word mayācitta is uncertain; read as māyācitta, “illusion-like mind.”)

(The Buddha answers:) For those confused about mind-only, I teach illusion, non-existence and existence: things bound up with arising and perishing, yet free of both the marked and the mark (lakṣya and lakṣaṇa, the thing characterized and its characteristic).
Conceptualizing (vikalpa) is what is called manas (the thinking mind), together with the five sense consciousnesses. Like reflections, like water in a flood, the seed of mind keeps rolling on.

cmp.note: 梵文说分别「叫做 manas（意）」。实叉难陀译成「分别名意识」，把 manas 换成了意识（manovijñāna），这两个在唯识里是不同的层次。白话「意」照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says conceptualizing “is called manas.” Śikṣānanda writes 分别名意识 (fēnbié míng yìshí, “conceptualizing is called mind consciousness”), swapping manas for manovijñāna, which in Yogācāra are two different layers. The plain Chinese 意 (yì, “manas”) follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: When mind, manas, and consciousness no longer run, one gains the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya, a body produced by will rather than by karma) and the buddha-stage.

Conditions, elements, aggregates (skandhas, the five heaps that make up a person), the particular marks of things, names, the person, and mind: all are like a dream, like the hair-net seen by someone with diseased eyes.
Seeing the world as like an illusion or a dream, one should rely on reality (tattva). For reality is free of all marks and lies beyond reasoning and causes.
One should always keep in mind the dwelling of the noble ones, which each knows within himself. The world, confused by reasoning and causes, should be led into reality.

cmp.note: 梵文是「应当把（被推理迷惑的）世间引入真实」。实叉难陀译成「执世间为实」，意思几乎反过来，变成迷惑的人把世间当真。白话和英文都照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says one “should lead the world into reality.” Śikṣānanda writes 执世间为实 (zhí shìjiān wéi shí, “they cling to the world as real”), nearly the opposite: it describes what deluded people do. The plain Chinese and the English follow the Sanskrit.

verses.en: When all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is stilled, the deluded mind no longer runs on. As long as wisdom keeps conceptualizing, delusion keeps running.
Being without own-nature (svabhāva), being, emptiness, permanence and impermanence: these are the views of those who teach arising, not of those who teach non-arising.
People imagine the world as coming from oneness, from difference, from both, from a creator god (Īśvara), from chance, from time, from primal matter (pradhāna), or from other conditions.
Consciousness is the seed of saṃsāra (the round of birth and death); it runs when there is something to be seen. Like a painting that needs a wall, it ceases once it is fully understood.
Just as a magician’s illusory man seems to people to die and be born, so for fools, through delusion, bondage and liberation go on.
Inner and outer, the two kinds, phenomena and conditions: contemplating this, the yogi stands in the imageless (nirābhāsa, where no appearances arise).
Mind is not split apart by habit-energies (vāsanā), nor is mind mixed with them. Mind’s character is undivided, though it is wrapped in habit-energies.

cmp.note: 梵文两句都是否定：心不被习气分裂，也不和习气在一起。实叉难陀第一句译成「习气不离心」，变成习气离不开心，和梵文的方向不同。白话照梵文。
cmp.en: Both Sanskrit lines are negations: mind is not split by habit-energies, and is not together with them. Śikṣānanda’s first line reads 习气不离心 (xíqì bù lí xīn, “habit-energy is not apart from mind”), which points the other way. The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: For one whose habit-energy, born from mind consciousness (manovijñāna), is like dirt, the mind, which is like a white cloth, does not shine because of the habit-energies.
Just as I say that space is neither being nor non-being, so the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) in the body is free of both being and non-being.
Mind that has turned away from mind consciousness is free of murkiness. Because it awakens to all phenomena, I call mind “buddha,” the awakened.

cmp.note: buddha 在梵文里既是「佛」这个称号，也是普通的过去分词「觉醒了的」。这里两层意思都在：觉了一切法，所以叫它觉者。白话「佛（觉者）」两层都保留；英文同样用 buddha 再加 the awakened。
cmp.en: Buddha in Sanskrit is both the title “Buddha” and an ordinary participle, “awakened.” Both senses are at work here: because it awakens to all things, mind is called awake. The plain Chinese 佛（觉者）(fó, juézhě, “Buddha, the awakened one”) keeps both; the English likewise pairs “buddha” with “the awakened.”

verses.en: Cut off from the three continuities (meaning unclear; perhaps the streams of affliction, karma, and birth), free of existence and non-existence, released from the four alternatives (is, is not, both, neither), becoming is always like an illusion.
Two of the natures belong to the seven stages, which arise from mind; the remaining stages and the buddha-stage would be the perfected (nature).
The realm of form, the formless realm, the realm of desire, and nirvana: all of this, in this very body, is said to be the field of mind.
As long as anything is grasped as found, delusion keeps running. Once one awakens to one’s own mind, delusion neither runs on nor turns back.

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「既不运转，也不退回（止息）」：觉悟自心后，迷乱没有什么要灭。白话译「也不必去止息」，意思对，但多了「不必」的语气；实叉难陀只译「迷惑则不生」，丢了后半句。英文照字面。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit literally says delusion “neither runs on nor turns back”: once one wakes to one’s own mind, there is nothing left to stop. The plain Chinese 也不必去止息 (yě bùbì qù zhǐxī, “nor does it need to be stopped”) gets the sense but adds “need to”; Śikṣānanda keeps only 迷惑则不生 (míhuò zé bù shēng, “delusion does not arise”) and drops the second half. The English is literal.

verses.en: In non-arising there is no cause; in being, the whole of saṃsāra is gathered up. Seeing things as like an illusion and the rest, one should not conceptualize marks.
I teach three vehicles, one vehicle, and no vehicle: for fools, for the slow-witted, and for the solitude of the noble ones.

My teaching arises in two ways: as marks and as realization. There is a fourfold method of reasoning, taught both as established doctrine (siddhānta) and as teaching by reasoned explanation. (The verse is compressed; the exact sense is unclear.)
Seeing delusion in the differences of shape and outward form, one conceptualizes. Apart from name and shape, own-nature is the field of the noble ones.
As long as one imagines through conceptualizing, there is the imagined (parikalpita) mark. When conceptualizing and imagining are gone, own-nature is the field of the noble ones.

Reality that is constant and eternal, the lineage (gotra, the spiritual family one belongs to), the own-nature of things, suchness (tathatā, things just as they are): this is free of mind and rid of all imagining.

If there were no real thing at all, there would be neither purification nor defilement for anyone. But since mind is purified and defilement is also seen, reality must be a real thing, pure, the field of the noble ones.

cmp.note: 梵文论证是：如果（真实）根本不是实在之物，就谈不上清净和杂染；既然两者都看得见，真实就是实在的。实叉难陀压成「以有清净心，而有杂染现」，把论证的结构丢了。白话和英文都保留了这个「如果……那么……」的推理。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit argues: if (reality) were no real thing, there could be no purity or defilement; since both are seen, reality must be real. Śikṣānanda compresses this to 以有清净心，而有杂染现 (yǐ yǒu qīngjìng xīn, ér yǒu zárǎn xiàn, “because there is a pure mind, defilement appears”), losing the shape of the argument. The plain Chinese and the English keep the “if… then…” reasoning.

verses.en: Whoever sees the world as born of conditions and free of conceptualizing, like an illusion, a dream, and so on, is liberated.

cmp.note: 梵文说世间「离开分别」。实叉难陀译成「增长于分别」，意思正好相反。白话「离开分别」照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the world is “free of conceptualizing.” Śikṣānanda writes 增长于分别 (zēngzhǎng yú fēnbié, “grows through conceptualizing”), the exact opposite. The plain Chinese 离开分别 (líkāi fēnbié, “apart from conceptualizing”) follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: All sorts of habit-energies of corruption (dauṣṭhulya, the coarse heaviness left by defilement) are bound up with mind. People see them as outside, and that is not the true nature of mind.
The true nature of mind is pure; mind is not born of delusion. Delusion is made of corruption, and that is why mind is not seen.
Reality would be delusion itself; reality is not found anywhere else. It is not in conditioned formations, nor somewhere else, but comes from seeing the formations (as they are).
When one sees the conditioned as free of both the marked and the mark, it is shaken off, for one then sees the world as one’s own mind.
Having climbed up to mind-only, one should not imagine outer objects. Standing on suchness as one’s object, one should go beyond mind-only.
Having gone beyond mind-only, one should go beyond the imageless too. The yogi who stands in the imageless sees the Mahayana.

cmp.note: 梵文是「他看见大乘」。实叉难陀译成「不见于大乘」，多了一个否定，意思反了。白话照梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “he sees the Mahayana.” Śikṣānanda writes 不见于大乘 (bù jiàn yú dàchéng, “does not see the Great Vehicle”), adding a negation that reverses the sense. The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The effortless state is peaceful, purified by vows. The supreme, selfless knowledge is not seen in the imageless. (Perhaps: it is beyond seeing there; the sense is unclear.)
One should see the field of mind, see the field of knowledge (jñāna), and see the field of wisdom (prajñā); then one is not confused by marks.
The truth of suffering belongs to mind; its origin is the field of knowledge; the remaining two truths and the buddha-stage are where wisdom works.
Gaining the fruit, nirvana, and the eightfold path as well: by awakening to all phenomena, the Buddha’s knowledge is purified.
The eye, visible form, light, space, and attention: from these, people’s consciousness arises, born from the storehouse consciousness.

cmp.note: 这里的 manas 列在眼、色、光、空间之后，是眼识生起的条件之一，意思更接近「作意」（注意力）。实叉难陀就译成「作意」；白话译「意」，容易和末那识混淆。英文译 attention。
cmp.en: Here manas is listed after eye, form, light and space as a condition for eye consciousness, so it means something closer to “attention.” Śikṣānanda renders it 作意 (zuòyì, “attention”); the plain Chinese has 意 (yì, “mind / manas”), which could be confused with the thinking mind. The English uses “attention.”

verses.en: What is grasped, the grasping, and the grasper do not exist; a name has no real thing behind it. Those who think conceptualizing has no cause are not wise.
A name does not arise in its object, and an object does not arise in its name either. One should not conceptualize a conceptualizing that is born from a cause or from no cause.
The own-nature of all things is unreal, and speech too is unreal. Not seeing emptiness (śūnyatā) or what emptiness means, the fool runs this way and that.

Seeing how truth is set up through conceiving, the teaching is mere designation. Oneness and the fivefold are not established, and this truth is let go. (Meaning unclear; the Sanskrit is compressed and possibly corrupt.)

One should pass beyond conceptual proliferation, the splitting caused by Mara, and existence and non-existence. Because one sees selflessness, there is no longing for becoming, which is a false notion. (The second half is uncertain.)
Eternalism and the belief in a maker are kept going by mere argument. The highest truth cannot be put into words; seeing the Dharma lies in cessation.
Resting on the storehouse consciousness, manas runs; resting on mind and manas, consciousness runs.
Superimposition (samāropa, attributing to things what is not there) as it is superimposed, suchness, and the true nature of mind: contemplating this, the yogi gains the knowledge of mind-only.
In practice the yogi does not think of manas, marks, or things as permanent or impermanent; nor does he think in terms of arising or non-arising.

They do not imagine a twofold object, for consciousness is born from the storehouse consciousness. One does not know a single object with two minds, since both arise from it. (The second line is uncertain.)
There is no speaker and nothing spoken, and since mind is seen, nothing is empty. Because one does not see one’s own mind, the net of views spreads.
Conditions come from nowhere, and there are no sense faculties at all, no elements, no aggregates, no passion, and nothing conditioned.
There is no earlier karma (the text here reads “fire,” agni, which looks corrupt), nothing done, nothing conditioned; no limit, no power, no liberation and no bondage.
There is nothing indeterminate (avyākṛta, morally neutral), no Dharma and no non-Dharma; no time and no nirvana; even the true nature of things (dharmatā) is not found.
There is no Buddha, no truths, no fruit and no causes; no inversion, no nirvana, no passing away and no coming to be.
There are no twelve links (of dependent arising), no finite and no infinite. To cut off all views, I teach mind-only.
Afflictions, paths of action, the body, the doers and the fruit are all like mirages and dreams, like a gandharva city (a phantom city seen in the clouds).
Because mind-only is established, the mark of things is set aside. Because one stands on mind-only, one sees eternalism and annihilationism for what they are.
In nirvana there are no aggregates, no self, and no marks. By entering mind-only, one turns back from grasping at liberation.

cmp.note: 梵文是「从对解脱的执取中退回」：连解脱也不去抓。白话照这个意思；实叉难陀译成「转依得解脱」，变成正面的得到解脱，丢了「放下对解脱的执着」这一层。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says one “turns back from grasping at liberation”: one stops clutching even at freedom. The plain Chinese keeps this; Śikṣānanda writes 转依得解脱 (zhuǎnyī dé jiětuō, “by the turning of the basis one gains liberation”), a positive statement that loses the point about letting go of the craving for liberation.

verses.en: The fault caused by the earth and other visible things appears to people as something outside. Mind arises from what cannot be seen, and so mind is not seen. (The first line is uncertain.)
People’s habit-energy shows itself as body, possessions, and dwelling place. Mind is neither being nor non-being; it does not shine through habit-energy.
Dirt shows up on white, but white does not show up on dirt. Like the sky behind thick clouds, mind is not seen.
Mind piles up karma, knowledge takes it apart, and through wisdom one reaches the imageless and its power.

cmp.note: 梵文用同一个词根玩文字游戏：cīyate「堆积」，加前缀 vi- 变成 vicīyate「拆开、分析」。中文「积聚」和「分析」看不出这层关系；英文用 piles up / takes apart 尽量保留一点对仗。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit plays on one root: cīyate “is piled up,” and with the prefix vi-, vicīyate “is taken apart, sorted.” The Chinese 积聚 (jījù, “accumulate”) and 分析 (fēnxī, “analyze”) lose the link; the English “piles up / takes apart” tries to keep some of the echo.

verses.en: Mind is tied to its objects; knowledge runs in reasoning; but in the imageless, in what is truly distinctive, knowledge comes fully into play.

Mind, manas, consciousness, and perception (saṃjñā) are free of imagining. Those who reach the non-conceptualizing nature of things are disciples (śrāvakas), not the children of the Victor (jina, a name for a buddha). (The point of the contrast is unclear.)
Through patience upon patience (kṣānti, acceptance of the truth), at the distinctive stage, the pure knowledge of the Tathagata arises for a distinctive purpose, free of active functioning.
The imagined nature exists; the dependent (nature) is not found. What is imagined is grasped through delusion; the dependent is not imagined.
Mind arises from what is unreal; mind is nowhere to be seen. People’s habit-energy shows itself as body, possessions, and dwelling place.
Not all form is made of the elements; there is form not made of the elements. The gandharva city, the dream, the illusion, and the mirage are not made of the elements.
My wisdom is threefold, and by it the noble is brought to light. Mind arises from what cannot be seen, and so mind is not seen.
People’s habit-energy shows itself as body, possessions, and dwelling place. (One kind of wisdom is that) by which marks are imagined and which picks out own-natures. (The second line is unclear.)

There is a wisdom free of the two vehicles and free of images; one that works among disciples through clinging to arising; and the stainless wisdom of the Tathagata, which comes from entering mind-only.
If things arise through conditions from being or from non-being, then those who think so are bound to rely on views of oneness and difference.
Just as the many kinds of rebirth are conjured up and an illusion is never real, so the variety of signs, when imagined, is never established. (The first line is uncertain.)
Bondage made of signs (nimitta) and corruption is born of mind. Those who do not understand the imagined (nature) conceptualize it as the dependent (nature).
The very thing that is imagined is itself the dependent. The imagined appears in many forms, and it is conceptualized as the dependent.

There is conventional truth (saṃvṛti) and ultimate truth (paramārtha); a third, based on causes, does not exist. The imagined is called conventional, and cutting it off is the field of the noble ones.
Just as for yogis a single thing shines out as many, though no manyness is really there, so it is with the imagined mark.
Just as people with an eye disease imagine all sorts of forms they see, while the disease itself is neither form nor not-form, so the wise see the dependent (nature).
Just as gold becomes pure, water becomes free of murk, and the sky becomes clear when there are no clouds, so what is conceptualized becomes pure.
My disciples (śrāvakas) are of three kinds: those magically emanated, those born of vows, and the disciple free of passion and hatred, born of the Dharma.
Bodhisattvas are also of three kinds. Buddhas have no marks, yet in each and every mind of living beings an image of the Buddha is seen.
If one holds that the imagined thing does not exist while the dependent does exist, then the conceptualizing of superimposition and denial (apavāda, denying what is there) is never destroyed.

If the imagined were non-existent while the dependent existed by its own-nature, there would be being without non-being, and being would arise from non-being. (The reasoning is compressed; the sense is partly unclear.)
Relying on the imagined, the dependent is obtained; from the link between sign and name, the imagined is born.
When (the imagined) is seen as utterly unestablished, and what arises from others is seen as arising through imagining, then the pure, ultimate own-nature becomes known.
The imagined is of ten kinds and the dependent of six; and for one who has realized it within, suchness has no distinctions.
The five dharmas (name, sign, conceptualizing, right knowledge, and suchness) are reality, and so are the three natures. Contemplating this, the yogi does not stray from suchness.
Mind appears to people in the shapes of stars and clouds, like the moon and the sun; it looks like something seen, stirred up by habit-energy.
The elements have a nature that cannot be found; there is neither the marked nor the mark. If form were made of the elements, then all the elements would be made of elements too.
The great elements are unborn, and in the elements there is nothing made of elements. The great elements are the cause; earth, water and the rest are the effect.
Form that is substance, form that is designation, form produced by illusion, the form of dreams and of gandharva cities, and the mirage as the fifth.
There are five kinds of icchantika (those cut off from the roots of good), and likewise five lineages; five vehicles and the non-vehicle; and nirvana is of six kinds.
The divisions of the aggregates are twenty-four, and form is of eight kinds; there are twenty-four buddhas, and the Victor’s own children are of two kinds.
There are a hundred and eight methods of teaching, and likewise three kinds of disciple. The buddhas have just one land, and likewise there is just one Buddha.
Likewise there are three liberations, and the flow of mind is of four kinds; selflessness, as I teach it, is of six kinds, and the knowable is also of four kinds.
Free of causes, rid of the faults of views, known by each within, unshakable: this is the unsurpassed Mahayana.
Arising and non-arising come in eight or nine kinds; realization may be all at once or step by step, yet the established doctrine is just one.
The formless realm is of eight kinds, and the divisions of meditation (dhyāna) of six; the way out for solitary buddhas and the Victor’s children is of seven kinds.
The three times (past, present, future) do not exist, nor do permanence and impermanence. Action, karma, and its fruit are like things done in a dream.
Buddhas, disciples, and the Victor’s own children have neither end nor beginning and never arose. Mind, free of anything seen, is always like an illusory thing.
Entering the womb, turning the wheel (of the Dharma), birth, leaving home, the Tushita heaven, and going to every buddha-land: all this is seen, yet (the buddhas) are not born from a womb.
Passing from life to life, wandering on, beings, teaching, nirvana, the truths, the lands, and awakening: all of these are set in motion by conditions.
Worlds, forests, continents, selflessness, the ways of the tirthikas (tīrthikas), meditation, the vehicles, the storehouse consciousness, attainment, the field of the inconceivable fruit,
the lineages of the moon and stars, the lineages of kings, the abodes of the gods, the lineages of yakshas and gandharvas: these are born of karma and arise from craving.

There is also the inconceivable death by transformation (the subtle death that advanced beings still undergo), still bound up with habit-energy. When death is cut off and is no more, the net of afflictions ceases.
Money, grain and gold, fields and property, cattle and goats, slaves, and horses, elephants and the like are conceptualized (as things to possess).

cmp.note: 梵文这句的动词是 vikalpyate「被分别」，字面只说这些财物「被分别（出来）」，没有直接说「不应蓄存」。白话和实叉难陀都按上下文的戒律意思译成「不应蓄存」，读起来更通顺；英文照字面，在括号里补一句「当作要拥有的东西」。
cmp.en: The verb here is vikalpyate, “are conceptualized”: literally the verse only says these possessions are “conceptualized,” not that they must not be kept. The plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda both read it in light of the monastic rules that follow and say 不应蓄存 / 不应畜 (bù yīng xùcún / bù yīng xù, “should not be kept”), which reads more smoothly. The English stays literal and adds “as things to possess” in parentheses.

verses.en: One should not sleep on a pierced bed (meaning unclear; perhaps a bed with holes or a raised, ornate bed), nor plaster the ground. One should not have bowls made of gold, silver, bronze, or copper.
Blankets may be blue or red; using cow dung, mud, fruits and leaves, the yogi should always dye white cloth to the ochre color (kāṣāya) of a monk’s robe.
For a bowl, the yogi may keep one made of stone, clay, iron, conch shell or crystal, holding a full Magadha measure.
His knife should be four fingers long and curved, for cutting cloth. A yogi devoted to practice should not study crafts and technical skills.

cmp.note: 梵文这一句「不学工艺」在本颂下半；实叉难陀把它挪到下一颂开头（勿学工巧明），这一颂改成「修行者听畜」。白话跟梵文走，所以两边的分颂不一样，意思没少。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit puts “should not study crafts” in the second half of this verse. Śikṣānanda moves it to the start of the next verse (勿学工巧明, wù xué gōngqiǎo míng, “do not study the craft sciences”) and ends this one with “the practitioner may keep it.” The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit, so the verse division differs but nothing is lost.

verses.en: A yogi carried along by practice should not buy and sell. That should be done by the monastery’s lay attendants. This is the Dharma I teach.
One who guards the senses, understands the meaning of the sutras and of the monastic rules (vinaya), and does not mix with householders — that is the one I call a yogi.
The yogi should make his dwelling in an empty house, a cremation ground, at the foot of a tree, in caves, on a heap of straw, or in the open air.
Always wrapped in the three robes, at a cremation ground or wherever he is, he should arrange for cloth when he needs it, and accept what someone gives in good will.
He should walk looking only a yoke’s length ahead, intent on alms food. As bees go among flowers, so he should go for alms.

cmp.note: yuga 是牛车的轭，yugamātra 就是「一轭的长度」，大约一人身长，意思是走路眼睛只看前方几步。白话译作「一轭远」照字面；实叉难陀用中国的长度单位「一寻」。英文照字面译 a yoke’s length。
cmp.en: Yuga is the yoke of an ox cart, so yugamātra is “the length of a yoke,” about a body’s length: the monk keeps his eyes a few steps ahead. The plain Chinese 一轭远 (yī è yuǎn, “a yoke away”) is literal; Śikṣānanda uses a Chinese unit, 一寻 (yī xún, “one fathom”). The English stays literal.

verses.en: Whatever comes from a crowd, from a place mixed up with crowds, or from among nuns is tied up with making a living, and it is not proper for yogis.
A yogi devoted to practice should not go to kings, princes, ministers or rich merchants to ask for food.

Food from a house where someone has died or a child has just been born, food given out of friendship and affection, and food from where monks and nuns are mixed together — these are not proper for yogis.
Food from a monastery where smoke always rises from cooking done by the rules, and food made specially for him — these too are not proper for yogis.
The yogi should regard the world as free from arising and perishing, rid of the two sides of being and non-being, and bound up with what is marked and the marks that mark it.
If the yogi does not imagine arising, before long he will have the power of concentration (samādhi), the higher knowledges (abhijñā, supernormal powers) and the masteries.
He should not imagine the world as coming from causes such as atoms, time or primal matter (pradhāna). The yogi should not imagine the world as produced by causes and conditions either.

The yogi should always see that the world is imagined by his own conceptualizing (vikalpa), many-sided, and stirred up by habit-energy (vāsanā, the traces left by past acts and thoughts), and that existence is like a magic show or a dream.
His view should always be free of denial and of superimposition. He should not conceptualize the three realms of existence, which appear as body, possessions and dwelling place.
Having eaten his alms food, he sets his body firmly upright and bows again and again to the buddhas and bodhisattvas.

cmp.note: 梵文是「吃完了乞来的饭」，白话照译。实叉难陀作「不思想饮食」，意思变成心里不惦记吃的，和梵文不同。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “having eaten his alms food,” and the plain Chinese follows it. Śikṣānanda has 不思想饮食 (bù sīxiǎng yǐnshí, “not thinking about food”), which shifts the sense to not dwelling on food.

verses.en: One who knows practice gathers the truth from the monastic rules, the sutras and reasoning, and contemplates the five dharmas (name, sign, conceptualizing, right knowledge and suchness), his own mind, and selflessness (nairātmya).
The purity of the Dharma-nature realized within oneself, the stages (bhūmi), and the buddha stage — the yogi who contemplates these is consecrated on a great lotus.
Having wandered through all the destinies of rebirth and feeling dread of existence, he goes to the auspicious path (a cemetery) and takes up various practices.

cmp.note: śivapathī 字面是「吉祥的路」，是坟场的委婉说法。白话把两层都放进去（吉祥清净的坟场），实叉难陀直接说「冢间静处」。英文先照字面，再括注是坟场。
cmp.en: Śivapathī literally means “the auspicious road,” a polite word for a cemetery. The plain Chinese keeps both layers (吉祥清净的坟场, jíxiáng qīngjìng de fénchǎng, “auspicious, pure cemetery”); Śikṣānanda simply says 冢间静处 (zhǒngjiān jìngchù, “quiet place among the tombs”). The English gives the literal phrase and notes in brackets that it means a cemetery.

verses.en: The yogi sees masses of light shaped like the moon and the sun, shining like lotus petals, like fire in the sky, like a painting.
These varied signs lead him onto the path of the tirthikas (tīrthikas), or make him fall into the state of a disciple (śrāvaka) or the range of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha).

When he has shaken all these off and is free of images, then buddhas from every land gather, their hands like suns, and stroke his head; the sign that follows is in accord with suchness (tathatā, things as they really are) (meaning of the last phrase unclear).

cmp.note: 这个复合词可以读成「手如太阳的诸佛」，也可以读成「诸佛（如）太阳，用手……」。白话取前一种，英文也一样。最后半句 nimittaṃ tathatānugāḥ 语法不顺，可能有错漏，英文标了意思不清。
cmp.en: This compound can be read “buddhas whose hands are like suns” or “buddhas, like suns, with their hands.” The plain Chinese takes the first reading, and so does the English. The last half-line, nimittaṃ tathatānugāḥ, does not parse cleanly and may be corrupt, so the English marks it as unclear.

verses.en: Some say that a thing exists in a formless way, free of eternalism and annihilationism. Having left behind the sides of being and non-being, they will imagine this to be the middle.

cmp.note: 梵文是「以无形相的方式」存在。实叉难陀译「无因生」，好像他的底本是「无因」（ahetu），正好接下一颂讲的无因论。白话照现在的梵文。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the thing exists “in a formless way.” Śikṣānanda has 无因生 (wú yīn shēng, “arises without cause”), as if his text read ahetu (“without cause”), which fits the theory of no cause in the next verse. The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit we have.

verses.en: They imagine things within a theory of no cause, and no cause is the view of annihilation. Not understanding external things, they will destroy the middle.
They will not let go of grasping at things, for fear of falling into the view of annihilation. They will teach the middle by way of superimposition and denial.
By waking up to mind-only, external things lose their support. The turning away of conceptualizing — that alone is the middle path.
Mind-only does not see; since there is nothing seen, it does not arise. This is the middle path, taught by me and by others.

cmp.note: 梵文这半句很简短，可以理解为「唯心，没有（外在）可见之物」。白话译成「唯心，看不见所见之物」，实叉难陀译「惟心无有境」，更清楚。英文照字面，读者可以对照这两种理解。
cmp.en: This half-line is terse: roughly “mind-only, nothing (outside) is seen.” The plain Chinese says 唯心，看不见所见之物 (wéixīn, kàn bú jiàn suǒ jiàn zhī wù, “mind-only, no object seen”); Śikṣānanda is clearer: 惟心无有境 (wéixīn wú yǒu jìng, “mind only, no objects”). The English stays literal.

verses.en: Arising and non-arising, being and non-being, emptiness (śūnyatā), and the lack of own-nature (svabhāva) in things — he should not conceptualize these pairs.
