Fools imagine that the stopping of conceptualizing is liberation. But as long as one does not understand how the mind works, grasping at duality is not abandoned.
By understanding what is seen as one’s own mind, grasping at duality is abandoned. Abandoning means fully knowing; it does not destroy what is conceptualized.
From fully knowing what the mind shows, conceptualizing does not start up. When conceptualizing does not start up, that is suchness, free of mind.

cmp.note: 梵文是「离开心的真如」，白话照译。实叉难陀作「真如心转依」，把「离心」换成了「心转依」，是从修行结果的角度说的。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “suchness free of mind,” and the plain Chinese follows it. Śikṣānanda writes 真如心转依 (zhēnrú xīn zhuǎnyī, “suchness, the mind’s turning of its basis”), describing the result of practice instead.

verses.en: If a coming-forth is seen that is free of the faults of the tirthikas, the wise should accept it; and its stopping is not destruction.
Awakening to this is buddhahood, as I and the buddhas have taught. Imagining it any other way leads to the doctrines of the tirthikas.
Unborn, they show birth; undying, they show death. Like the moon in water, they are seen all at once in millions of lands.
Becoming one and becoming many, they rain down and blaze with fire. Becoming thoughts within people’s minds, they teach mind-only.
Among minds there is mind-only; even no-mind arises from mind. All the varied forms and shapes come down to mind-only (meaning somewhat unclear).
In the forms of the lord of sages (the Buddha), of disciples, of solitary buddhas, and in many other forms, they teach mind-only.
To formless beings they show formlessness, to hell beings the form of hell; they show forms to beings as the cause of mind-only.

cmp.note: kāraṇam 可以是「原因」，也可以是「为了……的缘故」。白话取后一种（为了让人明白唯心），实叉难陀取前一种（皆是惟心作）。英文照字面译 cause，保留这个两可。
cmp.en: Kāraṇam can mean “cause” or “for the sake of.” The plain Chinese takes the second (so people will understand mind-only); Śikṣānanda takes the first, 皆是惟心作 (jiē shì wéixīn zuò, “all made by mind-only”). The English keeps “cause” to leave both readings open.

verses.en: Having turned around at the base (parāvṛtti), they gain the illusion-like concentration, the mind-made body, the ten stages and the masteries.
Through the distortions of their own conceptualizing and the stirrings of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), fools are bound by ideas in what they see, hear, think and know.
The sign belongs to the dependent (paratantra) nature; the name laid on it there is the imagined (parikalpita). The imagined sign comes forth from the dependent.
When examined with insight, there is neither the dependent nor the imagined. And a perfected (parinispanna) thing does not exist either — so how could insight imagine it?
If a perfected thing does exist, free of being and non-being, then how could there be two natures, both free of being and non-being?
The two natures rest on the imagined nature. What is imagined is seen as varied; what is purified is the range of the noble ones.
The imagined, appearing in many forms, is conceptualized on the dependent. To imagine it any other way would be to rely on the doctrines of the tirthikas.
It is called “imagining, imagining” because it is seen to arise from causes. What is free of the two kinds of conceptualizing — that alone is the perfected (meaning somewhat unclear).
Lands, buddhas, emanations, the one vehicle and the three — I do not enter nirvana. All things are empty (śūnya) and free from arising.
There are thirty-six divisions of buddhas, each with ten divisions of its own. These lands are the mind-streams of beings, not containers (meaning unclear; possibly “vessels”).

cmp.note: 这里可以拆成 kṣetrāṇi abhājanam（刹土不是容器），也可以读成 kṣetrāṇi bhājanam（刹土是容器）。白话取「不是容器」；实叉难陀作「随众生心器」，像是读成「容器」。原文可能有讹误，英文两种都提了。
cmp.en: This can be split kṣetrāṇi abhājanam (“the lands are not containers”) or kṣetrāṇi bhājanam (“the lands are containers”). The plain Chinese takes “not containers”; Śikṣānanda’s 随众生心器 (suí zhòngshēng xīnqì, “according to the mind-vessels of beings”) looks like the other reading. The text may be corrupt, so the English mentions both.

verses.en: Just as an imagined thing appears as a varied spectacle, yet there is no variety in it, so it is with the Buddha’s Dharma and with the world.
The Dharma-buddha is the true Buddha; the rest are his emanations. When beings see buddhas, what they see is the stream of their own seeds (bīja).
From the tie between confusion and signs, conceptualizing starts up. Conceptualizing is nothing other than suchness, and conceptualizing is not the signs.
There is the own-nature body, the enjoyment body and the emanation body, and the five emanated from the emanation. Of the thirty-six groups of buddhas, the own-nature one is the Buddha.
Like blue, red, salt, conch, milk and sugar, astringent tastes, fruits, flowers and the rest, or like the rays of the sun —
they are neither different nor not different, like the waves of the ocean. In the same way the seven consciousnesses are joined with the mind.

The many kinds of waves are a transformation of the ocean. In the same way the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) comes forth in many forms that are called “consciousnesses.”
Mind, manas (the thinking mind) and consciousness are set up for the sake of describing characteristics. The eight are not different in character; there is neither a thing marked nor a mark.
Just as there is no distinction between the ocean and its waves, so no transformation of the consciousnesses can be found in the mind.
By mind, karma is gathered; by manas it is sorted; by consciousness one knows; and with the five one imagines what is seen.
Mahamati asked: “People’s consciousness appears in kinds such as blue and red. Tell me, great sage (muni, a name for the Buddha), why is the mind like waves?”
The Buddha answered: “Kinds like blue and red are not found in the waves. The mind is described as active only to explain its characteristics to fools.”
“It has no activity of its own; one’s own mind is free of anything grasped. When there is something to grasp, there is grasping, and that is established together with the waves.”
“People’s consciousness appears as body, possessions and dwelling place. That is why its activity is seen to resemble waves.”
Mahamati asked: “The ocean is clearly seen dancing as waves. Why is the activity of the storehouse consciousness not grasped by insight in the same way?”
The Buddha answered: “Because fools lack insight, the storehouse consciousness is presented through the comparison with the ocean, by the likeness of its activity to waves.”
Mahamati said: “As the sun rises equally on low and high people, so you, light of the world, teach the truth to fools.”
“Having set things up among the teachings, why do you not speak the truth?” The Buddha answered: “If I spoke the truth, the truth is not found in the mind.”
Like the waves of the ocean, images in a mirror, or things in a dream, which are all seen at one time, so is the mind in its own field. But because the objects are incomplete, it works by stages.
With consciousness one discerns, then with manas one thinks it over; what is seen appears to the five. In someone in concentration there are no stages.
Just as a painter or a painter’s apprentice mixes colors for a picture, so too is my teaching.
The picture is not in the colors, nor on the wall, nor in the dish. To draw beings in, a picture is imagined with colors.
The teaching varies, but the truth is beyond letters. Having first set things up in the Dharma, I teach the truth to yogis.

cmp.note: 这个词按连音可以拆成 deśanā vyabhicārī（教法会有出入），也可以拆成 deśanā avyabhicārī（教法不出错）。白话取前一种，和后半「真实离文字」对比，比较通顺，英文也这样读。
cmp.en: By sandhi this can be split deśanā vyabhicārī (“the teaching varies”) or deśanā avyabhicārī (“the teaching does not stray”). The plain Chinese takes the first, which contrasts well with “truth is beyond letters,” and the English reads it the same way.

verses.en: The truth is reached within oneself and is free of what is imagined and the imagining. This I teach to the children of the Victor (jina, a name for a buddha); to fools I teach differently.
Just as a magic show appears in many forms yet does not exist, so the teaching appears in many forms, yet it does not stray.

cmp.note: 这里有省音符号，很清楚是 avyabhicāriṇī，意思是「不偏离、不出错」：教法虽然形形色色，本身不走样。白话作「却因人而不一定」，把意思弄反了。
cmp.en: The avagraha makes it clear this is avyabhicāriṇī, “not straying, not failing”: the teaching looks varied but does not go wrong. The plain Chinese 却因人而不一定 (què yīn rén ér bù yídìng, “yet it varies from person to person”) reverses the sense.

verses.en: What is a teaching for one person is no teaching for another. Just as a doctor gives each patient a different medicine, so the buddhas teach beings mind-only (cittamātra).
From seeds of habit-energy left by external things, conceptualizing starts up. That by which one grasps is the dependent; what one grasps is the imagined.
The external object that is grasped arises in dependence on the mind. So confusion runs in two ways; there is no third cause.
That from which confusion arises and that on which it depends — the six, the twelve and the eighteen — I say are only mind.

cmp.note: 「六、十二、十八」指六根（或六识）、十二处、十八界。实叉难陀译作「六十二十八」，读起来容易误作「六十二」。白话分开写更清楚，英文也一样。
cmp.en: “The six, twelve and eighteen” are the six senses (or consciousnesses), the twelve sense-bases and the eighteen elements. Śikṣānanda writes 六十二十八 (liù shí èr shí bā), which is easy to misread as “sixty-two.” The plain Chinese separates them, as does the English.

verses.en: By seeing that the grasped object is tied to one’s own seeds, grasping at a self is abandoned. By seeing into the mind’s imagining, grasping at phenomena is abandoned.
Consciousness comes forth from the storehouse consciousness. The inner sense-field turns into the external through its own appearance.
Just as the ignorant see stars, hair-nets or dream images, the conditioned, the unconditioned and the permanent are imagined, yet they do not exist.
Like a city of gandharvas (a mirage city of celestial musicians), a magic show, or the water of a mirage, things that do not exist are seen. The dependent nature is just like that.
I speak of a self and of sense faculties in terms of the three minds only as a manner of speaking. Mind, manas and consciousness have no characteristics of their own.
Mind, manas and consciousness, the two kinds of selflessness (of persons and of phenomena), the five dharmas and the natures — this is the range of the buddhas.
In their characteristics they are three, but they have one cause, habit-energy. Just as a single color is seen as a varied picture on a wall.
Selflessness, non-duality, mind, manas and mind consciousness (manovijñāna), the five dharmas and the natures — these do not exist in my lineage (gotra, spiritual family).
Free of the marks of mind, rid of consciousness and manas, without phenomena or own-nature — this is how one gains the Tathagata lineage.
There, nothing good is done by body, speech or mind. The Tathagata lineage is pure and free of all active functioning.
Pure through the higher knowledges and masteries, adorned with the power of concentration, the mind-made body, the mind — this is the lovely Tathagata lineage.
Known within oneself, stainless, free of causes and marks, the eighth stage and the buddha stage — this is the Tathagata lineage.
Far-Going, Good Insight, Cloud of Dharma, and the Tathagata stage — these are the lineage of the buddhas. The rest lead to the two vehicles.
Because beings’ mind-streams differ, and to explain characteristics to fools, the buddhas, who have mastered the mind, teach seven stages.
In the seventh stage, the coarseness of speech, body and mind no longer arises. In the eighth, his support is like crossing a flood in a dream.
In the eighth stage and the fifth, the children of the Victor master crafts, learning and the arts, and become kings in the house of existence.
One should not imagine arising or non-arising, empty or not empty. Own-nature and lack of own-nature are not found in mind-only.
Conceptualizing “this is true, this is true, this is false” is a teaching for solitary buddhas and disciples, not for the true children of the Victor.
Not existent, not non-existent, not both; there is no momentary mark; not a mere name, not a real substance — none of this is found in mind-only.
Things exist conventionally; in the ultimate sense there are no things. The confusion about things without own-nature (niḥsvabhāva) — that is conventional truth.
All phenomena do not exist; I only make designations for them. Speech and everyday usage are for fools and are empty of truth.
A thing born of speech exists as an object of meaning. Once one sees that a thing is born of speech, one sees that it does not exist.
Just as there is no picture without a wall, and no shadow without a post, so the storehouse consciousness, when it is pure, does not shine in the waves.
The mind stands like a dancer, manas like a clown. Together with the five consciousnesses, it imagines what is seen as if on a stage.
The outflow of the Dharma that is taught, and what is emanated from that outflow — these are the original buddhas; the rest are emanated forms (“original” is uncertain).

cmp.note: paurāḥ 一般是「城里人、市民」，放在这里讲不通。白话和实叉难陀都作「根本佛」，像是读成 maulāḥ（根本的）。英文跟着这个读法，并注明不确定。
cmp.en: Paurāḥ normally means “townsfolk, citizens,” which makes no sense here. The plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda both have 根本佛 (gēnběn fó, “root buddha”), as if reading maulāḥ (“original, root”). The English follows that reading and marks it as uncertain.

verses.en: What is seen does not exist; the mind is bewildered by what is seen. The storehouse consciousness appears to people as body, possessions and dwelling place.
Mind, manas and consciousness, the natures, the five dharmas, and the two pure kinds of selflessness — these the guides (the buddhas) proclaim.
What the protectors teach is not the range of logicians, nor of disciples; it is the range reached within oneself.
Long and short and the like come about in relation to each other. Non-existence is what establishes existence, and existence is what establishes non-existence.
Having broken matter down into atoms, one should not conceptualize form. But the setting forth of mind-only does not win over someone with wrong views.
Do not conceptualize emptiness, nor again “not empty.” Existence and non-existence are just imagining; the object imagined does not exist.
Fools conceptualize form as a combination of qualities, atoms and substances. But not even a single atom exists, so the object does not exist either.
People’s own mind appears outside them in the shape of what is seen. What is seen outside does not exist, so the object does not exist either.

A painting, the hair-net that floats before diseased eyes, a magic show, a dream, a city of the gandharvas (a mirage city in the clouds), a whirling firebrand, a desert mirage — none of these exist, yet they appear to people.
Permanent and impermanent, one and the same, both, neither — fools, bound up with faults that have no beginning and confused, imagine things in these terms.

cmp.note: 梵文这里只写了 ekatvam(一性),「一与异」的「异」是白话补出来的；英文照梵文译成 one and the same，没有另加「异」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit only has ekatvam, “oneness”; the “different” in the plain Chinese 一与异 (yī yǔ yì, “one and different”) is supplied by the translator. The English stays with the Sanskrit and says only “one and the same.”

verses.en: There is really no fixed arrangement of vehicles; I teach one single vehicle. It is to lead fools along that I speak of different vehicles.

The three kinds of liberation, the selflessness of things, the knowledge of sameness, and what is called (the cutting of) the afflictions — the disciples (śrāvakas) lack these in their liberation. (The second line is compressed and its exact sense is unclear.)
Just as a log floating on the ocean is carried here and there by the waves, so the deluded disciple is carried along by appearances.
That is not his final destination, and yet he does not turn back from it either. Having gained a body of meditative absorption (samādhi), he does not wake up until the eon is over.

They are still bound to the afflictions that live on as habit-energy, though freed from the afflictions that actively flare up. Drunk on the intoxication of absorption, they stay in the realm free of outflows (the pure, untainted state).
Just as a drunk man sobers up once the liquor wears off, so they too will one day attain my body, the one called the Buddha-Dharma.
Like an elephant sunk in mud that cannot move this way or that, the disciples stay stuck, sunk in the intoxication of absorption.

cmp.note: 梵文是「沉在三昧之醉里」;实叉难陀只写「住三昧，昏垫亦复然」,把「醉」换成「昏垫」(昏沉陷溺),意思接近但少了酒醉的比喻，而上一颂正是醉汉的比喻。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “sunk in the intoxication of absorption.” Śikṣānanda writes 住三昧，昏垫亦复然 (zhù sānmèi, hūndiàn yì fù rán, “abiding in samādhi, dull and sunk just the same”), replacing “intoxication” with “dullness,” which loses the drinking image that the previous verse set up.

verses.en: The empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna, the sustaining power) of the kings among men (the buddhas) is purified by vows; it includes consecration, absorption and the rest, from the first stage up to the tenth.
Space, a hare’s horn, the son of a barren woman — these do not exist and yet people talk about them. Imagining about things works the same way.

The world has habit-energy (vāsanā, the lingering imprint of past acts) as its cause; nowhere is there being, non-being, or both being and non-being. Those who see it this way, skilled in the selflessness of things, are set free.
Name is the own-nature that is imagined; what arises from conditions is the dependent; the perfected is called suchness. I have always said this, in sutra after sutra.

cmp.note: 梵文用了很省的说法：parabhāva(依于他者的存在)、tantraja(从因缘之网而生),合起来就是三自性里的依他起。实叉难陀直接写成「缘起是依他」,白话也说「依他的存在由因缘而生」,两者都把这个术语讲明了；英文用固定译法 the dependent。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is very terse: parabhāva (“existence dependent on another”) and tantraja (“born of the web of conditions”) together name the dependent nature of the three natures. Śikṣānanda spells it out as 缘起是依他 (yuánqǐ shì yītā, “dependent arising is the dependent”), and the plain Chinese does the same; the English uses the fixed term “the dependent.”

verses.en: Letters, groups of words, and above all names — dull-witted fools get stuck on them like great elephants in mud.
The vehicle of the gods, the vehicle of Brahma, the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the Tathagata, and that of the solitary buddhas — these are the vehicles I speak of.
There is no end to vehicles as long as the mind keeps moving. But once the mind has turned around at its base, there is no vehicle and no one who rides it.

Mind (citta), conceptualizing (vikalpa), representation (vijñapti), manas (the thinking mind), consciousness, the store (ālaya, the storehouse consciousness), the three realms of existence, and activity — these are all other names for mind.

cmp.note: ceṣṭā 是「动作、活动」。白话译作「造作」;实叉难陀没有单列这一词，而把「本识作三有」连起来读，意思是阿赖耶识造出三界。英文照梵文把它当成单独一个别名 activity。
cmp.en: Ceṣṭā means “movement, activity.” The plain Chinese renders it 造作 (zàozuò, “making, activity”); Śikṣānanda does not list it separately but reads the line as 本识作三有 (běnshí zuò sānyǒu, “the root consciousness makes the three realms”). The English follows the Sanskrit list and treats it as one more name: “activity.”

verses.en: Life-span, warmth, consciousness, the store, the life faculty, manas, and mind consciousness — these are different names for conceptualizing.
The body is held together by mind; manas is always thinking; and consciousness, whose field is what mind presents, together with the other consciousnesses cuts that field up into pieces.

cmp.note: chindati 字面是「切、割」,这里指把境界切分成一个个对象。白话「切分开来」照字面；实叉难陀译成「了自心境界」,只说「了知」,把切割这个形象换掉了。
cmp.en: Chindati literally means “cuts,” here: cutting the field up into separate objects. The plain Chinese 切分开来 (qiēfēn kāilái, “cut apart”) is literal; Śikṣānanda has 了自心境界 (liǎo zì xīn jìngjiè, “discerns the field of one’s own mind”), keeping “knowing” but dropping the cutting image.

verses.en: Craving is called the mother and ignorance likewise the father; and consciousness, because it wakes up to objects, is taught as “the Buddha.”

The arhats are the latent tendencies; the Sangha is the group of five aggregates (skandhas, the heaps that make up a person). Cutting them off completely, with no gap left, is the “deed without interval.” (Read as a deliberate reinterpretation of the five worst crimes.)

cmp.note: 「无间业」本来指杀父、杀母、杀阿罗汉、破僧等五种直堕地狱的重罪。这里故意换了意思：要「杀」的阿罗汉是随眠，要「破」的僧是五蕴，nirantara-antara-ccheda(彻底断开、不留间隙)才叫 ānantarya。白话没交代这层反讽，读者容易看不懂；英文加了一句说明。
cmp.en: The “deeds without interval” are normally the five gravest crimes (killing father, mother, an arhat, splitting the Sangha, etc.) that send one straight to hell. Here they are deliberately reinterpreted: the “arhats” to be killed are the latent tendencies, the “Sangha” to be split is the five aggregates, and cutting them off “with no gap” (nirantara-antara-ccheda) is what makes the deed “without interval.” The plain Chinese 无间业 (wújiān yè) gives no hint of the twist, so the English adds a short note.

verses.en: The two kinds of selflessness, the afflictions, and likewise the two hindrances, and the inconceivable death by transformation — the Tathagatas are those who have attained (the end of) these. (The construction is loose and the exact sense is uncertain.)

The established doctrine and the way of teaching it, what is realized within oneself and the spoken instruction — those who see these and know how to tell them apart do not fall under the sway of reasoning.
Things do not truly exist the way fools conceptualize them. Then why do the logicians not accept liberation through non-existence?
Seeing the conditioned as bound up with arising and perishing, they feed the two views (of existence and non-existence) and do not understand conditions.
Only one thing is real: nirvana, free of manas. One should see the world as conceptualized, like a banana tree (hollow inside), a dream, a magic show.
Greed does not exist, nor hatred, nor delusion, nor a person. The aggregates that arise from craving exist only the way things in a dream do.
Between the night I attained awakening and the night I pass into final nirvana, I have not revealed anything at all.
I said this with reference to the inner realization and the abiding of the Dharma as it always is; between those buddhas and me there is no difference at all.

The self exists as a real substance, and the aggregates have no marks — so some think. In fact the aggregates exist as things, and no self is found in them. (The first line is probably an opposing view being stated; the Sanskrit does not mark it.)

cmp.note: 梵文前半句字面是「自我像实物一样存在，诸蕴没有相」,没有标明是谁的说法。白话加了「(有人说)」,英文也这样处理；实叉难陀则完全改写成「若实有我体，异蕴及蕴中，于彼求我体，毕竟不可得」,变成在蕴内蕴外找我找不到的论证。
cmp.en: Literally the first half says “the self exists like a substance; the aggregates are without marks,” with no sign of who is speaking. The plain Chinese adds （有人说） (yǒurén shuō, “some say”), and the English does the same. Śikṣānanda rewrites it entirely as an argument: 若实有我体，异蕴及蕴中 (“if a real self existed, apart from or within the aggregates”), one would look for it there and never find it.

verses.en: Whoever discerns the path of practice, (seeing through) the afflictions and the ties of human company, and sees the world as their own mind, is freed from all suffering. (The first line is corrupt and its meaning unclear.)
Those who think the world runs on causes and conditions, and who are caught in the fourfold alternatives (the tetralemma: is, is not, both, neither), do not understand my method.
The world is not born from being, nor from non-being, nor anywhere from both being and non-being. So how can fools conceptualize it in terms of conditions and causes?
When one sees the world as neither being, nor non-being, nor both, the mind turns back and one attains selflessness.
All things are unborn, because they come about through conditions. All conditions are themselves effects, and existence is not born from an effect.

An effect does not give birth to an effect; otherwise the effect would be doubled. And yet the absurdity of doubling does not mean the effect is found to be non-existent. (The argument is compressed; meaning partly unclear.)
When one sees the conditioned as free of grasping and what is grasped, then appearances are mind-only; it is this that I call mind-only.

“Only” means the standing of things in their own-nature, free of existence that depends on conditions — the ultimate, highest state beyond existence. This is the “only” I speak of. (The wording is difficult; meaning partly uncertain.)

cmp.note: brahma 在这里不是梵天，而是「最高、最清净的」意思。白话译作「最高的清净」,英文译成 the highest state,都没有把它当神名。
cmp.en: Brahma here is not the god Brahma but “the highest, the purest.” The plain Chinese 最高的清净 (zuìgāo de qīngjìng, “the highest purity”) and the English “the highest state” both avoid reading it as a divine name.

verses.en: The self is real only as a designation; as a substance it does not exist. In the same way the aggregates are aggregates by designation, not as substances.
There are four kinds of sameness: of marks, of causes, of what is produced, and fourth, the sameness of selflessness — this is for yogis who practice.
Turning away from all views, free of what is imagined and the imagining, no grasping and no birth — this I call mind-only.
Neither existence nor non-existence, beyond both existence and non-existence; suchness released from mind — this I call mind-only.

cmp.note: 这里有个看似矛盾的说法：真如「脱离了心」,却又被称为「唯心」。梵文就是这样写的，白话和英文都照译，没有替它圆。意思大概是：真正的唯心，恰恰不是被执着为实体的那个心。
cmp.en: There is an apparent paradox: suchness is “released from mind,” yet it is called “mind-only.” The Sanskrit says exactly this, and both the plain Chinese 脱离了心 (tuōlí le xīn, “freed from mind”) and the English keep it as is. The likely point is that true mind-only is precisely not a mind grasped as a thing.

verses.en: Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvana, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the mind-made body, mind — this I call mind-only.
Bound by the habit-energy of conceptualizing, a whole variety of things arises from mind and seems to people to arise outside. The world is mind-only.
There is no external thing to be seen; what is seen is the mind’s own variety, appearing as body, possessions and dwelling place. This I call mind-only.

Disciples have the knowledge of exhaustion (that the afflictions are used up); the buddhas’ knowledge keeps arising; that of the solitary buddhas and the Victor’s children (the bodhisattvas) proceeds from being free of defilement.

cmp.note: 梵文说诸佛的智是 janma-saṃbhava(生起、出生),字面不太通，可能有讹误。实叉难陀把三者重新分配：声闻是尽智，缘觉是寂静智，如来的智「生起无穷尽」;白话则照梵文把独觉与佛子放在一起。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit calls the buddhas’ knowledge janma-saṃbhava (“arising, birth”), which reads oddly and may be corrupt. Śikṣānanda redistributes the three: disciples have 尽智 (jìnzhì, “knowledge of exhaustion”), solitary buddhas 寂静智 (jìjìngzhì, “knowledge of stillness”), and the Tathagata’s wisdom 生起无穷尽 (“arises without end”). The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit in grouping solitary buddhas with the bodhisattvas.

verses.en: There really is no form outside; it is one’s own mind that is seen as outside. Because they do not understand their own mind, fools imagine the conditioned.

Not understanding external objects, deluded people, harnessed to the fourfold alternatives, use reasons to block the insight that what they see is the picture-play of their own mind. (The verb vāryate, “is blocked,” may be corrupt.)
If the wise know that it is their own mind that has passed over into objects, then they need no reasons, no fourfold alternatives, no examples or parts of a syllogism.
One should not conceptualize, by means of conceptualizings, what has the mark of being conceptualized; it is by relying on the imagined that conceptualizing keeps running.
Because the two are bound to each other inseparably and have one habit-energy as their cause, and because both are only visitors, people’s mind is not born from them. (Meaning partly unclear.)
Those who seek objects for mind and its mental factors conceptualize and are established in the three realms; whatever appears to them as objects is the imagined own-nature.
From the union of appearances and seeds come the twelve sense bases; and I describe the process (of cognition) as coming from the union of the support and its object.
Like a reflection in a mirror, or the hair-net seen by someone with cataracts, so fools see a mind covered over by habit-energy.
Conceptualizing arises on objects that were imagined by one’s own conceptualizing. The object does not exist outside in the way the tirthikas (tīrthikas) imagine.
Just as fools who do not recognize a rope take it for a snake, so those who do not understand that the object is their own mind imagine the object to be external.
In fact a rope, as a rope, is free of being one or other. It is only a fault of one’s own mind that makes the rope be conceptualized (as something else).
If something cannot be found when it is looked for as a certain kind of thing, that does not mean one should conclude it does not exist. This is the nature of things.
“Is not” presupposes “is,” and “is” presupposes “is not.” So one should not settle on “is not,” nor should one imagine “is.”
What is imagined, as it is being imagined, does not have that as its nature. Seeing what has no nature, how could conceptualizing arise?
Form does not exist with form as its own nature, and the same goes for pots, cloth and the like. Yet even though the thing seen does not exist, conceptualizing is born from it.

(Mahamati asks:) If your conceptualizing comes from confusion within the beginningless conditioned, then by what has the existence of things been confused? Tell me, sage (muni, a name for the Buddha).

cmp.note: 梵文问的是「事物之为有，是被什么弄迷乱的」,问的是迷乱的来源。实叉难陀简化成「何法令迷惑」;白话保留了「事物之『有』」这个说法，英文也照梵文保留。说话人是谁梵文没写，白话和英文都按上下文补了「大慧问」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit asks “by what has the existence of things been confused?” — a question about where confusion comes from. Śikṣānanda simplifies it to 何法令迷惑 (hé fǎ lìng míhuò, “what makes one confused?”); the plain Chinese keeps “the ‘existence’ of things,” and so does the English. The speaker is not named in the Sanskrit; both the plain Chinese and the English supply “Mahamati asks” from context.

verses.en: (The Buddha answers:) The existence of things does not exist; what is seen is only mind. Not seeing one’s own mind, conceptualizing starts running.
If what is imagined does not exist the way a fool imagines it, then it exists in some other way — yet that is not understood by the intellect.
If it exists for the noble ones, then it is not what fools imagine. But if it is false for the noble ones too, then the noble ones have become the same as fools.
The noble ones have no confusion, because their mind has been purified. Fools, whose stream of mind is impure, imagine the imagined.
It is like a mother who pretends to fetch a fruit for her son from the sky: “Here, son, don’t cry — take this pretty fruit.”

cmp.note: 梵文的意思是母亲假装从空中拿来果子哄孩子，下一颂才点明是佛的方便。白话「从天上给他摘来果子」像是真的摘，英文加了 pretends,让「哄」的意思清楚一点。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit means the mother pretends to bring a fruit out of thin air to soothe the child; the next verse spells out that this is the Buddha’s skillful means. The plain Chinese 从天上给他摘来果子 (cóng tiānshàng gěi tā zhāi lái guǒzi, “picks him a fruit from the sky”) sounds literal, so the English adds “pretends” to make the coaxing clear.

verses.en: In the same way I lure all beings with all sorts of imagined fruits, and then teach the method that is free of the extremes of being and non-being.
If a thing exists after not having existed, and is not put together by conditions, then it is born without having been born before, and has no self-nature that can be found.
What has no self-nature and is unborn is never found anywhere without conditions; and what has arisen, in your view, is never found anywhere without conditions either.
Seeing it this way in brief — nowhere is there being, non-being, or both — the wise do not conceptualize what is born from conditions.
Foolish followers of bad teachers talk about oneness and otherness; they do not understand conditions, and do not know the world is like a magic show or a dream.
The vehicle (beyond) the field of words is the Great Vehicle, the unsurpassed; I have set out its meaning clearly, yet fools do not understand it.

cmp.note: 梵文字面只说「名言境界的乘」,并没有「超越」一词，可能是省略或抄本讹误。实叉难陀和白话都按上下文译成「超越名言」,英文也补上 beyond,但用括号标出是补的。
cmp.en: Literally the Sanskrit says only “the vehicle that is the field of words”; there is no word for “beyond,” perhaps through ellipsis or scribal error. Śikṣānanda and the plain Chinese both read it as 超越名言 (chāoyuè míngyán, “beyond words”) from context; the English adds “beyond” too, in parentheses to show it is supplied.

verses.en: What the disciples and the tirthikas have laid down out of jealousy strays from the true meaning, because it was taught through reasoning.
Marks, things, shapes and names — these four: taking them as its objects, imagining starts running.

Those who fall under the sway of Brahma’s body and speak of one or many, and those who (argue from) the movements of the moon and sun — they are not my children. (The verb nāśenti is obscure; meaning partly unclear.)
Accomplished in the vision of the noble ones, having arrived at things as they really are, skilled in turning around perceptions, gone to the far shore of consciousness —
this is the seal of my liberated children in my teaching: freed from existence and non-existence, beyond coming and going.
If, when form and consciousness cease, karma were destroyed, then neither permanence nor impermanence would be reached, and there would be no cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra).

At the time of dissolution, form breaks up and leaves its place, but karma, free of the faults of “is” and “is not,” remains in the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds).
Form breaks up and falls, and consciousness (passes on) into the house of existence; yet karma, bound up with form and consciousness, is not destroyed.

cmp.note: bhava-ālaye 字面是「在有的住处里」,也可能暗指阿赖耶(ālaya)。白话译成「落入三有之中」,实叉难陀则改写成业令色识「于诸有中复相续」。英文照字面译成 the house of existence。
cmp.en: Bhava-ālaye literally means “in the dwelling of existence,” possibly also hinting at the ālaya (the store). The plain Chinese renders it 落入三有之中 (luòrù sānyǒu zhī zhōng, “falls into the three realms”), while Śikṣānanda rewrites it as karma making form and consciousness 于诸有中复相续 (“continue again in the realms of existence”). The English stays literal: “the house of existence.”

verses.en: But if people’s karma, bound up with them, were destroyed too, then once the tie of karma is destroyed there would be neither rebirth nor nirvana.
And if, though destroyed along with them, it is still born again in the cycle of rebirth, then form bound up with it will also come back, since they are not separate.
Mind and form are neither not-different nor different, because (both) come from conceptualizing. Things are not destroyed, since they are free of the extremes of being and non-being.
The imagined and the dependent (natures) have marks that cannot be separated from each other; like impermanence in form, they give rise to each other.
Free of being other or not other, the imagined cannot be pinned down. So how can it be said to exist or not exist? It is like impermanence in form.
When the imagined is seen clearly, the dependent does not arise; when the dependent is seen (for what it is), the imagined becomes suchness.
If they destroy the imagined, my guidance is destroyed, and they will add false claims and deny what is true within my teaching.

cmp.note: netrī 是「引导者、领路的」,也有「眼」的联想。实叉难陀译成「法眼」,白话译成「引导」;英文用 guidance,和白话一致。这里说「破坏遍计」会坏法，是因为一口否定一切现象(连作为方便的名相也不要)就成了断灭见。
cmp.en: Netrī means “guide, what leads,” with an echo of “eye.” Śikṣānanda renders it 法眼 (fǎyǎn, “Dharma-eye”), the plain Chinese 引导 (yǐndǎo, “guidance”); the English follows the latter. Destroying the imagined harms the teaching because flatly denying all appearances, even as useful labels, falls into nihilism.

verses.en: Whenever there are people like this who corrupt the Dharma, none of them should be spoken with; they are destroyers of my guidance.
The wise should not talk with them, and should give up doing a monk’s duties with them — those who destroy the imagined, who make false claims and false denials.
Their imagining is like a hair-net, a magic show, a dream, a gandharva city, a mirage, because they see in terms of “is not” and “is.”
Whoever keeps company with them is not training in the way of the buddhas; these people have fallen into the two extremes and they ruin others too.
But yogis who see the imagined thing as void, free of existence and non-existence — with them one should keep company.
Just as in the world there are mines that yield gold, gems and pearls, all different, which are not caused by karma and yet fools make a living from them,
so the families (gotra, spiritual lineages) of beings are varied and not made by karma. Because what is seen does not exist, there is no karma, and no destination born of karma.

cmp.note: 梵文说众生的种性形形色色，「不由业所造」。实叉难陀译成「业性亦如是，远离种种性」,并说「非不生诸趣」,和梵文「没有业所生的去处」方向正相反。白话照梵文译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says the lineages of beings are various and “not made by karma.” Śikṣānanda writes 业性亦如是，远离种种性 (“the nature of karma is like this, free of all kinds of nature”) and then 非不生诸趣 (“it is not that the destinies are not produced”), the opposite of the Sanskrit’s “no destination born of karma.” The plain Chinese follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: Things have no real existence in the way the noble ones discern; and yet things do exist in the way fools conceptualize them.
If things did not exist (even) in the way fools conceptualize them, then, since beings and things would be non-existent, nobody would have any defilement. (Reading na for the text’s va.)
Through defilement by the variety of things, the embodied, bound by ignorance and craving and equipped with sense faculties, run on in the cycle of rebirth.
For those for whom there is no thing even in the way fools conceptualize it, the sense faculties would not function — and then there would be no yogi either.
If the things that cause the cycle of existence did not exist, then fools would be liberated without doing anything.
Then how would the difference between fools and noble ones come about through existence and non-existence? For the noble ones who practice the three gates of liberation, there are no things.
The aggregates, persons, phenomena, particular and general marks, the markless, conditions and sense faculties — these I teach to the disciples.
No-cause, mind-only, the powers, the stages, and the pure suchness realized within oneself — these I teach to the Victor’s own children.
In times to come there will be people who corrupt my teaching, wearing the saffron robe, who claim that the effect already exists in the cause, or that it does not.
Things that do not truly exist do exist through conditions — this is the field of the noble ones. Yet the logicians will imagine that the imagined thing simply does not exist.
In times to come there will be fools of the school of Kanada (the atomist) who, with the wrong view that the effect does not pre-exist its cause, will ruin people.

cmp.note: asat-kārya-vāda 是胜论派「果在因中本无」的主张(羯那陀即胜论派祖师)。白话「果本无而生」照梵文；实叉难陀却译成「无因论」,和梵文不同：胜论派讲因，只是说果事先不在因里。
cmp.en: Asat-kārya-vāda is the Vaiśeṣika doctrine that the effect does not exist beforehand in its cause (Kaṇāda founded that school). The plain Chinese 果本无而生 (guǒ běn wú ér shēng, “the effect arises from not having been”) follows the Sanskrit; Śikṣānanda instead writes 无因论 (wúyīn lùn, “the doctrine of no cause”), which misstates it: that school does teach causes, only that the effect is not already in them.

verses.en: With wrong views they will teach that the world arises from atoms, that the atoms themselves have no cause, and that the nine substances are permanent.
Substance is built up from substances, and qualities likewise from qualities — and so they will destroy the other, real nature of things.
If the world came into being after not existing, it would have a beginning. But I say the cycle of rebirth has no first point.
If the three realms and everything counted in them came into being after not existing, then dogs, camels and donkeys would grow horns, no doubt about it.
If the eye, form and consciousness came into being after not existing, then mats, crowns, cloth and the like would come out of a lump of clay.

You don’t get a mat out of strips of cloth, and you don’t get cloth out of reeds. If a thing could come about from conditions just anywhere, why doesn’t everything arise from any conditions at all? (The second line is compressed; its exact wording is partly unclear.)
“The soul is the same as the body,” and “something that did not exist comes into being” — these are all other people’s doctrines, and I have only quoted them.
I first state the opposing position in order to block their way of thinking; once their thinking is blocked, I teach my own position.
That is why I have recited the doctrines of the tirthikas (tīrthikas): so that my disciples do not get confused and fall back on a position of being or of nonbeing.
Even the dull-witted followers of Kapila teach their disciples that the world arose from primal matter (pradhāna), and that it is a transformation of the qualities (guṇas).

cmp.note: pradhāna 是数论派（迦毗罗一派）说的「原初物质」，一切从它展开；guṇa 是它的三种性质。白话沿用旧译「胜性」，实叉难陀则把 guṇa 音译成「求那」。英文直接说 primal matter 和 qualities，括号里留梵文。
cmp.en: Pradhāna is the Sāṃkhya (Kapila school) term for “primal matter,” from which everything unfolds; the guṇas are its three qualities. The modern Chinese keeps the old rendering 胜性 (shèngxìng, “supreme nature”), and Śikṣānanda simply transliterates guṇa as 求那 (qiúnà). The English says “primal matter” and “qualities,” with the Sanskrit in parentheses.

verses.en: It is not what already exists, nor what does not yet exist; it is not by conditions, and the conditions are not conditions either. Since conditions have no real existence, what does not exist does not come into being.
My own position is free from the sides of being and nonbeing, free of causes and conditions, without arising or perishing, and beyond anything that could be pointed to by a mark.

When you always see the world as like an illusion or a dream, free of causes and conditions, without any cause, conceptualizing (vikalpa, the mind’s habit of carving things up into this and that) does not arise.

When you always see existence as like a city of gandharvas (a mirage city in the sky), a heat-shimmer, or a net of hairs (the floaters seen by someone with an eye disorder) — free from the sides of being and nonbeing, free of causes and conditions, without any cause — then the stream of the mind becomes pure.
(Objection:) If, seeing that no object exists, mind-only does not exist either — then without an object, how could there be a mind? Mind-only does not hold up.

cmp.note: 梵文这一颂没有标出说话的人，只从内容看出是反方的质疑。白话加了「（有人问：）」，英文也加了「（Objection:）」，都是补出来的；实叉难陀用「若言……」带出反问。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit does not mark who is speaking; only the content shows it is an objection. The modern Chinese adds （有人问：） (yǒu rén wèn, “someone asks”), and the English adds “(Objection:)” — both are supplied. Śikṣānanda signals it with 若言 (ruò yán, “if one says”).

verses.en: People’s minds arise by taking an object as their support. Without a cause, how can there be a mind? Mind-only does not hold up.
(Answer:) Thusness (tathatā, things just as they are) and mind-only belong to the noble ones’ way of seeing reality. Those who say they exist, or say they do not exist, have not understood my method.
If the mind operates as something grasped and something grasping, that is just ordinary worldly mind; mind-only does not apply to it.
If the appearance of a body, possessions, and a place to live arises the way a dream does, it would follow that there are two minds — yet the mind does not have two marks.
Just as a sword cannot cut its own edge and a finger cannot touch its own tip, so the mind cannot see itself.

In the imageless state there is no dependent nature (paratantra), no imagined nature, and no object either; the five dharmas (name, sign, conceptualizing, right knowledge, suchness) and the twofold mind are not there at all.

cmp.w: na paraṃ na ca vai tantraṃ
cmp.note: para 和 tantra 很可能是为了凑格律把一个词 paratantra（依他起）拆成两半。白话把它们分成「他者」和「依他起」两项；实叉难陀只译出「依他起」。英文按一个词处理。
cmp.en: Para and tantra are most likely one word, paratantra (the dependent nature), split in two to fit the meter. The modern Chinese treats them as two items, 他者 (tāzhě, “the other”) and 依他起 (yītāqǐ, “the dependent”); Śikṣānanda renders only 依他起. The English treats them as one term.

verses.en: Things have two kinds of mark: what produces and what is produced. When I say things are without own-nature (niḥsvabhāva), I have what produces in mind.
And if conceptualizing arose from the variety of shapes, then empty space and a rabbit’s horn would also show up as objects.
If the mind showed up as an object, that object would not be something imagined. But an imagined object is never said to be anything other than the mind.
Throughout beginningless saṃsāra (the round of birth and death) there has never been an object anywhere. Without anything to feed it, how could the mind go on appearing as objects?

cmp.note: puṣṭa 是「被喂养、被滋养」。这里和后面几颂一直用「喂养」打比方：心要有东西喂才能长出影像。白话照字面作「没有得到滋养」；实叉难陀改成「心无有起处」，比喻没了。英文用 feed，保留这个比喻。
cmp.en: Puṣṭa means “fed, nourished.” This verse and the next few keep the feeding image: the mind needs something to feed on before it can grow appearances. The modern Chinese keeps it literally, 没有得到滋养 (méiyǒu dédào zīyǎng, “not nourished”); Śikṣānanda changes it to 心无有起处 (xīn wú yǒu qǐchù, “the mind has no place to arise from”), losing the image. The English uses “feed” to keep the metaphor.

verses.en: If nonexistence could feed something, then a rabbit’s horn would grow too. Conceptualizing does not arise by being fed on nonexistence.
Just as it does not exist now, it did not exist before either. Where there is no object, how can a mind tied to an object go on operating?
Thusness, emptiness (śūnyatā), the limit of reality, nirvana, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the non-arising of phenomena — this is the ultimate own-nature (svabhāva).
Fools fall into “it is” and “it is not” by imagining causes and conditions, because they do not understand that existence is without cause and unborn.

Mind shines forth; there is nothing out there to be seen; the differences have a beginningless cause. (Question:) But if even from beginningless time there has been no object, what gives rise to the differences?
If nonexistence could feed something, a poor man would become rich. With no object, how does a mind arise? Tell me, sage (muni, a name for the Buddha).
(Answer:) All this is without cause: there is neither mind nor any sphere for it to move in. The mind is not fed by anything, and the three realms of existence are free of any doing.
To put an end to the idea of arising and to establish non-arising, I teach the doctrine of no cause — but fools do not grasp it. All this is unborn, and yet it is not that things do not exist.

(Question:) Things called gandharva cities, dreams, and illusions exist without a cause. On what grounds do you tell me they are unborn, without own-nature, and empty? (The Sanskrit reads “own-natures” here, probably a slip for “without own-nature.”)
(Answer:) When a thing, taken out of its combination of conditions, can no longer be seen, then I call it empty, unborn, and without own-nature.
Dreams, a net of hairs, illusions, gandharva cities, and heat-shimmers are seen even though they have no cause; the variety of the world is just like that.

In the same way, combination itself, taken as a single thing, does not exist, because what is seen does not exist. But this is not destruction as the tirthikas view it: combination simply does not exist. (The force of “single” here is unclear.)
By analyzing things through the doctrine of no cause, one should establish non-arising. When things are established as unborn, my guidance is not lost.
When the doctrines of no cause are taught, the tirthikas grow afraid: “How, by whom, from where, and in what could something arise without a cause?”
When the wise see that things are not caused and yet not simply causeless, the view that keeps talking about perishing and arising falls away. (The first line is compressed; this is a best reading.)
(Question:) Is non-arising just nonexistence? Is it the mark of arising and coming into being? Or is it a name for some existing thing, or a word with no meaning? Tell me.

cmp.note: 梵文这里问的是「生起、出生的相」，没有提到缘。白话写成「缘生起的相」，是照着下一颂佛答的 pratyayalakṣaṇa（缘的相）补进去的。英文照梵文字面译，不加「缘」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit here asks about “the mark of arising and coming into being”; conditions are not mentioned. The modern Chinese writes 缘生起的相 (yuán shēngqǐ de xiàng, “the mark of arising from conditions”), borrowing pratyayalakṣaṇa (“the mark of conditions”) from the Buddha’s reply in the next verse. The English follows the Sanskrit literally and leaves conditions out.

verses.en: (Answer:) Non-arising is not nonexistence, nor is it the mark of conditions; it is not a name for some existing thing, nor is it a word with no meaning.
What lies beyond the reach of disciples (śrāvakas), solitary buddhas, tirthikas, and those who have reached the seventh stage — that is the mark of non-arising.

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「声闻与佛」。在这种并列里，「佛」指的是独觉（pratyekabuddha），不是如来，所以白话译成「独觉」。英文也写 solitary buddhas，否则读者会以为连佛也达不到。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit literally says “disciples and buddhas.” In this pairing “buddhas” means solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas), not fully awakened Tathagatas, so the modern Chinese gives 独觉 (dújué, “solitary awakened one”). The English also says “solitary buddhas”; otherwise readers would think even a buddha cannot reach it.

verses.en: Turning away from causes and conditions, rejecting any maker, and establishing mind-only (cittamātra) — this is what I call non-arising.
Things occurring without a cause, free of both the imagined and the imagining, released from the sides of being and nonbeing — this is what I call non-arising.
Freedom from what the mind sees, freedom from the two own-natures, the turning around of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti, the transformation at the root of the mind) — this is what I call non-arising.
Not the external existence of things, and not the mind’s grasping, but the abandoning of all views — that is the mark of non-arising.
So one should look at all phenomena as empty, without own-nature, and so on — not empty with a mere emptiness, but empty in the sense of non-arising.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「不是以（单纯的）空而空」，没有「断灭」一词。白话补成「断灭的空」，点出要否定的是什么都没有的那种空，意思通，但多了一层解释。英文写 a mere emptiness，没有加「断灭」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only “not empty by (mere) emptiness”; there is no word for annihilation. The modern Chinese adds 断灭的空 (duànmiè de kōng, “annihilationist emptiness”), making explicit that the rejected sense is sheer nothingness — reasonable, but an added layer of interpretation. The English says “a mere emptiness” without adding annihilation.

verses.en: A cluster of conditions comes into being and falls apart; what stands separate from the cluster is neither born nor does it cease.
No other thing exists anywhere apart from the cluster — not in the way the tirthikas conceptualize it, as either one with it or separate from it.
A thing is not born from what is, nor from what is not, nor from what both is and is not; it is only this cluster that comes into being and falls apart.
This is only a convention, arising from a chain of things that depend on one another. Apart from the chain of conditions, no produced thing exists.
Non-arising means there is no produced thing; it is free of the tirthikas’ faults. I teach that there is only the chain, but fools do not grasp it.
Anyone who holds that some produced thing exists anywhere apart from the chain should be recognized as a no-cause theorist, someone who destroys the chain.

If someone holds that there is some thing anywhere apart from the chain, then for them the chain would merely reveal it, the way a lamp reveals objects and their kinds. (The wording is compressed; meaning partly unclear.)
Whatever phenomenon fools imagine as existing apart from the chain is by nature without own-nature and unborn, like the sky.

This is a different non-arising: the nature of what the noble ones attain. And the non-arising of that — that would be the acceptance of non-arising (anutpādakṣānti, calmly accepting that nothing is truly born).
When one sees this whole world as just a chain — “this is only a chain” — then the mind settles into concentration.
Ignorance, craving, karma and the like make up the inner chain; a churning stick, clay, a rod, a potter’s wheel and the like, or seeds, the elements and so on, make up the outer chain.
Those who think a thing is born somewhere from something other than itself, through conditions, rather than being only a chain, do not stand on either reasoning or scripture.
(Question:) If no produced thing exists, from what condition would cognition arise? (Answer:) These things are conditions for one another; that is why they are called conditions.
Heat, wetness, motion, and hardness are conceptualized by fools as real things. But this is only a cluster; there is no such thing in itself — and that is why things are without own-nature.
Just as doctors vary their treatment according to the patient’s condition, while the medical science itself does not vary — only the disorders vary —

cmp.note: doṣa 在印度医学里是「体液失调」（风、胆、痰），引申为病、过失。白话直接译成「病」，好懂；英文用 disorders，保留一点医学味。下一颂又用 kleśadoṣa（烦恼之过），正是借这个医学词打比方。
cmp.en: In Indian medicine doṣa means an imbalance of the bodily humors (wind, bile, phlegm), and by extension illness or fault. The modern Chinese simply says 病 (bìng, “illness”), which reads easily; the English uses “disorders” to keep a medical flavor. The next verse says kleśadoṣa (“the faults of the afflictions”), playing on this very medical word.

verses.en: so too, knowing the strength of the faculties in beings whose mind-streams are badly tainted by the faults of the afflictions (kleśas), I teach the method to the simple-minded.
My teaching is not split apart by differences in afflictions or faculties. There is only one vehicle: the auspicious eightfold path.
The nonexistence of a rabbit’s horn is stated on the basis of pots, cloth, crowns, and horns. Understand that whatever arises from causes does not exist either.

Nonexistence is what establishes existence, and to say “nonexistence does not exist” makes no sense; existence depends on nonexistence, and each is the cause of the other through mutual dependence. (The first line is ambiguous; it could also mean “there is nothing that establishes existence.”)
Some people hold that one thing appears by depending on another. But then the thing depended on would be without a cause, while the thing depending on it would not be.
And if that in turn depends on something else, and that appears from something else again, you get an endless regress, and nothing at all could come to be.
Just as an illusion is conjured by relying on leaves, sticks and the like, so people see variety by relying on some real basis.
The web of illusion is not the leaves, not the sticks, not the pebbles. Fools see only the illusion, and what it rests on is the illusionist.
Likewise, if something perishes while resting on a real basis, then at the moment of seeing there are not two things — so how could anything be conceptualized? (Meaning partly unclear.)
What conceptualizing conceptualizes does not exist, and conceptualizing itself is not found either. And with conceptualizing not found, there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvana.
With conceptualizing not found, conceptualizing does not arise. (Objection:) If the mind does not operate, how can there be a mind? Mind-only does not hold up.
Because opinions are so many and so divided, the teaching has no core. Without a core there is no liberation, nor any variety in the world.
What is seen outside does not exist the way fools conceptualize it. The mind, set spinning by habit-energy (vāsanā, the lingering imprint of past experience), appears like a reflection.
All things are unborn; they do not arise from what is, from what is not, or from what both is and is not. All this is mind-only, free of imaginings.
It is fools who describe things as arising from conditions, not the wise. The mind freed from own-nature and from mind is the peaceful mind the noble ones arrive at.
The Samkhyas, the Vaisheshikas, the naked ascetics, the brahmins, and the Pashupatas all fall into views of being and nonbeing and miss the meaning of solitude.

cmp.note: vivikta 原义是「分开的、独处的、空出来的」，在这里指离开一切执取、空寂的状态。白话和实叉难陀都译成「寂静」；英文 solitude 更贴近「独处、隔开」的字面。
cmp.en: Vivikta originally means “set apart, secluded, emptied out”; here it points to a state cut off from all grasping. The modern Chinese and Śikṣānanda both give 寂静 (jìjìng, “stillness”); the English “solitude” stays closer to the literal sense of being set apart.

verses.en: (Question:) Without own-nature, unborn, empty, like an illusion, stainless — to whom did the buddhas teach these things, and to whom do you explain them?
(Answer:) To yogis whose minds are pure and free of views and speculation: the buddhas teach the practice to them, and I explain it to them too.
(Question:) If all this is mind, what is the world resting on? And by what are people seen coming and going on the ground?
(Answer:) Just as a bird, pushed along by conceptualizing, moves through the sky with nothing to stand on and nothing to hold, as though it were walking on the ground —
so all embodied beings, pushed along by conceptualizing, walk to and fro in their own mind, like a bird in the sky.
(Question:) Tell me how the mind comes to appear as a body, possessions, and a place to live. How, and by what, do appearance and activity arise? Explain mind-only to me.
(Answer:) Body, possessions, and dwelling, appearance and activity, arise from habit-energies. For those who are undisciplined, appearance and activity arise from conceptualizings.

cmp.note: ayukta 字面是「没有相应、没有在瑜伽里」的人，即心不收摄、不修行的人。白话译成「不如理思维的人」，实叉难陀作「不如理」，都偏向「想错了」；梵文更偏「没修持、心散乱」。英文用 undisciplined。
cmp.en: Ayukta literally means someone “not yoked” — not engaged in yoga, with an unrestrained mind. The modern Chinese gives 不如理思维的人 (bù rúlǐ sīwéi de rén, “those who do not think in accordance with reason”), and Śikṣānanda 不如理 (bù rúlǐ), both leaning toward “thinking wrongly”; the Sanskrit leans more toward “unpracticed, scattered.” The English says “undisciplined.”

verses.en: The object is something conceptualized, and the mind arises out of the object. By fully understanding that what is seen is mind, conceptualizing stops.

cmp.note: 这个复合词可以拆成「所见与心的遍知」，也可以读成「遍知所见即是心」。白话取前一种（「遍知所见与心」）；实叉难陀作「了境是惟心」，取后一种。英文跟实叉难陀，因为这一章反复讲的正是「所见只是自心」。
cmp.en: This compound can be split as “full knowledge of the seen and of mind,” or read as “fully knowing that the seen is mind.” The modern Chinese takes the first: 遍知所见与心 (biànzhī suǒjiàn yǔ xīn, “fully knowing the seen and the mind”); Śikṣānanda takes the second: 了境是惟心 (liǎo jìng shì wéixīn, “understanding that objects are mind only”). The English follows Śikṣānanda, since this chapter keeps saying that what is seen is only one’s own mind.

verses.en: When one sees that the imagined thing is not bound to its name — the name is not in the thing named — and is free of knower and known, then one is released from the conditioned.
This is what knowing and the known come to: seeing clearly that the name is not in the thing named. Those who understand it any other way are not awakened and cannot awaken others.
The five dharmas, the three own-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of no-self — these take in the whole of the Great Vehicle (Mahayana).
When one sees the world as empty of knower and known, there is no name, and conceptualizing no longer arises.
By seeing the mind, activity, words, and conceptualizing come to an end; by not seeing one’s own mind, conceptualizing arises.
The four formless aggregates (skandhas) cannot be counted. Since the elements each have different characteristics, how could form be made of many?
Once the marks are given up, there is neither element nor anything made of elements. And if form had other marks of its own, why would it not be produced by the aggregates?
When one sees the sense-fields and aggregates as released and without marks, then the mind turns back, because it sees the no-self of phenomena.
Through the difference of objects and sense faculties, consciousness arises in eight ways; in terms of marks it is threefold; in the imageless it ceases.

The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds), the self and what is mine in manas (the thinking mind), and consciousness — these arise from grasping at two, and cease through full understanding.

cmp.note: 梵文只是并列：阿赖耶、意中的我与我所、识。实叉难陀译成「意缘阿赖耶，起我我所执」，把唯识宗的说法（末那识把阿赖耶识当成「我」）直接写进去了。白话照梵文并列，英文也照字面。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit simply lists them: the ālaya, the self and what is mine in manas, and consciousness. Śikṣānanda renders 意缘阿赖耶，起我我所执 (yì yuán ālàiyē, qǐ wǒ wǒsuǒ zhí, “manas takes the ālaya as its object and grasps at self and mine”), writing the Yogācāra doctrine — manas mistaking the storehouse consciousness for a self — straight into the verse. The modern Chinese keeps the plain list, and so does the English.

verses.en: When one sees it as free of “different” and “not different,” and no longer wandering on, then one stops imagining the two: self and what belongs to self.
What no longer arises no longer feeds anything, nor is it a cause of consciousness. Free of effect and cause, what has ceased does not arise again.
(Question:) Tell me on what grounds you call the world conceptualizing and mind-only, unconnected to causes, and free of what is marked and the mark.

(Answer:) It is one’s own mind that is seen in all its variety; the shapes of what is seen are conceptualized. Not fully understanding what the mind sees, people grasp objects as something other than mind.
When one does not see objects with insight, a view of nonexistence arises. Then how could a view of existence not arise for him out of the mind’s grasping? (Meaning partly unclear.)
Conceptualizing is neither existence nor nonexistence, so the view of existence does not arise. By fully understanding what the mind sees, conceptualizing does not arise.
With conceptualizing no longer arising, the turning-around (parāvṛtti) has nothing to rest on. This blocks the four positions — such as “things have causes” —
which are only differences in names; “made by whom?” is never proven. For them, the result would either be inferred by presumption or come forth from a maker. (Meaning partly unclear.)

cmp.note: arthāpatti 是印度逻辑里的一种认识手段，叫「义准量」：从已知事实反推出必然的前提（例如「白天不吃却发胖，可见晚上在吃」）。白话译成「靠推论得出」，实叉难陀没有译出这个词。英文用 presumption，并标明意思不太确定。
cmp.en: Arthāpatti is a recognized means of knowledge in Indian logic, “postulation”: inferring the premise a known fact requires (the classic example: “he is fat but doesn’t eat by day, so he must eat at night”). The modern Chinese gives 靠推论得出 (kào tuīlùn déchū, “arrived at by inference”); Śikṣānanda leaves the word out. The English uses “presumption” and flags that the meaning is uncertain.

verses.en: By pointing to the coming together of causes and conditions, a maker is denied; and if the conditions are impermanent, the fault of permanence is avoided.
The impermanence that fools talk about gives neither arising nor perishing; nothing that is itself perishing is ever seen to act as a cause.

Since that is never seen, how, and by what, could existence arise from what is impermanent? One should tame beings with the ways of drawing people in (saṃgraha), bring them under control with moral discipline,

cmp.note: saṃgraha 在这里指菩萨的「四摄」：布施、爱语、利行、同事，是把人吸引过来、带上路的四种方法。白话写「种种摄受」；英文写成 the ways of drawing people in。另外，这一颂后半其实开启了新话题，与下一颂连读；实叉难陀只译了前半。
cmp.en: Saṃgraha here means the bodhisattva’s four “means of gathering” — giving, kind speech, helpful action, and sharing others’ lives — ways of drawing people in and setting them on the path. The modern Chinese writes 种种摄受 (zhǒngzhǒng shèshòu, “various ways of embracing”); the English says “the ways of drawing people in.” Note also that the second half of this verse starts a new topic that runs into the next verse; Śikṣānanda translates only the first half.

verses.en: destroy wrong views with wisdom, and help them grow through the liberations. Everything the tirthikas teach is false — it is all Lokayata (the materialist “worldly” school).
Because they take effect and cause to be real, they have no genuine position of their own. I alone have a position of my own, free of effect and cause,
and I teach it to my disciples, free of Lokayata: there is only mind; nothing seen exists; the mind appears in two ways, as grasped and grasper, free of the extremes of permanence and annihilation.
As long as the mind keeps moving, that is Lokayata. For one who sees the world as his own mind, conceptualizing does not arise.

cmp.note: lokāyata 本来是印度的唯物派（只承认四大、不承认来世）。但在这几颂里，佛把它的范围放得很宽：只要心还在动、还在讲常无常、因果，就都算 lokāyata，几乎等于「世俗的思辨」。白话一律作「顺世论」，读者容易以为只指那个学派；英文保留名称，并在第一次出现时加了说明。
cmp.en: Lokāyata originally names the Indian materialist school (only the four elements, no afterlife). But in these verses the Buddha stretches it very wide: as long as the mind keeps moving, talking of permanent and impermanent, cause and effect, it all counts as lokāyata — almost “worldly speculation” in general. The modern Chinese consistently writes 顺世论 (shùnshìlùn, “the doctrine that follows the world”), which readers may take to mean only that one school; the English keeps the name and glosses it at first mention.

verses.en: Coming is the production of an effect; going is seeing the effect disappear. By fully understanding coming and going, conceptualizing does not arise.
Permanent and impermanent, made and unmade, the higher and the lower (or: this world and the next) — all these and the like are Lokayata.
Gods, asuras (titans), humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and the realm of Yama — these are called the six destinies, where embodied beings are born.
Beings are born into them through low, high, or middling karma. By guarding all that is wholesome, one reaches the highest distinction — that is, liberation.
You teach the community of monks that dying and being reborn happen moment after moment. Tell me what you mean by that.
Just as one form gives way to another form, the mind comes together and then breaks apart. That is why I teach my disciples the chain of births that happen moment by moment.
In form after form, conceptualizing arises and passes away in just the same way. A living being is really nothing but conceptualizing; apart from conceptualizing, no other being is found.

Saying “moment after moment” is not quite fitting; it was said in terms of this-conditionality (idaṃpratyayatā, things arising because these conditions are present). Once free of grasping at form, there is no birth and nothing breaks apart.

cmp.note: idaṃpratyaya 可以读成「此缘性」（依这些条件而有），也可以读成「为此缘故而说」。白话取前者；实叉难陀「我为此缘故」取后者。英文跟白话走，但这里两种读法都讲得通。
cmp.en: Idaṃpratyaya can be read as “this-conditionality” (things existing because these conditions are present) or as “said for this reason.” The plain Chinese takes the first; Śikṣānanda’s 我为此缘故 (wǒ wèi cǐ yuángù, “for this reason I”) takes the second. The English follows the first, but both readings work here.

verses.en: Conditions and what arises from conditions — ignorance, suchness (tathatā, things just as they are), and the rest — run as two kinds of phenomena. Suchness, though, would be non-dual.
If conditions and what arises from conditions were set apart as distinct phenomena, then permanence and the like would become an effect, and a condition would become a maker-cause.

Then, since it would take in both effect and cause, your teaching and the buddhas’ would be no different from that of the tirthikas (tīrthikas), and so it would not be noble, great sage (mahāmuni, a name for the Buddha).
In this body, just a fathom tall, I teach the children of the Victor (jina, a name for a buddha) the world, the arising of the world, and the path that leads to its cessation.
By grasping the three own-natures, ordinary people form views of the grasped and the grasper, and they conceptualize worldly and world-transcending phenomena.
So own-nature is first taken up as the opening position to be examined (pūrvapakṣa); but in order to block views, one should not conceptualize own-nature.

Picking holes in others’ faults brings no certainty, and the mind does not settle either. Grasping at a twofold activity is the problem; suchness would be non-dual. (The first line is hard to construe.)

Ignorance, craving, karma, consciousness and the rest arise without a proper source (ayonija). Positing a further cause brings infinite regress and makes existence something manufactured; but existence does not come about by being made. (Meaning partly unclear.)

cmp.note: ayonija 字面是「不从胎生的」「没有出处的」。白话把它当成 ayoniśo（不如理）来译，作「由不如理而生」；实叉难陀这里只说「邪念复有因」。英文照字面译作「没有正当来源」，并注明这句意思不全清楚。
cmp.en: Ayonija literally means “not born from a womb,” “without a source.” The plain Chinese reads it as ayoniśo (“improper attention”) and renders 由不如理而生 (yóu bù rúlǐ ér shēng, “arising from improper thinking”); Śikṣānanda just has 邪念复有因 (xiéniàn fù yǒu yīn, “wrong thoughts have a further cause”). The English stays literal, “without a proper source,” and flags the verse as partly unclear.

verses.en: The unwise talk about four kinds of destruction of things. For conceptualizing, which works in two ways, there is really no being and no non-being. The truth is free of the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi: is, is not, both, neither) and leaves both views behind.
Conceptualizing works in two ways; once that is seen, it no longer runs on. With unborn things, because an understanding arises about them —
— and with born things too, because that is also conceptualizing, one should not conceptualize. Protector, tell me the reasoning that wards off two-sided views,

so that I and others may never mix up “is not” and “is.” [The answer:] It is untouched by tirthika doctrines, out of reach of the disciples (śrāvakas) (the phrase jina-varjitāḥ is unclear), the practice that the Victors realize, in which the Victor’s children never fall away.

cmp.note: yathā 在这里是「好让」，aham「我」是大慧自己：「好让我和其他人永远不把有与无混为一谈」，接着上一颂的请问。白话译成「（答：）就像我和其他佛一样」，把说话人换成了佛，与梵文不合。实叉难陀「令我及余众，恒不堕有无」是对的。
cmp.en: Here yathā means “so that,” and aham (“I”) is Mahamati: “so that I and others never confuse is and is not,” continuing the request of the previous verse. The plain Chinese has （答：）就像我和其他佛一样 (jiù xiàng wǒ hé qítā fó yíyàng, “[answer:] just like me and the other buddhas”), shifting the speaker to the Buddha, which the Sanskrit does not support. Śikṣānanda’s 令我及余众，恒不堕有无 (lìng wǒ jí yú zhòng, héng bù duò yǒu wú, “so that I and others never fall into being or non-being”) is right.

verses.en: The cause of liberation and the non-cause share one single mark: non-arising. People use different words for it and so confuse it; the wise should always stay clear of that.

All things are like clouds, banks of mist, a rainbow, a mirage, a net of hairs (keśoṇḍuka, the floaters a diseased eye sees), a magic show: they come from one’s own conceptualizing. The tirthikas conceptualize the world in terms of their own causes.
Non-arising, suchness, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi, the very edge of the real), emptiness — these are names of form. One should not conceptualize them as non-existence.

cmp.note: 梵文说这些是「色的名称」，白话照译。实叉难陀改成「此等异名说」，只说它们是同一回事的不同名称，没提色。英文照梵文译，但读者可以把它理解为同一实相的异名。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says these are “names of form,” and the plain Chinese follows it. Śikṣānanda changes it to 此等异名说 (cǐděng yìmíng shuō, “these are different names”), simply calling them synonyms without mentioning form. The English follows the Sanskrit, but it can be read as different names for one reality.

verses.en: Just as in the world a hand is called hasta or kara, and Indra is called Shakra or Purandara, so too with all things: one should not conceptualize them as non-existence.
Emptiness is not something other than form, and the same goes for non-arising. Since they are not different, one should not imagine them as different, or the fault of wrong views follows.
Conceiving (saṃkalpa) and conceptualizing come from taking hold of things and their marks; long, short, round and so on come from taking hold of imagination (parikalpa).
Conceiving is the mind (citta); imagining is manas (the thinking mind); conceptualizing is mind consciousness — and all are free of what is marked and what marks it.

cmp.note: 三个词都带「想」的意思，梵文靠前缀区分：saṃkalpa 是起念，parikalpa 是周遍计度，vikalpa 是分别。白话译作想念、周遍计度、分别；实叉难陀用总分别、遍分别、别分别，把三者都当作「分别」的种类。英文只能用 conceiving、imagining、discrimination 勉强分开。
cmp.en: All three words mean some kind of “thinking up,” told apart by prefix: saṃkalpa is forming a notion, parikalpa is imagining all around, vikalpa is conceptualizing. The plain Chinese has 想念 (xiǎngniàn, “conceiving”), 周遍计度 (zhōubiàn jìduó, “pervasive reckoning”), 分别 (fēnbié, “distinguishing”); Śikṣānanda treats all three as kinds of conceptualizing: 总分别, 遍分别, 别分别 (zǒng / biàn / bié fēnbié, “general / pervasive / particular conceptualizing”). English can only roughly separate them as conceiving, imagining, and conceptualizing.

verses.en: The non-arising that the tirthikas imagine and the non-arising imagined by those who hold views within my own method are no different, and the fault of wrong views follows.
Those who know the purpose of non-arising and the meaning of non-arising, who understand reasoning, are the ones who grasp my method.
Its purpose is to shrink views; non-arising has no place to settle (anālaya). Because I want both these meanings understood, I teach non-arising.
Great sage, tell me: do unborn things exist or not? Teaching non-arising sounds like the no-cause doctrine, and teaching activity sounds like the tirthika view.
The no-cause doctrine and the doctrine of non-arising are the crooked views of the tirthikas. I teach mind-only, free of “is” and “is not.”
One should give up arising and non-arising when they rest on views. In the no-cause doctrine there is non-arising; in arising there is reliance on a maker-cause.

There is no effortless action, and if there is action, views get mixed in. Tell me about the view that comes with skillful means, vows and the rest. If all phenomena are unreal, how does the seat of awakening (maṇḍala) come about?

cmp.note: maṇḍala 原意是「圆」「坛场」，这里指佛成道的处所（bodhimaṇḍa）。白话和实叉难陀都译作「道场」；英文没有现成对应词，译作 seat of awakening。
cmp.en: Maṇḍala basically means “circle” or “sacred enclosure”; here it means the place where a buddha awakens (bodhimaṇḍa). The plain Chinese and Śikṣānanda both use 道场 (dàochǎng, “place of the Way”); English has no ready equivalent, so it says “seat of awakening.”

verses.en: Once grasped and grasper come apart, there is neither activity nor stopping. The view that one thing turns into another thing arises from the mind itself.
And how is it that phenomena are unborn? Tell me this. If beings do not understand, that is why it has to be made clear.
Great sage, explain everything that seems to clash between earlier and later statements, free of the faults of the tirthikas and free of crooked, causeless ideas.
Best of speakers, tell me about non-activity and stopping, free of “is” and “is not,” in a way that does not wreck effect and cause.

Tell me how the stages (bhūmi, the levels of the bodhisattva path) connect in order, and tell me the mark of the Dharma. The world has fallen to the two extremes and is thrown into confusion by views.
Because of non-arising, arising and the like, the cause of peace is not understood. I have no seat of awakening at all, and I do not teach any nature of things (dharmatā).
Where there is duality there is fault, and the buddhas have cleared duality away. Things are empty, momentary, without own-nature, and unborn.
Those covered over by talk of bad views imagine such things; the Tathagatas do not. Tell me how conceptualizing starts up and how it stops.

In what way, and by what means, does an object arise and come face to face with us? It is put together by conceptual proliferation, from a rich combination of colors and shapes. (The second line is somewhat unclear.)
Seeing form outside, conceptualizing starts up. But by fully understanding that very form, by seeing its meaning as it really is, the mind falls in with the noble lineage and no longer starts up.
Once the elements are set aside, no arising of things is found. One should always see the mind, which takes on the look of the elements, as unborn.
Don’t conceptualize conceptualizing; the wise are free of conceptualizing. Whoever conceptualizes conceptualizing is left with duality, not nirvana.
For someone who asserts non-arising, the principle of illusion is also in view. To say that illusion comes about without a cause is the mark of a self-defeating doctrine.
The mind, steeped in beginningless thinking, is seen like a reflection. It takes on the look of objects, yet no object is there. See it as it really is.
Just as a form in a mirror is seen, free of being one with it or other than it, and yet is not nothing, so it is with the mark of arising.

Just as a city of the gandharvas (a mirage city in the sky), a magic show and the like have the marks of causes and conditions, so it is with all things: they do come about; it is not that they never come about.
Conceptualizing takes the shape of a person and runs in two ways, through figurative talk of a self and of phenomena; fools do not see this.

There is the disciple who depends on many conditions, and likewise the arhat; one depends on his own strength, one depends on the Victor; one should guide the fifth kind of disciple too. (Meaning unclear.)
Gaps in time, destruction, the ultimate, and change from one into another: fools who do not understand imagine these four kinds of impermanence.
Fools fall to the two extremes, taking qualities, atoms and primal nature (prakṛti) as causes. Because they cling to the positions of being and non-being, they do not know the way to liberation.
Just as dull-witted fools take the fingertip for the moon, so those attached to the letters do not know my truth.

cmp.note: 梵文是「把指尖当成月亮」——不是只看手指不看月，而是把手指错认成月亮本身。白话译作「抓着指尖而不看月亮」，意思近但稍有不同。英文照梵文译。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says fools “take the fingertip as the moon” — not just looking at the finger instead of the moon, but mistaking the finger for the moon itself. The plain Chinese 抓着指尖而不看月亮 (zhuāzhe zhǐjiān ér bú kàn yuèliang, “clutch the fingertip and don’t look at the moon”) is close but slightly different. The English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: The elements each have different marks; how could they produce form? This is just an arrangement of the elements; what is derived from them is not made by the elements.
Fire burns form, the water element has the nature of soaking it, and wind scatters form. How then could form come from the elements?
Form and consciousness: the aggregates (skandhas) are just these two, not five. I teach the aggregates under a hundred different names.

cmp.note: 梵文「我以百种方式讲说诸蕴的异名」。实叉难陀作「我说彼如怨」（我说它们像仇敌），像是读成了 śatru（敌人）而非 śatadhā（百种）。白话照现存梵文。
