cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “I teach the different names of the aggregates in a hundred ways.” Śikṣānanda has 我说彼如怨 (wǒ shuō bǐ rú yuàn, “I say they are like enemies”), which looks like a reading of śatru (“enemy”) instead of śatadhā (“a hundredfold”). The plain Chinese follows the surviving Sanskrit.

verses.en: Through the division into mind and mental factors, what is present goes on. When forms are taken apart, form is the mind, not something derived from the elements.
White depends on blue and the rest, and blue depends on white. When effect and cause are produced, emptiness both is and is not. (Second line somewhat unclear.)
The means of proof, the one proving, the thing to be proved; cold and heat; the marked and its mark — none of these, and nothing of the kind, is ever established by the logicians.

Mind, manas, and the other six consciousnesses, bound up together and free of being one or other: this is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) at work.

cmp.note: ātma-saṃyutā 可以读成「与自我相连」，也可以读成「彼此相连」。白话取前者；实叉难陀「诸识共相应」取后者。英文取「彼此相连」，因为下文说的是阿赖耶识，不是自我。
cmp.en: Ātma-saṃyutā can mean “joined with a self” or “joined with one another.” The plain Chinese takes the first, 与自我相连 (yǔ zìwǒ xiānglián); Śikṣānanda’s 诸识共相应 (zhū shí gòng xiāngyìng, “the consciousnesses are joined together”) takes the second. The English goes with “bound up together,” since the verse is about the storehouse consciousness, not a self.

verses.en: The Samkhyas, the Vaisheshikas, the naked ascetics, the logicians and those who preach Ishvara (a creator god) have fallen to the positions of being and non-being and are far from the meaning of solitude.
What is derived from the elements is nothing but a particular shape and look of the elements. The tirthikas talk of the elements being born, and of what is derived being born too.
Because things are unborn, those other tirthikas imagine them with causes. In their delusion they do not understand, relying on the positions of being and non-being.
Joined with the mind, apart from manas and the rest, the essence whose mark is pure stays together with wisdom.
If karma were form, with the aggregates and objects as its causes, then beings would have no grasping and could not stay in the formless realm. (Meaning partly unclear.)

Since there would be no beings, a teaching about beings would turn into a denial of self altogether; whoever teaches such selflessness falls into annihilation, and consciousness could not arise either.
Consciousness has four stations; how could they exist without form? With nothing inner and nothing outer, consciousness does not start up.
Just as the logicians accept aggregates in the in-between state (between death and rebirth), why should there not be a formless existence for someone born in the formless realm?
Liberation would come without effort, without beings and without consciousness. That is the tirthika doctrine, no doubt about it, yet the logicians do not see it.
If form exists there, in the formless realm it is not seen. If it does not exist, the doctrine falls apart, and there is no vehicle and no one who travels in it.
Consciousness arises from habit-energy (vāsanā) and is joined with the senses. Part of the eightfold [consciousness] is not grasped in a moment of time. (Meaning unclear.)
When form does not start up, the senses are not senses. That is why the Blessed One teaches that the senses and the rest are momentary.
If form is not pinned down, how will consciousness start up? And if it has not started, how will knowing give rise to samsara (the cycle of birth and death)?
The Guides do not teach destruction right after arising. Things have no unbroken continuity in this course where conceptualizing flickers.
Senses and sense objects belong to the deluded, not to the wise. Fools grasp by the name; the noble ones understand the meaning.
The sixth [consciousness] is not to be taken as without grasping or as with grasping. The noble ones call it undeterminable, free of the faults of saying “it exists.”
Logicians without wisdom are afraid of eternalism and annihilation. These childish people do not tell the conditioned and the unconditioned apart from the self.
If it is one, grasping is found; if it is other, grasping is found too. Oneness is with the mind, and otherness is with manas and the rest.
When grasping is pinned down as the mind, and is called the mental factors, how through grasping could it there be fixed as one? (Meaning unclear.)
They will try to prove a perception with grasping, by karma, birth, action and so on, using fire as the example and reasoning from like and unlike cases.
Just as when fire burns, the burned and the burner are there at once, so too the self with its grasping: why don’t the logicians take it that way?
Whether in arising or in non-arising, the mind is always luminous. Why don’t the logicians who try to prove a self use that as their example?
Lost in the thicket of consciousness, the deluded logicians, who have missed the right method, run here and there in their eagerness to build a doctrine of self.
The self that is reached by inner realization, whose mark is purity — that is the Tathagata-womb (tathāgatagarbha, buddha-nature), and it lies beyond the logicians’ range.

cmp.note: 这几颂里的 ātman 是「自我」，但指的是如来藏那种清净的「我」，不是外道的我。实叉难陀特意译作「真我」以示区别；白话只译「自我」。英文用 self，靠上下文区分，读的时候要记得这不是普通意义的自我。
cmp.en: In these verses ātman means “self,” but it refers to the pure self of the Tathagata-womb, not the self of the tirthikas. Śikṣānanda deliberately says 真我 (zhēnwǒ, “true self”) to mark the difference; the plain Chinese just says 自我 (zìwǒ, “self”). The English uses “self” and relies on context, so keep in mind this is not the ordinary self.

verses.en: If one knows the marks of grasping and the grasper, and of the division of the aggregates, then knowledge, the right method, arises.
Taking the storehouse consciousness as shaped like a womb and joined with a self is a view described by the tirthikas; these are not the teachings proclaimed [by the Buddha].
By sorting these out, there is liberation and the seeing of truth, and the afflictions (kleśas) to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation are cleared away.
The mind, luminous by nature, is the pure Tathagata-womb. It is what beings grasp at, and it is free of limits and the limitless.
Just as the luster of gold, pure gold and gravel are seen only after refining, so is the essence of beings within the aggregates and the storehouse consciousness.
The Buddha is not a person, nor the aggregates; he is undefiled knowledge. Seeing him as always at peace, I go to him for refuge.
Best of speakers, you teach that the mind, luminous by nature, is joined with the secondary afflictions, with manas and the rest, and with a self. [Please explain this.]
The mind is luminous by nature; manas and the rest are other than it. Because of the karma they pile up, the two of them become defiled.
The self, luminous by nature, gets stained by afflictions that are incidental and beginningless, and like a cloth that has been soiled, it can be washed clean.
Just as a cloth without its dirt, or gold without its flaws, remains and is not destroyed, so does the self without its faults.
It is like someone who doesn’t understand hunting for the lovely sound inside a lute, a conch or a drum; looking for a person in the aggregates is just the same.
Treasures, gems, and water under the ground are there but are not seen; so it is with the person in the aggregates.
Clusters of mind and mental factors, each with its own qualities, joined with the aggregates, are not grasped by those who don’t understand; so it is with the person in the aggregates.
Just as the child in a pregnant woman’s womb is there but is not seen, so the self is in the aggregates; someone who doesn’t understand reasoning does not see it.
Just as people who don’t understand reasoning do not see the potency in medicinal herbs, or the fire in firewood, so it is with the person in the aggregates.
Just as fools do not see the impermanence and the emptiness that are present in all things, so it is with the person in the aggregates.
The stages, the masteries, the higher powers (abhijñā), the supreme consecration, the samadhis (deep meditative absorptions) and their special qualities — without a self, none of these exist.
If a nihilist comes and says, “If it exists, show it,” the wise person should answer him, “Show me your own conceptualizing.”
Those who preach no-self should not be spoken with; exclude them from the monks’ communal acts. Holding views of the positions of being and non-being, they undermine the buddhas’ teachings.
Free of the tirthikas’ faults, this teaching of the self blazes up like the fire at the end of an age, burning down the forest of no-self.
In lumps of sugar, sugarcane, refined sugar, honey and the like, and in curd, sesame, ghee and so on, each has its own flavor, but it cannot be known without tasting it.
The self, sought in five ways in the heap of the aggregates, is not seen by the ignorant; the wise see it and are set free.
Even with examples drawn from knowledge and the like, the mind cannot be pinned down; where, from what, and for what the collection is, cannot be pinned down. (Meaning unclear.)
Phenomena have different marks, and the one mind is not grasped; so the logicians end up with no cause and no starting up.
A yogi watching the mind does not see mind in the mind. The seer is born from what is seen; and what is seen — from what cause does it arise?
I am of the Katyayana clan, come down from the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa, the highest heavens of the form realm). I teach beings the Dharma that leads to the city of nirvana.
This is an ancient path. I and those Tathagatas taught nirvana in three thousand sutras.
A buddha does not awaken in the desire realm or in the formless realm; he awakens in the form realm, in the Akanishtha heaven, among those free of passion.
Objects are not the cause of bondage; the cause is being bound to objects. Afflictions are to be cut down by wisdom — this practice is like walking a sword’s edge.

If the self is unreal, how can illusion and other such phenomena be said either to exist or not to exist? Suchness (tathatā, things just as they are) shows itself even to fools — so how can it be nonexistent just because it is without a self? (The verse is compressed; the sense is partly unclear.)
Because things are either made or unmade, there is no cause that sets them going. All of this is unborn, yet fools do not see it.
The makers are unborn, and so are the made things and the conditions. Since neither of these two produces anything, how can anything be imagined in terms of makers?

Logicians (tārkikas, those who argue by speculation) say the cause comes before, after, or at the same time as its effect, and they explain how things come to be with examples like a lamp lighting up a pot, or a teacher and his pupil.

Buddhas do not possess the marks (lakṣaṇa, the bodily signs of a great being) by way of marks that are manufactured. Such things are the virtues of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin, a universal monarch); they are not what the buddhas declared.

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「这些不是佛所宣说的」，白话照字面译。实叉难陀译成「非此名如来」，意思变成「有这些相好并不能叫作如来」，讲的是佛的定义，而不是佛说过什么。两种读法都通，但梵文本身只说前一种。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit literally says “these are not what the buddhas declared,” and the plain Chinese follows that. Śikṣānanda renders it 非此名如来 (fēi cǐ míng rúlái, “this is not what is called a Tathagata”), shifting the point to what makes someone a buddha rather than what a buddha taught. Both readings make sense, but the Sanskrit states only the first.

verses.en: The mark of the buddhas is knowledge, free of the faults of views. Its range is what is seen within oneself, and it destroys every fault.
The deaf, the blind, the one-eyed, the mute, the old, those who live in hostility, and above all fools — for them there is no holy life (brahmacarya, the celibate religious life).

Those whose minor marks are hidden become gods; those whose major marks are hidden become wheel-turning kings. Some, with their marks plainly showing, go forth into homeless life — but not the other teachers. (The Sanskrit is very compressed; this follows the likely sense.)

cmp.note: 梵文最后一句是「其他论者则不然」。实叉难陀没有译这一句，反而加了「此二着放逸」（这两种人沉溺放逸），梵文里找不到。白话照梵文译出了「其他论者则不然」。
cmp.en: The last clause in Sanskrit says “but not the other teachers.” Śikṣānanda leaves it out and instead adds 此二着放逸 (cǐ èr zhuó fàngyì, “these two are attached to carelessness”), which is not in the Sanskrit. The plain Chinese keeps the Sanskrit clause.

verses.en: Vyasa, Kanada (founder of the Vaisheshika school), Rishabha (a Jain teacher), Kapila (founder of Samkhya), a “leader of the Shakyas” — these and others like them will appear after I have passed into nirvana.

cmp.note: 梵文里「释迦导师」和毗耶娑、迦那陀等并列，都是主格，看起来是将来会出现的人物之一（后面第 797 颂也说涅槃后会出现「释迦族之子悉达多」这类外道）。实叉难陀和白话都把它读成说话者自己：「我释迦灭后」。英文按梵文的并列结构译。
cmp.en: In the Sanskrit, śākyanāyaka (“leader of the Shakyas”) stands in the same list as Vyasa, Kanada and the rest, so it reads as one of the figures who will appear later (verse 797 likewise lists a “Siddhartha, son of the Shakyas” among future sects). Śikṣānanda and the plain Chinese both take it as the speaker himself: 我释迦灭后 (wǒ Shìjiā miè hòu, “after I, Shakya, pass away”). The English follows the Sanskrit list.

verses.en: A hundred years after my nirvana there will be Vyasa and the Bharata (the Mahabharata epic), the Pandavas, the Kauravas, Rama, and after them the Mauryas.

The Mauryas, the Nandas and the Guptas; then the barbarian (mleccha, foreign) kings, the lowest of rulers. After the barbarians comes an upheaval of weapons, and after the weapons, the Kali age (the last and worst of the four world ages). At the end of the Kali age, people will no longer cultivate the true Dharma.
When these and other things have passed, the world turns like a wheel. Fire and the sun come together, and the desire realm (kāmadhātu, the world of sense desire) is torn apart.
Then the heavens will take shape again, and the world will start up within them once more: the four castes, the great kings, the seers, and the Dharma itself.

The Vedas, sacrifice and giving — the established order will turn again. And through tales, legends and the like, through prose, short pieces and commentaries, through texts that begin “Thus have I heard,” the world will fall into confusion.

Taking cloth that is bright red and cutting it, one should discolor it on top, staining the cloth with blue, mud and cow dung. All one’s garments should be of mixed color, free of the badges of the tirthikas (tīrthikas). (The opening phrase is unclear in the Sanskrit.)

The yogi should show forth the teaching; this is the banner of the buddhas. He should drink water strained through cloth and wear a waist cord, and take the alms food that comes his way at the proper time, avoiding what is low.
One kind of birth is divine, from heaven; the other two arise among humans. One endowed with the jewel-marks, born of the gods, becomes lord of the world.
Ruling by the Dharma, he enjoys heaven-like pleasures over the four continents. But after enjoying the continents for a very long time, he is ruined by craving.
There are the Krita age, the Treta, the Dvapara, and the Kali (the four world ages, from best to worst). I and the others belong to the Krita age; Shakyasimha (“lion of the Shakyas”) to the Kali age.

cmp.w: ahaṃ cānye kṛtayuge śākyasiṃhaḥ kalau yuge
cmp.note: 梵文是「我与其他（佛）在圆满时，释迦狮子在斗争时」——说话者把自己和释迦狮子分开，这和第 804 颂「我离尘与其他佛都出在圆满时」一致。白话写成「其他佛出在圆满时，我释迦狮子出在斗争时」，把「我」和「释迦狮子」合成了一个人，意思反了。实叉难陀「余佛出善时，释迦出恶世」则干脆没译「我」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “I and the others in the Krita age; Shakyasimha in the Kali age” — the speaker sets himself apart from the Shakya lion, matching verse 804, where he names himself Viraja among the Krita-age buddhas. The plain Chinese writes 我释迦狮子出在斗争时 (wǒ Shìjiā shīzi chū zài dòuzhēng shí, “I, the Shakya lion, appear in the age of strife”), merging “I” and Shakyasimha into one person and reversing the point. Śikṣānanda’s 余佛出善时，释迦出恶世 (yú fó chū shàn shí, Shìjiā chū è shì, “other buddhas in the good age, Shakya in the evil world”) simply drops the “I.”

verses.en: Siddhartha, son of the Shakyas, Vishnu, Vyasa, Maheshvara (Shiva) — these and other such tirthika sects will arise after my nirvana.
In this way the teaching of the Shakya lion, which begins with “Thus have I heard,” will become Vyasa’s ancient legend (itihāsa, old stories of the past).
Vishnu and Maheshvara too will teach that they created the world. Things like this will happen after my nirvana.
My mother is Vasumati, and my father is the brahmin Prajapati. I belong to the Katyayana clan, and my name is Viraja (“Stainless”), the Victor (jina, a name for a buddha).
I was born in Champa. My father, and my grandfather as well — he was named Somagupta — came from the lunar dynasty. (Who exactly bears the name is ambiguous in the Sanskrit.)
Having kept my vows and gone forth, I will teach a thousand ways of Dharma. Then, after giving Mahamati his prediction and consecrating him, I will pass into final nirvana.
Mati will hand the Dharma on to Dharma, and Dharma will hand it on to Mekhala. Mekhala, the disciple, out of weakness, will let it perish at the end of the eon.
Kashyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanaka the guide, and I, Viraja, and others besides — all of these are Victors of the Krita age.
After that, in the Krita age, a guide named Mati will appear, a great hero who awakens to the five things to be known.
Not in the Dvapara, not in the Treta, nor later in the Kali age do the protectors of the world appear; they awaken in the Krita age.
So that it cannot be stolen and carries a mark, one should piece the upper robe with “moons” — patches like the eye-spots on a peacock’s tail — together with uncut fringes.
Between one moon and the next there should be two or three finger-widths. Pieced any other way, it would only tempt the foolish.
Let the yogi always quench the fire of passion and bathe in the water of knowledge. At the three junctures of the day he should diligently take the three refuges.

cmp.note: 梵文 triśaraṇa 是「三皈依」，白话照译。实叉难陀却译成「惟畜于三衣」（只保存三件衣），可能他看到的本子是「三衣」（tricīvara）一类的字，或者把这句和前面讲袈裟的几颂连起来理解了。英文按梵文 three refuges 译。
cmp.en: Triśaraṇa means “the three refuges,” and the plain Chinese renders it that way. Śikṣānanda instead has 惟畜于三衣 (wéi xù yú sān yī, “keep only the three robes”), perhaps from a manuscript reading like tricīvara or under the pull of the preceding verses about robes. The English follows the Sanskrit: three refuges.

verses.en: Arrows, stones, sticks and the like are driven by a throw: one is thrown, one falls. So it is with wholesome and unwholesome action too. (The point seems to be that each act has its own result.)
One thing does not become many, for nowhere is a difference of characteristics found. Otherwise all receivers would be like the wind and givers like a field. (The second line is unclear.)
If one thing really became many, everything would be unmade, and what is made would have to perish. That is the logicians’ line of reasoning.
You may say it is like a lamp or a seed — but that is only likeness, so how is it “many”? “One becomes many” is the logicians’ line of reasoning.
Mung beans do not grow from sesame, and rice does not have barley as its cause; wheat and the other grains each come from their own kind. So how can one become many?

Panini, who laid down grammar, Akshapada (founder of the Nyaya school of logic), Brihaspati, the founders of the Lokayata (the materialist school), and Brahmagarbha will appear. (The last words could also mean “Brahma will become an embryo”; the meaning is unclear.)
Katyayana the author of sutras, and Yajnavalkya too, and the astrology of Bhudhuka and the like will appear in the Kali age. (“Bhudhuka” is obscure.)

Out of a world built by merit, and through the good fortune of the people, a mighty one will arise: a king, powerful lord of the earth, protector of all laws. (Balī, “mighty,” may also be the name of King Bali.)
Valmiki, Masuraksha, Kautilya and Ashvalayana — these greatly fortunate seers will appear in the future.

cmp.note: 这几个都是人名。白话按人名音译并加了说明（蚁垤是《罗摩衍那》作者，考底利耶写《政事论》）。实叉难陀却按字面意思把名字译出来了：vālmīka 是蚁丘，译「青蚁」；masura 是扁豆，译「赤豆」；kauṭilya 有「弯曲」义，译「侧僻」；aśva 是马，译「马行」。读古译时要知道这些其实是人名。
cmp.en: These are all personal names. The plain Chinese transliterates them and adds notes (Valmiki wrote the Ramayana, Kautilya the Arthashastra). Śikṣānanda instead translated the names by their word meanings: vālmīka “anthill” → 青蚁 (qīng yǐ, “blue ants”), masura “lentil” → 赤豆 (chì dòu, “red beans”), kauṭilya “crooked” → 侧僻 (cè pì, “slanted”), aśva “horse” → 马行 (mǎ xíng, “horse-going”). A reader of the old version needs to know these are really names.

verses.en: Siddhartha, son of the Shakyas, Bhutanta, Pancacudaka, Vagbali, and then Medhavin will appear in later times.
While I was living in the forest, Brahma, the great lord, gave me an antelope skin, a wooden staff, a girdle and a round vessel.

cmp.note: 动词 dadāti 是单数，所以 maheśvara（大自在）在这里更像是梵天的称号「大主」，送东西的只有梵天一位；实叉难陀也只说「梵王来惠我」。白话写成「梵天和大自在天（湿婆）」两位，多出了一个神。另外 cakramaṇḍala 字面是「圆轮」，实叉难陀译作「军持」（水瓶），英文取中性的 round vessel。
cmp.en: The verb dadāti is singular, so maheśvara (“great lord”) is most likely a title of Brahma, and only one god gives the gifts; Śikṣānanda also has just 梵王来惠我 (Fànwáng lái huì wǒ, “King Brahma came and gave me”). The plain Chinese makes it two gods, Brahma and Shiva. Also, cakramaṇḍala literally means “wheel-circle”; Śikṣānanda renders it 军持 (jūnchí, a water flask), and the English uses a neutral “round vessel.”

verses.en: “There will be a great yogi, the sage (muni, a name for the Buddha) named Viraja, a teacher who points the way to liberation. This is the banner of the sages.”
Brahma, with hundreds of Brahmas and many gods of mine, let the antelope skin fall from the sky, and then the master vanished right there.
Indra, Virudhaka (one of the four guardian kings) and others, together with the gods, give me robes of every color and an alms bowl in the forest.
If someone who teaches non-arising still accepts a cause, then the unborn would have to be born again. When he sets out to prove non-arising, it is only words.
They say ignorance is the cause that sets these minds going. But in between, what state is it in, so long as it does not yet know form? (The sense is partly unclear.)
The moment just before has perished and another mind starts up. Form does not stay for even an instant — so what will the new mind take as its object?
If, wherever mind starts up, it has a false cause and is not established, how can its perishing in a moment be determined?
The meditative attainment of yogis, gold, the relics of the Victor, the palaces of the Radiant gods (Ābhāsvara) — worldly causes cannot destroy these.
The settled states, the things attained, the buddhas’ perfection of knowledge, being a monk, receiving the vows — these are seen to last. How could they be momentary?

How could the forms of a gandharva city (a mirage city), an illusion and the like be momentary? What is unreal has no elements; and the elements — where would they be, where would they come from or go? (The last line is unclear.)
Mind, caused by ignorance and piled up since beginningless time, is imagined by the logicians as bound up with arising and perishing.
The Samkhya doctrine is of two kinds: one says things are transformations of primal matter (pradhāna); the other says the effect already exists in primal matter and is accomplished by its own-nature.

Primal matter is held to exist together with things, and difference is said to come from the qualities (guṇa, the three strands of nature in Samkhya). But in transformation, no variety of cause and effect is to be found.
Just as pure mercury is not stained by impurities, so the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna, the base layer of mind that holds all seeds) is pure — the support of all embodied beings.
The smell of asafoetida and of onion, a pregnant woman’s visible pregnancy, saltiness from salt and the like — why don’t these work like a seed? (The argument is obscure.)
Identity, difference, both, neither — it is the same with each. Its existence has no basis to grasp; it is neither nonexistent nor conditioned.

The self exists the way a horse does, which lacks the nature of a cow — so too with the aggregates (skandha, the five heaps that make up a person). Conditioned and unconditioned, sayable and unsayable: these are said of own-nature. (The verse is compressed; the reading is uncertain.)

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「自我像马一样存在，没有牛的性质」，看起来是在转述某种主张自我存在的说法（马不是牛，自我也不是诸蕴，但自我仍存在）。实叉难陀「马中牛性离，蕴中我亦然」和白话都把它读成否定：诸蕴中没有自我。英文保留了梵文的字面，并注明读法不确定。
cmp.en: Literally the Sanskrit says “the self exists, like a horse, lacking cow-nature” — apparently reporting a view that the self exists (a horse is not a cow, the self is not the aggregates, yet the self is real). Śikṣānanda’s 马中牛性离，蕴中我亦然 (mǎ zhōng niú xìng lí, yùn zhōng wǒ yì rán, “in a horse there is no cow-nature; in the aggregates likewise no self”) and the plain Chinese both read it as a denial of self. The English keeps the literal wording and flags the uncertainty.

verses.en: With reasoning and scripture, through bad views and speculative views, they have stained it. They say the self cannot be pinned down — it is neither in what is grasped nor anywhere else.
Here is their fault: they imagine the self by way of the aggregates, and whether it is one with them or other than them, the logicians do not understand.
As an image is seen in a mirror, in water, or in the eye, and is neither one with nor other than its source, so is the person (pudgala) in the aggregates.
Meditation to be cultivated, the path, and the seeing of the truths — those who cultivate these three are set free from wrong views.
Like lightning seen and gone, like a wheel glimpsed through a hole in a house: so is the transformation of all things. One should not conceptualize it the way fools do.
Taking nirvana as existence or nonexistence bewilders the minds of fools. Nirvana is the presence of the noble vision, the seeing of things as they actually are.
One should regard transformation as free of arising and perishing, free of existence and nonexistence, and released from both the marked and the mark.
One should regard transformation as free of the tirthika doctrines, without name or shape, a dwelling in inner seeing.

cmp.note: 这个复合词可以读成「安住于内在的观照」，白话就这样读；也可以读成「（执）内我之见的处所」。实叉难陀取后一种并加了否定：「内我见亦灭」（连内在的我见也灭了）。英文取正面读法 inner seeing，与白话一致。
cmp.en: The compound can be read as “a dwelling in inner seeing,” which is how the plain Chinese takes it, or as “the seat of the view of an inner self.” Śikṣānanda takes the second reading and adds a negation: 内我见亦灭 (nèi wǒ jiàn yì miè, “the view of an inner self also ceases”). The English follows the positive reading, as the plain Chinese does.

verses.en: Through pleasant contact there are gods, and through torment there are hell beings. There is no intermediate existence (antarābhava, the in-between state after death) set going by consciousness. (The sense is uncertain; the next verse affirms the intermediate state.)

cmp.note: 梵文字面是「不存在由识推动的中有」，白话照这个译。可是下一颂又说胎生、卵生等都由中有而生，前后像有矛盾。实叉难陀译成「若无彼中有，诸识不得生」（如果没有中有，识就无法生起），意思正好相反，可能他的底本不同，或者他按上下文改读了。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit literally says “there is no intermediate existence set going by consciousness,” and the plain Chinese follows that. Yet the next verse says womb-born, egg-born and other beings all arise through the intermediate state, which seems to contradict it. Śikṣānanda has 若无彼中有，诸识不得生 (ruò wú bǐ zhōngyǒu, zhū shí bù dé shēng, “if there were no intermediate state, consciousness could not arise”) — the opposite sense, perhaps from a different manuscript or a reading adjusted to the context.

verses.en: The womb-born, the egg-born, the moisture-born and the rest all come about through the intermediate state. One should see how varied the bodies of beings are as they come and go among the destinies.
Things that depart from reason and scripture, that wipe out the side free of defilement — the babble of tirthika views — a wise person should not practice.
First the self has to be determined; then it can be distinguished from what it grasps (upādāna). To distinguish it without determining it is like describing the son of a barren woman.
Not with the eye of flesh but with the divine eye and wisdom, I see beings — the embodied forms of all creatures, set free from the aggregates of samsara (saṃsāra, the round of birth and death).

Ugly or fair in color, marked as freed or not freed — with the divine eye one sees those who have left formations (saṃskāra, conditioned mental and physical factors) behind and those who still dwell in them.
The embodied being at the juncture between destinies lies outside the logicians’ range. The destinies beyond the human, I see them — not the other, false logicians.
“There is no self, yet mind arises — what does it come from?” Why not say it flows out the way a river, a lamp’s flame or a seed does?
If consciousness has not arisen, ignorance and the rest are not there; and without them there is no consciousness. So how does it arise as a continuous stream?
The three times, the timeless, and a fifth, the inexpressible — these are things the buddhas know, yet the logicians make loud claims about them.
The inexpressible exists by way of formations; knowledge has formations as its cause; it grasps what lies within formations, and so knowledge is called a “formation.” (The sense is partly unclear.)
“When this exists, that comes to be”: the conditions are not causes in the sense of makers. They are spoken of as what makes things appear, and apart from them there is no maker.
Wind fans a fire into burning, but it does not give birth to it; having fanned it, the wind also blows it out. So how can such examples prove a being’s self?
Both the conditioned and the unconditioned can be described as free of grasping. How then do fools imagine fire as the proof of the self?
Fire arises for people because things lend strength to one another. Then who sets a being going, that you imagine it to be like fire?
Is not manas (the thinking mind) and the rest the cause of this cluster of aggregates and sense bases (āyatana)? Not-self, like a caravan leader, always travels along with the mind.
These two are always luminous and free of effect and cause. Fire does not prove them, and the logicians do not understand this.
Mind, beings and nirvana are luminous by nature. Though stained by faults without beginning, they are undivided, like the sky.

Like “lying like an elephant” and other such practices, they have been stained by tirthika views. Covered over by mind consciousness (manovijñāna), they are thought to be purified by fire and the like. (The text is corrupt here; “lying like an elephant” is a guess at an ascetic practice.)
When these are seen as they really are, the afflictions (kleśa) are torn apart by that very seeing. Leaving the thicket of examples behind, such people reach the domain of the noble ones.
Because knowledge and the knowable are split apart, difference is imagined. The dull-witted do not understand this and call it “inexpressible.”
Just as fools claim a drum is made of sandalwood and nothing else, false logicians take their knowledge to be as precious as sandalwood and aloeswood. (The comparison is obscure.)
After eating, one rises, keeping only what rests in the bowl. Clearing away faults such as the taste left in the mouth, one should handle food in a clean way. (The sense is partly unclear.)
Whoever examines this teaching with reasoning — serene in faith, devoted to yoga, free of imagining, relying on nothing, intent on the meaning — will light the golden lamp of the Dharma’s way.

The bewildered imagining about existence, nonexistence and conditions, the stained net of wrong views, together with passion, fault and aversion — all of this falls away from him. He becomes spotless and is anointed by the hands of the buddhas.
Tirthikas are lost about the cause; others are thrown into confusion by conditions; still others, holding that there is no cause at all, settle into annihilationism and take it for the noble view.

The transformation that comes from ripening (vipāka, the maturing of past actions) is of consciousness and of manas: manas arises from the storehouse consciousness, and consciousness arises from manas.
From the storehouse consciousness all minds arise like waves. All of them have habit-energy (vāsanā, the lingering imprint of past acts) as their cause, and each arises according to its conditions.
Linked in a chain of separate moments, they grasp as objects what is really their own mind. With shape, marks and forms they arise from manas, the eye and the rest.

Bound up with faults without beginning, rising from habit-energy as the appearance of objects, the mind is seen as if outside. Understanding this wards off tirthika views. (The middle compound is ambiguous.)
With that as its cause and that as its object, another consciousness starts up. When views arise, samsara rolls on.

Things are like illusions and dreams, like a gandharva city, like a mirage, like the moon in water. See them as your own conceptualizing (vikalpa, the mind’s habit of carving things up into categories).

When the activity of mind is transformed, there is suchness, and right knowledge rests on it; and then come the Illusion-like, the Heroic March (Śūraṃgama) and the other supreme concentrations (samādhi).

By entering the stages (bhūmi, the levels of a bodhisattva’s path), one gains the higher powers (abhijñā) and the masteries, a body of knowledge that is like an illusion, and the anointing of the Sugata (“Well-gone,” a name for the Buddha).
When the mind turns back and sees the world as having ceased, one reaches the stage called Joyful, and reaches the stage of a buddha.
Once the basis has turned around, one does the work of beings like a jewel that shows every color, like a reflection in water.
Free of the sides of being and non-being, of “both” and of “neither,” gone beyond what belongs to the solitary buddhas and the disciples (śrāvakas) — this would be the seventh stage.

cmp.note: 梵文是「超出独觉与声闻，这就是第七（地）」，白话照译。实叉难陀译成「过于二乘行，亦超第七地」——不但超过二乘，还超过第七地，把第七地本身也算进被超越的东西里。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “gone beyond the solitary buddhas and disciples — this would be the seventh (stage),” and the plain Chinese follows it. Śikṣānanda has 过于二乘行，亦超第七地 (guò yú èr shèng xíng, yì chāo dì qī dì, “beyond the two vehicles, and beyond the seventh stage too”), turning the seventh stage itself into something left behind.

verses.en: One should teach the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna): about the things directly seen within oneself, purifying the true stages, free of the outside tirthikas.
The turning around of conceptualizing, free of passing away and of destruction, like a jewel made of rabbit’s hair — this is the way one should teach to those seeking liberation.

cmp.note: 梵文是「兔毛（做的）摩尼宝珠」，白话照字面译。实叉难陀写成「兔角摩尼」，用了佛典更常见的「兔角」（本不存在的东西）。不管是兔毛还是兔角，意思都是「这样的宝珠并不实有」，英文照梵文译 rabbit’s hair。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “a jewel of rabbit’s hair,” and the plain Chinese is literal. Śikṣānanda writes 兔角摩尼 (tù jiǎo móní, “rabbit-horn jewel”), using the more familiar Buddhist image of a hare’s horn, something that does not exist. Either way the point is that such a jewel is not real; the English follows the Sanskrit.

verses.en: If text fits with text, and reasoning fits with reasoning in the same way, then it is sound reasoning. Otherwise, do not make things up.
The eye, karma and craving, and likewise ignorance and unwise attention; the eye and form, and manas too, and the manas of one who is clouded. (The verse is fragmentary; its point is unclear.)
Here ends the Mahayana sutra called The Noble Entry of the True Dharma into Lanka (Ārya-saddharma-laṅkāvatāra), together with its verses.
Of the things that arise from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause, and also how they cease. This is what the great ascetic (mahāśramaṇa, a title of the Buddha) teaches.
